raw_text:
Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

A nine-second long video clip is has gone viral on social media, showing a man assaulting a puffed rice vendor. In the video, the man is seen overturning the box hanging from the snack seller’s neck and pouring all the food items onto the vendor’s face before they scatter onto the street. As this purported attack unfolds, the vendor stares at the man helplessly.
The video was posted by X user Alka Maurya on September 16 and has garnered more than 2,85,000 views and shared over 1,500 times till publication time. The caption of the post, translated from Hindi, reads: “(He) must be feeling so proud after doing something like this.” (Archive)
कितना गर्व महसूस कर रहा होगा ऐसे करके हैं ना …… pic.twitter.com/F6upi4I2ZD
— Alka Maurya (@MauryaAlka76391) September 16, 2026
Apart from Maurya, film actor Kamaal R Khan posted the same video with the caption: “How will you fix this mentality which has developed in last 10 years. India can’t be fixed now.” (Archive)
How will you fix this mentality which has developed in last 10 years. India can’t be fixed now. pic.twitter.com/o2T2AJzGoj
— KRK (@kamaalrkhan) September 17, 2026
Other social media users circulated the viral clip with similar captions, condemning the man seen purportedly attacking the vendor.
As a billboard visible in the video reads ‘Welcome to Patna Junction’, the Patna police was tagged in the comment section of certain posts, requesting them to take stringent action against the man who allegedly assaulted the vendor.
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the viral video clip, we ran reverse image search on several relevant keyframes. It led us to a video posted by content creator Sonu Paswan on Instagram. With 1,79,000 followers, he posts scripted videos highlighting the helpless condition of the working class people in India. Paswan has a social media presence on Facebook and YouTube as well. And according to his social media bios, he is from Darbhanga, Bihar.
In all of his videos, accessible on his Facebook page, Paswan himself can be seen playing different “poor characters” being harassed and attacked by others as he helplessly accepts his fate.
On September 18, Friday, Paswan posted a video on his Instagram page, where he clarified that he enacts emotional scenes on poverty as ‘content’ on his social media platforms. He clarifies that the viral clip does not depict a real attack on him, but is in fact a prepared skit. “I want to tell you that in the video you are seeing, the vendor is me and the man who is attacking me is part of my team. I want to let you know that we, as a team, make emotional videos on poverty. I request you to take this video purely as entertainment, and not believe that this is real,” he said.
The caption of this video reads, translated from Hindi, “Because we make emotional videos on the poor…You all give me so much love…but you guys have taken this clip to heart.
I know I have hurt you guys with this video. Please delete the video from your channel…I request you not to share this video any further.”
View this post on Instagram
After the clip started going viral and attracted significant backlash, on September 17, most of his videos on YouTube and all of his previous videos on Instagram had to be deleted. In the aforementioned video, Paswan urges audiences to not share the viral clip and excerbate his situation even further. “I request you to not share the clip on your personal profiles, please do this much for your brothers,” he said. He shared the same clarification on his YouTube page.
Moreover, Paswan posted videos of the guy who is acting as the attacker in the video, also clarifying the viral clip is indeed a skit, on his Instagram and YouTube pages. “The video you guys are watching and getting emotional and taking to heart is just our content…its not real…please stop roasting this video. Because of you [sharing the viral clip as real] all my efforts have gone to waste, all my videos, over 300 videos…I have had to delete them all. I request you to keep supporting and loving us,” he states in the video.
View this post on Instagram
Given that their skit went viral, misleadingly as a real incident, the content creators said they received backlash and trolling, compelling them to remove their previous videos. At present, Paswan’s Instagram page only features the two clarification videos and his YouTube page features the same. However, his Facebook still displayed his earlier content. The description of his Facebook page, translated from Hindi, also reads: “I make emotional videos on poverty.”
True to the description, Paswan’s Facebook page contains videos similar in theme to the viral video. In these videos, visibly destitute people or poor vendors are seen being humiliated or suffering at the hands of others, while accepting their fate.
Paswan can be identified acting in all of these videos, and a visual match can be established, indicating that he was indeed the person seen in the viral video. Thus, it can be concluded that a scripted video made by a content creator has gone viral, leading netizens to falsely believe that it depicts a real incident of attack on a puffed rice vendor.

All Public Sector Banks and Regional Rural Banks will remain open and function normally on Sunday, September 27, 2026, in view of the proposed three-day nationwide bank strike from September 28 to 30.
The strike has been called by the United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU) and comes after the weekend holidays on September 26 and 27.
The move has been taken to ensure that banking services remain available to customers and that their genuine banking needs are not affected over an extended period.
The Reserve Bank of India has approved the opening of all bank branches, offices, ATM-link branches and Currency Chests on September 27.
The government and bank managements have appealed to the unions to defer the proposed strike and said measures have been taken to ensure uninterrupted delivery of essential banking services.
The Department said the welfare and convenience of bank customers remains a priority.

Elephants use medicinal plants to treat themselves, researchers find
- Published
African elephants use dozens of different medicinal plants to treat themselves and their families when they are sick.
This is the conclusion of a study which interviewed people who live and work alongside the elephants in the Mount Elgon region of Kenya.
These particular animals have long intrigued scientists with their extraordinary behaviour - they are known as salt-mining elephants, because they go into caves and scrape the rock with their tusks to extract minerals for their diet.
This newly published research suggests that the same elephants use several different plant species in the forest for medicinal purposes.
One of the lead researchers, Dr Elodie Freymann from Brown University in the US, said the study raised the question of whether destruction of forest habitat deprives animals - and humans - of the medicines they need to thrive.
"This shows just how entangled our medicines are with the non-human world," Dr Freymann told BBC News.
Medicine for baby elephants
The scientists collaborated with the conservation charity the Mount Elgon Foundation, external. They interviewed local people, including wildlife scouts and community elders.
Accounts described elephants selecting particular plants when they seemed unwell, and mothers reportedly giving medicinal plant material to their calves.
From this, the researchers concluded that the elephants use 35 different plant species, and that 25 of those are known locally to have medicinal uses.
The study, published in the journal Scientific Reports, external, did not name the interviewees - keeping participants anonymous so they felt free to share their stories.
Their accounts reveal some intriguing details. In one testimony, a wildlife scout described seeing elephants using a plant known as Angurweet "as medicine to give to babies".
Angurweet is used as a remedy for ailments including stomach ache. The scout, who described elephant mothers mixing it in their mouths - "removing the leaves and chewing it until smooth, along with the roots of some other trees".
He also recounted that he had seen mothers mix this plant material with their own milk. "They give it to the babies, who chew on it themselves and spit out the solids".
Professor Michael Huffman, a primatologist based in Japan, currently at Nagasaki University, said this particular account was "tantalising", but more evidence would be needed to prove that elephants provided bespoke medical treatment for their calves.
The scientists have already embarked on gathering that evidence - giving the local wildlife experts they worked with cameras to record the behaviour they witness.
They are also analysing plants that the elephants use - looking for new medicines that the elephants themselves may have discovered.
Another lead reearcher on the project, Dr Fabien Schultz from the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg, told BBC News: "Local knowledge has given us a map".
"We [now] want to follow the elephants and investigate whether they select particular plants in particular health contexts, and whether those plants have relevant biological activity."
Natural medicine factories
Many animals treat themselves with plants and other natural remedies.
The earliest scientific accounts of elephants practicing "self-medication" date back to the early third century.
Roman author Claudius Aelian in his text De Natura Animalium (On the Nature of Animals) described an elephant that, after being wounded by spears and arrows, consumed flowers and oil from an olive tree. The elephant made a full recovery.
Centuries later, these scientists are delving into what we can learn from wildlife about the properties of plants in the forest habitats they evolved in.
"There are medicine-producing organisms on this planet that have this incredible capability," Dr Freymann told BBC News." Medicine factories that exist all around us."
Prof Huffman, who was not involved in this study, added: "We now know that mosquitoes and drosophila (flies) self-medicate, bees self-medicate, as do many other species all the way up the evolutionary ladder to the great apes of Africa and Asia.
"WIth each new species studied, we have gained a greater understanding of our medicinal past."
For Dr Freymann, the findings also contain a lesson for our future.
"So many of the medicines we buy in a pharmacy were derived from compounds from trees, algae, from fungi, from coral reefs.
"It's a win-win for us to protect these forests and keep those natural pharmacies around... long enough that we can discover new natural products that could save us down the line."

Union Minister Jitan Ram Manjhi, in a letter addressed to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, has said that MPs belonging to the Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) are not “given adequate time” to speak during discussions on important Bills in Parliament.
Mr. Manjhi heads the Hindustani Awam Morcha (Secular), an ally of the ruling National Democratic Alliance (NDA).
In his letter dated September 16, Mr. Manjhi referred to an “NDA sansad samooh samvaad baithak” (NDA MP Group Dialogue Meeting) held at his residence on August 5. He said that BJP Lok Sabha MP Gajendra Singh Patel, who represents Khargone, a reserved tribal constituency in Madhya Pradesh, had pointed out that MPs belonging to SC/ST communities were not being given adequate time to speak during discussions on important Bills in Parliament. Mr. Manjhi urged the Lok Sabha Speaker to take steps to rectify the situation.
Common demand
Mr. Patel, a two-time MP, speaking to The Hindu over the phone from Khargone, said this was a sentiment expressed by many MPs and not by him alone. He also insisted that it was an “informal” recommendation. “This issue was flagged by many who were present at the meeting. I was not the only one to say so. Moreover, this was something that was discussed informally. Sometimes we get the opportunity, and sometimes we don’t. Of course, all parliamentarians want more floor time,” Mr. Patel said.
Mr. Manjhi, speaking to The Hindu, said the NDA MPs’ groups meet once every quarter. “These meetings are designed to give a platform to the NDA parliamentarians to air their grievances, and the leader chairing the group then conveys these concerns to the respective Ministry or department. At the August 5 meeting, Mr. Patel raised the issue on behalf of several first-time MPs from the SC and ST communities. Everyone should have the right to speak in Parliament. That is what I conveyed in my letter to the Lok Sabha Speaker,” he said.
Mr. Manjhi clarified that the group that met on August 5 was not made up exclusively of SC/ST MPs.
Recently, Mr. Manjhi made headlines for supporting the sub-categorisation of SC/ST reservation and the introduction of a creamy layer within reservation. He argued that the benefits of Scheduled Caste reservation were reaching only some relatively empowered Dalit communities, while extremely marginalised groups such as the Musahar and Musahar-Bhuiyan communities, which fall under the Mahadalit category, continued to be deprived of these benefits. His Cabinet colleague from Bihar and LJP(RV) chief Chirag Paswan strongly opposed the idea, arguing that reservation is based not on economic status but on historical “social discrimination and untouchability”.
In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, the BJP won 55 of the 131 seats reserved for SCs and STs, a sharp decline from its 2019 tally of 77 seats. The party has since sought to strengthen its outreach among these communities.

Sales of Chinese hybrid cars have rocketed in the EU in the past four and a half years, new data shows, underlining growing concerns in Brussels over the future of the European car industry.
In 2022, just 659 Chinese-made fully hybrid cars (vehicles in which the petrol or diesel engine charge the motor and battery) were sold in the EU. However, after Brussels imposed anti-subsidy tariffs on fully electric cars from China in 2024, sales of hybrids have shot up to 160,662 in the first seven months of this year.
Eurostat figures show that sales of Chinese-made plug-in hybrid vehicles – models popular for longer driving distances which can recharge via both the fuel engine and an external power source – have also soared, rising from 56,706 sold in 2022 to 217,764 from January to July this year.
The volume of Chinese hybrids on the roads is now spooking the car industry and Brussels, which has asked China to voluntarily reduce its hybrid exports to the EU or face safeguards, likely to be quotas.
According to new figures released by the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), hybrid cars now account for almost 37% of the overall market, with electric cars making up just over 21% of the market.
ACEA figures showed three Chinese manufacturers – BYD, Chery, and Leapmotor – making significant inroads with triple-digit growth in the EU.
A fourth firm, Geely, has had a steady 8% increase in the first eight months of the year, and remains the most popular Chinese brand in the EU with 205,000 cars sold in the first eight months of the year. Its brands include Sweden’s Volvo and Polestar, the EU’s only all-electric car manufacturer.
BYD is catching up with Geely with sales year-on-year rocketing 163% with 177,000 units sold.
Both firms, along with a fifth Chinese manufacturer, SAIC, are now firmly ahead of Elon Musk’s Tesla which sold 142,000 cars across the bloc in the first seven months of the year.
European car manufacturers still dominate with the Volkswagen group selling 2m cars in the first eight months of the year.
Sales of electric cars are also growing fast in parts of Europe including Germany, up 75% to 69,000 units in August, and in France, where sales are up by 112%. In Slovenia sales have increased by 266%. This compares with the UK, up 27% in August to 28,000 EVs sold and Ireland up just 7% to 2,200 units.
Earlier this month, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, described the now €1.18bn-a-day trade deficit between the bloc and China as having reached an unsustainable “tipping point”.
The EU’s trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao will meet on 8 and 9 October to try to build a truce.
Also hoping for a trade truce are Donald Trump and Xi Jinping who meet in their third summit in 12 months in Washington on Thursday.
Trump agreed in South Korea last October to drop tariffs on certain Chinese imports in exchange for a suspension of China’s export restriction on rare earths, critical to the car industry across the US, EU and the UK.
Some believe a deal may not have been reached yet and the suspension may not be announced until the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference next month.

Russian woman mauled to death by bear as attacks surge across Siberian region
The attacks have been attributed to climate change and human carelessness

A Russian woman has died after being mauled by a bear in her garden, making her the seventh person to be killed by the animals in her Siberian region this month, according to state investigators.
The attack comes amid a wider series of deadly encounters across Russia that experts attribute to climate change and human carelessness.
Video footage released by officials in the Krasnoyarsk region of Siberia, located approximately 3,000 km (1,864 miles) east of Moscow, showed team members walking through woodland to inspect the body of the brown bear responsible for the mauling.
State news agency TASS reported that the 51-year-old woman was killed in the village of Voznesenka after discovering the animal attempting to gain entry to an outdoor pen where she kept domestic livestock.
"The bear lunged at the woman. The predator was shot dead by a neighbour of the deceased," TASS reported.
Experts quoted in Russian media explained that brown bears - which have launched attacks in at least 11 regions across Russia this year, causing at least 20 deaths - have been compelled to search further for food because an unseasonably early and dry spring left a shortage of wild berries in September.
Human activity has also contributed to the problem, with people leaving food waste exposed outdoors where it attracts bears and ignoring safety protocols, according to experts. Authorities in at least one region have also been accused of failing to keep bear numbers under control.
Milder and shorter winters, among other factors, have led to Russia's bear population more than doubling since 1990, when it stood at 130,000.
Environment ministry figures show that Krasnoyarsk accounts for nearly 27,000 of the 308,000 brown bears nationwide. On Wednesday, investigators in the region launched a criminal case into the local environment ministry, accusing officials of negligence that resulted in the deaths of six people — a figure that reached seven following the attack on the woman in her garden — in September alone.
State bodies had a legal responsibility to track bear populations and intervene immediately if human lives were endangered, investigators said.
"Despite numerous warnings of danger, officials from the ministry and other authorised officials failed to take measures to regulate the predator population and prevent their appearance in areas inhabited by people," investigators said in a statement.
"Monitoring data show that the brown bear population in the Krasnoyarsk region has increased 2.5-fold, reaching over 26,000 animals. Residents... have submitted more than 120 reports of brown bears entering the boundaries of settlements in more than 15 districts of the region, as well as in the cities of Krasnoyarsk, Zheleznogorsk and Zelenogorsk," they said.
Investigators warned residents to stay clear of woodland and to delay plans to go mushroom and berry picking, a widely popular Russian pastime.
"If you encounter a large predator, you have virtually no chance of survival," the statement said.
Other fatalities in the Krasnoyarsk region this month include a 39-year-old male logger and two women who were gathering mushrooms.
In Siberia's Irkutsk region, an elderly male mushroom picker was killed by a bear this month, alongside two men gathering wild plants in woodland.
During one of the most high-profile incidents this year, a bear attacked two tourists in their tent in the Altai region in August. It dragged a 29-year-old female camper from the tent, killed her, and buried her body in the forest.
In the Siberian region of Tuva, ice hockey coach Alexander Kuzmenko — father of NHL player Andrei Kuzmenko — died this week after being attacked by a bear during a fishing trip.
The environment ministry has attempted to downplay the surge in fatal attacks.
"In recent years, around 20 to 30 cases of bear attacks have been recorded annually," it told the RBC news outlet.
"The only abnormal spike was in 2014, when there were 166 cases. The thing is, nowadays everyone has a smartphone, and information spreads quickly via the internet and social media, which creates the impression that the problem is widespread."

High drama unfolded near Bairamangala Circle in Bengaluru South district on Friday as farmers protesting against the Greater Bengaluru Integrated Township, also known as the Bidadi township project, blocked the Bidadi-Harohalli Road, prompting police intervention.
Over 50 people, including several women farmers, were detained, while the police have yet to decide on filing a case, a senior police officer told The Hindu.
On Friday, over 100 people gathered at Bairamangala Circle, where the farmers were on a hunger strike and had blocked the main road, cutting off connectivity between Bidadi and Harohalli.
The farmers parked tractors and bullock carts in the middle of the road, while tying cows along the sides to block the road completely. Along with this, they also set up a Ganesha pandal in the middle of the road. In the afternoon, the Bidadi police visited the circle and requested the farmers to vacate the place, but to no avail.
According to the farmers, the protest was against the government-set-up committee’s “sluggish work” in re-examining the project and the mandates it had set for farmers to participate in expressing their views.
Police action
Soon, the police deployed more officers, including women staff, and brought in a police bus. However, several people lay down on the road and refused to move.
A senior police officer said that tensions escalated as farmers who were ready to part with their lands also visited the location and began arguing with the farmers protesting at the site.
“So, we had to intervene. Moreover, the whole stretch was blocked. We have detained members of both groups. We are yet to decide on filing an FIR,” the officer said. The farmers accused the police of trying to “silence” them.
Public notice
The committee — led by Guhanathan Narendar, a former judge of the High Court of Karnataka and former Chief Justice of the Uttarakhand High Court — set up by the Karnataka government to re-examine the Bidadi township project announced that it would hear the farmers’ objections on September 30 and October 1.
However, the committee has made it mandatory for farmers to register at the deputy tahsildar’s office by submitting RTC and Aadhaar cards before meeting the committee.
Yashavantha T., State general secretary, Karnataka Prantha Raitha Sangha, said that many farmers would not have RTCs for various reasons and making it mandatory would mean they would miss out on expressing their views.
Devanahalli, Doddaballapur farmers oppose KIADB land acquisition proposal
Farmers from Devanahalli and Doddaballapur on Friday submitted a memorandum to the Deputy Commissioner, Bengaluru Rural, opposing land acquisition for General Industrial Area Phase-3, reportedly proposed by the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board (KIADB).
Nagaraj Govindappa, a resident of Koira village near Devanahalli, claimed that the KIADB had proposed acquiring about 1,200 acres spread across five villages. “These fall under the Arkavati basin and cannot be acquired. The Deputy Commissioner has said that the matter will be looked into,” he told The Hindu.

United Nations, Sep 23: President Donald Trump said US and Iranian officials met Tuesday, an unexpected engagement that came even as he threatened in his address to the UN General Assembly that he may “annihilate” the Islamic Republic if a deal isn't reached soon to end the nearly seven-month war.
Trump told reporters that his chief envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met with the Iranian officials on the sidelines of the annual gathering of world leaders but he offered few details about how the discussions transpired or the substance of the exchange.
“It was a very good meeting,” Trump said. The president later added that the Iranian officials were “not the highest level, but it's something.”
The engagement comes after months of US-Iran communications languishing following the collapse of a short-lived ceasefire that was brokered in June.
US and Iranian negotiators met separately with Qatari and Pakistani mediators in Doha in early July for indirect talks.
Earlier Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Trump is open to meeting with Iran's president, Masoud Pezeshkian, while he's in New York for the General Assembly.
“This is a president that will meet with anybody for the most part, because he believes that engaging with people is important if you're going to solve problems,” Rubio said on NBC's “Today” show. “It doesn't mean you're going to end up agreeing with them, but it's important.”
Trump also met on Tuesday with leaders and senior officials from Gulf Cooperation Council nations - Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and United Arab Emirates - as well as Jordan to discuss the way ahead with the war in Iran.
In his address to the General Assembly, Trump made the case that he's shown fortitude while other leaders have equivocated as he defended his decision to start a war with Iran.
But Trump also suggested that he could be at a crossroads in the conflict even as he called on the Islamic Republic to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and return to the negotiating table to find a settlement to end the conflict.
“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world. Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
The president's comments came in his wide-ranging address to the international body in which he also celebrated this year's US military operation to oust Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from power, a new agreement to expand the US military presence in Greenland, and pushed back against calls for greater regulation of the artificial intelligence industry.
But at the heart of the address was a fulsome defence of the war and pushback on the notion that Iran has shown a measure of resilience.
“The terrorist regime is behaving badly, not because they are strong and confident, but because they are weak and desperate," Trump said.
Most of Iran's delegation walked out of the chamber as Trump railed against the Islamic Republic.
After his speech, Trump gathered with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the General Assembly to sign a new security agreement.
The deal, announced last week, came together after Trump repeatedly threatened to “take over” Greenland, a territory of NATO-ally Denmark, by military force if necessary.
Trump said Tuesday the US will immediately begin the process of developing a larger military presence in Greenland including “building two very major military bases”.
Under the deal, Greenland remains Denmark's territory.
Trump also held talks with new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
He's expected to hold a more informal meeting on Tuesday evening with Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodriguez, according to the White House.
Trump also took part in an event on the Shield of Americas, an initiative Trump launched with Latin American countries earlier this year focused on combatting violent cartels.
The visit to the UN comes as Trump's foreign policy approach - particularly his decision to start a war with Iran - has become a drag on his fellow Republicans' hopes of retaining control of both chambers of Congress during the coming midterm elections.
Nevertheless, Trump made the case in his speech that the world is better off for his leadership.
“I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day," Trump said.
In last year's address at the UN, Trump claimed the US had “demolished” Iran's nuclear capabilities after he ordered the June 2025 bombardment of three key facilities.
He returned to the General Assembly nearing the seven-month mark of a new war against Iran that he insists is necessary to address a nuclear threat posed by Iran.
The war has grown more complicated even though strikes by the United States and Israel have killed much of Iran's top leadership and destroyed its air force and navy, while a US blockade of Iranian oil has left Tehran in economic shambles.
The energy market continues to be spooked by the war and oil prices remain elevated.
Saudi Arabia earlier this month shuttered a key pipeline that acted as a relief valve for oil blocked in the Gulf. The kingdom made the move after the pipeline came under attack by Iran-backed militants in Iraq.
At the same time, territorial grabs by the Yemen-based Houthi rebels, another Iranian-backed group, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait has now made it treacherous for oil carriers to use that Red Sea shipping lane.
In his address, the president also touched on Russia's continuing war against Ukraine - a conflict that during his 2024 campaign he predicted would be resolved on Day One of his second term. He once again expressed hope that the conflict will soon be resolved.
Trump hasn't obscured that his patience is being tested by Ukraine's targeting of Russia's diesel refineries - an issue that's added to the global oil markets' volatility - and Russia's targeting of Ukraine's energy grid.
Trump last week asserted that he got the two sides to agree to not target each other's energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy had said he was willing to go along with Trump's plan if Russia abided by it. Russia said it could only go along with Trump's energy truce proposal if Western energy sanctions on Moscow were lifted first.
The two sides have continued carrying out strikes on refineries and other energy infrastructure.
Trump noted that last week he signed a new sanctions bill targeting Moscow. It empowers him to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas.
The legislation includes an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. Trump, however, has yet to enact the stiff penalties.
“If necessary, I will have to use them,” Trump said. “It's time to stop the killing.”

India is producing more green energy - but wasting a lot of it
- Published
On a hot July afternoon this year, electricity generated from renewable energy briefly met over half of India's peak power demand - only the second time this happened. The first instance was around the same period a year ago.
While it was only briefly that power generated from solar, wind, hydro and nuclear sources collectively outstripped coal-based output, it was a milestone moment reflecting the astonishing growth of non-fossil fuels to the country's electricity mix over the last decade.
"It showed that renewable energy is no longer a marginal source sitting at the edge of the power system," Sumant Sinha, CEO of ReNew Power, one of India's largest Nasdaq-listed clean energy companies, told the BBC.
To be sure, coal-based power plants still continue to generate 70% of India's electricity on average because they run on a higher load factor, or for more hours than solar or wind. Yet, the country's push for clean energy appears to have reached a crucial inflection point.
A decade ago India's installed renewable energy capacity was barely 4GW. It now makes up 300GW or 54% of its total 552GW installed capacity, external - a target that's been achieved five years ahead of schedule.
For a nation long seen as the poster child for dirty coal dependence, this rapid transition points to a remarkable achievement in decarbonising its grid.
Yet, the gains are tempered by some serious challenges.
Foremost among them is a shortage of grid capacity. The renewables' build out has significantly outpaced transmission infrastructure, a point of major concern for policymakers.
"In the first quarter of 2026, transmission constraints accounted for nearly two-thirds of all renewable energy curtailment at 300 gigawatt-hours (GWh)," according to Ember, a global energy think-tank.
Put simply, that means a bulk of the clean energy that was produced in India was wasted because the country's transmission lines have been dogged by missed targets, with one out of four inter-state projects facing delays of over a year.
The difficulty lies in matching the speed of generation projects with the grid build-out, says Sinha.
"Generation projects can be constructed in 18-24 months… Transmission can take much longer because they involve right-of-way, land acquisition, approvals and coordination across many agencies. It is an execution issue that becomes more important as the system gets larger," he adds.
Vibhuti Garg of the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis also blames "poor planning" for the problem.
The grid was able to absorb new capacity as long as India was generating 10-15GW annually, she told the BBC. But that pace has dramatically increased, reaching a record 51GW last year, and the infrastructure is no longer able to cope.
The concentration of renewables projects in the north-western states of Gujarat and Rajasthan has also compounded the challenge of evacuating power in the face of such grid shortages.
Analysts at Ember now believe this growing mismatch between fast-moving generation projects and slower-moving transmission infrastructure, is the "most critical operational risk to the country's 2030 target of 500 gigawatts (GW) of non-fossil electricity".
A quick solution to addressing this gap would have been to build battery storage systems at renewable pooling stations to integrate the power into the grid.
"Had that been the case, India could have stored the energy and used it during evening hours rather than wasting it," says Garg.
But storage capacity has not grown because of a huge jump in the price of batteries, raw material shortages due to the war in the Middle East and a fall in the value of the Indian currency which has jacked up financing costs for Indian companies.
"Many storage projects that were meant to come up fell through as a result," Garg adds.
Yet, finance isn't a constraint merely for storage projects but an industry wide problem.
While ample global capital is available for green transition across the developed world, getting access to it remains a persistent struggle for Indian clean energy companies, despite the strides that the country has made in its renewables commitments.
Estimates suggest the country will require $400-$500bn to meet its 500GW renewables target by 2030, external. But currently, around 83% of India's finance for climate mitigation is sourced domestically, according to the government's economic survey. While the Paris Agreement clearly mandated developed countries to provide financial resources to the tune of $100bn annually up to 2025 to developing countries for their climate action, that money has been hard to get.
"Emerging and developing economies outside China receive only around 15% of global clean-energy investment, despite accounting for roughly two-thirds of the world's population," says Sinha.
According to him, while India does not necessarily need developed countries to finance its entire transition, help is needed in the form of cheaper loans, guarantees and protection against currency losses so that private investors are encouraged to put in more money into the space.
Plugging these critical gaps in finance, transmission infrastructure and storage will be critical given this transition is under way at a pivotal moment, say experts.
India is the world's third largest emitter of greenhouse gases and facing a sharp rise in electricity demand, which has grown at a compounded rate of over 7% every year. It is expected to further accelerate with the expansion of industries like data centres and chip manufacturing.
The International Energy Agency, external predicts India's electricity demand will increase by 80% by 2035, the sharpest jump among emerging economies. It also credits the country's robust expansion of its renewables as a major contributor for slowing emissions in the developed world this year, even as energy related CO2 emissions rose more strongly in advanced economies for the first time since the 1990s.
How successful India is in achieving its targets on time will thus have an outsized impact on the world's ability to meet its climate goals.

A tropical cyclone brewing in the Philippine Sea is set to intensify over the weekend and take aim at Okinawa, the latest storm to menace Japan in a busier-than-normal season.
Tropical Storm Surigae is currently 791 kilometers south-southeast of Okinawa, packing top sustained winds of 74 kilometers per hour, according to the U.S. Joint Typhoon Warning Center. It’s forecast to intensify into a typhoon by Sunday, and strengthen to the equivalent of a Category 1 hurricane as it makes its closest approach to Okinawa on Monday, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency.
The tropical cyclone is the 11th system to approach Japan since June, above the historical norm of around 9 for the period, JMA data show. It follows an exceptionally active August, which saw 10 tropical cyclones form in the west Pacific basin — the highest number since 1966, according to the JMA.
Surigae also comes barely a week after Typhoon Dujuan hit Tokyo and surrounding areas with torrential rain, leaving at least nine dead and causing an estimated ¥5.7 billion ($36 million) in economic losses, according to preliminary estimates by Weathernews.
Fueling the abnormally active storm season this year is a “chain-reaction triggered by the El Nino background,” said Takahisa Nishikawa, a senior meteorologist at Atmospheric G2.
A strong El Nino expands a warm ocean pool across the Pacific, he said, triggering a number of changes in winds and clouds that eventually create a “steady conveyor belt” of what are known as tropical easterly waves — atmospheric ripples that pulse across the tropics, bringing rain and thunderstorms, which in turn spawn tropical cyclones.
“Most storms through mid-August formed directly from these atmospheric ripples,” Nishikawa said, citing JMA analysis.
After passing south of Okinawa early next week, Surigae is expected to continue tracking northeast toward Japan’s main island, according to Weathernews, although the forecast remains uncertain.

Ahead of World Heart Day on September 29, Prathap C. Reddy, founder and chairman, Apollo Hospitals, has urged people not to think they are healthy simply because they exercise, but to continue exercising, consult a medical professional, and undergo preventive health screening from the age of 25. A doctor can help determine if an individual is truly healthy and identify any risk factors or underlying health concerns, he said on Friday.
“Earlier, we recommended preventive health checks from the age of 30 to 60. Now, we are asking people aged 25 and above to get screened. Get yourself completely screened once in your lifetime. A person should know if he/she is free from diseases and is healthy or is predisposed to any of the diseases,” he said.
‘A serious problem’
Dr. Reddy pointed out that non-communicable diseases were among the most serious problems India was facing. These include heart attacks, strokes, cancers, and diabetes, with obesity and mental illness also adding to the list, he said.
Heart attacks are preventable, he said, adding, “It gives you enough time and warning. It is important to detect early and eliminate the risk factors.” With heart attacks occurring at younger ages, he said, apart from genetic factors, smoking, stress, inactivity, lack of diet restrictions, hypertension, diabetes, and family history of heart attacks were among the risk factors for young people.
“We can handle diseases, particularly heart diseases. We perform a large number of heart surgeries with better outcomes. We do minimally invasive cardiac surgeries as well as robotic cardiac surgeries,” Dr. Reddy said, adding that in terms of skills, healthcare professionals — doctors, nurses and paramedics — had proven that they could give excellent outcomes. “Cardiac treatments are improving every day, with more private hospitals providing care and the governments activating their own programmes,” he said.
Dr. Reddy stressed the need to prioritise women’s health. “Women take care of the health and wellbeing of their family. The incidence of heart attacks in women is no less. We are seeing only 25% of women coming for our preventive health checks and this must increase,” he said, urging families to focus on the health of women. “Prevention is best. Everybody should make health a priority. Then we will see a healthy and happy nation,” he added.

'It's like a dog set loose on us' - fear over Kenya's crackdown on foreign traders
- Published
For Ndaikech Ali, who has been traversing the streets of the Kenyan capital eking out a living as a tuk-tuk driver for the past nine years, Nairobi's traffic - not xenophobia - has been his biggest concern.
During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses.
"Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home.
"The threats are many… even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten."
President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials.
During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans.
Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country.
"We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food. When those jobs are taken away, the only option left is to return home."
Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees"
Other Burundians and some other foreign nationals have rushed to border crossing points to leave the country, with reports suggesting that a number have ended up stranded there.
Some couples fear they will be forced to separate - and some families have already been divided.
"I have been here from 2019," said a Burundian man, who identified himself only as Prosper and who has a child with a Kenyan woman.
"When I heard the announcement, it was very painful because when I go, I'm forced to leave my family... and I love my family," he told the BBC.
In Nairobi's low-income neighbourhood of Majengo, Kenyan Grace Wamaitha said her Burundian husband had already gone - leaving the day after the president's 3 September directive.
She is distraught as she has been left trying to feed their five children - and has taken on extra work washing clothes.
"Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees? I don't know what to do. Let them come back," she told the BBC.
In Nairobi and other major towns, migrants from the region can be found working in barber shops and salons, construction, operating motorbike taxis and street vending, as well as selling clothes, food and household goods.
Some have fled conflicts or economic hardship at home, while others have moved to Kenya in search of better opportunities. Within the East African Community (EAC), a regional bloc made up of eight countries, including Burundi and Kenya, the relative free movement of people is allowed - but employment and long-term residence do require permits.
Kenyan law also recognises the right of refugees to work and operate businesses, although they are also required to obtain the appropriate documentation.
Filmon Eyob, a co-ordinator within Nairobi's Eritrean community, agrees with concerns that the crackdown order will be used as pretext to harass foreigners.
He told the BBC that while many Kenyans had been supportive and welcoming, some Eritreans and Ethiopians had closed their businesses and stayed at home over the last week as a precaution.
The president's remarks also sparked a diplomatic row, with the Burundian foreign affairs minister warning that "hate speech against Burundi" could have repercussions for Kenyans abroad.
The authorities in Kenya have struggled to contain the fallout - and as the matter came to a head, Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'Oei visited and apologised to Burundians at the embassy this week, assuring them of protection from violence.
Critics argue that Ruto's remarks were a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia, although the government has denied this.
Since then, a series of official statements have sought to clarify the directive.
The government has now given a 90-day window for undocumented foreign nationals running small business to register and comply with local laws. During the process, those undergoing registration will be presumed to be living legally in Kenya.
Yet observers and those affected argue that it did not have to be this way.
Academic Hesbon Owilla told the BBC the president's comments were bound to be misinterpreted, especially by people who did not have the right documentation.
He says that while the proposed policy is good for Kenya and in line with global migration protocols, the communication about it ought to have been more diplomatic.
For those not in the audience, Owilla says people interpreted the president words as saying: "We are kicking these guys out."
The president did not stop at small-scale traders. A day later, he ordered India's Tata Chemicals to leave the country, saying the company had not provided sufficient benefits to the local Maasai community in Kajiado county.
Tata has been mining soda ash for years in Lake Magadi, a vast area often covered by a whitish salt crust. The lake's extreme briny environment sustains algae blooms that attract flamboyances of pink flamingos that thrive in the area.
Mining operations began at the lake in 1911 under a British colonial arrangement that is said to have remained largely intact, despite long-running land and resource disputes pitting the company and its predecessors against community and the government.
Economist Odhiambo Ramogi argues that the move to restrict foreign nationals from businesses is too broad - and could do with finessing.
He points out that Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees as well as other migrants, mostly from the EAC region, as well as other international investors.
Ramogi says that Ruto's intention seemed to go beyond "just protecting jobs for Kenyans".
The president's remarks have prompted a wave of support for foreign nationals, including by civil society groups and ordinary Kenyans who have criticised his approach.
In the wake of the criticism, Ruto, who is up for re-election next year, has sought to counter the backlash.
"Kenya will remain an open, secure and welcoming country, protecting opportunities for its citizens, safeguarding the rights of all persons lawfully within its borders," a statement by his spokesman said.
"Kenya's commitment to the East African Community of the African continent remains firm."
Ramogi says that in the end, it is Kenya that stands to lose when citizens of neighbouring countries are targeted.
He points out that Kenya earned $56m (£41m) in exports to Burundi last year, adding that the country would still benefit by allowing competition, as "locking out aliens simply means you don't want a competitive economy that gets to grow a lot faster".
"Now, if you got $56m out of a country, why are you worried about a hawker who's just trying to make, say, $200 in a month?
"It absolutely makes no sense what the president has done."
For Nairobi resident Lima Kabura, whose husband is Tanzanian, the president's remarks were just too hasty. She says he should have first established those who were in the country illegally.
"When they are forced out, I'm left with no work, no business and no husband," she said.

Takeaways from the Trump-Xi state visit: Pageantry and pandas
President Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi Jinping this week for the first state visit that the Chinese leader has made since 2015.
The visit comes at an important time for both men. For Trump, the state visit comes about six weeks before the midterm elections. Xi has an important calendar ahead as well, with a key Communist Party meeting scheduled for next month that should set up a widely expected announcement next fall that Xi will rule for another five-year term.
But there were a few commitments that came out of the meetings in Washington this week and more emphasis put on pageantry.
Expectations were low for major takeaways
The U.S. says the two countries will extend by two months a trade truce that lets the U.S. access rare earth elements from China, and for China to access some advanced American semiconductor chips.
But the two delegations did not announce crucial details about two still-unformed boards of trade and investment, Boeing purchases and pending Chinese agricultural purchases.
Instead, the two men relied on cordial remarks that glossed over the significant trade and economic complaints that have driven recent tension in the U.S.-China relationship. At a state dinner of about 145 guests, Xi toasted to Trump's health and a "new chapter" in bilateral relations, while Trump highlighted the long history of commerce between both countries.
Xi "wielded many of the usual feel-good tropes of Chinese diplomacy," said Lucy Hornby, author of The Last Man, an upcoming biography on Xi, such as panda diplomacy.
In his opening remarks, Trump referenced the intertwined histories of the U.S. Marines and Chinese Communist fighters during World War II, a conflict during which "Look at the greatness that we had together fighting in World War II," he said.
"Neither side is really in a position from a domestic standpoint to work out the really complicated issues at the heart of the conflict between the two," Samm Sacks, a senior fellow at the think tank New America, said.
Trump played up his personal relationship with Xi. Xi focused on geopolitics.
The two men and their delegations spent about three hours together in meetings inside the White House on Thursday, but much of the time was spent on a personal tour Trump gave to Xi of the South Lawn, lingering on the new helipad Trump has had constructed there and climbing inside the new Marine One helicopter.
Beijing views the U.S. relationship through sweeping, historical terms, with Xi invoking the "Thucydides trap" in his opening remarks on Thursday — a concept plucked from academia but is increasingly referenced by senior Chinese policymakers to describe possible conflict when a rising power threatens a declining power.
Yet China indicated it considered the visit had gone smoothly. A read-out of the Thursday meetings highlighting positive "aspirations for the future" in the relationship, and praising the diplomacy as "a significant step toward finding the right way for the two nations to coexist."
And Trump announced he is planning to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in southern China in November, and that Xi is planning to attend the upcoming G20 Leaders' Summit in Miami this December.
From Taiwan to technology, significant differences remain
Before Trump and Xi had concluded their meeting Thursday, China's state news agency issued a statement calling on the U.S. to come out against Taiwan's formal independence. The U.S. has no formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, and it has long maintained a position of "strategic ambiguity" as to whether it would defend the self-ruled democracy militarily if China were to use force.
Sacks, the New America fellow, said China sees Trump as being pro-China, more so than anyone around him in his Cabinet and anyone in Congress, which means they think that now is a really rare window to get a deal, even a shallow deal or symbolic deal.
"Because they know there are China hardliners who want decoupling waiting in the wings. The next president, Democrat or Republican, is very likely not to be as amenable to working with Xi Jinping the way we've seen," Sacks added.
Xi raised guardrails around the development of artificial intelligence with Trump, according to China's state news agency, urging the two countries to "work together to prevent the misuse and abuse of artificial intelligence."
Trump, by contrast, has argued forcefully against regulating frontier AI, and he wrote on Truth Social before his meeting with Xi that on artificial intelligence, "I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China's position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ!"
Yet at a state dinner Thursday evening, Trump and Xi warmly praised their countries' relationship, highlighting a long history of commerce with one another.
"Whenever he meets an American president, [Xi] frames the two countries as equals who can jointly sort out global problems; whereas in meetings with leaders of other countries, especially Russia or developing countries, he talks about solidarity against the "hegemonic" U.S.," said Hornby.
Sacks said it's possible a "cooperative path" on AI has opened after U.S. and Chinese officials deliberated this week ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting. There were discussions over an information-sharing system for alerting AI incidents related to national security. It's unlikely that a deal gets formalized between Trump and Xi, but Sacks said it's still significant.
"The bar is low, but they've set up a mechanism to keep talking," Sacks said.
Was the pageantry worth it?
The red-carpet VIP treatment of the leader of the world's top competitor to American power has raised eyebrows among those who've spent their careers helping manage the U.S.-China relationship.
"This is our most difficult relationship in the world," Nicholas Burns, former U.S. ambassador to China, told NPR's Leila Fadel on Morning Edition.
"American people want their president to be polite and civil to a foreign leader, but the over-the-top flattery by President Trump of President Xi, the red carpets, the pomp and circumstance, the marching bands, President Xi is not going to be swayed by that," Burns said. "He's highly intelligent. Obviously, he is not sentimental and he's very cynical about the United States. And his government's aim is to overtake us in power."
But other observers have argued that the pomp can only help what has become a bitter and tense relationship between the world's two largest economies.
"I don't want to understate the importance of pageantry at this moment. Because things have been so toxic," said Sacks of the New America think tank. "And so the pageantry itself creates a kind of breathing space that is stabilizing."
Stability between the U.S. and China seems to be the aim of this visit for Xi, as it is for Trump. But that stability still leaves the remaining issues between the two countries, including Chinese exports of rare earth minerals, the trade truce, and to what extent the two countries agree on an off-ramp from the potentially dangerous development of AI technology.

U.S. President Donald Trump is seeking to bring a major part of national funding for health research under the control of his political appointees, Politico reported on Saturday (September 20, 2026).
Mr. Trump has directed his budget director, Russ Vought, to draft an executive order to create a board that would decide which grants would be funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the news outlet said, citing two administration officials familiar with the meeting.
The board would include NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya and Mr. Vought, the director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, and would be required to reach unanimous decisions on grant awards, the report said.
The proposed arrangement would give Mr. Vought a direct role in determining how the health research agency distributes its congressionally-appropriated money, the report added.
The Office of Management and Budget, the White House and the Health and Human Services Department that oversees the NIH did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours.
The reported move comes amid mounting criticism of the U.S. government’s research funding cuts, undertaken last year to target federal spending at major universities, resulting in the freezing or cancellation ofgrants at numerous institutions.
The Trump administration says these cuts are necessary to ensure the government funds only solid science and to reverse years of misguided priorities.

Some people online have said they would not buy Tillamook products because of the halal label, but it is unclear how large the movement is. We have reached out to the company to ask whether its sales have been affected and if so, how.
In September 2026, a rumor spread that there was a U.S. conservative movement to boycott Tillamook cheese over its halal certification label.
In one Instagram video, a man said, "MAGA is having a meltdown over cheese," referring to people who adhere to U.S. President Donald Trump's movement, Make America Great Again (archived):
"Tillamook added halal labeling so more people can know whether its cheese fits their dietary needs. That is it. Nothing was taken from anyone. But apparently inclusion is too spicy for some people," said the poster in a comment.
Other posts on Instagram, X and Facebook made the claim that people were boycotting Tillamook products due to its halal label. A report by Qatar-based news organization Al Jazeera also relayed the rumor.
It is true that some prominent conservative social media accounts have said they would stop buying Tillamook products due to a halal certification label and urged others to do the same.
It is also true that some Tillamook products bear the halal certification seal. It is unclear how long Tillamook has been labeling its products with this label. We reached out to the company to ask about this, as well as to inquire if it has seen any drop in sales following calls for a boycott. We await a reply.
Tillamook product boycott?
Searches on various social media platforms revealed that some prominent conservative social media users said they would no longer buy Tillamook products, pointing to the halal certification label. This included posts on X, Instagram and Facebook.
For example on Instagram, Jack Hibbs, a pastor at Calvary Chapel Chino Hills in California and host of the show Real Life
Hibbs said that "until today," he and his wife bought Tillamook products, suggesting they no longer would. We reached out seeking confirmation.
At a grocery store in Brooklyn, New York, Snopes confirmed that Tillamook packaging for Sharp Cheddar, Extra Sharp Cheddar and Monterey Jack cheeses bore a halal certification label, as seen in the feature image.
On its website, Tillamook explained the halal certification on some of the company's products. "The majority of our cheeses are halal certified, and you can check the packaging for a Halal Certification symbol to know whether they are certified or not," the website read, adding that the ice cream, butter, yogurt, sour cream and cream cheese were not halal-certified despite being vegetarian-friendly.
Contrary to some claims, a halal certification does not mean that buying a product contributes to funding terrorism. Instead, it means that these products meet Islam's dietary laws and Muslims can eat them without fear of breaking the rules.
In the U.S., the Islamic Food and Nutrition Council of America delivers halal certifications. The process of receiving it is complex and requires a thorough investigation of the supply chain. In the case of dairy, the producers must demonstrate that they respected animal welfare. Often to simplify the process, producers follow organic practices. We reached out to IFANCA for more details on what it takes to certify cheese and will update this story should we receive a response.
Snopes covered several rumors regarding Islamic dietary rules, including the claim that Starbucks changed its rule on pets to make its shops halal.

The government’s attempts to provide 24×7 specialty care services in general and district hospitals is faltering, with the Health department barely able to run round-the-clock services in Punalur taluk hospital, where the initiative was piloted, despite concerns raised by stakeholders about the acute shortage of human resources in Health Services.
Health officials said that the idea had been to redeploy doctors with PG qualification, working in the periphery hospitals as assistant surgeons, at Punalur. However, this proposal has reportedly been met with stiff resistance from the local political leadership as well as the people.
Many PG doctors who had been pulled from institutions in Yeroor, Neendakara, Thevalakkara, Mayyanad, Kundara, Pathanapuram, Nedungolam, could not be retained at Punalur because of political interventions at the local level, who demanded their return.
It was last month that the Health Minister made the announcement that in the first phase, 24x7 services specialty services will be provided in General Medicine, General Surgery, Orthopaedics, Anaesthesia, Paediatrics, and Gynaecology.
The Kerala Government Medical College Officers’ Association (KGMOA) had pointed out that there are 799 vacancies of doctors in the Health Service — of which, 300 vacancies are in the specialty cadre — making it impractical that round-the-clock service provision can be made possible through just working arrangements, without post creation.
The government had, however, maintained that they had studied the patient load in various institutions and that judicious redeployment of specialist doctors from hospitals where patient load was much less, was enough for the time being to provide round-the-clock specialty services in many districts. It was pointed out that even some senior residents from Kollam Government Medical College could be utilised on working arrangement basis to provide specialty services at Punalur.
The government later placated the KGMOA that the plan was to provide specialty services from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., and teleconsultation services from 8 p.m. to 8 a.m. It was also stated that a minimum of nine specialist doctors in each medical specialty will be ensured in all hospitals so that 24x7 specialty services can be run smoothly.
Key challenges
“We could run the scheme if at least six specialist doctors could be made available in every speciality. Even that has not happened and the pressure from local political leadership could not be overcome. As for doctors, none are keen on seeing this initiative work and are unwilling to step out of their comfort zone,” a Health department official said.
At present, Punalur has just two or three PG doctors in each specialty against the nine promised.
In Malappuram, the idea was that the 24x7 specialty services can be introduced at Tirur and Nilambur by redeploying doctors from Manjeri Medical College on a temporary basis but this has not happened reportedly due to non-cooperation from doctors.
KGMOA State president PK Sunil denied that government doctors were resisting the initiative as it would affect the private practice that they are legally allowed to do after work hours.
“Only about 30% of the government doctors have the so-called “lucrative” private practice. The basic issue is that unless the human resource shortage is resolved, this plan will not work. We are not resisting the initiative but when a specialist is moved from the periphery hospital, there will be local protest,” he said.
Post creation is not as straightforward as it is being made out, as the Finance department is is no position to approve such proposals. Even during the previous government’s term, the Health department secured only 202 posts out of the 1,520 positions it sought, and that result was achieved after prolonged negotiations.
The Health department has now pushed a proposal to the government for the creation of 1,120 posts of specialist doctors and that of 520 posts of casualty medical officers, sources said.
