Why this break has come at the worst time for De Zerbi & Spurs
- Published
Big spending always means big ambitions, but shelling out so much money on so many players the way Tottenham did this summer produces problems for any manager, and there is no quick fix.
If I was given a bundle of cash and asked to buy an outfit for a wedding, and I spent every penny of it on pink shoes, brown trousers, yellow shirt and orange tie, then I am sure you would all say that just doesn't work.
That is similar to what has happened at Spurs, where the board backed Roberto de Zerbi to the hilt with an outlay on new players of around £400m.
It was an almost unprecedented occurrence from a club that has always been renowned for being careful with investment in their team, and it sent expectations from many Spurs supporters through the roof.
The club had just avoided relegation two seasons running, finishing 17th twice in a row, but suddenly some fans were looking forward to a season competing for trophies and a top-four finish.
Their early results and performances have been disappointing, of course, but fans have to understand all the different factors that affect you when you are building a team - and it is ridiculous to suggest De Zerbi should be under pressure already, especially after he kept them up last season.
Let's give De Zerbi a chance
Finding a way for your club to win takes a manager in lots of different directions but they all involve time - on the grass or with social interaction with the players.
Not only has De Zerbi not been given that early time and opportunity, the majority of his players have now been taken away from him for another three weeks on international duty.
De Zerbi has many other issues to deal with, from Tottenham's poor home form to their inability to recover from conceding the first goal in games.
But his biggest challenge right now will be to fit those players who have just arrived in with the ones already at the club, into a unit that plays as a team and produces results so that the money the club has spent is justified.
All of this will take time, and patience, and all the kinds of little detail that supporters never see.
In my day, we were given time to create a team, and a family. For today's managers, time seems more limited than ever.
We are only five games into the season but there are already some Spurs fans who seem to think De Zerbi is the worst manager in the world, even though he has proved elsewhere how good he is.
I like De Zerbi's passion, and his approach. That will count for nothing if Spurs don't eventually produce, but let's give him a proper chance.
Combinations can take time to click
De Zerbi is a very passionate, straight-talking and ambitious manager who demands total commitment and backing from his board.
He has definitely had that at Spurs, which has left people wondering why he has made such a slow start.
But, before the season started, I thought his biggest challenge with so many different types of players arriving would be to put players together that fit as a team, not as a group of individuals.
I've been in that situation myself, for example in my early days at Stoke, when I signed Gerry Taggart and Michael Duberry to play together, two centre-halves who were complete opposites in relation to how they dealt with space on the pitch.
Gerry always wanted to drop off deeper because he wasn't overly quick, whereas Michael was fast and didn't ever worry about leaving space behind him.
I couldn't make Gerry any quicker, so common sense locked in and I had to convince Michael that he would have to take a step away from his main strengths of pace and power and work along Gerry's lines instead.
We spent a great deal of time on the grass in training until we finally got both working in unison. Both were different, but they understood the importance of working together as a pair for the benefit of the team. Even so, it still took time for it to click.
For any manager trying to build a successful team by developing combinations like that, the main thing you need is time with your players.
It can happen where a lot of new players settle in quickly at the same time and the team starts well - like Sunderland last season, or Brighton pretty much every year when they have lost several key players - but the difference is that while those clubs might also have changed their manager, they have not changed their identity.
Whether it is Sunderland and Brighton, or Brentford and Bournemouth, they all have a set identity so that when they look for a player to fit in a certain position, he has to have certain strengths.
When you don't have that solid base behind you, knowing exactly what is needed for certain positions, then bringing 10 new signings and all in one window like Spurs have just done, is going to create many issues for the coach.
Each player has a different personality and needs different amount of time to settle in, not only to a new environment but also to adjust to the demands of a very single-minded and demanding coach like De Zerbi is.
This settling-in period would have been covered if all the players had had a pre-season together, to get up to speed with their team-mates and what De Zerbi is asking of them, with his front-foot style of play.
That did not happen, and then even after the season started, Spurs were still adding to their squad.
Finding out who understands importance of teamwork
Coaching a team to be a team takes time, patience and a sound idea of the strengths of all your players.
Even when you have got that, trying to knit every player together takes time, and that is still De Zerbi's issue now.
For starters, he was always playing catch-up. Because all of his players were not in place when the season began, he missed the opportunity to assess his squad and impose his own principles on his top group of players.
He is a coach at heart and will want to be out on the training pitch conducting a system of work for the team, in and out of possession, that he believes will bring success to the club. This international break means he cannot do that with all his players.
Another issue De Zerbi has is that he has only been in the job a few months and he is still getting to know the existing players, not just the new ones, on and off the grass.
On it, you need to find out who understands the importance of teamwork and who doesn't, to iron out shortcomings and and see what works and what doesn't.
An example of when you realise something doesn't work was my experience at a club who had just bought a right-back from a top Premier League team, for more than £1m which was big money at the time.
We were struggling at the bottom of the league when I came in and needed a direction on the pitch that would bring better results.
During the defensive work we were doing in training, the full-back kept picking up what were, in my opinion, poor positions while covering from the opposite side to where the ball was.
I must have stopped the session on at least four occasions to remonstrate with him and give my view, but in the end the lad told me that this is not what he believed was right.
I immediately replaced him with a young full-back from the reserves who had been playing for the opposition in the drill, who understood his role was for the team, and not for himself.
Getting to know your players' characters too
Getting things right off the pitch is so important too, and that involves getting to know what your players' characters are like, finding out what they are like as individuals, and understanding their lifestyles.
I had three South American players at West Brom who were fantastic lads but we still had to look after them.
I spoke to my assistant, David Kemp, about taking them and their families out for dinner, and by spending time with them and their children and their wives I believe we won a degree of respect and trust that we would never have had if we had not bothered to meet them all together as a family.
You have to realise that players from different cultures can be used to living a different lifestyle, and this can make a difference to how quickly or how well they fit in.
I had one player in the Premier League whose routine I just could not believe, yet he became such an integral part of keeping a struggling club up.
His 24 hours typically played out like this - training from 8.30am to 1pm, home and bed until 9 or 10pm and then up and out again for dinner and then a casino or whatever, until the early hours.
Then he would be up for training, and he would go again.
It took me a few weeks to get to the bottom of this but, once I confronted him, he was adamant that his routine suited his lifestyle. He certainly knew the best restaurants around town, but his performances were always of the highest quality on the pitch.
Did he heed my advice? I think he did, but he was such a great lad, top player and a great team member that he wasn't a problem anyway.
He had been a bit isolated from the rest of the squad at first, but it just took him some time to integrate.
Again, finding out about him as an individual and making personal contact with him, was important, and it was something I always saw as vital with all my players.
Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

Students strike across Germany in protest against military service
- Published
School strikes are taking place across Germany to protest against the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service.
One of the organisers of the strike, Bela Breitner, from School Strike Against Compulsory Military Service said the federal government was "serious about gradually reintroducing compulsory military service".
At one protest in Hamburg, demonstrators waved flags and held up banners emblazoned with the words "We won't take part in your wars".
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has made boosting Germany's military a priority following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
A new law introducing voluntary military service came into force in January, with the aim of recruiting volunteers to increase the number of soldiers.
However, if the security situation worsens or if too few volunteers come forward, a form of compulsory military service could be considered by Germany's Parliament, the Bundestag.
Under the law, all 18-year-olds in Germany are being sent a questionnaire asking if they are interested and willing to join the armed forces.
One protester, 16-year-old Elias Bernhard, from Hamburg, said that the responses to the questionnaires "show that young people do not want to join the Bundeswehr [Germany's army]".
"That is why I am out on the streets today. That is why we are serious about striking until compulsory military service is off the table. We will carry on."
The questionnaire is mandatory for men and voluntary for women. All 18-year-old men will have to take a medical exam to assess their fitness for possible military service.
The organisers of the protests, say the trigger came after some 18-year-olds in the northern German towns of Kiel and Flensburg, were sent official invitations for medical exams, even though they expressed no interest in joining the army on their registration forms.
The group says over a hundred demonstrations are planned across Germany, including in Kiel, Hamburg, Berlin and Frankfurt.
A spokesperson for the Defence Ministry told the BBC that under the law, the obligation to undergo a medical examination applies "to all men liable for military service who were born after 31 December 2007".
This also applies to people who have stated that they have no interest in compulsory military service. The spokesperson said that since July around 1,000 18-year-old men, who showed no interest in the army, have had the medical exam.
During the Cold War, Germany, like many other European countries, had a large army. But it reduced its armed forces during the 1990s after the fall of the Iron Curtain.
Germany's former Chancellor, Angela Merkel, ended compulsory military service in 2011.
But now, in the face of perceived threats from Russia and heavy pressure from Germany's traditional ally, the US, Merz has vowed to transform the Bundeswehr into Europe's strongest conventional army.
The Bundeswehr currently has around 186,700 troops. By the early 2030s, Germany wants to raise the number to 260,000, supplemented by around 200,000 reservists, in order to meet new Nato force targets and strengthen Germany's defences.

As many as 71% of consumers surveyed in Mumbai said chemists never or rarely refused to sell medicines without a doctor’s prescription, compared with 64% nationally, according to a LocalCircles survey published on September 18, 2026. The findings come as the Centre has proposed mandatory CCTV surveillance at medical stores selling prescription drugs, and the Maharashtra FDA has intensified enforcement against retailers.
The Mumbai survey by LocalCircles, which received more than 20,000 responses across its questions, also found that only 28% of respondents said they were assisted by a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 21% said they were assisted by someone who was not a qualified pharmacist.
On prescription checks, 36% of 3,697 Mumbai respondents said chemists never refused to give them medicines without a prescription and another 35% said they did so very rarely. Only 9% said chemists refused such sales most of the time and 5% said they always did so.
The gap was also visible in home deliveries. Of 3,122 respondents, 18% said their chemist never demanded a doctor’s prescription during ordering or delivery and 40% said this happened very rarely. Only 23% said a prescription was sought most of the time or always.
The survey showed that neighbourhood chemists remain the main source of medicines in Mumbai. Of 3,012 respondents, 57% said they visited or sent someone to a local chemist, while 26% ordered from their chemist through phone calls or WhatsApp for home delivery. Only 17% primarily used e-pharmacy apps.
The national survey, published a day earlier on September 17, 2026, showed similar, though somewhat lower, levels of reported non-compliance. Across India, 64% of consumers surveyed said their chemist never or rarely insisted on a doctor’s prescription, while only 15% said chemists did so most of the time or always. Only 31% said they were assisted by a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 13% said the person assisting them was not qualified.
The nationwide survey received more than 106,000 responses from consumers across 327 districts. It also found that 41% said chemists never or rarely sought prescriptions during home delivery, compared with 58% in Mumbai.
The findings come as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has floated draft amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, proposing mandatory CCTV surveillance at medical stores supplying medicines sold on a registered medical practitioner’s prescription.
The draft, issued through Gazette notification G.S.R. 791(E) dated September 8, proposes inserting a new sub-rule after Rule 65(2). It states that retail supply of prescription medicines should take place under CCTV surveillance installed and maintained at the premises. The proposal is aimed at strengthening oversight of the sale of Schedule H, H1 and X drugs and curbing sales without valid prescriptions. The government has invited objections and suggestions before finalising the amendment.
The proposed rule comes amid a sharper enforcement drive by the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration. Between June and August 2026, the FDA inspected 2,902 drug establishments, including 2,295 sales establishments and 607 manufacturing units, and initiated action against 880 licensees.
Of these, 677 licences were suspended, and 203 were cancelled, with 740 of the 880 actions involving retailers and wholesalers. During the same three-month period, the FDA conducted 104 search-and-seizure operations, seized illegal drugs and cosmetics worth Rs 11.41 crore, registered 20 FIRs and made 21 arrests.
FDA inspectors flagged several of the same issues reflected in the consumer survey, including the sale of medicines without registered pharmacist supervision, dispensing prescription medicines without valid prescriptions, incomplete Schedule H1 records and sales without proper invoices. Other violations included expired medicines being kept in sale stock and inadequate temperature controls for products such as insulin and vaccines.
The Mumbai survey also found billing gaps. While 76% said they generally received a printed GST invoice and 3% received a manually prepared GST bill, 20% effectively did not receive a proper GST bill.
LocalCircles said the Mumbai findings would be shared with the Maharashtra FDA, Union Health Ministry and CDSCO, and called for stricter verification of registered pharmacists, prescription checks for phone and WhatsApp deliveries and better documentation of medicine sales.

Our son's death could have been prevented by FA - Billy Vigar's parents
- Published
"You swing from sadness to anger because you just feel it could have been prevented."
That is the view of Camilla Vigar, whose son Billy, a former Arsenal academy player, died a year ago today from a "significant brain injury", five days after colliding with a concrete wall surrounding a pitch.
The 21-year-old striker was playing for Chichester City at Wingate and Finchley FC in north London.
In their first broadcast interview since their son's passing, the Vigar family accuse the Football Association of doing "nothing" after previous similar incidents.
"[Billy] had his whole life ahead of him. He was 21 years old and he lost it playing football when he didn't need to," she told BBC Sport.
"I personally feel that the FA could have stopped Billy losing his life because they had so many warnings."
They give the example of amateur footballer Ben Hiscox, who died in 2015 after colliding with a clubhouse near Bristol.
After the coroner warned the FA about the risk of future deaths, padding was added to Stoke Gifford United's clubhouse and the run-off between it and the pitch was increased.
The Vigars also point to the life-changing injuries sustained by Alex Fletcher in 2022.
Fletcher fractured his skull when colliding with concrete barriers next to the pitch at Bath City's ground, and was forced to retire in 2024.
The FA conducted a review of clubs after that incident.
"As far as I'm aware, nothing was done with that information and it just sat there. One of the clubs as far as I'm aware that was highlighted as being one of the high-risk clubs was Wingate [and Finchley], where Billy then lost his life," said Camilla Vigar.
When asked by the BBC what was done with the information it had gathered, the FA provided no comment.
Changes needed at 169 clubs
At the time of Vigar's accident, the FA's stadium accreditation criteria, which applies to the National League System in men's football and the Women's National League, said clubs needed to have a "permanent" barrier around the pitch "of sound construction (eg concrete and steel)".
In light of what happened to Vigar, the FA launched a safety review of more than 900 clubs, which was conducted by independent experts.
As a result, the stadium criteria was updated last month and "no longer permits solid brick, breeze block or concrete barriers around pitches".
The BBC has been told 169 clubs in the men's National League System and women's National League were notified they would need to make changes "as soon as is reasonably practicable".
Where walls are structural, they must be "covered with suitable protection", such as padding.
The FA said: "This important work is under way, and we will continue to fully support the clubs involved."
Funding is being provided by the FA and the Premier League.
BBC Sport approached hundreds of affected clubs in an effort to gauge their views on the changes and understand the status of their remedial work.
Bromsgrove Sporting near Birmingham, which has a concrete wall surrounding its pitch, told BBC Sport the changes were "completely understandable and long overdue". It added: "We are fully supportive of this and are grateful for the 100% funding from the FA."
The club said it had been given a deadline of the end of this season but "being high risk it would be good to complete this side of Christmas".
Meanwhile, Sheppey United, in Kent, has a concrete supporting wall around two sides of its 3G pitch, which will be covered in padding.
Asked for their thoughts on the changes, the club said: "There is always an element of risk in all sports and they can't all be mitigated, unfortunately in this instance the remedial works are more a reactive response rather than a proactive one. If the funding wasn't in place I think it would make it difficult for some clubs to fund this."
Bath City, where Fletcher's incident happened, has solid perimeter walls on all sides of its pitch.
The club told BBC Sport: "We welcome the ruling as it seeks to improve player safety and recognises that funding needs to be available to support clubs to implement this fundamental change to the ground grading regulations."
Keith Vigar, Billy's father, said: "I work in the health and safety industry, and the main thing is you don't go to work and expect to get injured, let alone even die at work in the workplace."
The Vigars want the regulations extended above and below the National League.
"It needs to change basically at all levels, not just at the levels that have changed," said Keith Vigar.
That is a view shared by Fletcher, who said the FA had "ignored" his years of campaigning on the issue of pitch perimeter safety.
"It wasn't until Billy's passing that [the FA] came to the table on this issue," he said.
"So for me, that is a complete dereliction of duty on their part, and there should be accountability for that failing."
Fletcher also said he is worried the ban on concrete, breeze block and brick walls does not cover all levels of the game and wants that explored urgently by the authorities.
"There could be still situations where football is being played at some level, to some degree, organised football in this country, with these unsafe pitch perimeters. I would like to see that guidance, or the regulation, extended to consider all of football."
Billy was 'something different'
Compared to many youngsters, Billy Vigar joined the football system late - and yet his talent was still recognised.
He was scouted by Arsenal while playing for local club Hove Rivervale in Sussex, and joined the Premier League side's academy.
"It was just an amazing feeling," said his father.
"Sort of like your son's been chosen. And I'd always promised him a decent pair of football boots if he joined an academy. So yeah, since then it's cost me a fortune.
"He was something different, Billy. I think most, even at Arsenal, they saw something different in him. He was a great athlete, basically. And that started from an early age with his brother, who quickly learned there's not much point trying to challenge him because he wanted to win."
Injuries followed, and Vigar was recuperating from one such setback while playing for Chichester City FC, where he had made an instant impression.
Darin Kilpatrick, the club's first-team manager, said: "He was so coachable, he would run in behind, he would drop in short. His hold-up play was excellent and obviously he had an eye for a goal which all strikers have to have.
"To be fair, the way Bills was playing in his last couple of games that we had him, we would probably have only been able to keep him another six months before we moved him on into the higher levels where he belonged."
Asked what level he was aiming for with Billy, Kilpatrick said: "He would have gone into the National League or [English] Football League, without a doubt."
Watching football again has been difficult for Keith Vigar.
"It did become less important, far less important to start with, the struggle to get back into it," he said. "When we went to see Chichester in that sense, first off, it's hard because you're just thinking, 'Billy should be out there, Billy should be playing' and that sort of thing. That's been hard."
The Vigars said Chichester FC have been "amazing" during the past year, including designing a kit that makes moving but subtle references to their son.
They want accountability and answers. They are awaiting the inquest, which is likely to take place next year.
But today, as they mark the one-year anniversary of their son's tragic accident, they will pour all their focus into climbing Snowdon with their children Phoebe and Ollie, and the family of Billy's girlfriend Lois.
"I think it just gives us something to focus on and gives us a challenge to do," Keith Vigar said. "And I know he'd have liked to do that. I'm sure he will be with us somewhere, looking over us in some way or form, having a laugh at us, no doubt, in the rain."

Drinking at football matches - would fans welcome it?
- Published
When UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham embarked on his trip to the United Nations in New York, he might not have been expecting a question about football fans drinking alcohol in grounds.
Burnham firmly believes the law that prevents supporters from having a beer at their seat during a match is outdated.
It's a position the Everton supporter has long held, and when asked was happy to reaffirm.
"I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination," said Burnham, who feels football fans are singled out compared to those of other sports and events.
There is no suggestion this is about to become official government policy, and last year MPs rejected a Conservative amendment to the Football Governance Bill that would have forced ministers to launch a formal consultation on scrapping the rule.
That was, of course, before Burnham returned to Downing Street.
It is a complicated and divisive issue, about not just safety. But it it something that match-going supporters actually want?
What the law says
Drinking alcohol at football grounds in England and Wales has been strictly controlled since the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act was introduced in 1985.
It was brought in to counter escalating hooliganism through the 1970s and into the 1980s.
The ban impacts clubs in the Premier League down to the National League. While beer can be sold, it must be consumed in areas that do not have a view of the pitch.
Yet fans who support teams in the National League North and South and below can drink alcohol around the pitch.
The ban is more strict in Scotland, with a law in place since 1981 that alcohol is only available in hospitality areas and not for other fans.
It was initially imposed following a riot during the 1980 Scottish Cup final between Rangers and Celtic at Hampden.
However, attitudes have been changing in recent seasons.
It was lifted as part of a pilot scheme last year, with several Scottish clubs selling alcohol in clearly defined, monitored areas of the stadiums. It started with lower-level clubs, eventually being extended to the Premiership.
The Scotland national team joined the trial for the friendlies against Japan and Curacao earlier this year. It has been extended to games against Switzerland on 29 September and Slovenia next month.
The Women's Super League in England has just completed two seasons of successful trials and the rule preventing drinking in the stands has now been removed by the league's governing company, WSL Football.
The women's game is not governed by the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act, enabling the competition organiser to make the change.
Is there support for the move within English football's corridors of power?
Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said in August the competition had not "got a specific view" and "we'd need to give it some really careful thought".
The English Football League, however, issued a statement on Thursday that said it would be "receptive to discussions around reviewing the current legislation".
It added member clubs had already provided "a mandate to lobby for appropriate reform" which had "not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding".
Fans' views differ on drinking in stands
The Football Supporters' Association has for some time backed changing the law.
Like the prime minister, it considers it to be unfair on football fans.
"I think it is outdated," FSA chairman Tom Greatrex told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme.
"If you go to watch football in Germany or in other places around the world, then it's perfectly acceptable.
"It is civilised and appropriate. There's no reason why that shouldn't be the case for football fans, as it is for fans of rugby league, watching Oasis, or anything else that happens often in the same stadiums in the same seats."
The FSA's position is that clubs should have the choice, in consultation with supporters, to sell alcohol.
Clubs might want to offer it in all stands, others in designated areas, while a few might choose not to do so at all.
Other sports offer designated alcohol-free sections, something that football clubs may wish to copy for some families and supporters who do not consume alcohol because of their religion.
The FSA acknowledges this, but believes having the option to make such decisions is important.
It believes relaxing the law would be more popular the further down the leagues you go, where alcohol sales could potentially provide a crucial additional income stream.
The UK Football Policing Unit rejected the suggestion, arguing alcohol plays "a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour" and that "other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour" that football does.
Yet for Greatrex, there is already proof police are not open to ideas through their previous opposition to safe standing.
Before it was introduced four years ago, Mark Roberts, who has been the national lead for football policing since 2014, told the BBC it would make it "easier to throw missiles, engage in hate chanting, racism, sneak alcohol in, take cocaine".
"[The police] were telling everybody that we couldn't have standing at football again, that it would jeopardise safety, " Greatrex said.
"Actually, what we saw then was a controlled, managed pilot projects to get that re-established.
"There hasn't been the level of disorder that some of the police sources were saying there would be. I think the police should have more of an open mind and engage in this in a sensible and mature way."
For many match-going fans, however, the prospect of beer being thrown and potential anti-social behaviour outweighs the opportunity to watch a game with a pint.
Dave, a Chelsea fan from Twickenham, told Nicky Campbell on BBC Radio 5 Live, that he was "100% against it".
"Have a look at some of the footage you see on social media at Boxpark, for instance. A goal goes in and there is beer and lager thrown everywhere," he said.
"I don't want to go round stinking of other people's beer and there is a fashion among certain supporters to throw their beer everywhere.
"If people can't go without drink for a 45-minute period there is something the matter with them."
Adrian, from Leicester, claimed it would be the "worst idea you could come up with".
"There is enough trouble with other things in football, with the flares, drug taking and other things," he added. "You throw the alcohol in as well. Football is tribal whereas other sports they aren't."
But Ryan, a Wolves fan in Banbury, said "a solution that suits everybody" is to provide designated areas for drinking in stands.
What is it like in other sports and different countries?
Football is in the only sport in the UK which faces restrictions on the consumption of alcohol.
Some of these sports have issues with alcohol-related and anti-social behaviour, but none have the same reputation as football.
The restrictions differ around Europe.
There is a strict ban in the top two divisions of Spanish football, where only alcohol-free beer can be sold outside of hospitality areas. It can, however, be taken to seats.
In the German Bundesliga, there is no ban on drinking at your seat. So relaxed is the approach to alcohol at games that you will even find people selling bottles of beer from shopping trolleys outside grounds.
In the Italian Serie A it is similarly as relaxed, though to a limit of 5% ABV. Some games which are designated "high risk" have sales suspended in and around the stadium.
In France, the Evin Law was introduced in 1991 which is pretty much in line with Scotland, as far as football is concerned. Alcohol cannot be sold at any sports event, other than in VIP areas.

The Ministry of Home Affairs on Friday extended the classification of most of Manipur as a “disturbed area” under the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act (AFSPA), 1958, while keeping 13 police station areas outside its purview. The notification will take effect from October 1, and remain valid for six months, unless the Centre revokes it before the period ends. Under Section 3 of the AFSPA, 1958, a “disturbed area” is an area officially declared through a notification in the Official Gazette where the situation is sufficiently disturbed or dangerous that the use of armed forces is considered necessary to assist the civil administration. The law allows such a declaration when there are severe disturbances, violence or conflicts involving different religious, racial, linguistic, regional, caste or community groups. Under AFSPA, armed forces personnel in a declared ‘disturbed area’ can: Use force: After giving due warning, use force, including lethal force, against people violating orders prohibiting certain assemblies or possession of weapons/explosives. Destroy armed facilities: Destroy arms dumps, fortified positions, shelters or structures used for armed attacks, training or as hideouts. Arrest without warrant: Arrest without a warrant anyone who has committed, or is reasonably suspected of committing or about to commit, a cognizable offence. Search without warrant: Enter and search premises without a warrant to make an arrest, rescue a person believed to be wrongfully confined, or recover suspected stolen property, weapons, ammunition or explosives. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop parent Purple Style Labs managed to trim its net loss for the June quarter of fiscal year FY27 (Q1 FY27) by 12% to ₹88.1 Cr from ₹100.3 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Sequentially, the recently listed company’s net loss jumped 40% from ₹62.9 Cr loss incurred in Q4 FY26.

One horse refused to jump, another tested positive for tick fever and a third never got its blood work done leaving it unable to travel for competition.
India’s hopes in the eventing team in the equestrian competition ended with one day to go after Arjan Nagra was disqualified following his horse Cooley Goodwood’s refusal to attempt two obstacles in the jumping event of the competition. Two other Indian riders – Fouad Mirza on Camouflage 38 and Ashish Limaye on Willy Be Dunn managed to complete the jumping competition.
The eventing competition consists of three events – dressage, jumping followed by cross country. Although each country is allowed four riders, only the top three scores are considered for the team competition.
The Indian trio completed the dressage event. However, following Nagra and his horse’s disqualification, the Indian team were left with only two riders, forcing their disqualification as well from the team event. All three riders were still eligible to continue in the individual category.
“Our Rider Ashish Limaye remains in contention for an individual medal. Currently lying 6th but likely to move up after the cross-country today. Our 3rd rider, Arjan Nagra, was eliminated in the show Jumping phase due to 2 refusals. We were a 3-member team due to Aahan kumars horse testing positive for piroplasmosis at the last moment before quarantine, with no time remaining to replace him due to quarantine restrictions. As a team, we are eliminated but have a chance for an individual medal depending upon the outcome of the cross-country (sic),” Lt. Col. Sandeep Dewan (Retd.), Member of Administration for the Indian Olympic Association (IOA)-appointed ad-hoc committee running the Equestrian Federation of India (EFI), wrote to Sportstar when asked about the elimination from the team event.
The next day, Mirza and his horse retired from the cross-country stage. India was already eliminated from the team event, which meant Limaye was the only one still left in contention to finish the eventing discipline. He and his horse, Willy Be Dunn, eventually finished the cross-country stage with a score of 44.50 after nine penalty points, eventually ranked 12th in the event by the end.
Although India had planned to send four riders, only three riders were finally sent because the horse of the fourth - Bolivar Gio Granno of Ahaan Kumar – tested positive for tick fever and was not allowed to travel to Japan.
Although the ad hoc committee currently running Equestrian Federation of India had also appointed a reserve player – Pradeep Jhangam, it is learned that his horse didn’t get its blood work (which is how a horse is tested for fitness and infection and thus declared fit to travel) would be unable to travel to Japan as well.
Order of events in equestrian eventing
At the eventing team events in Tokyo, India was one of only two teams out of eight teams to not feature four riders (China was the other one).
It is also learned that although India didn’t send a fourth rider or a reserve rider, some 50 lakh rupees had already been spent towards the transportation of eight horses although only seven were actually sent.
India have had a history of success in the team event, winning medals at three consecutive Asian Games between 1998 and 2006. However they have only medalled once (in 2018) since then.

Odisha reports 24 minor pregnancy cases in tribal school hostels over 2 yrs: Gond
Twenty-four minor girls staying in government-run tribal school hostels in Odisha became pregnant during the last two academic years
Twenty-four minor girls staying in government-run tribal school hostels in Odisha became pregnant during the last two academic years, with 15 cases reported in 2025-26, school and mass education minister Nityananda Gond told the state Assembly on Friday.
Replying to a question by Congress MLA Tara Prasad Bahinipati, Gond said nine cases were reported in 2024-25 and 15 in 2025-26. Of the nine cases reported in 2024-25, three were from Rayagada and one each from Balasore, Debagarh, Keonjhar, Koraput, Malkangiri and Mayurbhanj.
In 2025-26, Kandhamal reported the highest number of cases at five, followed by Koraput with four. Debagarh, Keonjhar, Malkangiri, Mayurbhanj, Rayagada and Sundargarh reported one case each, Gond said. In Malkangiri district, a minor student engaged in a physical relationship with a boy from a neighbouring village, while in Mayurbhanj district, the incident occurred during the summer vacation, while another involved a youth from the victim’s home village. In Kandhamal and Rayagada, multiple cases were similarly attributed to private individuals and outsiders.
Gond said action had been taken against those accused in the cases. Some of them were arrested, while FIRs were registered in other cases, he said.
The disclosures come amid concerns over teenage pregnancy and the safety and supervision of minors staying in residential educational institutions, particularly in tribal and remote districts where many students live away from their families for extended periods.
Odisha has recorded a modest improvement in teenage motherhood and pregnancy, with the proportion of girls aged 15-19 who were already mothers or pregnant at the time of the National Family Health Survey-6 (2023-24) declining to 6.5% from 7.5%. However, the prevalence remained considerably higher in several districts, including Keonjhar at 15%, Mayurbhanj at 14.8%, Malkangiri at 14.1%, Rayagada at 12.8% and Dhenkanal at 11.5%.

A review of available evidence has linked exposure to air pollutants with an increased risk of death by suicide or suicidal thoughts, with particulate matter PM2.5 and PM10 and nitrogen dioxide (NO2) posing the greatest risks.
The findings, published in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health, underscore the need to consider environmental exposures as potentially modifiable risk factors in suicide prevention strategies, researchers said.
The team from Queen's University Belfast in the UK analysed results from 29 studies that looked at the effects of air pollution exposure on suicide and suicidal thoughts.
The interplay of individual, biological, and contextual factors means that suicide prevention is really a public health issue, they said.
However, while the effect of environmental exposures on mental health outcomes, such as depression or anxiety, has been extensively studied, the potential role of environmental factors on the risk of suicide is less well understood, the researchers said.
"This meta-analysis shows statistically significant positive associations between short-term exposure to PM2.5 and PM10, long-term exposure to PM2.5 and NO2, and risk of death by suicide, attempted suicide and suicide ideation," the authors wrote.
Positive links might exist for other air pollutants, including sulphur dioxide and ozone, and noise pollution, the team added.
"The results highlight the importance of considering environmental exposures as modifiable risk factors in suicide prevention," they said.
The researchers explained that air pollutants and water polluted with arsenic, lead, lithium or nitrate, have been linked to neurological effects, including chronic inflammation and nerve damage, which can impair brain function and influence mood and stress resilience.
Further, traffic and other environmental noise and light pollution has been suggested in studies to increase stress levels through a disruption of the body clock, they said.
Ben Mullins, professor at Curtin University's school of population health in Australia, said the study has undertaken one of the first meta-analyses exploring the link between air pollution and suicide.
"It is well known that many air pollutants, specifically many metals, may cause wide-ranging neurological effects, including depression, anxiety, etc. Therefore, a link between air pollutant exposure and mental health disorders, including suicide, is not unexpected," Mullins, not involved with the study, said.
"However, the effect sizes in the included studies were relatively small, and the authors did not adequately address confounding factors or other explanatory variables," Mullins said.
The professor added, "For example, other studies have found stronger links between weather and climate extremes and suicide. These extremes are however, in turn, often associated with air pollution events." "More work to decouple these effects, as well as socio-economic or other confounders, is needed in order to better understand this important issue, including causation mechanisms and potential mitigation," Mullins said.

By mid-September, the Pennsylvania Department of Health had reported four confirmed measles-associated deaths, surpassing the highest annual number of measles-associated deaths in the United States since 1992. Pennsylvania public health professionals are sounding the alarm as the number of measles cases statewide exceeds 800, with cases clustering among communities with a history of vaccine hesitancy.
But if you look at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s measles dashboard page, it shows just one measles-related death so far this year, with an asterisk.
Amid a tussle between Pennsylvania and the federal government, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., recently stated that the CDC will only “report measles-caused deaths when the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) reports measles as the underlying cause based on death record information submitted by the states.”
When we first read this, as former senior leaders at NCHS, we questioned the approach. This new method deviates from how CDC historically has relied on notifications from state medical officials, including information about symptoms, hospitalizations, and deaths, to immediately publish real-time “associated” death cases that include any deaths with a positive laboratory result for the outbreak condition. By doing so during active outbreaks, CDC has played a key role in making real-time state-level public health surveillance information available for effective and timely responses.
Shifting away from the rapid notification approach and relying strictly on mortality statistics generated by NCHS will not provide the surveillance information needed at the beginning of an active outbreak when counts are low.
To see why, we need to understand the center’s mission and data processing and reporting procedures.
As the nation’s principal federal statistics agency, NCHS’s mission is to produce high-quality, trustworthy, statistical information for informing public health policy and actions. Collecting, compiling, and releasing information on death certificates is part of its mission.
Before death counts are released by NCHS, death certificates are first completed by state and local medical officials including physicians, medical examiners, and coroners. The medical officials must determine all causes of death — underlying and contributing — listed on the death certificate by adhering to established national guidelines. States’ vital registries then submit death certificate information to the NCHS National Vital Statistics System. The time between death occurrence and data submission to NCHS can vary from state to state.
When the data are received, NCHS verifies and codes the certificates using automated systems, with all causes of death coded with the International Classification of Diseases system. Once coded by NCHS, data are made available in CDC WONDER, a primary repository for disseminating NCHS mortality data within one to two weeks.
A small portion of the certificates with inconsistent or complex information, or that identify rare causes of death, are manually adjudicated, sometimes by referring the certificate back to the state. Manual adjudication for such cases can extend the time needed for release, ranging from weeks to even months in some cases. Data in CDC WONDER, including information on underlying and contributing causes, are available to anyone who needs the information, including HHS and infectious disease specialists at the CDC.
Regarding the Pennsylvania measles cases, even when NCHS eventually verifies that those death certificates have measles as an underlying cause of death and make the data available in CDC WONDER, death counts on the CDC measles tracker dashboard will remain with an asterisk for some time. This asterisk notation is a result of strict data suppression rules enforced by NCHS for protecting the confidentiality of the decedent. NCHS does not report death counts in any category from one to nine. The total number of measles-causing deaths in the U.S. without naming Pennsylvania or any other localities must surpass the threshold of 10 before CDC WONDER will show the actual death count for any use, including for the CDC measles dashboard.
The CDC now will shift to recognizing measles-causing deaths on its tracker dashboard only when measles is identified as the underlying cause, not contributing cause, of death on a death certificate.
Although using only the underlying cause of death is consistent with NCHS’ standard practice for its official national mortality statistics for purposes of annual ranking and trending analysis, the new CDC approach effectively precludes the federal measles dashboard from being used to track “measles-associated deaths,” a traditional epidemiological outbreak definition that includes measles as either the underlying or a contributing cause essential for tracking the severity of the current outbreak. Nonetheless, CDC WONDER contains both underlying and contributing causes of death for researchers and decision-makers for use to make informed decisions.
Contrary to the new CDC plan, Pennsylvania needs to actively track measles-associated deaths because even if measles is not the underlying cause of death, measles severely weakens the immune system, substantially increasing a person’s risk of fatal secondary infections or complications.
A discrepancy between how federal and state public health officials determine measles deaths will only increase public confusion about how dangerous the measles outbreaks have been and add to the public’s mistrust of conflicting information from governmental public health institutions.
Furthermore, by not recognizing the broader death definition and relying only on NCHS reporting, HHS could refuse to act until the death counts with measles as the underlying cause rise to more than nine, compromising our ability to effectively contain the country’s deadliest measles outbreak in over two decades.
Denys T. Lau, Ph.D., is the AJPH editor-in-chief and was with NCHS for more than 11 years, first as director of the Division of Health Care Statistics and then as senior science adviser of the Division of Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys. Jennifer D. Schoendorf, Ph.D., is the AJPH senior deputy editor and retired from NCHS in 2024 after nearly 30 years, most recently as the director of the Division of Research and Methodology.

Srinagar, Sep 22: The Government of Jammu and Kashmir has formally relieved Mohammad Zaid Malik, a 2001-batch officer of the Jammu and Kashmir Police Service (JKPS), to join the National Investigation Agency (NIA) in New Delhi as Superintendent of Police.
The Home Department issued an official order permitting his deputation to the central counter-terror agency. Malik will now serve in NIA , adding field experience from north and south Kashmir to the agency’s investigation and operations work.
Before the national assignment, he served as Senior Superintendent of Police of Baramulla, taking charge in late August 2024. Baramulla, a sensitive LoC-adjacent district, has long been a focus of anti-infiltration and law-and-order work.
Malik’s career has been built around operational and district commands. He has served as SP Operations in Baramulla, Anantnag and Bandipora, and as district SSP of Awantipora and Bandipora. In those postings he handled complex law-and-order situations and anti-terror operations, work that colleagues and security partners have often described as grounded in ground-level coordination with the Army and other forces.
A 2023 farewell by the Rashtriya Rifles in Bandipora, when he demitted charge as SSP there, underlined that record: Army officers credited him with intelligence-led operations, jointmanship and efforts to curb crime and narcotics in the district. He had assumed the Bandipora charge in March 2021.

Priest killed and four injured in knife attack at Polish abbey
- Published
A priest has been killed and four other people injured in a knife attack in south-east Poland, officials have said.
A 31-year-old Ukrainian man was arrested after the stabbings on the grounds of a Catholic abbey in the town of Jarosław.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki said Thursday's attack "has shaken us all and demands a firm response from the state", while his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky said "we are shocked by this evil".
Reports in Polish media said the attacker first injured a priest in a nearby cafe, and then another four people inside the abbey itself. A police investigation into the attacker's motives is now under way.
Polish police said four men and one woman were stabbed in the attack on Thursday morning on the abbey grounds.
The name of the murdered priest has not been publicly released.
Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said psychological support was now being provided to all those affected by the incident.
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the perpetrator "will be punished with the full severity of Polish law".
Echoing his words, President Zelensky said "the perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility according to the law", adding that Ukraine was counting on "a quick and thorough investigation of all circumstances".
The Ukrainian embassy in Poland also condemned the attack.
In a statement, it said: "In such difficult moments, it is especially important to support each other, remain steadfast in respect for human life, and not allow pain to escalate into hatred or new violence. Responsibility for a crime must be based solely on the law."
Poland has recently seen a number of often violent incidents involving its citizens and Ukrainians, many of whom have fled their home country after Russia's full-scale invasion.

Welcome to Sportstar’s LIVE coverage of the shooting events from Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026. This is Santadeep Dey, bringing you all the updates from the Aichi Prefectural General Shooting Gallery.
Decoding the 50m 3P rules
In qualification, 40 shots are attempted in each of kneeling, prone and standing positions. There is decimal scoring, and the top eight advance to the final.
The finalists fire 10 kneeling and 10 prone shots within a combined 22-minute phase, with athletes free to manage the transition between the two positions. They then shoot 10 shots standing, after which the bottom two are eliminated. Standing then continues with single shots, eliminating the lowest-ranked athlete after each.
How does the 10m air pistol mixed team qualification work?
In the qualification round, two shooters will get to fire 30 shots—three series of 10—each in a total of 40 minutes. The top four teams make the final.
In the new final format, each shooter initially fires three five-shot series. The teams then move into the eliminations round, wherein after three single shots per shooter, the team with the lowest cumulative score is eliminated in fourth place.
After another three, the lowest of the remaining teams takes bronze. After a final three shots, the top two teams are separated for gold and silver.
There are no separate bronze and gold medal matches anymore.

The New South Wales government’s crackdown on “AI-doctored” rental listings has hit a wall, after it made an example of a supposedly manipulated ad that turned out to be a genuine photograph of a $5,000 courtyard mural of Bondi beach.
In a media release on Friday announcing protections against misleading rental ads, the state government provided a link to a property in Leichhardt, claiming it was an “AI-doctored rental listing in Sydney’s Inner West”.
But the listing agency IB Property denied the images were altered.
A spokesperson confirmed the photograph shows a mural of Bondi beach on an internal courtyard wall visible through the unit’s windows, rather than a false digital depiction of coastal views.
“We can confirm that the image has not been altered or digitally generated using AI, Photoshop or any other image-editing software,” the spokesperson said.
Leichhardt is about 12km away from Bondi beach.
When Guardian Australia visited 2/14 Norton Street, the artwork was not visible from the street. IB Property explained the mural sits within an internal courtyard and provided photos taken inside the unit confirming it remains in place.
“The mural was commissioned and paid for by the landlord at a cost of approximately $5,000, and we can also confirm that there are no plans for it to be removed,” the spokesperson said, adding that the property was leased in February 2026 and has not been advertised since.
The better regulation and fair trading minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, whose office issued the media release, didn’t respond directly to questions from Guardian Australia, but did issue the following statement:
“Every renter knows the frustration of seeing a property online, only to turn up and find it looks nothing like the listing.
“These laws are about putting an end to misleading practices and making sure renters get a fair go. We will always stand on the side of renters.”
Tackling ‘housefishing’
Despite the mix-up, the new laws target an increasing market issue.
Under the legislation, real estate businesses in NSW will face fines of up to $22,000 for failing to disclose digitally altered or AI-generated property images.
The bill targets the rapid rise of “housefishing” – where digital alterations distort the true size and condition of a home.
Chanthivong said the new laws would establish strong protections against misleading property marketing and support ethical AI use. The regulations take effect in early 2027.
Virtual staging v distorting reality
The legislation arrives as generative AI embeds itself in property marketing nationwide.
Tim McKibbin, the chief executive of the Real Estate Institute of NSW, said generative AI complicates pre-existing digital enhancement in the industry.
“This technology has been available for some years now … people have used Photoshop,” he said. “People were removing trees and removing telegraph poles … clearly that is false and misleading.”
McKibbin draws a line between virtual staging and false advertising. “I’ve seen instances where agents have put furniture into the photographs … Now, that is merely giving you an indication of what you could do,” he said.
Stewart Bunn, of First National Real Estate, said consumer trust is being tested by poor industry examples, referencing a 2024 instance where an LJ Hooker branch used AI to generate a listing with nonexistent schools.
“We have seen examples across the industry where AI-generated images have depicted renovations that have not occurred, furnishings that create an unrealistic impression of scale, landscaping that does not exist or finishes that materially differ from the actual property,” Bunn said.
“The best practice is simple: if a buyer would be surprised by what they see when they arrive at the property, the advertising has gone too far.”
AI ‘hallucinations’
An RMIT University report led by Dr Leah Li, funded by the Australian Property Institute, found a “significant lack of sector-specific AI frameworks to guide responsible AI practice within the property profession”.
Public confidence remains fragile: a 2026 Cotality study showed only 40% of Australians trust AI-generated outputs, compared with 62% in Canada, 52% in the US, and 46% in the UK.
Dr Shuai Wang, a research fellow at the University of Queensland, said generative AI systems prioritise visual appeal over accuracy. In real estate, this can manifest as “hallucinations”.
“AI hallucinations can occur when AI-generated images introduce features that were never part of the property,” Li said, fundamentally changing a prospective tenant’s perception of “size, layout, condition, or amenity”.
Leo Patterson Ross, the chief executive of the Tenants’ Union of NSW, said deceptive imagery can artificially inflate rental markets by creating fake demand.
“By inflating the number of people who appear interested in a place and increasing pressure on someone to rush to put in an application or even offer above the advertised rent.”
Patterson Ross said stricter measures were necessary, rather than just disclosure. “The bill only requires disclosure of the use of digital alterations. We think any use of imagery that misrepresents the property should be disallowed.”
Li said long-term resolution will require national coordination combining “transparency requirements, professional accountability, industry standards, regulatory oversight, and consumer education”.
“Trust does not come from simply adopting AI; trust comes from transparency about how AI has been used and confidence that it is being used responsibly.”
‘Haunted houses with a digital paint job’
For tenants navigating tight rental markets, AI distortion has added a frustrating layer of deception.
Roxanne Gardiner, 26, said AI-generated imagery was “rife” during her search for a rental in Brisbane’s eastern suburbs.
“I was constantly getting scammed by listing photos,” she said. “What’s so embarrassing is we didn’t even realise one of the first houses we saw was AI until we rocked up there.
“The AI furniture is not accurate to the rooms and would usually make them look bigger than they were.”
Beyond virtual staging, Gardiner observed artificial greenery and soft lighting that changed the true character of a home.
“It feels cheap … lazy and insulting,” she said. “We just stopped going to AI listings, period. We started asking: ‘What are they compensating for?’” Gardiner’s group eventually signed a lease on an unedited property within three days of manually filtering out AI-altered ads.
Matt Stitt, 25, faced similar issues searching in south Brisbane.
“Listings had completely replaced floorboards to look new, edited in area rugs that near-covered entire rooms,” he said. “It was such a waste of time seeing these haunted houses with a digital paint job.”
Crackdown on data collection and hidden fees
The NSW legislation also protects privacy for more than 2.3 million renters by curbing excessive data harvesting. Landlords and property managers must use standardised application forms, banning requests for personal photos, social media handles, tattoo details or children’s information.
Sensitive identity documents, such as driver’s licences and passports, will only be collected from the single preferred applicant prior to lease signing, eliminating roughly 187,000 document collections annually, according to the government.
Penalties for privacy breaches will reach up to $11,000 for individuals and $49,500 for corporations. The bill also mandates the disclosure of embedded utility networks upfront.
Chanthivong said privacy protections build on broader rental reforms, including fee-free payment options and ending no-grounds evictions.
“Whether you have a tattoo, or what school your kids go to, is not relevant to whether you’ll be a good tenant.”

WASHINGTON — Heidi Overton, President Trump’s nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration, was grilled by senators on hot button topics like China, vaccines, and abortion access in her hearing before the committee that will decide whether to send her nomination for a vote of the full Senate.
Throughout the two-hour hearing, Overton, a preventive medicine physician from rural New Mexico who worked in the White House during both Trump terms, revealed very little of her own feelings on top issues facing the FDA. Instead, she referred repeatedly to existing agency guidance and approvals for products like childhood vaccines and the abortion drug mifepristone — without saying whether she would endorse updating those guidance or altering approvals to satisfy the desires of Trump or health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

US President Donald Trump welcomed China President Xi Jinping to the White House for a lavish state dinner where both leaders touted a new chapter in their friendship.
The dinner was attended by billionaire business leaders, Trump administration officials, US tech CEOs and others. Their arrival was marked, however, by protesters loudly shouting from just outside the White House gates, some of whom were arrested.
Both Trump and Xi praised one another, pledging to continue talks to ensure stability between their two nations. But experts say that not much concrete has been yielded in talks so far.
The dinner came on the second day of Xi's three-day trip to Washington.
What did Trump say in his dinner toast?
Trump thanked Xi for making the long trip to the US, and said the relationship between the two men was strong.
"We've never gotten along better," Trump said.
He praised the long history of US-China relations, although he did take an unscripted detour to praise his ongoing ballroom project.
In the off-the-cuff moment, he said as a "special treat" the Chinese leader and his wife could be the first to enter the ballroom, which is still a year away from completion.
"Anybody who wants to walk into a construction site that's nice and clean and sparkling, it's our honour to have you do so," he said.
He also presented Xi with a sculpture of a bald eagle, America's national symbol, saying it embodied "the free and soaring spirit of America".
"We hope it will find a nice, wonderful place in Beijing. It's your honour," he said.
Trump added that he and First Lady Melania had participated in the design of the sculpture.
What did Xi say?
Xi thanked his hosts for receiving him and his wife with "meticulous care and consideration", making them "feel truly at home".
He said the two leaders are "making history in our bilateral engagements".
"We agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability," Xi said, adding that the two shared "sincere and in-depth exchanges" that will strengthen relations between the two countries.
Like Trump's, Xi's remarks were heavy on flattery, focusing on cultural ties and shared history between the US and China.
The relationship between the two countries was "forged in blood and fire" during the fight against Japan in the Second World War, before being furthered during the "ping pong" diplomacy of the Nixon administration, he said.
Towards the end of his speech, Xi said the US and China's goals can be "mutually reinforcing". He urged both sides to explore a "new approach for major countries to get along".
Who was in attendance?
When the BBC entered the dining hall for the dinner, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was standing over a table and appeared to be telling an entertaining story that had two others nearby barreled over with laughter.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth was at another table, with a serious look on his face. His wife is sat beside him, with Jared Kushner and White House chief of staff Monica Crowley nearby.
The White House invited scores of US officials, as well as conservative broadcasters, tech industry bosses, social media CEOs and other corporate executives.
Attendees included members of Trump's cabinet, as well as family members like his children Ivanka, Eric and Tiffany.
Bosses from the tech industry in attendance included Apple's Tim Cook, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Google's Sundar Pichai, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
Both Cook and Huang were seated at the same table as Trump and Xi. As was Musk, who previously worked in Trump's administration leading the effort to shrink government.
Other companies whose leaders were in attendance include General Motors, Visa, Paramount Skydance, ExxonMobil and more.
Social media mogul Mark Zuckerberg also attended, as well as Jeff Yaas, the American billionaire who owns a share of TikTok.
"Everybody wanted to be there," Trump said ahead of the event. "I would say you have the entire tech world, the entire banking world, and a lot more."
But one notable absence was Anthropic - one of the biggest and most valuable AI firms in the world. The BBC has asked Anthropic if it was invited, or if they chose not to be there.
What was on the menu?
The office of the First Lady Melania Trump, which planned the event, said the dinner menu would showcase "American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence".
For their first course guests enjoyed yellow squash, wild mushrooms and crispy pancetta. The ate off red tablecloths - red being a symbol of luck and good fortune in China.
For their main course they dined on a sesame-crusted sea bass, braised bok choy and roasted eggplant.
Dessert featured the two leaders and their fellow diners tucking into vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit, with an accompanying ice cream "made with harvested White House honey".
The wine chosen by the first lady included Schramsberg Blanc De Noir - a nod to President Nixon's 1972 "Toast to Peace" with former Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai, when they used a bottle from the same vineyard.
What's on the agenda for Friday?
Trump and Xi will begin their day with tea at the White House's Red Room with their wives.
The group then head to the US National Archives for a tour of the building and its exhibits.
Formally called the National Archives and Records Administration, the building holds some of the most important documents regarding the founding of the United States - including the US Constitution, the Declaration of Independence and the Bill of Rights.
Xi and his wife will depart Washington later in the day.

Chinese President Xi Jinping invoked an idea rooted in ancient Greek history during his White House meeting with US President Donald Trump on 24 September, saying that the “Thucydides Trap can be overcome”, Bloomberg reported. The reference came as Xi called for the US and China to keep their competition “within bounds” and urged the two countries' militaries to maintain regular dialogue and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention, Bloomberg reported. The phrase refers to the risk of conflict when a rising power challenges an established one. While the concept is named after the ancient Greek historian Thucydides, its application to modern US-China relations was popularized by Harvard political scientist Graham Allison. Quick answers to key questions The Thucydides Trap describes the heightened risk of conflict when a rising power, like China, challenges the dominance of an established power, such as the US. It's based on historical examples where such dynamics led to war. Xi referred to the Thucydides Trap to emphasize the need for better communication and crisis management between the US and China, urging that competition should be managed to avoid escalation into conflict. Xi believes the Thucydides Trap can be overcome by maintaining regular military dialogue and crisis-prevention mechanisms while promoting healthy competition between the US and China. The Thucydides Trap has significant implications for trade and technology, as ongoing geopolitical competition can affect trade arrangements, technology access, and investment decisions between the two nations. Yes, both countries should take the Thucydides Trap seriously as it highlights the risk of conflict due to their competitive actions, and managing this rivalry effectively is crucial for global stability. Xi had referred to the same idea during his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, when he asked whether the two countries could overcome the trap and build a different kind of relationship. His latest remarks in Washington were more direct: the trap, he said, can be overcome. The Thucydides Trap describes the heightened risk of conflict when an emerging power challenges the position of an established power. The term draws on Thucydides' account of the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta. Thucydides attributed the conflict to the rise of Athens and the fear that this generated in Sparta. Allison subsequently applied the historical idea to modern great-power competition. His Harvard Thucydides's Trap project examined 16 cases over the past 500 years in which a rising power threatened to displace an established power. According to his research, 12 of those cases ended in war. That figure, however, is not a prediction that the US and China are headed for war. Scholars have questioned Allison's case selection and methodology, arguing that some historical examples do not fit the framework neatly and that the small sample size makes it difficult to draw broad conclusions. Xi's reference came alongside a call for greater communication between Washington and Beijing. He said the two countries should strengthen communication, better understand each other, seek common ground while managing differences, and maintain regular military dialogue. He also argued that the two sides should avoid confrontation, Bloomberg reported. The timing is significant because the US and China remain competitors across several areas, including trade, artificial intelligence and technology. Taiwan also remains a major point of disagreement between Washington and Beijing. Xi's message, therefore, was not that the US and China had resolved their differences. Rather, the reference to the Thucydides Trap framed communication and crisis management as ways of preventing strategic competition from escalating into conflict. Xi has discussed the Thucydides Trap for years and has previously argued that it is not an unavoidable law of history. His latest comments return to that argument: the outcome of a US-China power transition is shaped by decisions made by both governments rather than predetermined by history. The Thucydides Trap is a framework for thinking about great-power rivalry, not a rule that says a rising power and an established power must eventually go to war. The idea is particularly relevant as Washington and Beijing compete while also trying to keep their relationship stable. Trade remains a major part of the relationship, while technology and AI have become increasingly important areas of strategic competition. The two countries are also managing disagreements over Taiwan and other geopolitical issues. For businesses and investors, the significance lies in how geopolitical competition can affect trade arrangements, technology access, supply chains and investment decisions. Xi's White House remarks were therefore a call for managing competition rather than evidence that the underlying US-China rivalry has disappeared. Xi's choice of words offered a relatively simple proposition: the US and China can remain competitors without allowing competition to become a military conflict. His call for regular military communication and crisis-prevention mechanisms points to the practical challenge behind the historical analogy. Even if Washington and Beijing disagree over trade, technology, or Taiwan, both sides have an interest in preventing those disagreements from escalating. Therefore, the reference to the Thucydides Trap matters. It was less a declaration that the US-China rivalry had been resolved than a statement about how Beijing wants it managed.
