The moment Antonelli knew he had been transformed as an F1 driver
- Published
Kimi Antonelli says he knew from the first moment he drove this year's Mercedes that he would be transformed as a Formula 1 driver in 2026.
The 20-year-old Italian, who is running away with the world championship in only his second season in F1, is reflecting on his breakthrough year in the sport in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport.
A difficult debut season last year had left external expectations of Antonelli low at the start of 2026. But on a typically damp and cold January day at Silverstone, he already sensed that something special might be on the cards.
"It was just a few laps in the wet," Antonelli says, "but I just felt better in the car, much better than I felt last year. Also the car felt well, but I just felt better mentally in the car. Less tense, more relaxed and more mature."
Last year, he says, was "not great". "I was driving very tense most of the time, I wasn't able to extract the potential out of me," he says.
"This year, it's a lot different. The mindset has been the biggest change."
Fast forward eight months and the effects of that new headspace are plain to see.
After 14 grands prix, and with either eight or nine remaining depending on the war in the Middle East, Antonelli is a massive 81 points clear of team-mate George Russell.
Not only that, but he looks so in control. Always fast, always composed, a factor in every grand prix. Everyone knows the championship is basically over, barring some kind of dramatic misfortune.
Even then, Antonelli says he is "still finding my way" in F1.
The journey Antonelli has been on in the past two years is remarkable, and he says even he is "surprised" by the extent of his progress this year.
He was comprehensively outperformed by Russell in 2025. So when it was obvious that Mercedes would start the new regulatory era with an advantage, it was the Briton who started the season as championship favourite.
Russell duly won the opening race in Australia, but Antonelli was less than three seconds behind him at the flag. This, he says, was the second moment of realisation of what might be possible.
"I had a big, big crash in FP3," Antonelli recalls. "But then thanks to the mechanics - who all throughout the season have done an incredible job, but on that specific occasion, it is a miracle - I was able to go back in the car and push again in the high speed and getting close to the limit.
"The crash, definitely it compromised a little bit qualifying and the race because we couldn't set up properly the car. I mean, the car was still very quick. But it was not easy.
"Still being able to stay close despite that, I was like, 'OK, you know, it's not going to be a walk in the park. It's going to be very tough', but I knew already that it was a different story compared to last year.
"If it would have happened last year, I wouldn't have been able to overcome that."
Monza 2024 memory made Antonelli 'afraid to do a mistake'
Antonelli's first season in F1 was haunted by an incident that happened the first time he drove on a grand prix weekend.
At the 2024 Italian Grand Prix, the day before they formally announced Antonelli was the replacement for Ferrari-bound Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes gave him an outing in first practice at Monza.
He was blindingly fast on his first flying lap - but then crashed heavily on his second.
Team principal Toto Wolff played it down at the time, saying he was well aware there would be mistakes from Antonelli as he found his feet in F1. But behind the scenes the incident had had a big impact on the young man.
"Monza stayed in my head for a very long time," Antonelli says. "I think all throughout last season, at least. Definitely that was a big thing that was kind of slowing me down.
"This memory of being afraid to do a mistake, also because going through the difficult period (in the middle of 2025), this memory was even stronger in my head, if you know what I mean.
"Because it was already a difficult period and I was like, 'If I even do a mistake or I crash, it's even worse.'
"So yeah, it's been a thing that has been bothering me a lot last year. This year I was able to just put it behind."
Doing so has involved a lot of work behind the scenes, analysing what happened in 2025, understanding what had gone well, what had not, and why, and what he could do to improve.
"The mindset going into this season, it was mainly trying to be able to extract more out of my potential," Antonelli says. "Trying to, first of all, do a better job than previous year. But as well trying to put things more together.
"The preparation that I did in pre-season was very, very intense. But it helped me a lot to arrive ready for this season.
"Plus, I did a lot of work with my mental coach. Trying to get my head right, my thoughts right on understanding the goal, and understanding that the most important thing is to be ready and to stay present in the moment.
"Not trying to think about final results or what would happen if I wouldn't achieve that. But just trying to be present and trying to do the best with what you can do in the moment."
'First win, first pole, took a lot of weight off my shoulder'
Still, though, he admits to be "definitely surprised" at how much progress he has made.
"I knew that I was going to be better than my first year," he says. "Obviously, because I think last year, towards the end of the season, I started to put things more together, starting to extract more performance. But still, it was still not great.
"Whereas this year, it's a lot different. Also as well, with the first win, the first pole, it took a lot of weight off my shoulder."
Antonelli has blossomed. Everything seems to be coming so easily to him. If he drops back in a race, he recovers seamlessly and quickly. Overtaking moves are done quickly and decisively. There's not been a circuit on which he has lacked pace.
Russell, by contrast, has admitted to struggling and - while not trying to take anything away from Antonelli, who he is always quick to praise - has expressed his opinion that his his driving style does not suit this year's new cars.
All of which raises a key question - how much of what is happening this year is Antonelli stepping it up, and how much Russell falling back?
"That's a very difficult question," Antonelli says. "I've definitely stepped up.
"This year definitely everything is new. So it requires also a little bit of a different approach. And trying to adapt to a different car, which hasn't been easy."
His consistency this year, he says, has come from the fact he has found "a nice rhythm in the season".
"I always try to follow my routines," Antonelli says, "the way I approach the weekend. I try to approach it all the time the same.
"I'm still finding my way, but I've found a way that helps me to be consistent and also helps me to be consistently ready when I go in the car."
There are still moments when he misjudges things, though. He cites the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix, just days after his outstanding win in Monaco, one of the most dominant at that storied track for years.
"Monaco was a very high moment for me in the season, and then I went to Barcelona and I was probably a bit too excited, especially over a single lap," he says.
"So I was overdriving, I was chasing the lap time and the result didn't come in qualifying. I was actually a bit far back and didn't do a good lap.
"But that's because I was trying to do a bit too much after a very high moment in my career. And then I understood that that is not the way."
The lesson was applied after his spellbinding win from 19th on the grid at Monza, his home race, a result that Wolff said "closed a cycle" from his 2024 crash.
Antonelli says: "After Monza, I reminded myself, 'Don't make the same mistake as you did after Monaco.'"
He won the Spanish Grand Prix seven days later, an eighth victory from 14 races so far this season.
Success has inevitably led to fame, and with it attention.
"Life has changed a lot," Antonelli says. "I'm not going to lie. It's been a big change, but it's nice to see so much support. Definitely, one side is very nice, but on the other side, you have to be careful. You've got to protect yourself a bit more because obviously you're more exposed."
All year, Antonelli has talked about focusing on process, about doing the best he can on every single day, not thinking about the big picture.
Now, though, for the first time, he acknowledges the title - an achievement that would make him the youngest world champion in F1 history - is on his mind.
"Yes, I thought about it," he says. "But again, thinking about it, I came always to the same conclusion that the earlier I finish all this, the better it is.
"So I've got to just keep pushing. I keep doing the best I can every race. Because, yeah, that's the way. Just not finish. And until it's done, it's not over."

When Meta first launched its AI-powered smart glasses in 2023, in collaboration with the trendy sunglasses brand Ray-Ban, it unleashed a storm of controversy.
There have been multiple reports of the devices being used to harass women and girls in particular, filming them without their consent, then sharing the footage.
The image problem doesn't seem to have been cured by Meta's enlistment this summer of Kylie Jenner, Kim Kardashian's sister, as their prime model. The devices have been dubbed "pervert" or "creepy" glasses. In the UK, JD Wetherspoon pubs, a handful of major theatres, Comic-Con, some schools, and Faslane, home of the UK's nuclear submarines, have all chosen to ban them.
On Thursday, Meta is unveiling a new version which does not contain a camera at all, called Ray-Ban Meta Audio. They will have the audio functions of the original glasses - including the ability to make phone calls or play music, with the sound funnelled directly into your ear - but with fewer implications for privacy.
To some in the industry, it looks like an interesting pivot - a response, perhaps, to the backlash over privacy.
The tech giant denies that the new glasses have been rushed out in response to public anger. They say the product has been in development for two years. The audio-only version is cheaper than its camera-enabled cousins, and Meta says it has a lighter frame and better battery life.
When I put it to Meta Glasses' head of product Ankit Brahmbhatt that I thought they might overtake the original camera-enabled glasses in sales, there was a pregnant pause.
"We have, I think, something for everyone," he said, choosing his words very carefully.
Does the release of a camera-free option represent a shift in how tech companies see the future of smart glasses? And is Meta's original vision getting further away?
Or should we see camera-free glasses as a niche side-product that serves a small market - a bit like how some mobile manufacturers are now releasing internet-disabled "brick" phones for people who are tired of social media?
Music, maps, and washing cars
There's no doubt that smart glasses have become controversial.
I was lent a pair of Meta Ray-Bans – with cameras - to try out. I was initially nervous about wearing them in public, in case someone got physical: I have heard of people knocking them off wearers' heads and smashing them in the street.
The reality was that I wore them on public transport and on foot in several cities including London, Glasgow and Portsmouth, and nobody batted an eyelid. It made me wonder whether awareness of them is really as high as both Meta and anti-glasses campaigners believe.
That said, some people quietly told me they would not be confident enough to approach someone wearing them even if they did spot them, for fear of the interaction being filmed and uploaded.
The glasses are designed to work as an extension of your phone. They use Bluetooth to sync with a handset via Meta's AI app. They are voice-activated, with open speakers in the arms funnelling sound into your ears. The result is a bit like wearing headphones without the addition of noise-cancelling features, so you can still hear the world around you.
My potentially cancellable opinion is that I found many of the glasses' features useful. Interestingly, none of them included the camera.
Listening to music and podcasts on the move without having earbuds stuffed into my ears felt safer. I felt more confident about avoiding the gamut of e-bike-riding phone thieves in central London without my phone physically in my hand.
And as someone with a pitiful sense of direction, I rely a lot on map apps. It was handy to have the directions spoken in my ears. The pay-off for this, however, was having to accept allowing the Meta AI app to know exactly where I was at all times. Meta is notorious for its hunger for personal data.
When I posted about using the Meta Ray-Bans on social media, I got a bit of a hard time. Less so when I showed them to people in my everyday life.
My hairdresser loved the idea of using them to record her clients' hair transformations. A builder I chatted to at the gym reckoned they would be useful on sites for recording what he was doing, either in the event of an accident or even to teach others new skills. My friend who runs said he would like to wear them on a jog.
Plenty of content creators are big fans. My son borrowed them to wash my car, and was proud of his film showing me how he delicately chipped away at a stubborn bit of bird poo without damaging the paintwork (I was pleased, and happy to take his word for it).
More broadly, smart glasses have been welcomed by the blind community. One user described them to the BBC as a "game-changer" because they can give audio descriptions of current locations and read out visible text like restaurant menu options. Earlier this year Meta donated 15,000 pairs to a charity for the blind in Ireland.
Calls for regulation
But still, anger over privacy has grown.
The glasses have a blinking white LED that switches on when the camera is active, but a whole industry has sprung up around finding technical workarounds to disable that light, some of which involve taking the glasses apart.
Meta says less than 0.1% of the frames it has sold worldwide have been physically tampered with. Exact sales figures are unknown, but Ray-Ban's parent company EssilorLuxottica has reported that it sold seven million last year.
Liz Hunter, a tech founder and parent who has set up a petition calling for urgent new regulation of smart glasses, is furious.
"They should never, ever have left the lab at Meta," she told me. "It's a real travesty of public trust, and of women's equality, and it's rolled back our privacy rights right before our very eyes."
Hunter thinks smart glasses should remain available for blind people, but not for the general population.
"We don't need them, we don't want them," she says.
A Polish developer has released an app called ZuckOff which uses Bluetooth to identify nearby smart glasses. It's been downloaded thousands of times, reports Wired magazine.
Ben Wood, from tech research firm CCS Insight, remembers first reading the phrase "pervert glasses" in the usually strait-laced Financial Times - a sign, he says, that it had prompted a "significant public backlash".
The furore has not deterred other companies from eyeing the market, however.
Samsung is reported to be working on a collaboration with the upmarket glasses brand Warby Parker. Google is also said to be working on a set. Snap, the firm behind Snapchat, has just launched Specs, which are retailing in the US for $2,195 (and £1,995 in the UK). Users can see data inside the glass, and snap their fingers to take a photo.
Snap founder Evan Spiegel says he thinks smart glasses will eventually replace phones, and he's not alone.
Step back or 'half step to the side'?
When Meta launched smart glasses in 2021, they were geared in part around what the user could see. The firm promised they would allow users to "easily record the world as you see it", and to "capture life's moments as they happen from a unique first-person perspective".
So Meta's latest announcement - glasses without a camera - is notable.
Janusz Swierczynski, a researcher at Oxford University's Saïd Business School, who is worried about smart glasses, says the release of a camera-free version is a "positive sign" that Meta seems to have listened to privacy concerns. "They're thinking about it and that they're responding," he says, though he thinks it's "not a perfect" response because the camera-enabled glasses are still on the market.
Others are less sure it represents a real shift.
"It's certainly not the end of cameras in glasses," says Wood, from CCS Insight. He thinks that smart glasses are largely about capturing information; the glasses collect as much data as they can from your surroundings and then use AI to tell you about it.
And glasses armed with a camera - trained on whatever you can see - are an "extremely good" source of that information.
"That is an invaluable data stream to an AI platform, which can then interpret that data and provide you with the best possible information related to it," Wood says. "So having the vision parts of it with the cameras is a key pillar for getting the best experience."

He imagines Meta has been working on the camera-free glasses for several years, and the current backlash over privacy provides "fantastic timing" for their release.
Indeed, Meta doesn't yet show any signs of slowing down its development of camera-enabled glasses. The company is bringing its third generation of the glasses to the UK next month. These can visually display data inside the specs' lenses. (As a live broadcast journalist who has talked openly about brain fog, I can see the appeal of glasses that can discreetly display a script).
Kate Winick, a tech analyst at the research firm Forrester, says it's not a step back from camera-enabled glasses but more of a "half step to the side, where they give users time to get comfortable with the technology… so that users themselves start to say, 'Oh, this would be so much more useful if it had a camera'."
And she says, paradoxically, the existence of camera-free glasses might help "take the heat" off people who wear camera-enabled glasses in public. "It's now clear that out in the market some glasses have cameras and some don't," she says. "You can't automatically get mad at everybody wearing Meta's glasses, because you may not know whether or not they have a camera."
Towards a social norm
And other companies are trying to address privacy concerns in different ways - without getting rid of the camera.
The Taiwanese firm HTC recently launched Vive Eagle glasses, which cost less than a quarter of Snap's.
Thomas Dexmier, a vice president at HTC Vive, says that if anyone near an Eagle specs wearer says "stop filming" or "stop recording", and it is picked up by one of the four microphones, the camera will deactivate.
And he adds that all recordings captured by the glasses are encrypted, and the firm itself cannot see them - though this also means HTC cannot flag harmful content.
"We acknowledge that there are some challenges, potentially becoming a real problem, especially for women," he said.
He said HTC Vive was working to make it as difficult as possible for the tech to be misused but said it was "too early to comment" on whether the firm would consider a version without cameras.
Ultimately, Wood thinks that camera-enabled glasses are "not going away".
He says the current moment reminds him of the 2000s, when some people said that mobile phone companies couldn't install cameras in their devices because of similar concerns over privacy. "There's an inevitability there," he says.
"We will have to find a societal norm, a framework for the use of these products."

If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “stalemate summit”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.
Instead, it was described as a celebration of “diplotainment” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo.
Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.
“The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.
But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.
One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.
To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.
With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.
That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.
On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.
William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”.
China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.
Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.”
Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.
On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.
For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely.
On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.”
For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

A study by Chennai-based diabetologists has attempted to find out how India has managed to reduce the prices of new and expensive diabetes drugs and what lessons this could possibly hold for other low- and middle-income countries (LMIC). The study, ‘Making Modern Diabetes Medications Affordable and Accessible: Lessons from India for Other Countries’, was led by V. Mohan, chairman, Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, Chennai, and was published in the journal Diabetes Care.
What did the study find?
Of the 589 million adults in the world with diabetes, 80% live in LMICs, the study noted. Modern diabetes therapies such as GLP-1 receptor agonists as well as SGLT2i (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors) improve cardiovascular and renal outcomes, while analogue insulins help reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia. However, affordability remains a barrier: diabetes requires lifelong care and management of complications.
India’s ability to maintain low medication prices is closely linked to its role as a major pharmaceutical exporter, the paper stated, noting the strategic legislative history of maintaining critical safeguards to prevent ‘patent evergreening’ and allowing for generic manufacture of drugs. It also found that the country has increasingly focused on strengthening domestic manufacturing capacity. There are concerns over global trade policies affecting prices and the availability of raw materials. A government incentive scheme has been introduced to promote domestic manufacturing of raw materials, and as of 2025, production has commenced for 26 molecules that were previously imported.
The paper notes that metformin and sulfonylureas continue to form the foundation of type 2 diabetes management in India - both are included in the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM). While DPP-4 (dipeptidyl peptidase 4) inhibitors, SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA have all been introduced, they are not currently in the NLEM. Initial uptake of these drugs was constrained by pricing. Following the competitive entry by multiple domestic manufacturers, the price of semaglutide, for instance in India, has dropped considerably now, and there has been a huge increase in sales; however, absolute monthly costs remain high relative to the household income in India, and, crucially, these are not covered by insurance, as they are, to a great extent, in the U.S.
Quick availability of generic and biosimilar drugs, deliberate regulatory and distribution strategies such as the government’s Jan Aushadi Kendras, and market competition have allowed for affordable drugs in India, the paper highlighted.
What does it propose for other LMICs?
Building local manufacturing capacity as a strategic public health investment, balancing patent governance that encourages easier access to newer molecules, predictable and structured price regulation, good distribution networks at reasonable retail prices and aligning pharmaceutical policy with health financing and ongoing monitoring of medicine quality, prices, prescription patterns and patient access can all help with improving access to affordable medicines, the paper noted. These core principles could also apply to high-income countries facing drug prices, the paper said.
Challenges ahead
Challenges that remain include urban-rural disparities in distribution and availability of medicines; tight regulations potentially affecting chances of drug innovation; differences in quality between generics and difficulties in maintaining strict pharmacovigilance; as well as limited formal evaluation of government schemes to look at their long-term impact on clinical outcomes.

Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly Speaker J.C.D. Prabhakar unveiled the logo and website for the 50th Chennai Book Fair on Friday.

Layola Mani, chairman of the Tamil Nadu Textbook and Educational Services Corporation and M. Kavitha, district library officer, Chennai also spoke at the event.
The website for the bookfair this year is www.chennaibookfair.com

AI superpower ambitions take centre stage as Trump and Xi meet
- Published
"Whoever wins AI, WINS!"
US President Donald Trump has been blunt about his AI ambitions, as well as about who he considers the US's main rival to be: China.
His Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, has not said anything so forthright - but it seems he holds a similar view.
"China very much sees it as a race, they very much think China should be the leading force in AI - they see AI as a power maximiser," says Rebecca Arcesati, from the Mercator Institute for China Studies.
You can look beyond the rhetoric for evidence of this: AI has been a cornerstone of China's technological ambitions for more than a decade, whether Xi emphasises it publicly or not.
For Trump, beating China to AI supremacy outweighs any risks of the technology to humans - something he has described as "a hoax".
China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hinder global AI governance, calling for cooperation to ensure it benefits all.
It means when the two presidents sit down on Thursday there will be few more important topics than their AI ambitions - and what they say and decide will matter to the whole world.
Is the US in the lead?
There's no doubt the US and China are global leaders in AI but who is ahead depends on how success is measured.
American companies lead on so-called frontier models, with the highest-performing systems on most benchmarks coming from firms such as Anthropic, Google and OpenAI.
In February 2025, an AI model by China's DeepSeek "briefly matched the top US model" and as of March 2026, Anthropic's top model led the pack "by just 2.7%", according to researchers at Stanford University, external.
Part of the US advantage stems from the vast sums being invested in leading AI companies as the frontier labs burn through mountains of cash to build the infrastructure to train new models.
The stock market is booming and a large part of the US economy's expansion relies on the enormous growth - and projected profitability - of AI companies.
So that might partly explain why President Trump sees AI as key to US success.
Another factor limiting China's ability is the sweeping government restrictions placed on US companies that prevent them from selling advanced microchips to Chinese firms - these are crucial for developing cutting-edge models.
China's advantage
Despite the chip restrictions, new AI models are coming out almost monthly in both countries and it's unclear what "winning" the AI race would actually mean, or whether there is a finish line at all.
Many companies are racing to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI), a theoretical form of AI capable of learning, reasoning and performing a wide range of tasks at or above the level of humans.
The Chinese AI industry has so far focused not on creating frontier models but releasing what is known as open weight models - downloadable and tweakable in a similar way to open source software.
This contrasts with the approach taken by many US firms, which largely focus on proprietary models accessed through paid subscriptions or company platforms.
Chinese open weight models are being released at a rapid pace, with benchmarks showing the country's top models trailing US rivals by only a few months.
Models such as Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 have become popular in China and overseas because they perform close to the frontier models while remaining freely downloadable and adaptable.
Beijing's focus is more about deploying the technology across its economy, China analyst Lizzi Lee from the Asia Society Policy Institute said.
"AI isn't the moon landing," she said. "The US may lead at the frontier, while China could still gain enormous economic and geopolitical leverage by making capable AI cheap, open and ubiquitous."
AI is also very energy hungry, and China is very well placed there, Rebecca Arcesati told Tech Life on the BBC World Service.
"Chinese AI companies are able to access the electricity they need for a much lower cost and that really is an advantage," she said.
In robotics - a field of AI that some believe will be world-changing - China has become the world's biggest manufacturer of robots, with more than two million working in the country's factories, the International Federation of Robotics estimated.
The nation is also the world's biggest maker of humanoid robots, accounting for more than nine-tenths of global shipments in the first half of the year, according to independent policy institute Chatham House.
Chinese AI developers have showed "remarkable resilience and innovation" in spite of the shortage of advanced American chips, analyst Lian Jye Su from tech research firm Omdia said.
But US officials and AI firms have also alleged that Chinese developers closed the gap by using distillation - a technique that enables models to learn from more advanced platforms.
China's foreign ministry said in response that AI development was "fuelled" by the country's "vision of extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit".
Safety concerns?
China and the US may be in fierce competition, but their governments' approaches to safety concerns are markedly different.
While some in the industry have recently warned that AI could pose an existential risk to humanity, Chinese researchers seem less concerned about that and are more worried about potential misuse of the technology and cyber war.
Responding to concerns over AI, Trump has said the US already has sufficient rules in place and that the only guardrails AI needs are a "high IQ" president.
"We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said this week, adding that the US was not going to "stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution".
Washington has prioritised innovation and sought to reduce regulation in an effort to "keep American labs ahead", said information security officer Jayant Dave from cybersecurity firm Check Point Software Technologies.
Beijing has taken a different strategy to the US hands-off approach.
Xi urged the country's leaders to keep a close eye on AI's risks and ensure the technology was always "under human control".
"China has taken a relatively cautious and centrally-coordinated approach," introducing guides on data usage and algorithms before many other countries, helping to address many underlying concerns, Dave said.
The use of guidelines, though not legally binding, sets expectations while giving developers room to innovate, said National University of Singapore AI ethics lecturer Jonathan Sim.
Will they cooperate?
Despite calls for international cooperation, it remains unclear how the AI superpowers plan to address the technology's potential dangers - if at all.
The two countries have previously cooperated on existential threats such as nuclear weapons, but that was based on a shared understanding of the threat, which is not currently the case with AI, Dave said.
"Washington worries about capability escaping control. Beijing worries about capability threatening domestic stability," he added.
Trump has dismissed proposals for an industry-wide slowdown, arguing that it could allow Chinese developers to close the gap.
Ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng discussed establishing a notification mechanism for serious AI incidents.
While the messaging from Trump on China in recent weeks has been "more antagonistic", the fact that AI is expected to be on the agenda was a "good start", said policy analyst Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
What we don't want, he added, was for an "unhealthy version of the race narrative to perpetuate", potentially escalating an already fierce rivalry in AI.

India had the highest number of children with no sanitation service in schools, with 50 million out of the world total of 244 million as of 2025, according to a new global report. Only Nigeria (34 million), Ethiopia (26 million), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (11 million) or Indonesia (8 million) had a comparatively large number of schoolchildren who had no access to sanitation service.
The data from ‘Progress on drinking water, sanitation and hygiene in schools 2015-2025’ shows the progress as well as the challenges India is facing in meeting the water, sanitation and hygiene goals that are part of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) set for 2030.
14% reduction in schools with no sanitation service
The report can also be seen as a decadal report card on the Swachh Bharat Mission, which was launched in India on October 2, 2014. The report cites the achievement of India which saw a 14% reduction in schools with no sanitation service.
Lack of hygiene service
The WHO/UNICEF report that is part of the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) shows that globally, 362 million children still had no hygiene service at their school in 2025. Of these, 20 million were from India.
It is not just lack of access that the WHO report flags about India but also gaps in data. “There is now sufficient data to estimate trends in basic hygiene coverage between 2015 and 2025 for all SDG regions except Central and Southern Asia where there were insufficient recent data to generate estimates for India, and therefore the region, beyond 2024.”
Drinking water
On the brighter side, India is among the 28 out of 62 countries that are on track to achieve universal coverage of basic drinking water in schools by 2030.
As of 2025, there were 258 million children who still had no drinking water service at their school. The number of children from Indian schools made up 12 million of this number or about 1 out 20 children in the world. The report shows that India has made a big progress in basic drinking water services in 2025 and average rates of change between 2015 and 2025. India, Panama, Syrian Arab Republic, Togo and Tuvalu increased coverage by over 4% per year, “demonstrating that rapid progress is possible”.
However, the report found that while gaps in basic water coverage persists between school levels and between rural and urban areas, this did not apply to India, Cambodia and Fiji.

Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial database to check voter citizenship
- Published
The US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration to use a controversial federal database that uses citizenship information and other sensitive data to identify voters suspected of being non-citizens.
Critics have questioned the reliability of the data, warning it could result in US citizens being wrongly removed from electoral rolls.
In June, a federal judge ruled that the system was illegal and violated the privacy rights of Americans.
But the top court's conservative majority ruled that the National Voter Registration Act prohibits broad purges of voter rolls in the weeks before an election, which limits any "potential impact" of the decision ahead of the midterms.
The three liberal-leaning liberals on the Supreme Court dissented from the decision.
One of the dissenting Supreme Court justices, Ketanji Brown Jackson, expressed concern that this could mistakenly revoke the voting rights of eligible voters.
"The harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the non-existent harm that the government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take," she wrote.
The Department of Homeland Security programme, known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, allows officials to verify the eligibility of voters on their rolls.
The database was first created in 1986 to help officials verify the citizenship or immigration status of those applying for public benefits.
But the Trump administration last year expanded its search capabilities by allowing bulk searches using sensitive information from Social Security rolls.
In June, however, US District Judge Sparkle L Soonnan - a Biden-appointee - ruled that the revamped system shows that the federal government "knowingly trampled on the privacy rights" of US citizens "in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote".
A federal appeals court allowed her ruling to stand, only to be overridden by the Supreme Court on Friday.
The top court ruled that a 1996 law allows DHS to seek citizenship and immigration data from federal agencies, and has "an obligation to respond" to states seeking that information.
The use of the Save programme by individual states is voluntary.
The previous judge's order, the Supreme Court ruled, "prevents the federal government from using the programme it believes is best suited to the task".
Lawyers for the Trump administration have long argued that the system is lawful and necessary to prevent non-citizens from voting. A total of 27 states currently use the system to check voter citizenship.
Critics, however, have pointed to a number of cases of the system already having led to mistakes.
For example, officials in Travis County, Texas, found that of nearly 100 voters identified as non-citizens, at least 10% of them - and potentially more - were US citizens, according to US media reports.
Since the state began checking its voter rolls with the Save system last year, only three non-citizen voters have been charged with illegally voting in Texas.
Since returning to the White House in January last year, the Trump administration has sought to reform the US electoral system, a process that has included a bid - rejected by the Supreme Court - to reign in mail-in ballots.
In 2024, for example, Texas Governor Greg Abbott announced that 1,930 people with a "voter history" had been removed from electoral rolls out of a total of nearly 18 million registered voters.
The figures are far below the hundreds of thousands of non-citizen voters that Trump and the Department of Homeland Security have previously suggested were on voter rolls.

SpaceX Starship's first orbital flight test on track after successful launch rehearsal
The vehicle is scheduled for launch on September 28.
SpaceX has successfully conducted a wet dress rehearsal for Starship, making sure it's in working condition for its next test flight that's bound to become a major milestone for the vehicle if everything goes according to plan. "Launch rehearsal complete ahead of Starship Flight 14," the company has announced on X.
In a wet dress rehearsal, the rocket goes through a full launch simulation. It's loaded with liquid propellants and powered on before it goes through final checks to ensure its fuel lines, software and communications with the ground team are all working. The launch team even runs it through the full countdown sequence, demonstrates procedures for scrubbing launches in the event of poor weather conditions and then drains the fuel to simulate offload procedures. In other words, the rocket goes through the whole launch sequence without actually lifting off.
With the success of this rehearsal, Starship is on track to launch for its 14th test flight scheduled for September 28, with a 75-minute launch window opening at 8:15AM Eastern Time. It will be the vehicle's first orbital flight after multiple suborbital tests. Starship will be orbiting our planet six times within the course of 10 hours before re-entering our atmosphere and crashing into the ocean. It will also ferry 26 Starlink V3 satellites to orbit, which will be the first next-gen models to be added to SpaceX's satellite internet constellation. You'll be able to watch the Starship launch on September 28 on X.

Trump is bracing to lose his latest fight with the press
Trump’s lawyers said he barred three news outlets from the White House on security grounds. A judge seemed skeptical.
A hearing on President Donald Trump’s White House press ban ended without a ruling this afternoon — an admittedly anticlimactic outcome, but one that will likely change very soon.
The Trump-appointed judge in the case, Timothy Kelly, appeared skeptical of the administration’s arguments for banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House grounds last week. Kelly said he would rule “as soon as possible.” Until then, the ban remains in place.
By all accounts, Trump’s case is a feeble one. While the Justice Department attempted to argue on Wednesday that the three outlets’ reporting jeopardized national security, Trump himself kind of gave the game away last week when he said he had singled these organizations out over what he characterized as negative and inaccurate stories.
The move sat poorly even with people and institutions you’d expect to be sympathetic to Trump: Fox News was one of several outlets that boycotted White House events this week to protest the ban, for instance.
And ahead of today’s hearing, Trump himself seemed primed to lose. In a Truth Social post on Monday, he promised he would “almost without question” appeal any decision against him.
Go a little deeper
This is all emblematic of how Trump has escalated his attacks on the news media in his second term: not just by insulting and demeaning the press, but also by weaponizing otherwise neutral-seeming rules.
Every administration has policies that regulate who can access the White House grounds and under what conditions, for instance. But in early 2025, the White House took control of the press pool — the rotating group of reporters that frequently travels with the president — and soon sought to exclude disfavored organizations.
More insidiously, Trump has mobilized regulatory agencies like the Federal Communications Commission against his perceived critics, in some cases even threatening to revoke the licenses of local TV stations that air coverage and commentary he disagrees with.
While no licenses have actually been suspended, the FCC has mysteriously pulled some up for unscheduled review. And just the prospect of government retaliation has been enough to force some content off the air: Just two weeks ago, the late-night comedy host Jimmy Kimmel said his show wouldn’t air a scheduled interview with Texas Senate candidate James Talarico because of the FCC’s new scrutiny of political content.
This playbook isn’t a Trump original, as my colleague Zack Beauchamp has explained. In fact, weaponizing broadcast regulations was also a favored technique of former Hungarian Prime Minister (and infamous strongman) Viktor Orbán, who successfully used licensing rules and other bureaucratic technicalities to force independent media outlets into submission.
Likewise, revoking the press credentials of critical reporters has long been a favorite tactic of Russian President Vladimir Putin, Nico Perrino, the executive vice president of the nonprofit civil liberties group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, said in a briefing on Wednesday: “These are things that are done by regimes that we do not want to emulate.”
Lest these comparisons get you down, however, recall that neither Hungary nor Russia has all the defenses that the US does. Defenses like, for example, an independent court system.

Yukon government struggling to keep rural health centres open
No nurse on site 214 days across the Yukon’s community health centres over past year
The Yukon’s rural health centres continue to struggle with temporary closures and disruptions.
This week, the territory's health department verified the number of interruptions to its community health centres over the past year.
According to CBC’s analysis of the data provided by the department, between August 2025 and August 2026 the territory's rural health centres saw a total of 214 days when there were no nursing services available.
That tally doesn’t totally reflect the latest partial closure at the Beaver Creek health centre from July 2 to Oct. 30. It also leaves out “reduced services” at the Carcross health centre from Sept. 16 to Oct. 14.
Furthermore, Faro is seeing a temporary closure from Sept. 25 to Oct. 2, Ross River from Sept. 4 to Sept 30, and Teslin from Sept. 23 to Oct. 14.
As the Official Opposition, the Yukon Party previously railed against the former Liberal government for its failure to keep health centres open for prolonged periods of time. During last year's election campaign, Currie Dixon, now the premier, vowed that his party was "going to change this.”
Lack of community nurses goes on
Beaver Creek's health centre saw the most days of closure or reduced service over the past year, at 82.
Pelly Crossing and Destruction Bay have also seen significant disruptions.
The problem is marked by a lack of nurses available to work at the rural health centres. It’s been a chronic issue for the community centres which aren't regularly staffed by physicians.
According to the health department, some services are still available during some health centre closures.
The department said in a statement that depending on the community, emergency services were still available, administrative staff could help with medical travel and bookings, and doctor clinics went on.
Health Minister Brad Cathers wasn’t available for an interview.
The health department said the model of community care is under review.
The government also said it’s continually looking for ways to recruit and keep nurses working in the territory, and expanding licensing pathways for qualified health professionals. It’s also “evaluating opportunities” for a more sustainable health-care system in communities.
National nurses association hears some frustration
Valerie Grdisa, CEO of the Canadian Nurses Association, travelled to the Yukon at the end of June and she spoke with dozens of nurses at Whitehorse General Hospital and also met with the health centre team in Carcross.
Grdisa said she heard about pride and innovation in the workplace, as well as frustrations around the ability to retain nurses who want to live and provide care in the communities.
Grdisa said nurses aren’t regularly considering the ability to get licensed and be registered in multiple jurisdictions. She added that there’s actually a rather large workforce in the country, with 518,000 registered or regulated nurses in Canada.
“I think we could do a better job in providing opportunities for people to be more mobile,” she said.
Grdisa also suggested health centres look to hire closer to home.
“I think the homegrown workforce pathways are the way to go, so investing in youth engagement,” she said. “We're talking in the middle schools and high schools, and then having local education programs and apprenticeships and return-of-service agreements.”

He also suggested that Opposition parties could be allowed occasional victories — “the crumbs” — to keep them participating and give voters the impression that there was a real electoral contest. Gyanesh Kumar is accused of overseeing revisions to voter rolls that have allegedly deleted millions of votes, raising concerns over fairness and potential manipulation of election outcomes. The impeachment process for a Chief Election Commissioner involves a motion introduced in Parliament, requiring a two-thirds majority in both houses, based on proven misbehavior or incapacity. Kenya destroys $63 million meth haul intercepted at sea
Kenyan authorities have destroyed a massive methamphetamine haul worth $63 million
MOMBASA, Kenya -- MOMBASA, Kenya (AP) — Kenyan authorities on Thursday destroyed a massive haul of methamphetamine worth an estimated $63 million, nearly a year after the drugs were intercepted in the Indian Ocean off the coast of Mombasa.
The consignment, weighing 1,024 kilograms (about 2,257 pounds), was placed in a high-temperature kiln and destroyed as government officials watched.
Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen oversaw the destruction and warned drug traffickers that authorities would step up efforts to disrupt the illicit trade.
Murkomen said Kenya was being used both as a “transit hub” and a “market” for illegal drugs, and pledged tougher enforcement to prevent drug trafficking and substance abuse.
He said suspected traffickers would face prosecution and that authorities would pursue the seizure of property linked to the illegal trade.
The Kenyan Navy intercepted the consignment on Oct. 25, 2025, about 630 kilometers (391 miles) off the coast of Mombasa in the Indian Ocean. The vessel was escorted to port under armed guard.
Six Iranian nationals arrested aboard the flagless vessel remain in court facing drug-trafficking charges.
Authorities described the seizure of more than a ton of methamphetamine as a major breakthrough in Kenya’s fight against narcotics trafficking.
The interception comes as Kenya confronts growing concerns over synthetic drugs, particularly along the coast, where health and law-enforcement officials have reported increasing problems involving methamphetamine and heroin.

'I have never felt heat like that' - a survivor on watching 33 cellmates die in Nigeria
- Published
Usman Muhammad pauses by the entrance to a tiny Nigerian prison cell and leans his forehead against the wall unable to speak.
The day before he had been trapped inside the stifling room, measuring roughly 6m (19.7ft) by 3m (9.8ft), with more than 50 other prisoners.
Thirty-three of his cellmates died in the cramped conditions in the prison in Minna, the capital of Nigeria's Niger state - and four died later in hospital.
The mass deaths caused an outcry and sparked protests, including attacks on public buildings, as relatives and locals demanded answers.
Federal officials had initially blamed the deaths on a diphtheria outbreak but exactly what happened is now the subject of an investigation.
"I have never felt heat like that in my life. When we touched each other's bodies, it felt like fire burning," Muhammad tells the BBC once he is able to gather his thoughts.
When he was locked inside, there was standing room only amid humidity levels of more than 90%, which in some circumstances can be dangerous to human health as it prevents the natural cooling mechanism of sweat drying on the skin.
The temperature outside was above 25C and the only ventilation came from a small, high-up window.
"One of us fainted and we started knocking at the [cell] door. When [a guard] came we asked him for water. He looked at the guy that fainted and closed the door. That's how they started dying one after the other," Muhammad says.
Like the others who had been detained, the young man, in his 20s, is an artisanal miner, eking out a living searching for precious metals at mine sites.
The federal government has tried to crack down on this alleged illegal activity as it says it costs the country revenue, damages the environment and can be linked to wider criminal activity.
Officers from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) had arrested a large group of miners near Minna last Tuesday and Wednesday.
The prisoners were held at its detention centre in the city, but the NSCDC has not shared either the names or the number of those it was holding.
As the hours inside the cell wore on, the heat and dehydration became unbearable and Muhammad says some of the detainees began drinking their own urine and collecting sweat from their bodies to try to stay alive.
He describes seeing people in distress and struggling to breathe.
"People were calling for help, some were already very weak."
But no-one came to help, he and others allege.
"While in the cell, we were shouting and telling them that people were dying," another survivor Adamu Isah told the Reuters news agency.
"We tried to break down the door when they refused to open it… At one point, a security officer came to the door.
"We were shouting and telling him that people were dying, but he said it wasn't his problem if people died."
Finally, on Thursday, the cell door was opened and the guards saw the dead bodies.
The NSCDC has not directly responded to the accusations of neglect and maltreatment but has said that 24 of its personnel are now in custody in connection with the deaths, including its suspended Niger state commandant Suberu Aniviye.
"The people who were killed are not flies. How can this go unlooked? We will get to the bottom of this," Niger state Governor Umaru Bago told the BBC.
As the organisation involved is a federal body rather than a force under his jurisdiction, such as the police, the governor is unable to exert direct influence but he welcomes the investigation that has been ordered by the government in capital, Abuja.
A 10-member committee has now been set-up to determine exactly what happened.
It has two weeks to establish the causes of the deaths and identify who was responsible and can recommend legal action against anyone found culpable.
No officer, regardless of rank, would be protected and any attempt to obstruct the investigation would be taken seriously, Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said.
As he leaves the cell after talking to the BBC, Muhammad says he hopes that by speaking out he can help find justice and bring some closure to this traumatic event.

The United States’ withdrawal from key aid programs has put has put healthcare in Africa and the Global South “under growing strain” a new report warns.
The report says the Trump administration’s cuts to programs such as US Agency for International Development (USAID), as well as the Covid-19 pandemic and rising costs of living globally have brought “new urgency” for the need to reform healthcare in the region.
The report, titled A Sovereign Future For Health, was created by the Accra Reset, a global health initiative led by John Dramani Mahama, Ghana’s president, that believes countries in Africa and the wider global south should have greater control over their health development rather than being dependent on aid from western countries and international institutions.
A key statistic cited by Mahama and Accra Reset is that Africa produces less than 1% of its vaccines while carrying about 25% of the global disease burden.
The report cites how abrupt changes to global health financing, such as the US withdrawal from several global health initiatives, forced countries within the global south to urgently restructure their finances. The report points to the Trump administration’s decision to dissolve USAID, which pushed Nigeria to absorb the 28,000 health workers who were previously employed by the agency at a cost of $200m.
External financing for health in Africa contracted by close to 70% between 2021 and 2025, the report notes, meaning that African countries historically dependent on aid were forced to adapt quickly.
The withdrawal of the US Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) funding for South Africa, which provided over $400m a year annually and is credited with saving 26m lives globally since 2003, led to HIV clinics closing across the country. That left 1.4 million people living with HIV to face uncertainty about their treatment.
Such funding cuts caused “severe and devastating” disruption globally, according to research presented at the 26th International Aids Conference in Brazil earlier this year.
At the World Health Assembly in May, Mahama said Ghana lost $78m following the closure of USAID programs which affected maternal healthcare, the treatment of malaria, nutrition and HIV/Aids interventions.
The initiative’s latest report, published on Monday, comes amid these major cuts to international aid and growing pressure on countries to take greater ownership of their health systems. Mahama refers to these aid cuts as a clear example that donor dependency is not sustainable.
“The Accra Reset is not an argument for traditional donors to do less on global health. It is an argument for doing it differently and doing it better. As countries take greater ownership of their health futures, donor countries should step up to support that transition – following the lead of countries that set their own priorities, and work alongside them to determine where outside support is most valuable,” said Naveen Rao, senior vice-president of the health initiative at the Rockefeller Foundation. “The Accra Reset shows how we can evolve to back country-led solutions while advancing our shared health and economic interests.”
Mahama notes in the report that the “past few years have shaken global health cooperation to its foundations”.
“The Covid-19 pandemic exposed the risks created by concentrated production and unequal access to essential health products; rising debt and fiscal pressures have constrained national health budgets; and declining development assistance is placing programs and services under growing strain,” he continued, adding: “These shocks have brought new urgency to reform debates that have continued for years with limited progress. It was in this context that we launched the Accra Reset and its Sovereign Health Agenda – to give renewed political force to the reform agenda and place the agency of countries of the Global South at its centre.”
The report comes alongside a recent survey revealing the progressive attitudes many US citizens have towards foreign aid. Some 75% of Americans – including more than one in two (52%) who primarily support Donald Trump – agree that the US should restore disease prevention aid to contain the Ebola virus, according to polling of over 2,000 US adults commissioned by the Rockefeller Foundation.
The polling also revealed that 65% of US adults support international cooperation even if it means compromising some national interests; 64% also believe Americans have a shared responsibility to others, including people in other countries whom they do not know.
The Guardian has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for comment.

Blessed by warm but hardly sweltering late summer sun — and no typical Basque txirimiri drizzle so common to other editions — the 74th San Sebastián also marks the last under festival director José Luis Rebordinos, who since 2011 has brought stability, sponsors, industry build and a close relationship to Cannes.
Fittingly enough, the hallmark of this year’s 74th edition is a phenomenon which Rebordinos has contributed significantly to — the build of Spain’s film and TV industry.
Just before San Sebastián, Los Javis “La Bola Negra” won the TIFF People’s Choice Award, boosting no end its status in the Oscars race. During San Sebastián, Spain scored five nominations for the International Emmy Awards and the Spain Film Commission announced that Spanish film and TV production hit an all-time high of €5.68 billion ($6.6 billion) in 2025.
Popular on Variety
10 takeaways from this year’s edition:
Brad Pitt Seduces San Sebastián, Jesse Eisenberg Endearingly Self-Deprecating
Brad Pitt spent an hour-and-a-half signing autographs and taking selfies and waxed lyrical on the performance of co-star Uber, a dog at his press conference, as David Ayer’s “The Heart of the Beast” produced by Plan B, proved one of the most popular at the festival, with critics and audiences alike. A typically self-deprecating Jesse Eisenberg said Jeremy Strong will be “amazing” playing Mark Zuckerberg in Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Network” sequel. Los Javis came saw and conquered with “La Bola Negra,” with Oscar Buzz fueled by its TIFF People’s Choice Award. They were also presented by Thierry Frémaux with a copy of their Cannes best director award so that both had a trophy.
Buzz Titles
Most well-received films in San Sebastián’s main competition, at least from international critics, take in Yesim Ustaoglu’s Turkish road movie “What Remains,” Japanese Novelist Maha Harada’s debut feature “In My Father’s Room,” Victoria Luengo starrer “Saints” and “Border.” Mike Leigh’s “Tender Loving Care” already tops Spanish reviewers’ poll in El Diario Vasco. So it might not be a surprise if he scores what would be a highly sentimental prize for his final film, or for Julianne Moore to build on her Toronto buzz for “The Debut,” also a hit with local scribes.
International Hurts
Yes, San Sebastián conversation turned on what the explosive breakout of “Obsession” and “Backrooms” really meant for the U.S. or world industry. It is not a quick fix, however, for international’s multiplying woes. San Sebastián coincided with a Variety news report that France of all places, the bastion of world arthouse cinema, is “in shambles.” And that merely seven months before a fateful presidential election which has the far right leading polls. In Brazil, despite boffo B.O. for “‘I’m Still Here” and “The Secret Agent,” “a lot of other Brazilian films make 10,000 admissions in theaters. And that kills the film.” In South Korea, “the number of films and revenues, everything’s shrinking, financiers are really struggling to invest money,” Heejeon Kim at Barunson C&C also said at the Creative Investors Conference. And France, South Korea and Brazil regarded as three of the strongest industry drivers in in the world.
Europe Courts New Money
With public funding stretched, European producers are turning to private equity, and The Marché du Film — Festival de Cannes is trying to give private investment in cinema more structure. In a first-time partnership, with San Sebastian’s Creative Investors’ Conference, its Investors Circle brought four investors for organized closed-door sessions with experts, running alongside the conference. “There’s for sure more demand on the investment side, and it’s because it’s getting harder and harder to finance films with public money, especially second, third and fourth features,” said Alexandra Zakharchenko, the Marché’s head of industry programs. Too many investors still confuse grants with equity, she argued: “Equity is not for every film. There has to be commercial viability and a clear path to recoupment.” The biggest lesson? “It became even more clear to me than ever how much it’s a human-driven business. It’s about trust.”
Another Way Forward: Sharing the Load
Another way forward is an advantageous financing model. Spain’s biggest series are no longer always straight platform commissions. Showcased at San Sebastán, ”Sira,” the sequel to “The Time in Between,” is produced by Buendía Estudios with Atresmedia and Netflix. It bows on SVOD service Atresplayer, moves to Antena 3, and goes international via Atresmedia Sales. “By combining different windows and territories across multiple licensees, the investment can be shared,” said Buendía Estudios director general Ignacio Corrales. The real prize is ownership: “We retain ownership of the IP, which means we are not simply producing a title for a single buyer: we are building and retaining an asset of our own.” Corrales admitted that’s not always possible. But the ideal, he said, is to share in content’s long-term value.
San Sebastián: Culinary Paradise
In the weeks building up to San Sebastian, industry attendees eagerly began passing round a Word file billed by one as “the most precious commodity.” Considered almost as sacred as the schedule of films and probably just as well-thumbed, the 16-page document — painstakingly put together and frequently updated by a much-loved festival regular — detailed the very best places to eat and drink across the city. Because, just as the festival lures both execs and talent with the chance to showcase their latest movies to a welcoming and cultured audience, in an almost dual-lead role is the city itself, considered one of the world’s culinary hotspots, where cobbled streets burst with cosy bars and restaurants serving local tapas, seafood and, perhaps top of the food chain, generous portions of meat (such as the famed massive Txuleta T-bone steak). There probably isn’t any other film event where most morning conversations begin by asking what people had to eat the previous night rather than what movie they watched.
Highflying Movistar Plus Unveils New Slate
What company in Europe can say it had a really good 2026, and for that matter a really good 2025? One strong candidate: the biggest Spanish pay TV/SVOD operator Movistar Plus. This year at Cannes’ main competition, it had two Movistar Plus Originals in “The Beloved” and “La Bola Negra,” and one with “Sirāt” last year when “Querer” and “Celeste” walked off with the two top prizes at Series Mania. Movistar Plus did so by giving Spain’s top, top younger auteur creative freedom and the economic resources to make the movies and TV shows they wanted. At San Sebastián, Movistar Plus presented its first new slate under new management, and reiterated its desire to continue as a national champion.The Spanish film industry is lighting a candle and saying a prayer that Movistar Plus will be able to execute on its now clearly stated support for the industry.
AI: Independent Industry Figures Don’t Say No
This was a festival where senior, highly respected industry independent industry figures – Vincent Maraval, Patrick Wachsberger – came out of the AI closet to recognise they were contemplating use of or would not object to the use of AI in specific circumstances on a movie. AI could be a make-or-break factor in a film getting made, so creating employment, Maraval argued in conversation with CAA Media Finance’s Roeg Sutherland at San Sebastián’s Creative Investors’ Conference. “I’m not suggesting at all that you use AI for any of the actors, but if you want to do extension or whatever, something to give scope to the movie, I’m all for it,” Patrick Wachsberger agreed in a final Conference panel.
Spain Preeminent at San Sebastián
Spain produced 423 movies last year, more than any other country in Europe, including the U.K. and France, according to the European Audiovisual Observatory. That powerhouse volume came across at San Sebastián. Made in Spain featured titles. Perlak framed screenings of La Bola Negra and The Beloved. Top players Movistar Plus, Atresmedia, the Spain Film Commission held press conferences. Spain’s Ministry for Digital Transformation hosted a whole conference. Much of the international industry and press come to San Sebastián to check out Spain. The festival delivered.
Not to Be Missed Clara Simón’s Latest Film, ‘Flamenco’
The best Spanish film showcased at San Sebastián with a preeminent director on hand didn’t even play in a festival section. On Tuesday, Clara Simón attended an ICEX showcase, to walk an audience Energized by three electric flamenco set-pieces, “Flamenco” talks of artistic and family legacy, in highly emotional terms. Like another short, from Rasalía director also talks about one thing which sets Spain apart: the still resilient deep impact of popular culture which has proved far more resilient in Spain than almost any other part of Europe. Such is part of Spain’s magic.
A San Sebastián Standout: ‘El Castillo’
The most warmly applauded of new Spanish fictions? As often at a Festival which world premiered Los Javis’ “La Mesías” and “Querer,” it was most probably a series: El Castillo, scribe Isabel Peña first TV so outing without Rodrigo Sorogoyen but partnering with Eduardo Villanueva, also a writer on “Riot Police.” A chronicle of how Spain’s pimp trade transformed into neo-capitalist organized crime of networked macro brothels, “El Castillo” has a triple POV: a Colombian single mother sex worker, the prostitution kingpin, and the cop out to catch him. Nuanced in characters, and told with telling tawdriness this is a series which tells it as it was.
And the Deals
*Martin Scorsese mentee Celina Murga (“The Freshly Cut Grass”) is prepping her next pic, “The Rehearsals,” about how caring for someone can also bring love, connection and a renewed sense of life.
*Mikel Gurrea’s awaited “Saints,” toplined by “The Beloved” star Victoria Luengo, was swooped on by M-Appeal in a deal announced just before the festival.
*Latido Films has picked up international sales rights to “Flamenco Sketches,” from double San Sebastián Golden Shell winner Isaki Lacuesta
*Main competition frontrunner “In My Father’s Room” was pre-sold to France, Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong ahead its san Sebastian world premiere. It now heads to Busan.
*Mexico’s Sula Films has boarded Tatiana Huezo’s anticipated “Galerna,” a top Industry Award winner at San Sebastián from “Roma” producer Pimienta Films
*Another Golden Shell contender, Chinese filmmaker Ah Biao’s feature debut “Border,” was picked up for sales by Paris-based Reel Suspects.
*New Regency acquired international rights to “Genesi,” detailing in part Ferran Adria’s transformation of El Bulli restaurant into a haute cuisine legend. Netflix will release in Spain, Europe, Latin America and the U.S.
*Lee Kang-sheng, Miranda de la Serna and Marcelo Subiotto are set to star in RT Features’ ‘Bodies of Summer,’ from Berlin winner Iván Fund (“The Message”).
*Filmax has swooped on Javier Giner’s “This Solitude,” one of the buzziest feature debuts at this year’s San Sebastián.
*Txintxua Films (“Intimacy”) boarded “This Is the Memory I Would Like to Have of Mom” a San Sebastián Forum title from Berlin Perspectives first Ffeature winner Martínez Bucio (“The Devil Smokes”).
*Mexico’s Martfilms is co-producing “Looking for Sam,” Mariana Rondón’s follow-up to her acclaimed coming -of-age drama “Bad Hair” (“Pelo malo”), and one of the major titles at this year’s San Sebastián Co-Production Forum.
*Urban Sales boarded Ricardo Alves Jr.’s religious cult thriller “The French Teacher” ahead of its San Sebastián premiere.
*Helsinki and London-based The Yellow Affair snatched up world sales rights to Rodrigo García Saiz’s buzzy drama “Morro” ahead of its world premiere at San Sebastián’s New Directors strand.
