WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

Anthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland, a remote state in north-eastern India bordering Myanmar, have expressed joy and relief that human remains belonging to their ancestors that had been on display in a British museum for nearly a century are finally being returned.
On Monday, the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford announced that 39 pieces of human remains – including parts of skulls, a finger and a piece of skin with hair – belonging to the Naga tribes, will be returned to Nagaland after six years of negotiation between the community and the museum.
For the Nagas, the repatriation is not just about “bones and ancestral remains … It is about memory returning to where it belongs,” the community said in a statement.
“We are at peace,” said A Peihwang Wangsa, an Indigenous Konyak man involved in the repatriation negotiations. “Our forefathers are coming back.”
Wangsa, whose ancestors’ remains are among those being returned, added that the homecoming would be a moment of “mourning and celebration”.
NT Thamlong Phom, a Naga community leader from the Phom sub-tribe, said: “I feel joy, I feel blessed.
“Ever since the announcement was made, my entire community has felt happy,” he said. “Our ancestors’ spirit will have a final resting place.”
Thejao Vihienuo, who is also part of the repatriation discussions and went to Oxford in 2025, said he had been “angry and unhappy” to see the remains of his ancestors, which he said had been “taken in a most dubious manner”.
“It was displayed as if it was a trophy, but they silently spoke of the atrocities the British committed on our people,” he said.
The return caused “mixed feelings”, he said, but added: “We owe it to our ancestors to bring their remains back and put them to peaceful rest. And also to our younger generation to decolonise their minds and show that our children are not inferior to any white man.”
The Nagas are a transnational Indigenous group of tribes living in India’s north-east and parts of Myanmar, once associated with headhunting but now predominantly Christian.
The Pitt Rivers Museum, home to one of the world’s largest ethnological collections, has more than 6,500 Naga objects, 898 of which were on display. Most of the collection was “coercively” acquired by the colonial administrators James Philip Mills and John Henry Hutton.
The human remains were displayed at the museum for 80 years. In 2020, they were put into storage during a revamp aimed at addressing the institution’s colonial past and how exhibiting human remains “reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking” of other cultures.
The museum said in a statement: “Thirty-nine Naga ancestors will soon begin their journey home from Oxford to Nagaland.”
In November, a Naga delegation will visit Oxford for a handover ceremony and the remains are expected to arrive in Nagaland before the end of the year. They will be laid to rest in a traditional community ceremony in the state capital, Kohima.
The repatriation negotiations were led by representatives from all of the Naga tribes.
“It has been a journey of redemption,” said Prof Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist. “This shows that we are no longer victims of colonial violence. We embrace our roles as people who find redemption and healing by giving dignity and honour to a very violent past.”
The negotiations started in 2020, when Kikon wrote to the museum after reading “an article in the Guardian that they were doing an ethical review” of the collection. “They replied within 24 hours,” said Kikon.
That was just the beginning of a lengthy process that soon expanded into a wider community-led campaign.
The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a community peace group, assembled a team known as Recover, Restore and Decolonise, bringing together Naga volunteers from across the region to work on the repatriation effort.
“They travelled to villages and organised meetings to inform people about the remains,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a Naga anthropologist who worked closely with Kikon to lead the initiative, which he described as “open and transparent”.
“It was an intergenerational journey that brought together students, civil society, tribal leaders and the church,” said Longkumer, who teaches at Edinburgh University.
A Naga delegation, including tribal leaders, visited Oxford in 2025 to officially register a claim to the remains.
“I had never known our ancestral human remains had been taken away like that,” said Wangsa. “I felt angry when I saw them.”
Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum and a professor of museum studies and ethics at Oxford University, said the museum was completing paperwork to enable the return of the remains.
“We will then start working towards the ceremonial aspects so we can have everything ready,” she said. “In our experience, handover ceremonies can be very emotional.”

Violence displaced members of more than half a million Mexican households in past 5 years
New figures from Mexico's national statistics agency reveal that violence has forced people from more than half a million households in Mexico to flee their homes in the past five years
MEXICO CITY -- Violence has forcibly displaced people from more than half a million households across Mexico in the past five years, according to new figures released by Mexico's national statistics agency, the first numbers that speak to the depth of what many have described as an invisible internal displacement crisis.
Until now, Mexico's government did not share comprehensive data on people who have been forced to flee their homes due to ongoing violence in many parts of Mexico, leaving civil society groups piecing together information to get a wider view of the problem.
The figures published this week by Mexico’s National Institute of Statistics and Geography, or INEGI — an autonomous government agency that has at times been at odds with Mexico's ruling party — offer the first wider snapshot of the ongoing crisis.
Between October 2020 and October 2025, people in 510,000 households across Mexico were forced to flee to another part of the country. That could range from a single person to an entire family. The displacement affected 1.6 million people, including those forced to flee and those left behind to cope with the consequences of the crisis.
The figures show the problem has reached every corner of Mexico, but the states with the highest rates of displacement from cartel violence were Zacatecas, Morelos, Michoacan, Queretaro and Colima.
Other autonomous agencies, civil society groups and Mexican state governments have published data on internal displacement, but their findings have often been limited in scope.
Tracking internal displacement can often be tricky because many people leave their homes in fear without the intention of being found or reporting their case, or hope to later return to their homes if they determine it's safe to return home down the line.
David Mora, Mexico analyst for International Crisis Group, described the new data as a “major breakthrough” that will pave the way for authorities and civil society to address the long-term humanitarian consequences of the crisis. Those who are forced to flee criminal violence have almost no resources to turn to when they disappear into the fabric of Mexico and often have to start from zero.
“For years, civil society and victims of forced displacement have been sounding the alarm on the issue and the federal government has not paid attention,” Mora said Friday. “So this coming from the independent INEGI, it’s a breakthrough. It’s huge that they’re trying to put a number on it, which is just the first step.”
The INEGI figures don't include people displaced before 2020, meaning the number of displaced people across the country is likely much higher. Cartel violence has raged in key areas of Mexico since the beginning of the drug war around 2006 under the administration of Mexican President Felipe Calderón. The data focuses specifically on internally displaced people, and doesn’t capture people who have fled to the U.S.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has said little about the issue, focusing instead on the government's efforts to reduce homicide numbers and crack down on criminal groups. She is also facing pressure from the Trump administration to show progress on security.
She has addressed specific cases of families being displaced from bursts of cartel violence, noting that authorities were working on finding a way for them to return home, but has largely not spoken about forced displacement as a widespread phenomenon.
At her morning news briefing Wednesday, Sheinbaum questioned the figures and said she had asked INEGI to provide further details about the data, including the questions and methodology used to reach those numbers.

Ethiopia risks a wider war. Here are 5 things to know
Renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia is threatening the fragile peace that ended the Tigray war
NAIROBI, Kenya -- Fighting has returned to Ethiopia’s Tigray region, where former enemies are joining forces against the government and the peace agreement that ended one of Africa’s deadliest recent wars appears close to collapse.
The crisis could merge conflicts in several parts of Ethiopia and draw neighboring Eritrea into another war. Here are five things to know:
Federal and Tigrayan forces accuse each other of restarting hostilities nearly four years after signing the Pretoria peace agreement.
Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to Tigray this week following the seizure of Mekelle airport by Tigrayan forces. Residents told The Associated Press that roads connecting Tigray with the neighboring Afar region had been closed, although AP could not independently verify the closures.
Internet monitor NetBlocks also reported disruptions across northern Ethiopia, reviving memories of the previous war, when Tigray was largely isolated and civilians struggled to obtain food, medicine and reliable information.
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front has joined six other opposition groups in an alliance that aims to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government.
Its members include the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army. Tigrayan and Amhara forces fought on opposing sides during the previous war.
Magnus Taylor, deputy project director for the Horn of Africa at the International Crisis Group, described the coalition as combining political opposition to Abiy with an “opportunistic military alliance.”
Effective coordination could force federal troops to fight across several regions. But it remains unclear whether groups divided by territorial disputes and deep grievances can conduct joint military operations.
The Pretoria agreement ended major fighting in November 2022 but left disputes over territory, security and accountability unresolved.
Taylor said the agreement was “on life support.” A TPLF spokesman told the AP this week that it was no longer valid.
Laetitia Bader, a regional director at Human Rights Watch, said key provisions had been violated for years. She cited continuing abuses, including what the organization describes as the forced expulsion of ethnic Tigrayans from western Tigray. AP could not independently verify the allegations.
Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal forces during the previous Tigray war. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara have since deteriorated sharply.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting armed opponents. Eritrea has accused Abiy’s government of preparing for war as Ethiopia presses for greater access to the Red Sea.
Taylor warned that the fighting could spread across Ethiopia and draw in Eritrea. That would create another regional conflict next to Sudan, which is already experiencing a devastating war and humanitarian crisis.
Researchers at Ghent University have estimated that the earlier war caused about 500,000 civilian deaths in Tigray alone. The estimate includes deaths from direct violence, but researchers attributed most of the toll to famine and the collapse of the region’s health system. The conflict also displaced millions of people across northern Ethiopia.
The war’s effects persisted after the ceasefire, with researchers later documenting deaths from hunger in Tigray.
Bader warned that another Ethiopian conflict could deepen the wider regional emergency. Transport and communications restrictions could quickly interrupt supplies of food and medicine while making civilian suffering harder to document.
Preventing a wider war would require an immediate halt to the fighting, renewed negotiations and sustained international pressure before Ethiopia’s separate conflicts converge.

Chennai: “There are things more important in life than TRP ratings,” the Madras High Court said on Friday while restraining the media, YouTube channels and digital platforms from meddling with the factual matrix in the sensational case of predatory child sexual abuse in which prominent industrialist Veeramani of Gem Granites is a key accused.
The court passed the restraining order a day after certain English TV news channels and other media outlets shared screenshot images of Veeramani from a video clip in which he was seen abusing a minor girl.
In a related development, the Chennai Police registered a case in connection with the leak of the video clip.
Court raises media trial concerns
“While this court cherishes the right to freedom of speech and expression and in particular, the freedom of the press to disseminate information, this court is also reminded of the gruesome Mumbai terror attacks. It was only on account of constant media coverage, all strategies of law enforcing agencies came to the know of things of the handlers of the terrorists,” Justice V Lakshminarayan said.
“Right has a corresponding duty and this duty is not only owed to the children but also the accused involved in the case,” the judge said while saying the Republic TV counsel was right that the press has the right to report “but whether this right to report includes a right to media trial would have to be probed into by this court.”
The judge made the observations while hearing a petition filed by Tulir Charitable Trust (for prevention and healing of child sexual abuse) against the telecast of Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse Material by prominent television channels.
Also Watch:
SIT to issue weekly updates
To ensure people get to know the progress made by the police in the investigation of the sensational case, the court directed an all-women Special Investigation Team (SIT), constituted by Director General of Police Mahesh Kumar Aggarwal to probe the case, to issue weekly press releases.
Justice Lakshminarayan restrained media outlets and others from publishing, broadcasting, transmitting, circulating, reproducing or otherwise disseminating any video or screen grab which touches upon the crime under investigation.

After the proliferation of AI adoption, enterprise India has started to ask whether its infrastructure is robust enough to survive the shift. With the country’s enterprise AI market expected to cross $71 Bn by 2030, boardroom mandates around AI are accelerating, cloud costs are spiralling, data pipelines are buckling under the weight of unstructured inputs, and CTOs are discovering that pilots that worked in isolation can collapse the moment they are pushed into production at scale. Therefore, enterprises across sectors are moving beyond productivity tools into core product development and delivery processes, including coding copilots, automated testing, and AI-driven IT service management. As a result, the conversation and its implementation are now shifting from experimentation to predictability, governance and cost control. To unpack this shift, India’s leading tech voices joined Inc42 and Oracle for CTO Dialogues, featuring a roundtable on ‘Building The Infrastructure Backbone For AI At Scale’, followed by a fireside chat and a session exploring where enterprise AI strategies often fall short. The roundtable was moderated by Sameer Dhanrajani, CEO of 3AI and AIQRATE, and featured the following speakers: Ankit Mehra, cofounder and CEO, GyanDhan Mashiyat Hussain, engineering lead, Backend, HYPD Nitish Gupta, SVP – technology, NimbusPost Sanjeev Singh, VP engineering, DeHaat Shubhanshu Chouhan, CTO, Pidge Vivek Gupta, senior director and head of technology cloud sales at Oracle India Building A Robust Infra Backbone For AI The roundtable, moderated by Dhanrajani, addressed the harder question of how enterprises actually operationalise AI at scale, with six leaders spanning cloud, fintech, D2C, agritech, logistics and last-mile delivery. Oracle India’s Vivek Gupta opened the conversation by arguing that enterprises chasing AI at scale are often solving for the wrong constraint. “AI at scale is not a GPU problem... It's an engineering problem that needs to be solved,” said Gupta. According to Gupta, the bottleneck for many companies when implementing AI is not compute availability, but the ability to define a clear business outcome before they begin building. That focus on the problem itself resonated with GyanDhan’s Ankit Mehra, who pushed back against the instinct to reach for AI as a default fix. Having run workloads at his own company for testing purposes, Mehra said he had seen more problems traced to poorly framed questions than to actual scale limitations. “Really solve for the problem that you're trying to solve rather than just running with the hype part of it,” Mehra added. But even when the problem is clearly defined, the data feeding these systems can present a different set of challenges. HYPD’s Hussain brought the conversation to data itself, describing the unpredictability of user-generated content on a creator platform, with comments arriving from varied regions and formats and no consistent pattern to model against. “Data variety is a major problem for us. We cannot always predict what kind of data we will receive. For example, on our platform, creators receive comments from people across different regions and backgrounds, making it difficult to predict the nature and variety of the data,” said Hussain. That unpredictability becomes even more complex when AI is layered on top of existing data challenges, and the VP of engineering at DeHaat, Singh, reiterated the same. According to Singh, the nature of the problem has shifted over the past decade, from a pure data-management challenge to a compounded one. “Earlier it was only a data problem, shuffling of data, creating or churning our money. Now it's a data-plus-AI problem. So, we have faced both,” said Singh. For businesses operating at scale, however, identifying the problem and managing the data is only part of the equation. The infrastructure itself has to be tailored to the use case. The SVP of technology at NimbusPost, Gupta, grounded the discussion in logistics, where infrastructure decisions vary sharply by use case and margin. Getting the right setup, he said, comes only through costly trial and error. “The right choice would come out of experimentation, and that experimentation would need a good amount of money... infrastructure is something wherein different industries would have different use cases,” he said. And that experimentation becomes even harder when AI is deployed in live operational environments, where a wrong decision can directly affect costs and performance. Chouhan, CTO of Pidge, concluded on a note of caution around automation in last-mile operations. Rider and delivery allocation, he said, still cannot be handed fully to opaque models. “We cannot rely on an ambiguous, black-box algorithm like AI to always make the right decision. If we put AI in that place, our costs will go up, and we cannot guarantee performance,” said Chouhan. Hidden Costs And Risks Of Scaling AI The conversation then moved from the roundtable to a fireside chat, where the focus shifted from the broader challenges of building AI infrastructure to the risks enterprises face as they scale these deployments from pilots. Dhanrajani, also moderating the fireside, opened the AI infrastructure conversation by pressing his two panellists, Ankit Gupta, CTO of Policybazaar for Business, and Nitin Kaushik, director of technology, Cloud Engineering, at Oracle, on where enterprise AI strategies tend to break down first. Building AI capability, Gupta argued, is not only an infrastructure and use-case problem. According to him, it is also a trust challenge that many organisations underestimate. He noted that, without the right controls, prompts and AI-agent interactions can create pathways to expose sensitive enterprise information. "Earlier we used to say, it is garbage in, garbage out, but today, the risk is that poorly governed inputs can lead to sensitive information getting out. That is why security, data governance, identity, and access controls must be designed into AI systems from the start,” Gupta said. Oracle’s Kaushik picked up the thread when the conversation turned to cost, an issue Dhanrajani termed as the "elephant in the room" for most enterprises deep into their AI rollouts. Token consumption, Kaushik said, is rising in ways many organisations are not prepared for. "I have met customers that are consuming trillions of tokens a day. We hear cases where organisations say their AI bills are beginning to approach – or even exceed – the value they associate with the business impact they are receiving." Infra Gap Behind AI Deployment Kaushik followed the fireside chat with a deeper look at why AI deployments break down after the pilot stage. According to Oracle’s director of cloud engineering, companies face three recurring challenges behind AI implementation. Cloud costs are often unpredictable, and data silos can create multiple versions of the same dataset – undermining the consistency and reliability of AI outputs. At the same time, cloud infrastructure has traditionally been built to prioritise availability over performance. According to him, Oracle rebuilt from the infrastructure layer up with dedicated compute and memory, off-box virtualisation to reduce network load on the CPU, and RDMA-based networking designed to deliver low-latency communication across GPU clusters. Taken together, the roundtable and fireside chat pointed to a common thread: enterprise AI's biggest constraints are not just computational, but organisational. Enterprises are grappling with engineering discipline, data governance, cost visibility and trust, rather than mere GPU access. Tech leaders across the sessions converged on the same view that these factors, alongside access to compute, will ultimately determine whether an AI deployment survives the move from pilot to production.

Microsoft's Copilot app adds Office, natural coding and automation
It's yet another facelift for Microsoft's AI app.
Microsoft may be taking a step back from shoving AI and Copilot features into Windows, but the company is still trucking along with upgrades for its dedicated Copilot app. Following a minor refresh earlier this year, the Copilot app will debut a new tabbed interface, as well as direct integration of Office apps. It's all part of a move towards making Copilot more useful for consumers and businesses, alike. While the company hasn't really made the case for serious consumer Copilot adoption, it's another story for enterprises who need to constantly process data, generate reports and create presentations.
The new Copilot app will feature a "Home" tab, where your typical AI chats and other work occurs. Eventually, the company says the Home tab will also be able to intelligently route your requests between Copilot's different modes. For example, a simple question may stay within the Chat mode, while a more complex query might trigger the Copilot mode, where you can delegate work to Copilot.
The "Code" tab, meanwhile, lets you create small tasks through natural language requests, no programming skills required. "Describe an app, tracker, dashboard, automation, or workflow in natural language, and Copilot chooses an approach and builds it," Jared Spataro, Microsoft's Chief Marketing Officer of AI at Work, said in a blog post today. Copilot can spit out things like simple desktop widgets, to dashboards for managing your data.
Finally, the new "Autopilot" tab unlocks agentic capabilities. You can have Copilot automatically respond to threads or deal with recurring tasks without any input from your end. "It can do things like set up and manage a full supplier review process: building the schedule and workback plan, then handling prep, meetings, and follow-ups on its own, right down to reaching out to stakeholders for updates," Spataro wrote.

“Treatable conditions can masquerade as Alzheimer’s disease, including autoimmune disorders and thyroid inflammation,” said Ennapadam S. Krishnamoorthy, founder and behavioural neurologist and neuropsychiatrist, Buddhi Clinic, stressing the importance of a specific diagnosis in people presenting with cognitive symptoms.
He was speaking at The Hindu Wellness Series webinar on Alzheimer’s dementia and the promise of brain stimulation, held on Sunday by The Hindu in association with Buddhi Clinic, marking World Alzheimer’s Day.
Dr. Krishnamoorthy said a detailed, case-based assessment was important to distinguish Alzheimer’s disease from other conditions that can cause cognitive symptoms and may be treatable. He also stressed the need to tailor care to the individual, noting that some medications may offer limited benefits or cause harm in certain patients. He said non-pharmacological interventions also had an important role in dementia care.
Vivek Misra, senior consultant – Neuromodulation and Clinical Neurosciences, Buddhi Clinic, discussed the potential of non-invasive brain stimulation as part of dementia care. The technique uses external stimulation to modulate activity in specific areas of the brain. “It does not require sedation or seizure induction and can be done in an outpatient setting,” Mr. Misra said.
He said brain stimulation should not be viewed as a standalone treatment, but as one component of a broader, precision-based approach to dementia care, with interventions tailored to the individual’s clinical profile and needs.
The session was moderated by Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, The Hindu.

Sixty-three per cent of the 3,253 Water Supply Schemes (WSS) taken up under the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) in Jammu and Kashmir are non-operational despite expenditure of around Rs 7,000 crore, a House Committee of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly has found, raising serious questions over planning, execution, procurement, quality control and monitoring of the flagship rural drinking-water programme.
The findings are contained in the voluminous 1253-page report of the House Committee constituted to examine alleged irregularities in the implementation of JJM in the Union Territory. The report was laid before the Legislative Assembly on September 21 by committee chairman Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi. The committee was constituted on April 9, 2025, to examine alleged irregularities in implementation of the Mission.
“The result is that 63 per cent of 3253 WSS involving an expenditure of Rs. 7000.00 crore are non-operational,” the report states. It adds that even the 37 percent of schemes claimed by the Jal Shakti Department to be functional were “not fully operational”.
The committee said the institutional mechanism established to oversee JJM had failed to discharge its responsibilities effectively, resulting in inadequate planning, supervision and monitoring.
“The House Committee is of the considered view that there has been complete abdication of authority,” the report said, referring to the Apex Level Committee, Executive Committee and District Level Committees.
The panel attributed the failure to achieve the Mission’s objectives within the stipulated timeframe to what it described as “gross negligence” on the part of these committees and the officers who manned them.
According to the report, 37 per cent of schemes claimed by the Jal Shakti Department to be functional were also “not fully operational” in several cases.
The committee also questioned official figures relating to Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTCs), saying discrepancies emerged between departmental records and ground conditions during field inspections.
The panel said records supplied to it contained what it described as “false claims” regarding the number of FHTCs provided in habitations and the number of habitations covered.
“On spot visits, the House Committee came to know that far less than the number of FHTC indicated in the record, have actually been provided benefit of the Safe and Adequate Drinking Water of the prescribed quality,” the report said.
The committee also questioned the department’s claim that 81 per cent of rural households in J&K had tap-water connections as of March 2025, saying the figures required physical verification.
The House Committee was headed by Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi. Its 13 members were Mohammad Yousuf Tarigami, Ali Mohammad Dar, Altaf Ahmad Wani, Aijaz Ahmad Jan, Rajiv Jasrotia, Ranbir Singh Pathania, Tanvir Sadiq, Javaid Riyaz Bedar, Muzaffar Iqbal Khan, Rafiq Ahmad Naik, Arjun Singh Raju and Iftikar Ahmad.
The committee subsequently undertook field inspections to assess the implementation of JJM works. It inspected schemes in Rajouri and Poonch, among other areas, before finalising its findings.
One of the major concerns highlighted by the committee was the failure to establish the sustainability and adequacy of water sources before executing schemes.
The panel found instances where expenditure had been incurred on pumping systems, storage facilities, transmission networks and distribution infrastructure without adequately establishing the viability of the underlying water source.
In WSS Shirpora Bangil, the committee found high sulphur and iron content in the source and said this had rendered the scheme useless. It termed the expenditure “unfruitful” and directed fresh testing of the source.
“Providing of FHTC is immaterial in absence of safe and viable source,” the committee observed.
The report also cited schemes affected by land and source disputes. These included WSS Dachnipora in Pahalgam, WSS Lelhara, WSS Syed Mantaqi Khrew and WSS Greenland Wuyan. In WSS Bugam Dooniwari, the committee said Rs 10 crore had been spent without benefiting the targeted population because of a source dispute.
The committee has also scrutinised the decision to shift from GI pipes to HDPE pipes during JJM implementation.
It noted that the Jal Shakti Department, Jammu, authorised Executive Engineers in April 2023 to use HDPE pipes instead of GI pipes depending on site feasibility. However, an earlier technical committee had recommended modification of DPRs before the change.
The panel said the national-level communications cited in support of the shift did not mandate compulsory replacement of GI pipes with HDPE pipes and questioned why the decision was taken several years after the Mission’s launch.
It said the decision had significant financial and operational implications and “ought to have been taken by the Apex Level Committee”.
The report also records allegations made by retired IAS officer Ashok Parmar concerning procurement orders and changes in pipe specifications. Parmar alleged that procurement orders worth Rs 4,000 crore were placed without approval and that HDPE pipes were ordered in violation of approved DPRs. The committee recorded these as allegations and evidence presented before it, rather than independently establishing every allegation.
The committee separately examined tube-well projects and raised concerns over tendering, technical qualifications, quality assurance and functionality.
It said some tube wells had failed to meet desired standards and noted submissions that water from certain sources was unsuitable for human consumption. The committee observed that quality-assurance mechanisms appeared to have been inadequately enforced.
The panel also questioned the effectiveness of third-party monitoring agencies hired for audit and inspection of JJM works. It said field observations regarding faulty execution indicated that such agencies had failed to discharge their obligations adequately despite being paid for monitoring and audit work.
The committee has recommended constitution of a High-Level Committee to conduct a comprehensive audit of JJM and retrofitting schemes, including procurement of DI, GI and HDPE pipes and execution of civil works.
It has recommended identifying officers and engineers responsible for irregularities and initiating action against those found responsible under applicable rules.
The panel has also called for scrutiny of officers who served on the Apex Level, Executive and District Level Committees from their constitution until March 31, 2025, with their actions and omissions examined against the respective terms of reference.
A comprehensive technical, financial and administrative review of tube-well projects has also been recommended, covering functionality, water quality, payments released, pending liabilities and possible additional expenditure.
The committee said the problems identified were not confined to isolated technical failures but indicated “possible systemic deficiencies in planning, procurement, quality control, contract administration and project oversight”.
Its central finding is that the success of JJM cannot be measured merely through construction figures or tap connections recorded in official databases. The ultimate test, the committee said, is whether households are actually receiving safe and adequate drinking water.

Tigray capital 'out of cash' as fighting escalates, resident tells BBC
A resident of Mekelle, the capital of Ethiopia's Tigray region, says that the atmosphere is calm but people are very stressed after fighting broke out between government troops and the party that controls the region on Wednesday, raising fears of a return to full-scale civil war.
He says that many banks have been running low on cash for months, leaving people to rely on mobile banking, with fears that could now be blocked.
An adviser to Ethiopia's prime minister accused the Tigray People's Liberation Front of launching an all-out offensive, including in the two neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara. The Tigrayans say they are engaged in defensive combat.

Woman who accused Jay-Z of sexual assault says her claims were false
A woman who had previously accused rapper and entrepreneur Jay-Z of assaulting her more than two decades ago has recanted her allegations.
Jane Doe, as she is identified in court documents to protect her identity, originally filed a civil lawsuit in 2024 claiming that Shawn "Jay-Z" Carter and media mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs drugged and raped her in 2000, when she was 13 years old. At the time of the filing, the woman was being represented by Texas attorney Tony Buzbee, who had filed more than a dozen sexual harassment lawsuits against Combs. (Separately, Combs was in the midst of a federal investigation for sex trafficking and racketeering conspiracy; he was later acquitted on the most serious charges.) Both men denied the allegations in Buzbee's filing, and Carter issued a statement claiming he was the target of an extortion campaign.
Jane Doe dropped the lawsuit against Combs and Carter several months later. In February of 2025, Carter sued Buzbee and Jane Doe for malicious prosecution and defamation. On Thursday, Doe filed a declaration in Manhattan federal court stating that all of her original claims against Carter were false, and that to her knowledge, her allegations were filed in court by the attorneys without conducting any independent investigation.
"Shawn 'Jay-Z' Carter never raped me," she wrote. "I have never met or spoken to Mr. Carter. Mr. Carter never engaged in any inappropriate conduct toward me whatsoever."
The woman has now been dismissed as a defendant from Carter's lawsuit. NPR reached out to the Buzbee Law Firm for comment, but has not heard back.
The developments come as Jay-Z is in the midst of a professional victory lap, celebrating the 30th anniversary of his debut album Reasonable Doubt with a series of concerts at Yankee Stadium and an HBO docuseries titled JAŸ-Z In 8, which explores his catalog and legacy.

Political candidates are attacking AI in ads, and they're focusing on the one thing scarier than a killer robot: a high electricity bill.
Republicans, Democrats, and Independents are peddling anti-AI messaging this year, with subtle differences. The attacks pose a challenge for AI companies looking to build political support for data centers and other infrastructure projects.
Business Insider reviewed 130 US political TV ads that mentioned artificial intelligence or data centers. More than AI safety or other hot-button tech issues, campaigns are mostly making noise about AI's costs, per our review of Senate, House, and gubernatorial campaign ads aired between January 2025 and last week, compiled by the ad intelligence firm AdImpact.
Data centers are "draining our water, driving up our power bills, threatening our way of life," Fred Simon, a Republican candidate who ran in the June 9 primary for Nevada's 2nd District, said in one ad.
All of the anti-AI political ads we reviewed aired in states like Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Texas, where data centers operate, are under construction, or have been proposed. Beyond electricity price increases, the ads criticized corporate or "billionaire" tax breaks for AI infrastructure, as well as water and land use.
"A number of candidates are linking data center concerns to broader affordability issues," said Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a public policy and governance think tank. "That makes the combination much more potent."
No party owns AI as a wedge issue
AI, as a political talking point, is still up for grabs. Neither Democrats nor Republicans have found a way to turn it into a wedge issue that they own.
About 37% of the candidates represented in AdImpact's dataset were Republicans, while 47% were Democrats and 16% were Independents.
The candidates' messaging often overlapped in Business Insider's review of TV ads. Regardless of party, the politicians often criticized increased electricity costs for voters, attacked incumbents who had supported data-center tax breaks, and said that AI had served corporate or billionaire interests.
"Big Tech billionaires are coming for Wyoming. They want massive data centers, more control over our land, our water, and our way of life," Republican candidate Chuck Gray said in a TV spot that aired around 670 times.
Blaming the wealthy serves as a "double whammy" for politicians who want to attack AI, said Michael Franz, co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project.
"Not only can you tie data centers to increasing costs, especially around energy costs, but you can also whack big elite interests at the same time," he said.
Republicans and Democrats do diverge slightly in the language they use to criticize AI's use of resources, Franz said.
Democrats are more likely to talk about data centers' effect on the environment from a conservation angle, while Republicans have brought up how the facilities take over private property or eat up farmland, he said.
Democrats also have at least one messaging advantage when it comes to AI: they don't need to defend the positions of the Trump administration, which has pushed back on Americans' AI concerns and recently launched a meme campaign to combat AI doomerism.
"Trump keeps telling people everything's OK, and there's nothing to worry about," West said. "People are worried about data centers, and they're concerned about AI taking jobs. The president can huff and puff all he wants. It's not changing public worries."
AI is making a 'mess'
AI infrastructure has quickly become a symbol of Big Tech overreach, and like Flock cameras, it's facing grassroots backlash.
Sixty-one percent of likely US voters oppose constructing data centers to support AI, according to a September poll from The New York Times and Siena University. About half of US adults are more "concerned than excited" about rising AI use in daily life, according to a June survey from the Pew Research Center.
Campaigns are trying to lock into those concerns in their 15- or 30-second TV spots.
"Big companies have come before, taken what they wanted, and left us with their mess to clean up. Now it's data centers," Paige Cognetti, a Democratic candidate for Pennsylvania's 8th district, said in an ad that aired around 400 times.
AI's salience in this election cycle is showing up across the campaign trail as governors in states like Pennsylvania and Texas flip from supporting data-center construction to delaying or blocking the facilities. It could become a much more influential political issue in the coming years if the technology ends up displacing jobs or harming society in other ways, as doomsayers warn.
"Data centers are a local issue, but the concerns have popped up in so many communities," West said. "People are worried about data centers whether they have one in their neighborhood or not."
While almost every TV spot we viewed was anti-AI, Business Insider did find one ad in the dataset that spoke positively about the tech.
It came from an AI-focused super PAC called Public First Action, backed by Anthropic, which supported Republican Tom Cotton in the Arkansas Senate race.
"American genius and resolve mean AI's future will be made right here," the ad, which aired around 1,100 times, said. "It's more important than ever that our chips don't fall into the wrong hands. Senator Tom Cotton is making sure of it."
Jobs, deepfakes, and other ways politicians talk about AI
Not all of the AI or data center discourse has centered on costs or resource usage. Business Insider found a slew of other themes that came up in political spots, including:
- AI safety: Candidates like Republican Congressman Abe Hamadeh talked about "common sense safeguards to keep the most dangerous AI away from terrorists."
- AI deepfakes: Some candidates complained about being AI deepfaked by opponents, accusing them of lying or mud-slinging. One AI-generated attack ad targeting Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed disclosed that it was "created in whole or in part with the use of artificial intelligence."
- AI taking jobs: Several campaigns brought up AI-related job losses in ads. Montana House Republican candidate Aaron Flint pledged to "create high-paying jobs that China can't steal, and AI can't replace" in an ad that aired about 1,180 times.
- Environmental impact: While water or land usage were common complaints in ads, some politicians spoke more broadly about AI's environmental effects. "Big Tech's invading Ohio, driving up our electric rates, damaging our environment, destroying our farmland," the campaign for Ohio Democrat Marcy Kaptur said in an ad that aired about 1,260 times.
Beyond TV ads, campaigns are bringing their anti-data center messaging online via Meta and YouTube ads, according to an analysis of digital-ad spend from Tom Egan, founder of the public-affairs firm Absecon Group.
Over 700 campaigns posted about data centers in digital ads this year, and 99.7% of ad spend has gone to critical messaging, Egan said.
"There's no other topic that everyone's talking about the way that they are about data centers," he said. "Voters across the country have concerns about AI, and the most tangible visualization of that is data centers being built."

It is sometimes called "momnesia," "mommy brain," "pregnancy brain" or "baby brain" — the forgetfulness, mental fogginess and cognitive changes that many women may experience during pregnancy. For instance, a woman might walk into the kitchen and forget why she did, or perhaps misplace her car keys in the bathroom.
Scientists know it is a real biological phenomenon, and now have found a possible explanation, identifying a specific brain circuit that becomes disrupted under the sustained high levels of oestrogen that accompany pregnancy.
They conducted experiments using laboratory mice designed to mimic the sustained elevated oestrogen experienced during pregnancy, finding that this led to temporary memory impairment in the animals without mood changes.
Underlying this in the mice, they found, was how the high oestrogen affected a neuronal pathway between two brain structures — the hypothalamus, which acts as a control center and integrative hub, and the hippocampus, which is central to memory formation.
High oestrogen increased the activity of hypothalamus neurons, which in turn suppressed activity in the hippocampus and impaired memory, they found.
"Momnesia" becomes most evident in late pregnancy and may continue into the postpartum period but usually dissipates after childbirth. Short-term and long-term memory can be affected, including spatial, social and verbal memory such as having difficulty remembering names or words, or struggling to recall familiar information.
"It is not serious or medically disabling, although it does affect daily functioning and confidence," said Zheng Sun, a professor of medicine at Baylor College of Medicine specialising in endocrinology and molecular biology and one of the leaders of the study published in the journal Science Bulletin.
"Typical examples include forgetting why one entered a room, misplacing an item, losing the thread of a conversation or needing reminders for appointments. It is widespread. About 80% of pregnant women notice those changes, but that figure largely reflects self-report and subjective experience rather than objective testing," Dr. Sun said.
The findings suggest that the phenomenon does not represent a general decline in cognitive ability.
"The important point is that pregnancy does not simply make someone 'less intelligent.' The effects appear to be more subtle and specific to certain cognitive tasks," said Yanlin He, director of the Brain Glycemic and Metabolism Control Laboratory at Louisiana State University's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and another of the study leaders.
Mouse experiments
The mouse experiments shed light on what is happening in the brain. Oestrogen is a hormone that governs a woman's pregnancy, menstrual cycle and puberty, spurring physical changes that help the body support the fetus, foster fetal development and prepare for childbirth. Its levels increase during pregnancy, peaking in the third trimester.
The researchers found that a protein called "oestrogen receptor alpha" transmits estrogen's signals into cells in the hypothalamus.
This region has abundant brain cells called GABAergic neurons that typically transmit calming signals to other parts of the brain. The study showed that high oestrogen levels over-activate the inhibitory signals by these neurons in the mice, and this directly affected the hippocampus.
The researchers performed memory tests including object and location recognition, finding impairment in mice given high oestrogen levels compared to those that were not.
When the researchers experimentally turned off the hypothalamus-to-hippocampus neuronal pathway, the mice no longer experienced oestrogen-induced memory problems. But experimentally activating the same pathway impaired memory in the mice, even without higher amounts of oestrogen present.
"When we genetically removed estrogen receptors from these hypothalamic neurons, estrogen-induced and pregnancy-induced memory problems in mice were also reversed. We suspect that a similar circuit may play a similar role in humans, although you cannot do this type of invasive study directly in humans," Dr. Sun said.
The researchers complemented the mouse experiments with a study assessing memory performance in 70 women, including some across different stages of pregnancy and some who were not pregnant, using tests of long-term, short-term and working memory. These tests revealed memory impairments that manifested during late pregnancy, correlating with high circulating oestrogen levels.
"Importantly, higher circulating estrogen levels were associated with poorer performance on several memory-related measures even after accounting for other potential contributing factors. This provides human evidence consistent with the mechanism we identified in mice," Dr. He said.
"However, we should emphasise that we did not directly manipulate or measure this specific neural circuit in pregnant women. Therefore, the human findings support the hypothesis but do not establish the same level of causality as the mouse experiments," Dr. He said.

Italy ministers agree to ban burqa and niqab in school and cap foreigners in class
- Published
The Italian government has approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools, along with a limit on the share of pupils who speak little Italian in any one class.
A 30% cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the measures as "common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate".
Opposition parties accuse the government of pandering to the policies of the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party, ahead of a general election next year.
Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara has said the limit is "purely linguistic" rather than one of citizenship, while he has sought to frame the ban on the niqab and burqa as a matter of gender equality.
"You must go to school with your face uncovered," Meloni said while announcing the plans on Sunday, adding that no-one could decide that a young woman should hide herself in the name of tradition.
There were several drafts of the decree ahead of Thursday's council of ministers meeting, however the core details were clear.
The veil ban would apply to the burqa and niqab, but not the hijab, which leaves the face visible.
The niqab is a veil for the face that leaves the area around the eyes clear. However, it may be worn with a separate eye veil. It is worn with an accompanying headscarf.
The burka is a one-piece veil that covers the face and body. Often there is a mesh screen around the eyes to see through.
Non-Italian citizens make up 11.6% of pupils in Italy's schools, according to the research institution Fondazione ISMU.
The 30% limit on pupils who speak limited Italian will cover separate stages of education differently.
In primary schools, it would cover non-Italian citizens who have either not been born in Italy or who have not attended at least two years of nursery school.
In lower- and upper- secondary schools, it would cover pupils without Italian citizenship who have not successfully completed at least three years in the Italian school system.
Local school offices would be asked to spread pupils with little Italian language skills more evenly among nearby schools. Where that is not possible, exemptions would apply, with extra Italian teaching.
The aim was to avoid "ghetto classes", the education minister explained.
The draft also goes further on parents, according to the Ansa news agency. Schools would have to report to social services cases in which persistent language barriers among those with parental responsibility hinder a child's integration. Free Italian courses would be offered.
The measure is a decree law, meaning it can take effect immediately, but must be ratified by parliament within 60 days.
Italy already has guidance on Italian language at schools. A 2010 ministerial notice under then-Education Minister Mariastella Gelmini set a 30% limit "as a rule" on pupils without Italian citizenship. The new decree puts the limit into law.
The political opposition says the plan is as much about politics as schools.
Opponents accuse Meloni of pandering to Roberto Vannacci, a retired military general who leads the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party and is seen as a threat to the governing coalition's right flank.
The leader of the centre-left Democratic Party (PD), Elly Schlein, called the plan propaganda and impossible to implement. PD deputy and chamber vice-president Anna Ascani also accused the government of propaganda at the expense of schoolchildren.
Valditara, speaking by video link from New York at a press conference rejected the charge.
"We are not chasing Vannacci; if anything, he is chasing us," he said.
Vannacci said he agreed with the measures, but they should have come years ago.
The League's Matteo Salvini, who launched a separate package of measures on what he called "political Islam" on Wednesday, accused Vannacci of "continually voting against the government".
Salvini said he hoped Futuro Nazionale would back the League's new proposals.

Public health experts have called for tighter regulation of celebrity endorsements of harmful products following President Droupadi Murmu’s appeal to artistes to refrain from promoting substances detrimental to health, made against the backdrop of Maharashtra’s action over a Vimal Elaichi advertisement featuring Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgn and Tiger Shroff.
The President, speaking at the 72nd National Film Awards in Gujarat on Tuesday (September 22, 2026), said popular artists, particularly those who influence children and young people, should promote disciplined lifestyles and refrain from endorsing substances harmful to health.
The remarks come as the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) examines whether the Vimal Elaichi campaign amounts to surrogate advertising for Vimal Pan Masala. The FDA has issued show-cause notices to the three actors, alleging that the advertisement creates an association with a pan-masala product whose manufacture, storage, transportation, distribution and sale have been prohibited in Maharashtra.
The issue has also reached the courts. The Delhi High Court on September 14 declined to entertain a challenge to the FDA notices on territorial-jurisdiction grounds and directed the petitioner to approach the appropriate court in Maharashtra. The court did not adjudicate on whether the advertisements amounted to surrogate advertising.
Public health advocates have long raised concerns that celebrity endorsements can give socially acceptable imagery to products associated with tobacco, areca nut and other harmful substances, particularly among younger audiences. Cancer specialists have also warned about the health consequences associated with tobacco and areca-nut consumption.
Also read| Due diligence: On surrogate advertising
The Vimal campaign is not the first instance in which Bollywood celebrities have faced scrutiny over such endorsements. Amitabh Bachchan, Salman Khan, Saif Ali Khan and Akshay Kumar have, at different times, been associated with advertisements for pan masala or related products. Kumar withdrew from a Vimal campaign in 2022 following criticism.
The renewed debate raises a broader public health question over whether regulations governing advertising are keeping pace with the influence of celebrity endorsements, particularly where advertisements for apparently permissible products may create associations with products that are restricted or harmful.
Speaking to The Hindu, Arun Gupta, convener of Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPi), said appeals to celebrities needed to be backed by a clear legal framework covering the endorsement and advertising of harmful products, including tobacco and ultra-processed foods.
“I wish appeals were taken seriously and work in India, especially when it comes to endorsement and advertising of harmful products which include ultra-processed food products and tobacco products,” he said.
Mr. Gupta said the government should act on the President’s appeal and enact a clearly worded law to prohibit the marketing of unhealthy products.
“This is the only way to curb the trend. Why I am saying this is because the current legal framework is more of self-regulation and is ineffective even though the government believes it to be working,” he said.
Sandeep Nayak, chairman — Oncology and executive director — Surgical Oncology and Robotic Surgery, KIMS Hospitals, Bengaluru, said the President’s remarks highlighted the public-health consequences of celebrity endorsements of tobacco-linked products.
“As oncologists, we witness daily the catastrophic impact of pan masala, alcohol and tobacco addiction in our clinics. When high-profile icons lend their names to these brands, they inadvertently glamorise carcinogenic products for millions of impressionable youth,” he said.
Dr. Nayak said products such as silver-coated cardamom and flavoured mouth fresheners marketed under tobacco-associated brand names could function as surrogate advertisements.
“Using identical brand titles, logos and colour palettes — whether for pan masala or alcohol extensions —” creates a strong association with the primary brand, he said, calling for tighter regulation of such brand extensions.
Giving an insight into the scale of tobacco use in India, the National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21) found that 21.4% of Indians aged 15-49 used smokeless tobacco, with the prevalence higher among men (29.6%) than women (12.8%). The latest Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS), conducted in 2016-17, estimated that 28.6% of Indians aged 15 years and above — nearly 267 million people — used tobacco. The survey also found that smokeless tobacco was the most prevalent form of tobacco use in the country.
A World Health Organisation study estimated the economic cost of diseases and premature deaths attributable to tobacco at ₹1.77 lakh crore in 2017-18, more than 1% of GDP, while treatment of tobacco-related diseases accounted for 5.3% of total health expenditure. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has estimated that smokeless tobacco and areca-nut use caused more than 120,000 oral-cancer cases globally in 2022, with 88% occurring in South-Central Asia.

The Bharatiya Janata Party felt the heat within its alliance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise on Friday, as Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas) leader Chirag Paswan and Rashtriya Lok Morcha (RLM) leader Upendra Kushwaha urged the Election Commission of India (EC) to dispel confusion in the minds of the people.
Both Bihar leaders issued statements amid the demand of the Congress that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign immediately after an Indian Express report claimed that two of the three Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had formally recorded objections at least 14 times over the last 10 months.
Speaking to reporters in Patna, Union Minister Paswan said, “Being a part of the government, I will not defend anyone. The Election Commission is an independent constitutional institution. If questions are being raised about the Commission, I believe it is the Commission’s responsibility, and specifically the CEC’s, to strongly present its own side. It makes no difference to me what the Opposition says, because the Opposition’s job is to engage in politics. After all, how else would they pursue their political agenda if they do not level allegations?”
He further said, “The Commission should present its position strongly to the people, and that is the beauty of democracy. If people lose confidence in the election process or if doubts arise, then it’s wrong. I feel the Commission should present its side. This is not to respond to Rahul Gandhi or the Opposition, but to ensure that no doubts remain in the minds of the people.”
Earlier this week, Leader of the Opposition in the Bihar Assembly Tejashwi Yadav had said reports had revealed how the BJP intends to dismantle the Constitution and democracy. He had even asked why there was silence over the questions raised by the two Election Commissioners. Mr. Yadav had further urged Mr. Kumar to come forward and respond to the allegations.
Mr. Kushwaha echoed the comments in a post on X. “A lot of confusion has arisen among the people over the controversy related to the SIR. The matter needs to be addressed. To dispel the confusion, the Election Commission should immediately come out with the clarification.”
On the other hand, Union Minister and senior Janata Dal (United) leader Rajiv Ranjan, alias Lalan Singh, came out in support of the EC.
“The Congress raises a hue and cry across the country over a media report concerning the Election Commission. The party ought to review the real reasons for its defeat. Attacking constitutional institutions has been a tradition of the Congress. The Congress has no issue against Prime Minister Narendra Modi,” Mr. Singh said.
Meanwhile, the Opposition Rashtriya Janata Dal burnt effigies of Mr. Kumar at district headquarters across the State, including in Patna, seeking re-election in five States, including Bihar and West Bengal.
In Patna, an effigy was burnt at the Income Tax office under the leadership of Patna district president Dinanath Singh Yadav, following the call for protest by national president Lalu Prasad and national working president Mr. Yadav.

You are hungry. Or you are not. It doesn't matter.
You open FoodNeverComes, pick from 22 cuisines and start scrolling. Butter chicken looks good. So does bibimbap. You add a few dishes, watch the total climb and hit checkout. A tracker says a rider is on the way.
Then you get a dummy AI-generated call from inside the site. He is outside your building, he says, but cannot find your street or door. Except there was never any food in the first place. The order exists only on the screen.
"Order the food. Skip the bill," says the site., external Its slogan is blunter: "The food never comes - but the dopamine does."
Built by two 26-year-old software developers - Purvansh Parmar and Anshul Sharma - from Udaipur in India's northern state of Rajasthan, FoodNeverComes says it has attracted more than 2.7m visitors since its launch in June.
It now offers 22 kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes, complete with fake prices, a simulated checkout and a fictional delivery experience.
FoodNeverComes belongs to a new internet genre: "dopamine sites", which recreate the rituals of consumption without the consumption. There are fake shopping sites, fake delivery services and even fake holidays.
The genre took off in South Korea, external and has since travelled well beyond, spawning a growing crop of sites - Dopamine Shop, external or Fakehaul, external, for example - that mimic everything from food delivery and shopping to travel.
What, exactly, are we enjoying when we enjoy buying something?
The idea began with the founders' own shopping habits. Parmar and Sharma met on a computer science diploma course and later started NeuroX AI, which builds software and AI products and makes Instagram content. They noticed it in their own lives: online baskets filling up with things they wanted, but never actually bought.
Sharma would browse electronics, fill an online basket and abandon it. Parmar's mother did much the same. "She would add things to the cart and say, 'I will order this later'," he recalls.
Parmar's own version ended at food delivery checkouts. During a two-month project in Mumbai, he says, he was spending 5,000-10,000 rupees a week on food, sometimes ordering treats he did not necessarily need: Belgian waffles, ice cream and, once, a large jar of sour cream he barely wanted and gave away to friends.
He believes "perhaps the real craving was not always for the food, but for the ritual of ordering it".
What begins as genuine hunger, the two argue, can become associated with the pleasure of ordering. Over time, boredom, anxiety or habit can trigger the urge even when the hunger has disappeared.
"Sometimes you're not hungry at all. You're bored or busy, and then you realise that ordering food makes you feel good. You start associating the act of ordering with that dopamine hit. Eventually, it's not just the food you want," says Parmar.
Ravi Dhar, director of the Yale Center for Customer Insights, calls this "anticipatory utility" - the pleasure of looking forward to consumption. It is especially strong with things that capture the imagination - a new pair of shoes, a holiday, a restaurant meal - because anticipation becomes part of the experience.
Sometimes, Dhar says, anticipation can be more pleasurable than ownership: "The thrill is in the chase." Once the object is acquired and the tension resolved, psychological arousal falls.
Neuroscience has a name for this gap between the chase and the catch, and it complicates a popular idea. Dopamine is not simply the brain's pleasure chemical, whatever the internet's talk of "dopamine hits" might suggest.
Kent Berridge, a University of Michigan neuroscientist who developed the theory of "wanting" and "liking", says they are separate processes. Wanting is the motivational pull towards something; liking is the pleasure of having it. They often travel together, but not always. Dopamine, in his account, drives the first, not the second.
Tempting food or products online are likely to activate this wanting system, which Berridge calls "incentive salience".
"Some situations can trigger 'wanting' by itself," he says. We can pursue something intensely even when the eventual pleasure is weak - or, in more everyday terms, want something more than we ultimately like it.
Dr Anna Lembke, a Stanford University addiction psychiatrist and author of Dopamine Nation, makes a similar distinction.
"To call dopamine a chemical of pleasure is an oversimplification," she told me. "Dopamine is the molecule that says 'get more of' or 'do more of', but it doesn't necessarily equate to pleasure."
What she adds is the role of ritual. Cues and habits attached to a reward can become reinforcing in their own right, she says: in addiction, the routines leading up to drug use can eventually matter as much as the drug itself. "Anticipation of reward can be as reinforcing as the reward itself," she says.
Can repeatedly ordering imaginary food satisfy a real craving? Berridge says the ritual could produce a "dopamine hit and strong 'wanting', and also evoke faint conditioned 'liking'".
But he would expect the "novelty to soon wear off", and would be "surprised" if many people returned to place more than about 10 imaginary orders.
Dhar is more open to the possibility that simulated consumption could serve as a kind of release valve.
"While we still need more empirical data to know if simulated shopping can satisfy a consumer urge, evidence from simulated consumption in gaming shows it can be highly effective," he says.
But there is an equally plausible danger: the ritual may simply rehearse the behaviour it is supposed to replace.
Lembke says the evidence is not in yet, and the effect may depend on the person. But her own bet is that, over time, the sites could "reinforce the same addictive neural networks they are trying to simulate".
"The one up side, though, is that people using these sites have on some level already admitted to themselves they have a problem, and that admission is often the first step in recovery," says Lembke.
Sharma ran an accidental experiment of his own. When his phone screen cracked, he spent a week on Amazon comparing six or seven replacements and adding them to his basket. Then he repaired the handset.
"I enjoyed the process of research and putting the phones in the cart," he says. "Eventually I didn't buy a phone."
He now catches himself doing the same on food delivery sites, particularly when anxious, filling baskets without checking out. "I realised that I suffer from this problem," he says.
The site's blog explores the "serious side" of the fake takeaway, from food-delivery addiction and why fake ordering feels good to cravings, guilt and the psychology of the shopping cart.
The founders have since taken the idea beyond food. A second site, TripNeverLeaves, lets users plan a holiday - destination, flight, seat, hotel and activities - then sends them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway. They say it has attracted more than 100,000 visitors.
Who those visitors are is harder to establish. But Lembke says younger people may be especially vulnerable to reinforcing digital rewards because the "developing brain is a vulnerable brain".
"In childhood and early adolescence, the front lobe, which acts like the brakes on appetite, is not yet fully connected to the emotion centres of the brain. Hence, teens are more likely to take risks without appreciating the negative consequences, and more likely to get addicted to reinforcing substances and behaviours, once exposed," she says.
For now, the founders say the sites are not about making money. They plan to keep them free and eventually share the data with neuroscientists and psychologists.
What looks like a joke about ordering too much food has stumbled into a bigger question about modern consumption: if so much of the thrill comes before we get the thing, do we need the thing at all?

Morning opening: Pope Leo visits France to meet Catholics, talk AI, united Europe
Jakub Krupa
Pope Leo will visit France this weekend, the first papal state visit to the country in 18 years, beginning with Paris today.
During the visit, Leo is expected to seek to repair the Catholic Church’s standing after abuse scandals in the country, as well as deliver a landmark speech on AI development at Unesco and talk about Europe’s future in Metz, with some other European leaders expected to attend.
He will visit the restored Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris, as well as the famed Catholic shrine in Lourdes, among other places.
The Pope’s plane is now in French airspace and expected to land at Paris Orly airport in the next half hour.
I will keep an eye on his trip and keep you up to date.
Elsewhere, I will bring you all the updates from Ukraine and across the continent.
It’s Friday, 25 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Pope Leo's plans in France today and over the weekend
Later today, Pope Leo will go to the Élysée Palace for (another) formal welcome and a meeting with authorities, civil society and the diplomatic corps, before visiting Unesco and delivering a speech on AI in mid-afternoon.
He is then expected to go on a stroll through the streets of Paris, before going to the restored Notre Dame Cathedral.
In the evening, he is due to meet with some 80,000 young people for a prayer vigil with young people at Stade de France (I decline to say what they consider as ‘young’, because I’m not happy their brackets.)
Tomorrow, he will visit Maison Bakhita social support and integration centre and hold a meeting at the Catholic Institute of Paris before hosting an open-air mass at Place de la Concorde and Avenue des Champs-Elysees and moving onwards to Lourdes.
He will spend all Sunday there, with a Sunday Mass in the Sanctuary of Lourdes, and a private meeting with victims of sexual abuse within the Church later that day.
He will then be in Metz on Monday, with a speech on the roots of united Europe, another stroll through the streets of the city, and a mass at Metz Cathedral, before flying back to Rome.
Church bells across France ring to mark Pope Leo's visit
To welcome Pope Leo to France, the bells of churches across France started ringing at 10am, just as his plane touched down at Paris Orly.
In fact, they are still ringing: it was agreed they would ring for seven minutes, which the Conference of Bishops of France said would be just right to “mark the solemnity of the event without disrupting civil life.”
It’s seen as “a symbolic gesture to mark the beginning of this apostolic journey and allow everyone to join in, wherever they are.”
Meanwhile, AP is reporting that in what will surely be seen as a swipe at Donald Trump, Pope Leo told reporters on board of his plane that they are always welcome to cover him, and affirmed the need for media scrutiny.
These comments came in response to a question about Trump ban at the White House, AP is reporting.
Last night Macron gave a rare prime time TV interview, answering questions about all sorts of current issues.
Talking to TF1 and France2, he denied media reports from Spain that the US Central Intelligence Agency warned Paris of a potential Russian strike across southern Europe, from the Mediterranean (Europe Live, Thursday).
“I can deny it. The CIA did not inform French services,” he said.
But he still repeated his warning about Russia’s “growing” hostile activities in Europe, saying all sensitive sites in France are subject to additional protection.
The French president also said that said any ban on US diesel exports backed by president Donald Trump would be a “bad” decision, including for the US economy.
Interestingly, French president Emmanuel Macron will meet with Pope Leo this morning and host him at the Élysée Palace, but will not attend tomorrow’s mass at Place de la Concorde in Paris.
