Actress Chahatt Khanna, who was recently seen in Hungama OTT’s Hasratein 4, has revealed that she was approached for the reality show Alliance, but she turned down the offer because of the show’s long filming schedule and no-phone requirement. In an exclusive conversation with Bollywood Hungama, the actress also opened up about possibly participating in The Traitors and taking her business to Shark Tank India.
EXCLUSIVE: Chahatt Khanna recalls being held by aunties in malls after her Bade Achhe Lagte Hain character turned villain; says, “It became difficult for me to step out,” reveals why she’d consider doing The Traitors over Alliance!
Chahatt Khanna reveals why she turned down Alliance
Chahatt revealed that she was approached for Alliance, but the commitment required for the show did not work for her. According to the actress, she was expected to spend several weeks away from her phone, which would have been difficult because she also runs a company.
“Yes, I was approached for Alliance. And they had come in touch with me. I think they wanted 40, 45, 62 days, without phone and all. I was like, I won't be able to do it. Because, I am running a company also,” she said.
Chahatt added that she could consider participating in a shorter-format reality show. “So, I will be able to do it for a few days, maybe for a show like The Traitors. But if you ask me to leave my phone for 60 days, what will happen to my company? So, I couldn't do it. The lines didn't work out.”
Chahatt Khanna says she could consider The Traitors
While Chahatt has not watched the recent season of The Traitors India in full, she said she has seen some episodes and heard stories about the show from contestant Sahil. “I haven't seen it. I haven't seen the first. I haven't seen this. I have seen some episodes. I have seen Sahil (Salathia). He is very funny,” she said.
The actress explained that her busy schedule leaves her with little time for television and reality shows. “I don't get time to watch TV. Hardly, I get time.”
Chahatt said she is selective about how she spends her free time. “If I will watch it anytime, I like to watch cinema. If I want to spend my time. If I want to spend my precious time, I like to watch what I like. Not just because it is new. I don't follow trends.”
She added, “I want to invest my time where it is meaningful for me. So, I am very, very confused when it comes to investing time. You ask me money, I will give. You ask me time, I can't.”
Chahatt Khanna open to taking her business to Shark Tank India
Chahatt also revealed that she has considered taking her business to Shark Tank India. While she has not committed to a timeline, the actress said it could happen this year or next year.
“Sometimes, I watch some episodes of Shark Tank,” she said when asked if she would consider taking her business to the show.
Asked about her plans, Chahatt said, “Yes, we can. Maybe this year or next year we can plan to do that.”
The actress, however, reiterated that her limited free time makes it difficult to keep up with reality television. She said that when she gets time, she would rather rest, scroll through her phone or watch something she finds meaningful.
Chahatt Khanna recalls the Bade Achhe Lagte Hain backlash
Chahatt also revisited one of her most recognised television roles, Ayesha from Bade Achhe Lagte Hain. The character initially won over viewers before being portrayed negatively, after which the actress began facing strong reactions from audiences in public spaces.
“Before she turned a bitch, everyone liked her. Then when she turned into a bitch, people used to stop her in the mall and ask her why she is after her sister's life and all,” Chahatt recalled.
She further revealed that some viewers would physically stop her to question the character’s actions. “Aunties used to hold me tight and scold me, ‘What do you want? Why are you after your sister's life?’ It was difficult for me to come out.”
Chahatt also spoke about what she learned while working on the show, crediting her co-stars Ram Kapoor and Sakshi Tanwar. “The spontaneity I learnt from Ram as an actor, you know, he is a very spontaneous actor. I learnt method acting from Sakshi. So, I think I learnt a very good mix from both sides.”
Meanwhile, Chahatt is currently seen in Hasratein 4. The actress said she initially turned down the project but changed her mind after reading the character.
“There was no casting process as such because it's been a while I'm in the industry so I got a call and then I initially refused for this because I was not really sure about the project but then when I read the character, it was very relevant,” she said.
Chahatt added that she ultimately agreed to the show because of the character. “For this, I said yes because of the character.”

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows the 136-year-old Gauripur Jama Masjid near Kolkata Airport being demolished by religious extremists to make way for a Ram temple. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows the 136-year-old Gauripur Jama Masjid near Kolkata airport being demolished by religious extremists to make way for a Ram temple.
Fact: The video shows an angry mob vandalising the house of Mustafa Pramanik, an accused in the rape and murder of a 10-year-old schoolgirl in Pabna, Bangladesh, in September 2026. It has no connection to the 136-year-old Gauripur Jama Masjid near Kolkata airport. While the mosque is set to be relocated due to airport security and runway expansion plans, there are no credible reports of it being vandalised. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we searched Google using relevant keywords and found (here, here) that the 136-year-old Bankra Masjid, also known as Gauripur Jama Masjid, is located within the premises of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport in Kolkata, about 165 metres from its secondary runway. It was built in the 1890s. In July 2026, prayers were suspended, and authorities supported relocating the mosque, citing airport security and runway expansion plans. The mosque will be moved, as stated by West Bengal Chief Minister Subhendu Adhikari. However, at the time of writing this article, we could not find any credible reports of the mosque being vandalised.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to several Bangladeshi news reports (here, here, and here) from September 2026 featuring the same visuals as the viral video. According to these reports, an angry mob attacked and vandalised the house of Mustafa Pramanik, who was accused in the rape and murder of a 10-year-old schoolgirl in Pabna Sadar Upazila. The incident took place in the Kulunia area. Pabna Sadar Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Md. Tariqul Islam said that the schoolgirl’s body, wrapped in a sack, was recovered from a pond seven days after she went missing. Local grocer Md. Mostafa Pramanik, 55, and his tenant, Md. Yasin Ali, were arrested in connection with the incident and sent to jail by a court.
To sum up, an unrelated video from Bangladesh is being shared as visuals of the demolition of a 136-year-old mosque near Kolkata Airport.

Fiji has declared an HIV national emergency after data showed one in 60 people in the South Pacific island nation is now estimated to have the bloodborne virus.
The country says it is boosting testing and treatment efforts to fight a surge in new infections, which have increased 12-fold over the last 15 years, according to the Joint United Nations Program on HIV and Aids (UNAIDS).
Latest figures showed there was about 9,000 people living with HIV in 2025 in a country which has less than a million people, according to the UN agency. It said only 39 per cent of patients knew their HIV status and just 22 per cent were receiving antiretroviral treatment.
Fiji said that one in every 60 adults in the country has HIV, compared with one in 167 five years ago.
"This means HIV is now a national crisis and the government is treating it like one. No more business as usual," Fiji's Health Minister Antonio Lalabalavu said in a video statement on Facebook. “More people in Fiji are living with HIV than ever before.” The government said it was finding more cases because its testing efforts are reaching more people. It will provide more free testing, clean needles for drug users and free treatment for people who test positive.

United Nations, Sep 23: In his inaugural speech at the UN General Assembly, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said world leaders must set up global standards to oversee artificial intelligence because “fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance”.
Burnham said the UK will try to persuade other countries to adopt rules on transparency and access to AI models - and, even tougher, to get tech companies to sign on, too.
He said AI has immense potential but will also be “a source of disruption to the way we live and work - and a multiplier of risk”.
Burnham also said Russia and other states are using AI-augmented misinformation and disinformation to corrode democracy, something he said Britain has faced in the decade since it voted to leave the European Union.
He said he has asked British security chiefs to set up a National Centre for Information Defence to counter the threat.
Burnham also chaired a meeting at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday on the Israel-Palestine issue, alongside French President Emmanuel Macron, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan.
He said the two-state solution to Israel-Palestinian conflict must be kept alive.
Burnham said failure to deliver a two-state solution will “corrode trust” in politicians who have talked about the issue but not taken action.
He told delegates from dozens of countries that the UK has banned trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank because the “E1” settlement expansion plan is “a deliberate attempt to block a two-state solution.”
“We all live in an era of low trust in politics. Many people in this room, many politicians around the world, have spoken for decades about a two-state solution. But if we fail to back those words with deeds, we will further corrode trust in the political, diplomatic and international process,” the UK prime minister said. (AP)

The Embassy of the State of Palestine to India has questioned the description of the 1918 Battle of Haifa as the “liberation of Haifa”, saying that Indian soldiers who participated in the battle were serving under British command as part of an imperial military campaign that resulted in the occupation of Palestine.
In a five-page position paper titled “Rewriting of India–Palestine history: The battle of Haifa: liberation or occupation?”, the Palestinian Embassy said the terminology surrounding the battle required “careful and scholarly reflection” and argued that the event should be understood within the historical context of British military occupation of Palestine.
The Embassy said Palestine, including Haifa, was under Ottoman rule before 1918 and that British forces defeated the Ottoman Empire during the First World War, bringing Palestine under British occupation. Indian soldiers participated in the campaign as part of the British Indian Army, under British command.
It argued that describing them retrospectively as having “liberated Haifa” risked attributing to India a sovereign military decision that the country did not possess in 1918, when it was still under British rule.
The paper pointed to contemporary British terminology, saying military and parliamentary records referred to the operations in Palestine using terms such as “capture”, “take”, “fall” and “conquer”. It also noted that following the British military campaign, Palestine was administered under the Occupied Enemy Territory Administration (OETA) until its replacement by a civil administration in July 1920.
The Embassy also cited India’s own historical records, including the 2014 publication Indian War Memorials Around the World, saying it does not describe the event as the “liberation of Haifa”.
According to the paper, the publication records that the “fortified town of Haifa fell to a cavalry charge by the Jodhpur Lancers” and that the 15th Imperial Service Cavalry Brigade “broke through and took the town”.
It also referred to the Teen Murti Memorial in New Delhi, stating that the memorial was established during British colonial rule to commemorate Indian soldiers who served and died during the First World War, and was not originally intended to commemorate relations between India and Israel.
The Embassy said the memorial refers to “Palestine and some of its cities” among the places associated with the military campaigns in which Indian soldiers served.
The paper further cited official Indian records to state that 491 Indian soldiers are recorded at Ramleh War Cemetery, 109 at the Gaza and Deir el Balah War Cemeteries and 47 at the Haifa Indian Cemetery, besides soldiers commemorated at other cemeteries and memorials across historical Palestine.
The Embassy questioned why Haifa had become the centre of a commemorative narrative when Indian soldiers had fought across a much wider region, including the Suez Canal, Gaza, Jerusalem, the Jordan Valley, Damascus and Aleppo.
It also said the first formal Israeli public ceremony commemorating the Indian soldiers was held in 2010, nearly a century after the battle.
The paper argued that Britain, rather than India, was the principal military power behind the campaign, as it financed, armed and commanded the operation. It questioned why the “liberation of Haifa” narrative centred on Indian soldiers while Britain’s role was not similarly emphasised.
The Embassy also stressed that the soldiers described as “Indian soldiers” served in the British Indian Army and came from different regions, communities and religions across British India, whose geographical and political boundaries differed from those of the present-day Republic of India.
The position paper placed the soldiers’ participation within the wider history of British colonial rule, noting that Indian troops were deployed in military campaigns far from their homeland.
It also referred to the Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, arguing that the broader record of British rule should be considered when interpreting the role of Indian soldiers in the First World War.
The Embassy cited Mahatma Gandhi’s opposition to the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine at the expense of its indigenous population, including his statement that “Palestine belongs to the Arabs in the same sense that England belongs to the English.”
It further pointed out that India voted against UN Resolution 181 in 1947, which proposed partition and allocated Haifa to the proposed Jewish state, and questioned how the 1918 battle could subsequently be presented as a foundation for India-Israel historical ties.
The Embassy said describing the 1918 occupation of Haifa as a liberation “raises serious questions and concerns in Palestine”. It maintained that Haifa should be recognised as a Palestinian city at the time and that the battle took place in the context of the British military occupation of Palestine.
At the same time, the Embassy said its position was expressed with “full respect” for the sacrifice and memory of Indian soldiers and for India’s sovereign right to commemorate its history and fallen soldiers.
It called for historical remembrance of the Battle of Haifa to remain grounded in accuracy, balance and respect for the historical experiences of all concerned, while emphasising that the document represented the Palestinian Embassy’s perspective and was intended to contribute to discussion on the historical and legal questions surrounding the battle.

Cardi B brings star power as Roberto Cavalli goes wild at Milan Fashion Week
Cardi B adds star power to Milan Fashion Week as she arrives at the Roberto Cavalli runway show
MILAN -- MILAN (AP) — Cardi B was thronged by photographers as she arrived at the Roberto Cavalli runway show Thursday, adding star power to Milan Fashion Week.
Looking glamorous in an animal-print coat, dark sunglasses and a blowout, the rapper took her seat next to stylist Kollin Carter and the show could go on.
Fausto Puglisi turned up the volume as he evolved the Cavalli vocabulary. His Spring-Summer 2027 womenswear collection piled animal prints, florals and feathers onto the house’s familiar foundation of exposed skin and embellished denim.
Flowing robes topped low-rise jeans worn with thongs and bra tops. Cropped jeans glittered with crystals and sprouted feathers, while a mesh minidress erupted into crinkled golden ruffles. Chiffon skirts fell into long shredded hemlines, and animal prints were pieced together in a mishmash suggesting a rumble in the jungle. Prints clashed joyfully in an exuberant collection that played on all the Cavalli codes of sex, glamour and animal instinct.
“What I like about Cavalli is that you have the possibility to create jeans as an object,’’ Puglisi said backstage. “You feel them, you have them and you put them in your wardrobe, and you feel better. It’s about joy.”

Concerns over the safety of drinking water have resurfaced in parts of Uri area of north Kashmir’s Baramulla district after residents of Gawalta village found a dead snake inside a pipeline supplying water to the locality, raising questions over the maintenance and monitoring of the public water supply network.
The incident comes weeks after a similar complaint from Karkroo Mohalla in Nambla, where residents had reported finding dead rats inside a water storage tank and supply pipelines.
Both incidents have generated severe resentment among the local population, who accused the Jal Shakti Department of not taking care of the water tanks, pipelines and other components of the supply network.
In the fresh incident, the residents said the Sokad-Gowlta Water Supply Scheme had remained non-functional for several days, leaving the village without regular drinking water.
They said that despite repeated requests to employees of the Jal Shakti Department, the problem was not addressed promptly.
“With the supply remaining disrupted, the local residents inspected the pipeline themselves on Monday and found a dead snake lodged inside it,” said Arif Hussain, a local resident.
The presence of the snake triggered concern among residents over the possibility of contamination and the overall hygiene of the water distribution system.
The residents of Gowlta have now urged the department to conduct an immediate inspection of the entire supply network, clean and disinfect the pipeline and ensure that only safe water is supplied to households.
They have also sought an inquiry into how the reptile entered the pipeline and demanded preventive measures, including regular inspection and sanitation of water infrastructure.
Residents said repeated complaints involving contamination or poor maintenance were a major issue in the area and the concerned authority should ensure monitoring of drinking-water schemes in the Uri area.

Salt, as an essential electrolyte, sits at the centre of human well-being, but being most prone to overuse and misuse, the condiment remains at the heart of illness as well. When Tamil Nadu Health Minister K.G. Arunraj took salt to the floor of the Assembly, he dragged it willy-nilly into public discourse. He announced plans to launch a multi-pronged mission to reduce salt intake, turning attention to the right quantities and forms that must be consumed. The Minister’s speech made it clear that the government’s plans were not merely about a dietary tweak, but instead, a recalibration of how wellbeing is perceived.
Salt, in the right proportions, facilitates hydration, nerve signalling, muscle function, and digestion and also has a role to play in stress physiology. However, in excess, or in ultra-processed foods, it can have a deleterious impact on health, increasing the risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney strain over time. On the other hand, very low salt intake can contribute to hypotension, fatigue, dizziness and brain fog, as well.
The health difference comes from the quantity of salt consumed and the overall diet patterns, undergoing rapid changes in favour of ultra-processed, packaged foods, and fast foods, that tend to be high in salt. The Indian diet itself, with its pickles and spicy curries, lends itself to tilting the salt cellar over a little too often. Surveys by the Indian Council of Medical Research show that in India, men consume an average of 8.9 gms daily, while women consume about 7.1 gms. Urban areas tend to consume higher amounts of salt, averaging around 9.2 gms a day. The WHO, which recommends keeping the intake under 5 gms of salt per day, released a set of guidelines in January 2025, recommending the use of lower-sodium salt substitutes, essentially including potassium chloride, and reducing the percentage of sodium chloride in table salt.
In Tamil Nadu, hypertension is a major public health concern. A 2024 study by Selvavinayagam T.S. et al., published in PLOS 1, showed adult prevalence of hypertension hovering around 33.9%, much above the national average of 28.5%. There is a direct link between consuming excess salt and hypertension — eating too much salt causes the body to retain extra water, which increases blood volume and puts higher pressure on the artery walls, leading to clinical hypertension.
Action plan
The Tamil Nadu government’s plan is appropriately comprehensive. For the first time, a statewide survey using urine samples will scientifically measure salt consumption. Salt will be gradually reduced in government-run kitchens, including the Nutritious Meal Programme, ICDS centres, government hospitals and hostels. The feasibility of introducing a low-sodium salt substitute will be examined.
This will be backed by a state-wide awareness campaign on how to read labels on packages, tasting before adding salt and using natural flavour enhancers. Researchers of a randomised, double-blind, controlled trial reported in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, in 2021, wrote that the replacement of salt with a reduced-sodium, added-potassium salt substitute is an acceptable and effective dietary intervention for lowering systolic blood pressure in persons with hypertension in rural India.
The State also intends to step up its hypertension control activities through its community health outreach programme ‘Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam’ and other public health care institutions. People diagnosed with hypertension will receive systematic counselling and anti-hypertension drugs. There is evidence that such closely-monitored health interventions succeed. A study published recently in Nature, Archana Ramalingam et al., studying the cascade of care between 2019-20 and 2023-24 in Tamil Nadu, showed that overall, hypertension care in Tamil Nadu improved, with increased use of public health facilities for treatment.
The Sapiens Health Foundation has welcomed the new salt reduction campaign of the Tamil Nadu government. Founder Rajan Ravichandran says: “This is a wonderful surprise; we have been knocking at many doors to bring in awareness of salt reduction in the public health sector. It can be very powerful in changing the way people consume salt. We just have to go back to 2005, when the campaign initiated by Graham MacGregor of the World Action on Salt, Sugar and Health resulted in a reported 30% reduction of salt in bread in the United Kingdom,” Dr. Rajan adds.
G. Sengottuvelu, senior interventional cardiologist, Apollo Hospitals, explains further: “Excess salt is one of the most important and preventable contributors to high blood pressure, heart attack and stroke.” His argument is that Indians’ preference for salty food is largely an acquired habit, often beginning in childhood, and the palate can adapt when salt is gradually reduced. Cutting down salt is a simple change that can make a major difference to cardiovascular health — less salt today can mean lower blood pressure, fewer heart attacks and fewer strokes tomorrow.
Incidentally, the regulator Food Safety and Standards Association of India’s submission of guidelines for ingredient labelling on packaged food has grabbed eyeballs. While experts point to lacunae within the labelling guidelines, it does seem that momentum is growing towards building a society that is aware of the importance of salt and regulating it, and reclaiming the kitchen staple as a transformative touchstone for improved public health. As Tamil Nadu rolls out its programme, hopefully with scientific vigour and cultural sensitivity, other States will do well to watch and emulate. If it is possible to cut down hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and kidney disease with adjusting the size of a single pinch, then, the question is why not?

If you want to understand the federal government’s new initiative to improve autism care and diagnosis, it’s helpful to understand its leader, Russell Shilling.
Sitting in his Fairfax, Va., office, Shilling is flanked by a colorful tableau: a coterie of medals from his time in the armed forces and a sky blue puppet from his six years working with Sesame Street. He shares his felt doppelganger’s glasses and close-cropped hair, though not its hue.
An experimental psychologist, Shilling has led many lives. During his time in the Navy and at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, he developed virtual reality therapy to help Iraq War veterans with PTSD and constructed early versions of chatbots to destigmatize mental health issues, bringing them into clinics.

Mohamed Salah given six-month driving ban
- Published
Former Liverpool footballer Mohamed Salah has been banned from driving for six months after his Rolls-Royce was clocked speeding.
Salah failed to tell police who was at the wheel when the car was caught by a speed camera driving at 36mph (58 km/h) on a 30mph (48km/h) stretch of road in Wilmslow, Cheshire, on 27 March, according to court documents.
The 34-year-old did not respond to the notice of the prosecution, brought by Cheshire Police, and did not enter a plea to the charge.
He was handed a six-month driving ban and ordered to pay £1,044 in a hearing at Warrington Combined Court.
A court spokeswoman said Salah was prosecuted under the Single Justice Procedure, which sees magistrates sit in private hearings, and was convicted of failing to give information relating to the identification of the driver of the Rolls-Royce.
The speeding offence came days after the Egypt captain announced he would be leaving Liverpool following nine years with the team.
Announcing his departure on 24 March, the club said he had "firmly established himself as one of the greatest players in Liverpool's history".
He scored 257 goals in 442 appearances for Liverpool, before transferring to Turkish side Trabzonspor following the 2025-26 season.

In an interview, former Chief Election Commissioner S. Y. Quraishi addressed the reported internal rift within the Election Commission of India involving CEC Gyanesh Kumar and fellow election commissioners. Quraishi stated that unilateral decision-making by a single individual within the multi-member body renders decisions invalid, remarking, "Any, all decisions taken by a single man, whosoever he may be, he may be the chairman of the Election Commission, but they're all illegal." He discussed opposition demands to nullify recent elections, noting that extensive voter deletions have compromised the electoral process. Quraishi observed that dissenting election commissioners face distinct operational pressures, citing historical instances where dissenting members were removed. Addressing public agitation and street ultimatums, he described the diminishing public trust in the commission as unprecedented. He also called for a technical and legal audit of all decisions taken by the Election Commission over the past two years.
In an interview with India Today, former Chief Election Commissioner OP Rawat discussed the controversies surrounding voter deletions, internal disagreements, and administrative functioning within the Election Commission of India. Addressing concerns over differences among commissioners, Rawat remarked, "Most of the issues are, a little frivolous or made up and, like this, centralization." He emphasized that internal dissent is manageable, noting that fellow commissioners hold majority decision-making powers if consensus is not reached. Rawat clarified that an election's sanctity cannot be challenged outside of an election petition under the law or Constitution. Regarding unaddressed emails from local officials, he stated that administrative supervision rests at the Deputy Election Commissioner and Director level rather than the commission itself, dismissing allegations of unilateral central control.

There are numerous reasons why you might want to record what’s happening on your phone. Maybe you’re having a problem with an app and you want to share what’s going wrong with a tech-savvy friend; or maybe you're the tech-savvy friend, and you want to show someone else how to fix a bug.
Perhaps you’re starting up a YouTube channel of smartphone tutorials. Or it could be that you want to capture evidence of a new high score in a mobile game—not just a screenshot of it, but the actual act of you achieving it.
For these reasons and more, screen recordings are useful, and they’re not difficult to capture no matter what the make and model of your handset. You’ll find instructions below for the two most well-known Android phone brands, and the iPhone.
Record Your Screen on a Google Pixel
If your phone of choice is the Google Pixel, unlock your handset then swipe down from the top of the screen with two fingers to bring up the full Quick Settings selection. You should see a widget for Screen recorder—if you can’t see it, try swiping left or right. If you still can’t see it, tap the pen icon (lower right) to add it to the Quick Settings menu.
Next you’ll see a panel of toggle switches: These options let you choose whether or not the screen touches are visible in the recording, and whether you want the selfie camera feed to be visible as an overlay (handy if you’re narrating or reacting to what’s on screen). You can also opt to include audio from your phone’s apps or from the microphone.
The drop-down menu at the top lets you decide between recording the entire screen or just a single app. When you’re happy, tap Start. You’ll see a short countdown, then the recording begins. To end the recording, tap the red recording timer in the status bar at the top, then Stop. The video will be saved to Google Photos.
Record Your Screen on a Samsung Galaxy
On Samsung Galaxy phones, the process is similar but not quite identical to screen recording on a Pixel. With your phone unlocked, swipe down from the top of the display, then swipe down again on the central pane (with icons for features including Wi-Fi and the flashlight) to reveal the Screen recorder icon.
This brings up a settings panel. You can choose between Full screen and Partial screen for your recording, and there are three options for audio: None, Media (whatever your phone is playing), and Media and mic (whatever your phone is playing plus the microphone input). There’s also a toggle switch for showing taps and touches on screen.
When you’re good to go, tap Start recording. You get a short countdown, and then the recording begins—up in the corner of the screen you’ll see a widget overlay for adding annotations or a selfie camera overlay, and for pausing or stopping the recording. When you tap the stop button, the video is saved in Samsung Gallery and (if you’ve got it installed) Google Photos.
Record Your Screen on an iPhone
For iOS, the screen recorder is launched by swiping down from the top right corner of the display, then tapping the screen recorder button (it’s a circle with another circle outside it). If the icon has been removed from the Control Center somehow, tap the + (plus) button in the top left corner to add it back.
You can either tap the record button once to start the countdown and launch the recording, or press and hold the record button to choose a different app for the recording besides the default Photos option—so you can use this to broadcast your recording to Facebook or WhatsApp for example.
Pressing and holding on the record button also lets you choose whether or not to include the iPhone mic audio. (The iPhone’s native output audio is always included.) To stop the recording, tap the recording indicator at the top of the screen, then the red stop button. You’ll find your saved video stored in the Photos app.
Third-Party Screen Recording Apps
It’s worth noting that iOS restricts what third-party apps can do in terms of screen recordings, for security and privacy reasons. Most apps in this category in the Apple App Store simply tap into the iPhone’s own recording capabilities, though Record It! is worth a look if you want to add commentaries and selfie cam reactions—you just need to add these after the main recording. Clips over three minutes require the $6 Pro purchase.
On Android, there are fewer limits on what apps can do. AZ Recorder has been a popular choice for years, giving you one-tap recording options, a choice of video quality settings, and some basic editing options included as well. To remove the ads in the app and the watermarks on your exported videos, you can pay $4.49 a month for the Pro version.
Mobizen Screen Recorder is another of the leading screen recorders on Android, and comes with a similar set of features as AZ Recorder: A widget overlay for instantly starting recordings, editing tools, and a few options for video quality (both resolution and refresh rate). Again, payment is required to remove the ads and watermarks—that will set you back $3.35 a month.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Friday said it has initiated legal action against Nestle India Ltd for alleged non-compliance with food safety norms in three infant nutrition products.
According to FSSAI, it examined NAN Excella Pro Stage 1, Lactogen Pro 1, and a follow-up formula along with their promotional material available on e-commerce platforms.
In NAN Excella Pro Stage 1, the regulator flagged claims relating to "5HMOs" and "Whey Protein," while in Lactogen Pro 1, it observed a claim describing "Whey Protein" as easy to digest, the regulator said in a social media post.
FSSAI said it had sought clarifications from Nestle India on these claims.
Both the products were found to be in contravention of Regulation 4(2) of the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, which restrict promotional claims or material aimed at increasing the saleability of infant foods, as well as Section 3 of the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992, which bars the advertisement or promotion of such products.
Separately, a sample of a follow-up formula manufactured by Nestle India was found sub-standard for Biotin content during laboratory analysis. The sample was sent for re-analysis, and the referral laboratory also found it non-conforming with the Biotin requirement prescribed under the 2020 regulations.
In light of these findings, FSSAI has filed three separate adjudication cases against Nestle India in respect of the three products, it added.
At 1.10 p.m., shares of Nestle India were down nearly 2% at ₹1,345.45 on the BSE.

Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 vs. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2: How these AI glasses compare
Meta's newest smart glasses are an iterative, expensive update.
Meta announced a slew of new smart glasses at Meta Connect 2026, including its first camera-free options, but the company's Ray-Ban Meta models remain the flagship. The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 carry over many of the improvements introduced in smaller updates over the last year, like the more prescription-friendly Ray-Ban Meta Optics or the affordable Meta Glasses, with new features that mostly rely on software rather than reinvented hardware.
Other than new colors and frame options, it's hard to tell how the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 glasses differ from the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2, unless you really dig into the specs. And you kind of need to, since understanding those differences is the only way to justify the new $449 starting price.
The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 last longer and listen better
The biggest changes Meta introduced to the Gen 3 are a longer battery life and the addition of more microphones. The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 lasts up to 9 hours on a charge — one hour more than the Gen 2 — and up to 50 hours with its charging case, two hours more than the Gen 2's 48 hours. In day-to-day usability this might not make a huge difference, especially when compared to the 12 hours of battery life the company is promising on the Ray-Ban Meta Audio. We'll need to do a full review of the glasses to see what the battery life improvements mean in real-world use.
The Gen 3's six-mic array, one more mic than what Meta offered on the Gen 2, is a similarly modest change. Meta says adding the extra mic and redesigning the microphone layout on the Gen 3 model has allowed for better background noise reduction for calls and AI interactions, but that will have to be tested to see if it's meaningfully different. One way the new mic on the Gen 3 could allow it to stand out from the Gen 2 is support for listening to and recording Dolby Atmos spatial audio, a feature the company says is launching later in 2026.
Meta has also ported over the action button it introduced on the Ray-Ban Meta Optics and Meta Glasses to the Gen 3. The button can summon Meta AI, act as a capture button, or be assigned as a shortcut for a variety of other Ray-Ban Meta features. The Gen 2 features a capture button that only works with Meta's camera features.
The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 are smaller and available in new styles
Smart glasses are fashion as much as they are anything else, so another way the Gen 3 are differentiated from the Gen 2 is the addition of two new frame styles. The Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) Aviator features lenses shaped like Ray-Ban's classic aviator glasses, with thick frames in multiple translucent and tortoiseshell colors. For something a little less in-your-face, the Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) Zena comes with more of a cat-eye shape in translucent, black and tortoiseshell colors. The only frame shape that's carrying over from the Gen 2 is the Wayfarer, Ray-Ban's most well-known frame. That doesn't mean Meta won't port more Gen 2 styles over in the future given its penchant for mid-cycle refreshes, but for now most Gen 3 glasses will look pretty different.
They're also, technically, a bit smaller. The best comparison point is the Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer. The standard-fit Gen 2 model is 131mm from hinge to hinge, while the Gen 3 model is only 129mm. The temples on the Gen 3 model are also slightly shorter at 149mm compared to 150mm on the Gen 2. The relationship is reversed when it comes to weight, though, where the Gen 3 model is a slightly heavier 51.5 grams compared to the Gen 2's 51 grams. Those changes might not be noticeable unless you have the glasses side-by-side, but it does suggest Meta is mostly trending towards smaller glasses overall.
Meta's new software features are coming to older models
Software and AI access define the experience of using Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses. And the vast majority of features the company announced alongside its Gen 3 model will be available on older Gen 2 models, too. That includes using the smart glasses' FDA-cleared hearing enhancement feature, interacting with the company's Muse AI agent, and taking photos with the glasses' new dynamic photo capture feature, which captures multiple shots at once and lets you pick the best framing.
Combined with the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3's higher starting price of $449, $70 more than the Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2, that makes justifying an upgrade hard. The company's new smart glasses will likely be a great way to jump into Meta's growing ecosystem, but if you can buy a used Gen 2 pair (assuming you don't need a prescription) you'll likely get a better deal.

Is Switzerland's neutrality at a crossroads?
BERN, Switzerland — The people of Switzerland are voting this weekend on whether to reinterpret their long tradition of neutrality.
For more than 200 years, the Swiss have stayed out of wars. Their neutral status was originally imposed on them by the big 19th-century European powers; France on one side, and the Austro-Hungarian Empire on the other - which wanted a buffer zone between them.
So, although not of their own choosing, neutrality allowed Switzerland to avoid the slaughter of two world wars, and, in later years, to use its neutral status to justify continuing its trade with repressive regimes, such as apartheid South Africa, that other governments had sanctioned.
That changed in 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine. After a few days' hesitation, Switzerland, which is not a member of the European Union, joined the EU's sanctions against Moscow, stopping trade, and freezing billions of dollars in Russian assets.
The move was welcomed by many younger Swiss. As its government agonised over how to react, Switzerland's cities had seen days of protests calling for solidarity with Ukraine.
But traditionalists were angry at what they saw as a weakening of neutrality. They collected the required signatures to force this weekend's nationwide vote, which would explicitly forbid Switzerland from joining economic sanctions unless they are approved by the UN Security Council – an unlikely prospect nowadays since the five permanent members (the U.S., China, Russia, France and the United Kingdom) agree on very little.
The proposal would enshrine neutrality in Switzerland's constitution, block the Swiss from joining military alliances like NATO, and define neutrality as permanent armed defence of Swiss territory only.
The campaign is led by the grand old man of the right-wing Swiss People's Party, 85-year-old Christoph Blocher. He has spent decades campaigning to keep Switzerland out of the European Union and even opposed the country's membership in the United Nations, which Switzerland ultimately joined in 2002.
Blocher claims his proposals will keep Switzerland safe. 'We've hurt our neutrality with these EU sanctions,' he told a rally of supporters. 'Now Russia thinks we're part of the war.' Campaign posters across the country sell the same idea, 'No war,' they promise, if voters say 'yes to Swiss neutrality.'
But opponents insist Switzerland cannot remain neutral in the face of clear injustice or unprovoked aggression. Fabian Molina, a member of parliament for the Social Democrats, sees Switzerland's refusal to join sanctions against apartheid South Africa as a shameful period in its history. 'We therefore supported directly the racist regime and prolonged apartheid in South Africa,' he said.
Not joining EU sanctions 'would put us in a similar situation now with Russia. And this is morally wrong.'
Molina is also somewhat suspicious of Blocher's motivations. The 85-year-old is a billionaire whose businesses traded with South Africa during apartheid, and also traded with Russia until 2022. 'With no sanctions, it's easier to trade with dirty regimes,' said Molina.
Opinion polls suggest Swiss voters too are also doubtful that Blocher's proposals for a stricter neutrality will keep them safe. Warfare is changing; this year, drones, believed to be Russian, were seen hovering over sensitive Swiss military sites.
The traditional armed neutrality, in which every family has a nuclear bunker, and every man serves in Switzerland's militia army, may not protect against the new threats.
The Swiss government also wants voters to reject the neutrality initiative. Ministers know the world is changing fast, with old friends becoming unreliable. The Patriot missiles and F35 fighter jets Switzerland planned to buy from the United States are either indefinitely delayed, much more expensive, or both.
New alliances, and new defence strategies, will have to be found urgently, and redefining neutrality on such strict lines could limit Switzerland's room for manoeuvre.

Dating startup Rivet has raised $10.5 Mn (about ₹100.6 Cr) in seed funding from Peak XV Partners, Shine Capital, and Blume Ventures to build and scale its community-driven matchmaking platform. The startup plans to use the fresh capital to develop its product, expand distribution, and scale across the US. It announced its nationwide US launch yesterday. Besides US, Rivet has an office in Delhi NCR, with its engineering and machine learning teams largely based in India. Founded in 2025 by former Tinder and Match Group executive Taru Kapoor and Rajat Sahni, who previously served as CEO of CarDekho’s used-car business, Rivet offers a dating platform built around community recommendations. The startup calls its model “social matching”. Users can join as “matchers” to assess potential pairs and recommend introductions they think would work. These recommendations contribute to a social matching score for each potential pair. Pairs with high scores are introduced to each other, after which both individuals independently decide whether to connect and begin a conversation. People who are not looking to date can also join solely as matchers. The startup describes its model as a “give-to-get” approach, allowing users to help others find connections while receiving recommendations for themselves. The startup also counts former Tinder and OkCupid CEO Elie Seidman among its early investors. Seidman advised and mentored Kapoor during Rivet’s development. The startup competes with dating and matchmaking platforms such as Tinder, Hinge, Bumble, The League, and Wingman. Its community-driven approach makes participation by people willing to recommend matches an important part of its expansion, alongside attracting singles seeking connections. Rivet’s pitch centres on addressing the frustration of browsing profiles without finding a connection. Kapoor argued that while dating apps expanded the pool of potential partners, they also made the experience feel transactional and isolating. The startup is betting that recommendations from other people can help surface potential matches that users might otherwise dismiss on swipe-based apps.

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has cautioned against the indiscriminate, repeated, or prolonged use of painkillers and antibiotics, citing the associated risk of chronic kidney disease and renal impairment.
In a circular dated September 21, 2026, the regulator said non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and antibiotics are regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the Drugs Rules, 1945, and are required to be sold and distributed on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner.
The CDSCO said most NSAIDs are included in Schedule H of the Drugs Rules and cannot be sold at retail without a prescription. Most antibiotics are included in Schedule H1 and carry warnings that they should not be taken except in accordance with medical advice and should not be sold without a prescription.
The circular directed stakeholders, including healthcare professionals, pharmacists, retailers, hospitals, and State drug control authorities, to ensure that such medicines are used only when clinically indicated, at the appropriate dose and for the appropriate duration.
‘Don’t self-medicate’
The regulator advised the public not to self-medicate with antibiotics or use them for conditions where they are not clinically indicated, including most uncomplicated viral infections. It also said antibiotics prescribed by a healthcare professional should be taken strictly as advised and should neither be shared nor used from leftover medicines.
People with pre-existing kidney disease or other risk factors for renal impairment have been advised to inform their healthcare professionals before taking NSAIDs. The CDSCO also urged people to seek medical advice if pain, fever, or other symptoms persist or recur instead of repeatedly taking painkillers or antibiotics on their own.
Advise for medical professionals
For healthcare professionals, the regulator recommended considering a patient’s age, comorbidities, other medicines and risk factors before prescribing these drugs. It said the lowest effective dose for the shortest appropriate duration should be considered when prescribing NSAIDs, particularly for those at increased risk of renal impairment.
Doctors have also been advised to follow antimicrobial stewardship principles while prescribing antibiotics and to avoid unnecessary combination therapy, inappropriate drug selection, incorrect dosing, and unnecessarily prolonged treatment.
Pharmacists and retailers have been directed to strictly comply with statutory requirements governing Schedule H and H1 drugs and not facilitate self-medication.
The CDSCO has also asked hospitals and healthcare institutions to strengthen systems for rational prescribing, prescription review, antimicrobial stewardship, and patient counselling. State and Union Territory drug control authorities have been asked to create awareness about the risks and regulatory requirements.

What is the cost of a life? For the wife and 20-year-old son Chongtham Vikram Singh, it is the lifelong grief and trauma of losing a family member. For Manipur, it is the loss of a homegrown musical talent, who began practicing his craft when he was a child, and made his way from Imphal to the big stages of Delhi. And for the rest of India, it is a reckoning with the systemic racism that has historically exposed Northeasterners living in other parts of the country to racial discrimination, harassment, bullying and violence.
The concerns are not new, nor were solutions entirely out of reach. The Bezbaruah Committee, set up by the Manmohan Singh-led UPA government to address the discrimination faced by people from the Northeast, had made a series of recommendations to the Modi cabinet in 2014. A key component of the proposals was making changes to the Indian Penal Code (IPC). Twelve years on, this is yet to be implemented.
Accused ‘Wanted to Teach a Lesson’ to the Manipuri Guitarist
Singh, a 55-year-old Manipuri guitarist, was allegedly beaten to death by a group of young men outside his home in Kilokari village of Southwest Delhi. On September 6, around 11:30 pm, Singh had objected to the loud noise and commotion being created by the accused outside his apartment.
According to the police complaint, when his son heard him shouting, he opened the door to see the group of men violently attacking Singh. After the altercation, Singh returned home but complained of breathlessness, he was then taken to Holy Family Hospital where he succumbed to his injuries at 6 am on September 7. CCTV footage showed the accused leaving the building. Seven men and a minor have been arrested in the case so far.
A Manipuri music teacher, Chongtham Vikram Singh, living in Delhi’s Ashram area was mob lynched by 8 people following a dispute over alleged noise and nuisance outside his residence.
Police said seven accused have been arrested and a minor detained in connection with the case.… pic.twitter.com/4V0LVeVLiJ
— Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear) September 7, 2026
The autopsy report revealed that Singh died of massive internal bleeding caused by severe physical trauma to his chest and abdomen. The accused allegedly kicked him on the chest and abdomen after he fell to the ground. During questioning, they told the police that they wanted to teach Singh a lesson.
While the police investigation so far has not revealed any racial motive behind the violent attack, his death has brought to the fore larger concerns around hate faced by people from the Northeast in the nation’s capital and beyond. It also brings the Bezbaruah Committee’s recommendations, and the fate of those recommendations, back into focus.
The Bezbaruah Committee and Administrative Inaction
The Bezbaruah Committee was formed in February, 2014, after the killing of Nido Tania, a 20-year-old hailing from Arunachal Pradesh, who was beaten to death with iron rods and sticks by three men after a verbal altercation in Delhi. The accused hurled racial slurs at Tania during the attack. The committee was constituted “to look into the various concerns of persons hailing from the Northeastern states who are living in different parts of the country, especially the Metropolitan areas, and to suggest suitable remedial measures which could be taken by the Government.” It submitted its report to the MHA of the BJP government in July, 2014. It can be read here.
The most crucial among the recommendations, perhaps, was a proposal to amend the provisions of the then IPC by adding Sections 153C and 509A. Section 153C would criminalise words, signs or acts that promote discrimination or violence on grounds of race or place of origin, with up to five years’ imprisonment and a fine. Section 509A would criminalise any word, gesture or act intended to insult a member of a racial group, with up to three years and a fine.
On January 2, 2015, then Union home minister Rajnath Singh said that the amendments were accepted and Sections 153C and 509A would be added as recommended by the Committee. However, In 2017, minister of state, home, Kiren Rijiju said in the Rajya Sabha the proposal was still under examination, with states’ views being sought. Later, when the IPC was being officially changed to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) in 2024 and discussions were being held from 2023, the recommended amendments were entirely overlooked. The provisions were never enacted.
On September 8, 2026, two days after Singh’s killing, the MHA’s monitoring committee on Northeast issues convened a meeting to discuss the recommendations made more than a decade ago. Joram Maivio, a special invitee to the monitoring committee, MHA, and member of the Bezbaruah Committee, spoke to Alt News.
“We were expecting most of the recommendations of the Bezbaruah Committee to be slowly implemented after we received a confirmation from the MHA in 2015. We deliberated extensively on this with the judicial division of the MHA, after which the recommendation was sent to the law commission and the law ministry. It kept going from one department to another. We were verbally, or in principle, informed that it had been accepted and that it would be included when the comprehensive amendment of the IPC took place,” Maivio said.
“The discussions continued through 2017, 2018 and 2019 as the Supreme Court had ordered the committee to meet at least every three years and in serious instances, meetings can be called at any point. In every meeting we kept discussing the issue of racial discrimination and questioning when the law would be amended so as to criminalise racism against Northeasterners. So when the comprehensive criminal law amendments came in 2023 — the BNS, BSA and BNSS — we were expecting this recommendation to be included. But surprisingly, it did not come up,” he added.
Maivio said that he had flagged this on the two or three MHA monitoring committee meetings and questioned the ministry why the amendments had not taken place, but did not receive any concrete answer.
Meanwhile, Delhi police data accessed by The Indian Express in June 2026 showed that more than half of the accused in cases registered over the past 12 years for crimes against people from the Northeast in Delhi remained “untraced” despite “the creation of a specialised police unit intended to address such cases”. Out of the 2,656 FIRs filed between 2014 and April 30, 2026, in 1,465 (or 55%) cases, the accused were classified as untraced. Only 33 cases resulted in conviction, producing a conviction rate of 1.82 per cent.
Asked about what transpired at the September 8 review meeting, Maivio said, “The committee director and joint secretary said that the amendments would be taken up but we were not given any clear timeline as to when.”
“We will keep following up to ensure justice to people from Northeast as incidents of racial violence are chronic and recurring. There is no quick-fix solution, but by denying the reality, we cannot solve the problem. The Government must continue to act decisively to address it and prevent such incidents,” he asserted.
Maivio noted that some measures were implemented in Delhi, including the creation a Special Police Unit for North East Region (SPUNER) with the helpline number, 1093, two special Delhi Police recruitment drives in the Northeast, and plans for a Northeast Social and Cultural Institute in Dwarka. However, he acknowledged that implementation has largely remained confined to Delhi, with little progress in other states.
Northeasterners Condemn Killing, Speak out Against Discrimination
The North Eastern Students’ Organisation (NESO) condemned Vikram’s killing and demanded an impartial probe. Chairman Samuel B Jyrwa, who in 2024 also demanded that Prime Minister Narendra Modi “breaks his silence” and visits the crisis-struck Manipur, told the media: “It is deeply disturbing that a person can lose his life merely for raising an objection to disturbance outside his own home…For years, Northeastern citizens living, studying and working outside the region have repeatedly reported being subjected to racial slurs, verbal abuse, physical attacks, social discrimination and other forms of humiliation because of their appearance, identity and place of origin.”
“It is a very big loss not just for us but also for the music fraternity…We want justice and we want the government to ensure that people from the Northeast are treated as Indians in Delhi,” said Singh’s brother, Chongtham Vivek, as the former’s mortal remains were brought back to Imphal.

It is a very big loss not just for us but also for the music fraternity. We want justice. An atmosphere should be created in the capitals of India… pic.twitter.com/QmHjnTkk3W
— ANI (@ANI) September 9, 2026
Speaking to Alt News, the convenor of Delhi-based The Mizo Welfare Association, Thangzamang Henry Simte, condemned the killing and said, “Our organisation was built to create a community and safe space for people from Mizoram and the Northeast living in Delhi, who regularly face racial discrimination and stereotyping in educational institutes, office spaces, or even while taking public transport. The root cause is lack of education in the rest of the country about the Northeast. Some people in Delhi don’t even know which part of India is Mizoram or Nagaland…they do not know the difference between foreigners from other Asian countries and Northeasterns of their country.”
Simte left Nagaland around 26 years ago and moved to Delhi due to ethnic conflicts in his region. He said in 2003, when he was still new to the city, he was routinely referred to as ‘Nepali’ by passerby on the road. “In one particular incident that stayed with me, a man in a suit and tie who was sitting next to me at a bike servicing centre, suddenly yelled ‘Nepali’ at me unprompted. When I retorted sharply, he asked me where I was from. As I replied ‘Mizoram’, he bluntly asked, ‘where is that? Is that in India?”
Alt News spoke to people from the Northeast living in various parts of India, who, like Simte, revealed the daily, oft-normalised patterns of racial stereotyping and harassment they continue to face.
Gopi Kishan Baro (28), who hails from Assam and is currently working as a graphic designer in Gurgaon, alleged that he was systematically discriminated against and bullied by a senior colleague at work. “A few weeks ago, when we were in the lift, he kept mocking me and said something which sounded rather like a warning, ‘Tumahari aankhein choti hai aur hum dikhte nahi, iska ye matlab nahi hum gayab ho gaye hai’ (Your eyes are small, so we are not visible to you but that doesn’t mean we have disappeared). It made me quote uncomfortable but I tried to laugh it off because I did not want to create a scene,” he alleged.
He continued: “Last Wednesday, when I was having tea by myself, he appeared and claimed I stayed aloof most of the time because I came from such a faraway corner. By the end of the conversation when I was leaving, he shouted at me, ‘Waapis chale jaa apne desh’ (Go back to your country). I wrote a formal email to the HR about his racist behaviour. They simply let him off with a warning, while I continue to live in anxiety and disgust, knowing that these insults are directed not just to me, but at my kin, my community, and the entirety of Northeast India as well.”
Heightened Racism During Covid-19
COVID-19 brought this prejudice into sharper focus, as Northeasterners in several places were subjected to racial slurs, harassment and stigma.
Twenty-eight-year-old musician Abhibyanjana, who hails from Sikkim, lived in Pune for her studies and later in Mumbai for work. “When I was studying, as part of my course we were required to visit several slum pockets for a survey in early 2020, during the beginning of the pandemic. I was constantly referred to as ‘Covid’ or ‘Corona’ by locals there. I was jeered at and humiliated but I continued my work regardless, I realised that if I cannot fight back deeply indoctrinated prejudice against people who look like me,” she said.
“I have to move to cities like Mumbai for opportunities because it is scarce in Gangtok. But as a musician working in Mumbai, I am often treated as an ‘outsider’. The discrimination and otherisation against the people of Northeast is pervasive and crimes against our people hardly receive national focus. On the flipside, this has created solidarity within our community, we look out for each other wherever we go,” she added.
A 2022 study, published in the International Social Science Journal, titled ‘‘You people have brought the virus here’: Othering experience of northeastern people amid COVID‐19 in Delhi, India’, focused on how the Covid‐19 pandemic exacerbated discrimination, violence, and othering against Northeasterners living in Delhi, by analysing nineteen qualitative interviews.
The study, conducted to understand their lived experiences in Delhi before and after the pandemic, found that the pandemic disproportionately impacted the Northeastern people living away from their home states. “The Mongoloid features make them ‘non‐belonging’ and outsiders. The experience of othering is an everyday phenomenon for northeasterners… Northeasterners’ experience amid COVID‐19 is dominated by stigmatisation and bullying, as they are being targeted and arbitrarily accused of spreading the virus,” the study highlighted.
An earlier study, commissioned by the Indian Council of Social Science Research (ICSSR) in 2021, further confirms the heightened harassment, abuse, stigmatisation and blatant labelling as ‘coronavirus’ that Northeasterners faced living in other parts of India during the pandemic. Over 60% of the respondents said that their studies, work, and psychological health was impacted by these experience.
“The highest number of incidents were reported from Mumbai (44.7%)…78% of the Northeast people believed that physical appearance was the most important reason for prejudice against them,” the study noted. Mumbai was followed by by Chennai (72%), Pune (67.3%), Delhi (64%), Hyderabad (48.7%) and Bengaluru (43.3%) in racial discrimination comprising offensive and abusive language against Northeasterners.
‘You Look Like a Chinese’
Caroline Devi-Singh (52), who hails from Manipur, moved to Delhi in 1994 to pursue her graduation at Delhi University. She later moved to Chandigarh and subsequently Chhattisgarh. She told Alt News that her experiences living in North India for so many years had been varied, but racial stereotyping was a constant. “In college, we were often called racial slurs, either ‘Chinese’ or ‘Chinki’ or ‘Momo’. As a young girl, I was always taught to be extra cautious, to a point where dressing how we do at home was a threat to my safety,” she said.
“So many years later, my son [now 25-years-old] faces the same racial attacks. He has grown up with the awareness of his rights, but the rest of India still lacks awareness… Nobody thinks twice before resorting to violence against Northeastern. We have been ignored by all the governments and the media has never paid attention to our issues. I stay in a small town now and I see that even educated people cannot differentiate between a person from China and a person from the Northeast… This comes from ignorance and a lack of information. I blame the overall education system and the government for this,” she asserted.
China call us Chinese, mainland Indian call us Chinese, but we call ourselves Indians. 🙂
— Neha Gurung (@nehaGurung1692) November 27, 2025
A former student of Ashoka University, who now lives near the campus in Sonipat, said, requesting anonymity, “I moved here in 2021 from Manipur. In university, I have faced racial slurs regularly. Whenever I have brought it up with the administration, they have simply let the accused go with a warning. Racism is not taken seriously on this campus, or in the NCR region at large.”
“When Northeasterners face racism, people think it is only our responsibility to speak against it… We are always on high alert because what happened to the Manipuri musician could’ve been me. It could’ve been any of us,” he added.
A Violent Pattern Entrenched in History
The cases point to a continuum of discriminatory mindset against the people of Northeast that stretches from racial slurs and stereotyping to intimidation, physical assault and, in the most extreme cases, death. In December 2025, 24-year-old Anjel Chakma, an MBA student from Tripura, died after being allegedly attacked by a group of men in Dehradun. Anjel and his younger brother Michael were reportedly subjected to racial slurs, including being called ‘Chinki’, ‘Chinese’ and ‘Momo’, before the confrontation turned violent.
In July, 2014, 29-year-old Akha Salouni from Manipur was allegedly beaten to death by five youths in Delhi following a road rage incident. Following his death, the deceased’s family and members of the Northeastern community held a candlelight vigil at Jantar Mantar, which also saw the participation of the mother of Nido Tania.
In May 2013, 22-year-old Manipuri girl Reingamphi Awungshi was found dead in her home in Delhi under suspicious circumstances. Delhi police initially said she died by suicide, stating that severe injuries on her face and body were caused by rodents. However, her family and rights groups demanded a deeper investigation, claiming that she was sexually assaulted and murdered, pointing to local stalking complaints and police bias against Northeasterners. After 11 years, in March 2024, the Supreme Court ordered a CBI probe into Awungshi’s case. Two years on, no headway into the investigation has been publicly reported.
More recently, in February 2026, three women from Arunachal Pradesh alleged that their neighbours in Delhi’s Malviya Nagar subjected them to racial and sexist abuse during a dispute over repair work at their rented home. The women said they were called ‘dhandhewali’ and ‘momo’ and that ‘Northeastern people are shit’. In a viral video, the accused woman can be heard asking the Northeastern women, “Rs 500 mei massage parlour mei kaam karne waali dhandhewali (You work at massage parlours as sex workers for Rs 500). Are you sitting here to do business? Have you opened a massage parlour at home?” Delhi police registered an FIR and later arrested the neighbours, a couple, invoking provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.
While speaking to Alt News, Maivio admitted that lack of awareness about the Northeast was the primary cause behind cases of racial discrimination. “We had recommended inclusion of the history and culture of the Northeast in school curricula and textbooks throughout the country. In our last meeting, we called the NCERT to find out what had been done so far. They said that they have included some content in Classes 9 and 10 in certain cities and that they would share it with us, which they are trying to implement countrywide. They are also preparing a documentary to be released countrywide, building awareness on the Northeast. But these have largely been verbal assurances, and we will have to see what has actually been included and whether it is sufficient,” he added.

- Sony's AI-powered matchmaking patent could use your search history and other data to match you with compatible players.
- According to the WIPO filing, the system will use your explicit and implicit data to evolve and refine your matchmaking profile to match your preferences.
- The patent also includes a percentage compatibility score to help pair you with players who prefer similar preferences across Sony's ecosystem.
Sony’s AI-powered matchmaking patent could use your search history to match you with other players on the PlayStation 5 or even the PlayStation 6, depending on when Sony implements the system. Sony filed the AI patent last year and published it on September 10, 2026. The WIPO filing details how Sony could integrate the feature across its ecosystem.
Sony May Use Your Data Across Its Ecosystem to Match With Compatible Players
Sony filed it under the name “Using ML models to match players together for gameplay.” According to its description, this system will use your explicit data “prior to engaging with a game or during profile creation.” This means Sony will use the types of games you play, what kind of player you are on the PlayStation console, which games you prefer, and the like, to match players.
Meanwhile, Sony will use your implicit data to gather information from your “time data information associated with one or more titles game environment, player skill levels, shopping cart information, social media information, and user search history information.”
Inputs could include chat data, biometric data, audio, and just about anything else Sony can use to find your perfect gaming match. At this point, Sony’s AI matchmaking system may raise some privacy concerns, especially since it could go beyond your in-game behaviour in multiplayer titles like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 or Fortnite.
Sony will track your data across its entire ecosystem and use your feedback to continually update and refine each matchmaking profile as your preferences and playstyle evolve. The AI matchmaking patent also includes a compatibility score that could help pair you with players who share similar preferences.
The description states, “A percentage compatibility may be computed based on the inputs and similarities between a first user’s preferences and a second user’s preferences.” In this case, the first user is you, and the second user is the one you’re matched with.
Sony states that, based on this percentage compatibility system, it may only show recommended player matches that meet the predetermined threshold, for example, “an 80% compatibility, an 85% compatibility, or a 90% compatibility”.
Sony has patented some interesting ideas before, including a possible touchscreen for the PS6 controller, but this one feels like it could take things a little too far. That said, what do you make of Sony’s AI matchmaking patent? Let us know.

Baljinder Singh, a resident of Sujanpur in Punjab’s Pathankot district, has reportedly been sentenced to death by a court in Saudi Arabia in connection with a drug trafficking case. Singh has reportedly been imprisoned in Saudi Arabia for around three years. His family members have appealed to both the Punjab government and the central government to intervene and provide assistance. They have sought help to understand the legal proceedings and explore possible avenues for relief. The case has drawn attention in Punjab, with the family seeking government support to pursue available legal and diplomatic options to help Singh (here, here, and here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows actor Shah Rukh Khan criticising Saudi Arabia and reprimanding the country over Baljinder Singh’s death sentence. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows actor Shah Rukh Khan criticising Saudi Arabia and reprimanding the country over Baljinder Singh’s death sentence.
Fact: The video has been digitally altered to depict Shah Rukh Khan criticising Saudi Arabia and speaking about Baljinder Singh’s death sentence. The original footage is from a 2015 event at the University of Edinburgh, where Khan spoke about life lessons. AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya, indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but found no credible reports confirming that actor Shah Rukh Khan criticised or reprimanded Saudi Arabia over Baljinder Singh’s death sentence. Had such a statement been made, it would likely have received significant media coverage; however, no such reports were found.
We also reviewed Shah Rukh Khan’s official social media handles (here, here, and here). Still, we found no reference to the case or any statement regarding Baljinder Singh’s death sentence that could substantiate the claim.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to an extended version of the same video uploaded on the University of Edinburgh’s YouTube channel on 16 October 2015. The background in the original video matches that seen in the viral clip, confirming that both videos are from the same event. In the video, Shah Rukh Khan speaks about various life lessons. At the event, the University of Edinburgh awarded him an honorary doctorate, and he spoke about lessons he learned through his film roles. One of the three attendees who was shot at Donald Trump's 2024 presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, has passed away from complications stemming from his injuries, according to the Pennsylvania attorney general.
Jim Copenhaver, 76, was struck twice when a gunman opened fire from a nearby rooftop. Another attendee, Corey Comperatore, was killed in the shooting and Trump's ear was grazed by a bullet.
Copenhaver died on Wednesday at a hospital in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, according to a statement from the Allegheny County medical examiner shared with local media.
The gunman, 20-year-old Thomas Crooks, was killed by Secret Service after he opened fire.

Republicans in the US House of Representatives also paid tribute to Copenhaver on Friday, saying in a social media post: "Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance."
