President Donald Trump is approaching the midterm elections with a historic 50 percent of Americans strongly disapproving of his job performance — shattering the rejection record he set before the 2018 midterms, CNN's polling guru said Friday.
“They don't just dislike him,” Harry Enten said. “There's record hatred for the president of the United States going into a midterm.”
Trump also fares worse with independent voters, with 56 percent expressing strong disapproval, Enten said.
"Among the group that determines elections in this country, you see the hatred for the president of the United States. This is what the voters are saying now," he said.
The White House didn’t immediately return an inquiry from The Independent.
Enten said Trump’s overall 50 percent “strongly disapprove” rating eclipses the 45 percent he notched in 2016.
Before that, President George W. Bush held the record when 41 percent of Americans strongly disapproved of his job performance ahead of the 2006 midterm elections, according to CNN’s chief data analyst.
And while Trump's “historically polarizing” effect on American voters has sometimes worked to his benefit, Enten said, it's not doing so now.
That's because the president's “strongly approve” rating is just 18 percent, one-third less than the average 27 percent for previous presidents going into the midterms — including Trump in 2018, Enten said.
“So, Trump actually has fewer people loving him than what we see with the average president,” he said. “What's going on here is normally Trump is able to counteract that strong hatred with strong love, but not anymore.”
The 2018 midterms took place during Trump's first term, when Democrats flipped six seats in the House and two in the Senate, but failed to win a majority in either chamber.
But Trump is now a lame duck, like Bush was in 2006, when Democrats gained control of both chambers by flipping 31 seats in the House and five in the Senate, along with two seats won by independents who caucused with them.
The latest so-called generic congressional ballot polling average shows Democrats with an 8.7 percent edge over Republicans, according to data posted Friday by Real Clear Polling.
Democrats have enjoyed an “incredible upswing” during September, when they began with a generic congressional ballot lead of 6.7 percent, according to the Silver Bulletin.
That's now up to 8.1 percent, or 8.8 percent with a “likely voter” adjustment, according to the Silver Bulletin.
The Cook Political Report also said that Democrats were on track to gain control of the House, with 15 races shifting in their favor, largely because voters are unhappy with Trump’s handling of the economy.
Democrats now hold 215 House seats and need just three more for a majority.
The Republican advantage in the Senate is 53-47, and The Cook Political Report described it Wednesday as a “true toss-up” after three races shifted toward Democrats.

My colleague Pranav Dixit attended Meta Connect this week and he stopped by AI Insider to share his thoughts with newsletter subscribers.
Here's how the Q&A went down, in longer form:
What was your biggest surprise while at the event?
The biggest surprise was how good Meta's upcoming VR glasses were. They're not coming out until spring 2027, and they'll cost around $1,300, so they're definitely not a mass-market product yet. But after spending about half an hour with them, I walked away really impressed.
I watched 3D movies, played Beat Saber, and even paired the glasses with a laptop so I suddenly had three giant virtual monitors floating in front of me.
The whole thing weighs about 100 grams, and after a few minutes, you kind of stop thinking about the hardware and just use it.
More than anything, it made me realize how far Meta has come. I kept thinking, this is what Apple should have released instead of the Vision Pro.
It obviously won't be for everyone, especially at that price, but it was the first time I'd tried something that made me think lightweight VR glasses might actually be getting close.
Which product/device were you most impressed by and why?
I already use Muse quite a lot for surprisingly complex tasks. I'll ask it to place a hold on a library book, send the ebook to my Kindle, or handle little chores that would otherwise have me bouncing between apps. It feels less like using a chatbot and more like having an assistant.
That's why I think bringing Muse to the glasses is such a big deal. The glasses themselves are just a tool. The real magic is being able to ask for something while you're walking down the street, cooking dinner, or driving, and have it quietly take care of it without you ever reaching for your phone. That starts to feel less like software and more like a superpower.
That feature hasn't launched yet. Meta says it's coming in the next few weeks. I can't say how well it works in the real world. But if it does work well, it's the first AI glasses feature I've seen that feels genuinely useful rather than just a gimmick.
Folks seem to like Muse much better than the metaverse. Why?
Can anyone really explain what the metaverse was? Was it a giant virtual world we were all supposed to hang out in? The vision always felt a little fuzzy. And to experience it, you had to buy an expensive VR headset and strap it to your face.
Muse is the opposite. It's an actual product you can use today. It lives on your phone, you can ask it to do things, and it actually gets things done.
Meta has also been moving incredibly fast. It's building Muse into all of its glasses, signing partnerships that let it book flights, order groceries, buy products, and connect to more and more services. You can see the road map unfolding in real time.
I think the biggest difference is that Muse solves a problem people already have. Everyone has little digital chores they don't want to do. The metaverse always felt like it was asking people to change their behavior. Muse fits into behavior people already have and just makes it easier.
That's why this feels much more tangible. It's here now, and you can actually imagine yourself using it every day in a way that was always harder with the metaverse.
Do you think Muse can become a true top-of-the-funnel platform like iOS and Google Search, with a huge user base and loads of developers?
I think there's definitely potential, but it's way too early to say. One thing Meta has going for it is distribution. It already has billions of people using WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, and Messenger every day, and it's now weaving Muse into all of those products, plus its glasses. That's a pretty unique advantage.
But building a great AI product and building the next iPhone or Google Search are two very different things. Those became platforms because millions of developers, businesses, and consumers built their lives around them over many years.
Muse is off to a promising start, but I think the real test is whether it becomes something people use dozens of times a day without even thinking about it. If it gets there, then you can start talking about it as a new computing platform. We're just not there yet
Any concerns/doubts? What could make Muse fizzle or fail?
Two big things I'm watching.
The first is platform risk. Meta is trying to build what could become a new computing platform, but today it's still living on someone else's platforms — iOS and Android. If Apple or Google decides AI agents are becoming a competitive threat, they could change App Store or operating system rules in ways that make Muse, or AI agents more broadly, much less capable. We've seen platform owners do that before.
The second is that the web wasn't really built for AI agents. It was built for humans. If websites decide they don't want agents browsing, clicking, or completing transactions on behalf of users, these products become a lot less useful. We're already seeing some early signs of that. Amazon has blocked Muse from shopping on its site, and services like Goodreads aren't available either.
Ultimately, AI agents are only as useful as the parts of the internet they can access. If the broader web decides not to play ball, that's a problem for not just Muse but for all AI agents.

New Delhi, Sep 23: The Congress on Wednesday alleged that for the Modi government, the UCC is not an instrument of considered legal reform but an instrument of division, disruption and diversion, as well as a tool for stoking prejudices and keeping society in a state of permanent polarisation.
The opposition party's assertion comes after former Bombay High Court judge Justice R C Chavan resigned from the Maharashtra government's panel to prepare a draft for implementing the Uniform Civil Code (UCC), citing serious reservations over its decision to restrict public feedback on crucial social issues to a "Yes/No" format.
Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh said the resignation of a former high court judge from the Maharashtra government's committee to draft a UCC for the state raises larger questions, apart from his several concerns on the functioning of this committee.
Posting his statement on X, Ramesh said, "A retired High Court judge has shown courage to resign from a committee set up by the Maharashtra government to prepare a uniform civil code for the state. Here is our statement on the non-uniform 'Uniform' Civil Codes (UCC) the HM is trying to bulldoze through in every state."
"Did the Constituent Assembly ever imagine a situation in which every state would enact its own separate version of a UCC? The answer is a resounding no," Ramesh said.
Did the architects of our Constitution led by Dr B.R. Ambedkar ever conceive states competing with one another to have different UCCs according to the political machinations and calculations of one political party, he asked.
"Again, the answer is a resounding no," Ramesh added.
He pointed out that on June 17, 2016, the Modi government referred the question of the UCC to the 21st Law Commission of India for detailed examination.
"After extensive research, the Commission published its Consultation Paper on Reform of Family Law on August 31, 2018. Its conclusion appearing in paragraph 1.15 on page 7 of the Consultation Paper was clear: 'The formulation of a Uniform Civil Code is neither necessary nor desirable at this stage'. Instead it recommended addressing nor discrimination within individual family laws while preserving India's legal and cultural diversity," Ramesh said.
The Modi government has chosen to disregard the findings of the very Commission it tasked with examining the issue because the facts, as usual, did not align with its political agenda, the Congress leader said.
Over the last three years, one BJP-ruled State after another bulldozed through its own version of a UCC, Ramesh said.
The UCC came into effect in Uttarakhand from January 27, 2025. Subsequently the Gujarat Assembly passed the UCC Bill on March 24, 2026, the Assam Assembly on May 27, 2026 and the Madhya Pradesh Assembly on July 21, 2026," he pointed out.
Ramesh said these State-level UCCs, never envisaged in the Constitution, are not uniform.
"They contain different provisions, different penalties, different procedures and significant exemptions. Contrary to claims, the Uttarakhand UCC, the only one in force, continues with a number of patriarchal traditions and is creating many problems for perfectly law-abiding residents of the state," Ramesh argued.
Union Home Minister Amit Shah has made a typically bombastic announcement that a UCC will be implemented in all NDA-ruled States before the 2029 Lok Sabha election, he said.
Evidently other NDA parties have lost their voices and are being silenced by the BJP, the Congress general secretary said.
"For the Modi Government, the UCC is not an instrument of considered legal reform to be implemented after the widest possible consultations and public debate and with the broadest possible consensus. It is, in reality, an instrument of division, disruption and diversion, a tool for harassment and intimidation, stoking prejudices and keeping society in a state of permanent polarisation," Ramesh said.
Later, asked about the statement, he said, "The UCC bulldozer is to permanently polarise society."
In a letter to the panel chairperson Justice Ranjana Desai (retd), former Bombay High Court judge Chavan criticised the committee's approach, stating that reducing complex societal questions, such as delayed marriages, perversions, infertility, and rising matrimonial disputes, to binary options undermined the primary purpose of consensus-building.
The former judge said he had misunderstood that the committee aimed to gather views of the people of Maharashtra and to generate a consensus to remedy the issues of late marriages, infertility, unstable marriages, time-consuming dispute resolution mechanism and so on.
"Now that the misunderstanding is removed, I realise that the aim is to just provide an opportunity to people who may care, to share their responses, in a 'yes or no' format to the questions posed so that analysis of data becomes easy," the letter said.
In July, the state government set up a seven-member committee headed by retired Supreme Court Justice Ranjana Desai to draft a framework for implementing the UCC, which seeks to establish equal laws across religions on issues about marriage, divorce, and property.
Justice Chavan, a former high court judge, resigned from the panel on September 19.
The Congress' statement also comes days after Shah said the BJP-led NDA governments in 21 states will introduce UCC before 2029. The next Lok Sabha polls are scheduled for 2029.

Last year, Maddie Kowalski was a regular sophomore attending the University of Florida. Then a series of burner accounts on X started proliferating explicit, nonconsensual videos of her. This week, Zoë Schiffer sits down with WIRED’s senior writer Ej Dickson to discuss the burnerverse, a sprawling, loosely organized network of anonymous accounts that have turned the sexual humiliation of young women into an online participatory sport.

Maddie Kowalski: When I heard that someone had sent a nude photograph of me to his friends at FSU, and in this picture I was heavily intoxicated.

Maddie Kowalski: So right after this, I started getting flooded with messages that I was being talked about all over my school's Yik Yak.
Zoë Schiffer: Yik Yak is a platform popular among college students where you can post anonymously if you're within a specific geographic radius.
Maddie Kowalski: Everything was just happening really fast, and I couldn't comprehend any of it.
Zoë Schiffer: What Maddie had heard about was a single photo, but there were a series of videos in which she was visibly out of it, naked, and performing sexual acts. Maddie remembers, well, she was really drunk that night.
Maddie Kowalski: I felt really detached from the girl in the videos because I had so little memory of the events.
Zoë Schiffer: Obviously, she hadn't consented to any of this, not to being filmed, and certainly not to those films being posted online. But now, it was all over X.
Maddie Kowalski: And at this moment, I just felt my whole world collapse. Everything was being shared and reposted so fast, and I couldn't do anything to stop it.
Zoë Schiffer: The videos had officially gone viral. #MaddieKowalski was trending on X nationwide, and it was viewed more than 8.5 million times. For the next 24 hours, Maddie sat paralyzed on her couch while anonymous internet people harassed her. They posted old photos from before the night the videos were taken. They called and texted her parents all throughout the night. One anonymous man told her father that he'd had sex with her and had since tested positive for HIV. People on X were placing bets on whether by the end of the week she would either start an OnlyFans or kill herself. Here's the thing. The people behind this weren't strangers in some far-off corner of the internet. In many cases, they were her literal classmates hiding behind anonymous burner accounts, mostly used to celebrate college sports. From WIRED's Uncanny Valley, I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor. WIRED senior writer Ej Dickson spent months following Maddie's story and what's become known as the burnerverse, a sprawling, loosely organized network of anonymous accounts that has turned the sexual humiliation of young women into a kind of participatory sport. Ej, thank you so much for coming on.
Ej Dickson: Thank you for having me.
Zoë Schiffer: Can you talk us through what exactly is the burnerverse? How is it organized? Who exactly is part of it?
Ej Dickson: So, the burnerverse is a very loosely organized network. It's unfair to even say network because it's just kind of an amorphous community of college sports fan burner accounts. So, they're all anonymous or mostly anonymous accounts. And I think it's important to note that a lot of them are pretty innocuous, but there is a segment of this community that has emerged that is pretty violently racist and misogynistic and antisemitic. And this is the corner of the subculture that has sort of made a sport out of systemically doxing women. So, I initially found out about the burnerverse in February 2025, a few months, about nine months, before Maddie went viral. And I found out about it because I saw this young woman's name trending on X, and her name was Mary Kate Cornett. And I was really curious. I was like, who is this person? And it turned out to be an Ole Miss college student who there was a campus rumor, a salacious, defamatory rumor, about her sex life that had gone viral on campus that had been elevated to the mainstream and was going viral on X nationally because a bunch of prominent people had picked it up. Barstool Sports personalities, Pat McAfee, talked about it on his podcast. So, I was like, how does this happen? How does a girl's name trend nationally based on a completely unverifiable rumor? This is a private citizen. There's no real news interest here. How does this happen? And that's how I started digging into the burnerverse and how burner accounts made her name go viral.
Zoë Schiffer: Going back to Maddie's story, she gets alerted to the fact that these images and videos are going viral on campus. What was her immediate response? What avenues were available to her, I guess, in terms of reporting or getting the content taken down?
Ej Dickson: So, she had the presence of mind to go to the police department in Gainesville, where she went to school, fairly early. And she was receiving harassing phone calls basically every second of the day at that point from these burner accounts, calling her slut, calling her parents, telling that she had AIDS, that she was a crack whore. Just the most horrible things you can possibly imagine. She couldn't even turn off her phone, she told me, because her phone was ringing so much. She couldn't even press the button to turn it off. And so, she went to the Gainesville Police Department to complain about this, and they basically just told her, "Change your phone number." And she was like, "Oh, OK. Well, that's not really going to do anything." Also, the university contacted her because the university found out about the images going viral before she did, even. That's how massively widespread they were. And they opened up a Title IX investigation, but it was closed after about a month because she says the university told her that there was no evidence that the videos had been filmed on campus, so it was not within their jurisdiction. So, her initial options for recourse were pretty limited, at least at first.
Zoë Schiffer: I'm curious, can you talk through her sorority's response? Were they helpful?
Ej Dickson: I think she considered that one of the biggest betrayals is how her sorority sisters responded to all of this. Her sorority basically disavowed her immediately. They allegedly held meetings discussing how this incident would reflect on them. Many of her sorority sisters blocked her, unfollowed her. Again, I mean, this was a girl who was struggling. She was in her second year of college, 19 years old, drinking heavily, needed support, and your sorority sisters are supposed to stick with you through thick and thin. I mean, you're supposed to be bonded for life. And basically the second that this happens, they completely abandoned her is the way she tells it.
Zoë Schiffer: And eventually, she and her family try and find a lawyer, and you write in the story that it was difficult for them to find someone who could understand the scope of the problem. I believe the line in the story is like, "This wasn't a typical revenge porn case. This was much bigger than that."
Ej Dickson: Yeah, I think that's what was confusing to law enforcement and to the lawyers that the Kowalskis consulted as well. If this had been a simple case of a spurned ex-boyfriend posting a nude or a pornographic video nonconsensually, that would've been much easier to prosecute. That's something that law enforcement has seen before, but this wasn't that. This was a network of total strangers posting the nonconsensual intimate images of a girl they didn't even know, for no apparent reason. And there were so many obstacles in the way. They didn't know who was behind these accounts. They didn't know why they were posting them. They didn't know how they had obtained these videos. To this day, Maddie is not sure how her video was leaked. And I also think it really speaks to the real chasm between the speed with which the viral news cycle evolves and the speed with which our legislation evolves. It simply can't keep up.
Zoë Schiffer: So, there's a moment where I believe it's when she's starting to consult with lawyers. What does she ultimately decide?
Ej Dickson: She ultimately decides to go after the burner accounts, the anonymous men who shared her nonconsensual videos. My understanding is that it took a couple of months for the Gainesville Police Department to subpoena X for these guys' records. Two freshmen boys in a fraternity, Theta Chi, who she did not know. And a third man was also charged, who I believe was a former UF student who had transferred at that point.
Zoë Schiffer: You also write that people don't have a lot of recourse in terms of getting X to take immediate action. This is happening years after Elon Musk has purchased the platform formerly known as Twitter. He famously got rid of much of the trust and safety team. The content policies have been relaxed from what they used to be. And so, how responsive was the platform in getting the content to go away?
Ej Dickson: Well, I mean, the platform didn't respond to me when I asked for comment, and I had a lot of questions for them. I mean, I don't think that this would've happened were it not for Elon Musk acquiring X and dismantling the regulations because X's algorithm amplifies divisive or inflammatory content in such a way that it doesn't really matter what's trending. It's just going to be broadcast nationwide. And it's like a game of whack-a-mole. You can file a take-down request, and apparently the Kowalskis said that X was pretty responsive in terms of actually getting the videos down individually once they filed the request because they're legally required to do that because of the Take It Down Act. But, if you remove one, 10 more pop up in their stead. That's just the way the internet works.
Zoë Schiffer: As things stand now, has anyone specifically been held accountable for what happened to Maddie?
Ej Dickson: So, the men are being charged with sexual cyberharassment which is a misdemeanor that is punishable by up to one year in prison and an $1,000 fine. I believe one of them is ... The police department is alleging that he'd financially profited off of her humiliation. When I reached out to Theta Chi, their fraternity, they said that they were on interim suspension and completely disavowed their activities and said, "This is not what Theta Chi is about." I don't know if that was prompted by my reaching out or if that had already been underway prior. I don't want to speculate, but I had said that she will see them posting from parties and stuff.
Zoë Schiffer: And where does this leave Maddie?
Ej Dickson: She's traumatized. I mean, can you imagine the worst moment of your life goes viral when you're 19 years old, and you don't even remember it? She doesn't think she'll be able to date and find love. She thinks this is going to follow her wherever she goes for the rest of her life. And the first time I met her, she wasn't even particularly emotional about it. It was just fact for her. And I was just sitting there. I'm a parent. It broke my heart. And that's the thing that really haunted me after reporting this and what really stuck with me when I spoke to her best friend who's quoted in the article. They stole her youth. They stole her girlhood. They stole her optimism and her sense of hope and belief that she could do something great with her life. Because that's what college is all about, right? You're kind of on the precipice of all of that. And that just seems like the most egregious theft of all.
Zoë Schiffer: Her experience also isn't an isolated incident, right? How far-reaching is this? How many people has this happened to?
Ej Dickson: So, there are degrees of it. All told, I was able to identify about a little less than a dozen women across the country who had been doxed in this fashion and on this scale. They were all young women in their late teens, early 20s, college students or recently graduated from college, conventionally attractive, and they had all been subject to some sort of salacious rumor or had nonconsensual videos or images of them circulating and were perceived to have transgressed the boundaries of sexual norms, I guess, in some way was kind of the unifying criteria. But, the burner accounts were also doing this on a much smaller scale to teenage girls whose photos were posted on college's incoming students' Instagram pages. They were taking their photos and posting them and making fun of their bodies and the way they looked and posting their full names. Girls who weren't even in college yet, incoming freshmen, they were doxing on a much smaller scale. And they do that pretty regularly. Or, they'll take photos of somebody's dating profile, some girl's dating profile or a message, and they'll post it, and they'll release her name and make fun of her. So, it happens all the time. I think that it's really the scale that differs, but the exposure aspect of it happens all the time.
Zoë Schiffer: Going back to Maddie's story, I'm curious how she felt. Like you said, you talked to her after the article came out. Obviously, it's this decision that I think a lot of sources face where it's like, do you not speak out and hope that the story kind of goes away? Or, do you take the chance and try and take back a little of the narrative?
Ej Dickson: That was really difficult. That was something I was really concerned about because I thought that there was a possibility that it could renew the harassment against her. And we had a number of conversations about that. And I think she understood and understands the impact that her story has and that she has an opportunity to speak for other women who have been through this and to sort of ensure that shame switches sides, that she doesn't need to be ashamed of what happened to her. I think she was a little overwhelmed, but she's a very strong person.
Maddie Kowalski: I'd like to end this with something really important. Although I don't have control over what happened to me, I can control what I do moving forward, and I want to move forward with healing.
Zoë Schiffer: Here's Maddie again. We thought she should close out the story in her own words.
Maddie Kowalski: These last few weeks have been the darkest and hardest moments of my life, but I'm still here, and that's something that I'm really learning to be proud of. I'm taking steps to rebuild myself, to feel safe again, and to understand that what happened to me doesn't define me. And I know that this is a long path. I've unfortunately also realized that there are so many women and girls as well as men who go through things like this in silence, feeling alone or ashamed or afraid to speak. And if sharing my story can help even one person feel seen or teach one person why consent and decency matter, then it's worth it.

The woman, known in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, also said: "My claims that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me while a third celebrity, [name redacted] watched are false. There is no truth to any of my claims against Mr Carter.
"I understand my false accusations have caused Mr Carter immense pain, suffering, and damage that can never be fully undone."
Jay-Z and family's 'trauma'
Carter had vehemently denied the accusations, saying they were a "blackmail attempt" and describing them as "frivolous, fictitious and appalling allegations".
When the accuser dropped her case in February 2025, the rapper, who is married to singer Beyoncé, said: "The trauma that my wife, my children, loved ones and I have endured can never be dismissed."
The woman, from Alabama, has now been removed from Carter's lawsuit.
She said she had not received any money from the rap superstar or anyone acting on his behalf, and had not been paid to make her latest declaration.

She also said Buzbee and other lawyers acting on her behalf filed it "without conducting any independent investigation, background inquiry, or due diligence, and without obtaining any corroboration of the allegations".

Buzbee also represents numerous other people who have made allegations against Combs.

Man City and the 115 charges - key questions answered
- Published
It has taken more than two years, but a judgement finally appears to have been reached on the 115 charges levelled against Manchester City over breaches of Premier League financial rules.
Following a four-year investigation, City were charged and the hearing finally got under way on 16 September 2024.
BBC Sport has now learned a decision has been made, after the Athletic reported City had been found guilty on all almost of the charges.
We are not at the end of this process, however. Far from it.
But what does this mean for City's titles? What about their Premier League status? Will there be an appeal? And how long will it be before this saga does come to an end?
What are the 115 charges?
In February 2023, City were charged and referred to an independent commission over alleged breaches that were said to have taken place between 2009 and 2018.
The charges - relating to Premier League financial rules - are:
- 54 x failure to provide accurate financial information from 2009-10 to 2017-18.
- 14 x failure to provide accurate details for player and manager payments from 2009-10 to 2017-18.
- 5 x failure to comply with Uefa's rules including financial fair play (FFP) 2013-14 to 2017-18.
- 7 x breaching Premier League profit and sustainability (PSR) rules from 2015-16 to 2017-18.
- 35 x failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations from December 2018 to Feb 2023.
City have always denied wrongdoing and BBC Sport has been told they would appeal were they found guilty.
But what does that actually mean?
German newspaper Der Spiegel published leaked documents, including emails purportedly sent between top City executives (some of whom remain at the City Football Group), across several seasons following the club's Abu Dhabi takeover in 2008.
It alleged these showed the club had inflated sponsorship revenue from state-owned airline Etihad and state-controlled telecoms firm Etisalat by disguising direct investment from their holding company (Sheik Mansour's Abu Dhabi United Group, or ADUG) as sponsorship income by channelling the funds through the companies' accounts.
This, it was alleged, was a means of meeting FFP rules introduced by Uefa in 2011 - and PSR brought in by the Premier League in 2012 - limiting clubs' permitted losses.
There then followed further allegations of misreporting financial information centred on documents that claimed to show secret 'off-the-books' payments to then manager Roberto Mancini via consultancy fees from a club in Abu Dhabi.
It is also alleged the club gave players more money than was officially going through the accounts so recorded spending was less than it actually was.
City, who have always maintained ADUG is a private fund rather than an arm of the state, refused to comment on any of Der Spiegel's revelations, saying the leaked emails were obtained illegally, and they were an "attempt to damage the club's reputation".
City - along with the companies involved - strongly denied breaking any financial rules. But that did not stop both Uefa and the Premier League launching investigations as a result.
What has been the timeline of the case?
November 2018: Football Leaks allegations emerge with Der Spiegel publishing claims Manchester City breached financial fair play rules.
March 2019: Uefa launches a formal investigation off the back of Der Spiegel's findings.
May 2019: City criticise the investigation and launch an appeal process.
November 2019: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) deems City's appeal inadmissible.
February 2020: Uefa announces a two-year ban for City from European competitions and a €30m fine.
July 2020: City's European ban is overturned after an appeal to Cas.
July 2021: City lose a jurisdiction ruling that allows the media to report the Premier League is continuing to investigate the champions for alleged financial breaches.
April 2022: Der Spiegel publishes a fresh report claiming the Premier League has been investigating the club for three years, providing detailed claims.
February 2023: The Premier League charges City with 115 financial breaches.
September 2024: The start of a 10-week hearing between the Premier League and City on the 115 charges.
February 2025: City manager Pep Guardiola says the club expect to learn the verdict "within one month". Guardiola left the Etihad at the end of last season.
September 2026: Reports emerge that a verdict has been reached, with sources telling the BBC that City have been found guilty of breaking the majority of the charges.
What punishment could Man City face?
It was never expected the verdict would come complete with the sanctions.
We now face a waiting game for even that verdict to officially be made public by the independent panel.
We don't know who was on the panel that heard and ruled on the case, and that will only come once a written judgment is released.
All options are open to the disciplinary commission:
- Points deduction (immediate or suspended).
- Financial penalties (immediate or suspended).
- Removal from the Premier League.
Being removed from the Premier League would mean City lose their membership and are demoted to a lower division from the end of the season.
That could also happen through a points penalty so severe they would effectively be relegated.
What has been said?
The Premier League declined to comment on the case when approached on Friday.
City issued a statement that showed frustration news of the verdict had leaked.
It read: "The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality.
"As such Manchester City FC's position remains consistent with the club's statement of February 2023.
"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence."
Will there be an appeal? How long would one take?
An appeal from City is expected to be a formality.
City's legal team is being led by Lord Pannick KC, who is reported to charge £5,000 an hour for his services. He helped City overturn their two-year European ban in 2020.
However, considering we are already eight years into this process - and two years beyond the start of the hearing itself - it is impossible to speculate when this could come to an end.
Until now, the case has been watertight, with no media leaks from any of the parties involved.
This is just the latest chapter.
However, while the commission's judgement can be directly appealed against, it is not possible for City to take it to Cas.
What titles did City win and who was affected?
City won the Premier League three times during the period in question.
That includes their first in the Premier League era in 2011-12, plus 2013-14 and 2017-18.
They won the FA Cup in 2011, and the EFL Cup three times - 2013-14, 2015-16 and 2017-18.
Since their 2008 takeover by ADUG, City have won eight league titles, and multiple cups including the Champions League as part of a Treble in 2023.
If the commission choses to hand City's titles to other clubs, this is who could benefit:
Premier League
2011-12: Manchester United
2013-14: Liverpool
2017-18: Manchester United
FA Cup
2010-11: Stoke City
EFL Cup
2013-14: Sunderland
2015-16: Liverpool
2017-18: Arsenal
Could affected clubs claim compensation from City?
Earlier this year, Everton were told they must pay Burnley £35m over the impact of a breach of the Premier League's financial rules.
The case - heard by a Premier League commission - relates to the 2021-22 season, when Everton were found to have broken PSR regulations over a three-year period.
Burnley argued the breach impacted their chances of staying in the Premier League, and sought compensation for the losses associated with being relegated.
The Clarets were awarded £26m in damages and a further £9m in interest.
Clubs who had their league positions impacted by City's offences could potentially claim a loss of chance to win potential honours.
These would need to be individually heard by an independent commission.
How much has the case cost?
This specific case was six years in the making, so legal fees on both sides were estimated at tens of millions of pounds before the hearing even started.
Whichever side 'wins' can be expected to make a claim for costs.
For context, the Premier League wanted Everton to pay the full £4.9m legal costs of their first PSR six-point deduction case.
However, an appeal board ruled Everton should pay £1.7m and the Premier League cover the remaining £3.2m legal fees.
Any costs being paid by the Premier League at the end of the City case would have to be spread across the 20 clubs which make up the league.
Have there been other cases involving Premier League teams?
Comparisons have been drawn to the cases brought by the Premier League against Nottingham Forest and Everton respectively over breaches of PSR.
During the 2023-24 season, both clubs were docked points for making more losses than they were permitted to for the three-year period from the 2020-21 to 2022-23 seasons.
Those cases were of a single charge, were easier to decipher and involved significantly less evidence.
Everton were twice deducted points. For the first charge, they were docked six points - reduced from 10 points on appeal. The second offence led to them being handed a two-point penalty.
Forest, meanwhile, lost four points.
However, these relate purely to PSR.
Why are the Man City and Chelsea cases different?
Chelsea have faced 74 charges of rule breaches, but these were quite different and primarily focused on transfers that happened between the 2010-11 and 2015-16 seasons, including deals for Eden Hazard, Samuel Eto'o and Willian.
The Premier League fined Chelsea £10m and handed out a suspended transfer ban after admitting making £47m in secret payments.
Importantly, Chelsea reached a settlement with the Premier League in relation to historical regulatory matters that were self-reported.
This has not been the case with City, who have always denied wrongdoing.
The Blues were also fined by Uefa and the Football Association.

Four civilians killed in Pakistani strikes in Afghanistan, Taliban says
- Published
Afghanistan's Taliban government said a wave of Pakistani air strikes had killed four civilians in the latest escalation between the two sides.
The strikes hit provinces including Kandahar, the Taliban's base of power, sources told the BBC. A resident told AFP news agency they heard a jet, followed by a large explosion and then a fire in the city.
Pakistan said its forces had struck 10 targets in Afghanistan, without specifying their locations, adding the strikes were "strictly limited to identified military objectives".
It's the second wave of Pakistani air strikes on Afghan territory in the past week, and comes after a deadly attack on a police facility in Pakistan on 18 September.
In a statement, the Taliban said there would be an "appropriate response" following the attack, while Pakistan said any further "provocative act" would be responded to.
Taliban government spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said the attacks were in Afghanistan's Kandahar, Paktia and Khost provinces.
In Paktia, an official said jets had bombed the Afghan Armed Forces' 203 Mansouri Corps, which is controlled by the Taliban, without providing any information on casualties.
In Khost, a spokesman said houses were damaged in the strikes, with no casualties reported. Abdullah, a local eyewitness, told Reuters news agency the strikes happened around midnight.
"People were shouting, and there was panic all around," he said. "Afterwards, the village elder arrived and called out to the houses, asking if anyone was killed. Thankfully, no one was killed."
Another local, Salamat Khan, told Reuters that "there is no military base here, nor are there any military personnel", adding "there are only the homes of ordinary civilians".
Zabihullah Mujahid labelled the attack as "reckless, careless, and hostile", and said it "will have adverse consequences for the Pakistani military".
Pakistan's Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the strikes were "deliberate, precise, calibrated, and proportionate, and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan".
The Taliban and Pakistan had enjoyed three months of relative calm, until fighting reignited following an attack on a mosque at a police compound in north-western Pakistan last week, which killed at least 31 people, according to AFP.
A group linked to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has waged a violent campaign against Pakistan for years, claimed the attack.
Islamabad has accused Kabul of harbouring the TTP. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies this, saying militancy is Pakistan's internal problem.
Following the attack on the police facility, Pakistan said earlier this week it launched air strikes in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, killing 28 militants.
Farid Dehqan, a spokesman for the Taliban government in Kunar province, told the BBC that three people were killed and four others were injured in the strike. The UN mission Unama also confirmed that at least three civilians were killed.
Then on Wednesday, Pakistan said it detected drones launched from Afghanistan into its territory and that all of them were "neutralised". Taliban officials denied that their government had launched drones against Pakistan that day.
Unama said in July that cross-border armed violence between Taliban government forces and Pakistani security forces killed at least 499 civilians and wounded 1,216 others between October 2025 and June 2026.
The worst single incident occurred in March, when more than 269 people were killed, external in a Pakistani air strike on Kabul, which the Afghan Taliban said hit a drug rehabilitation centre. Islamabad denied the charge, saying it "precisely targeted military installations and terrorist support infrastructure".
The neighbouring countries had agreed a ceasefire in March, but international mediation has failed to produce a lasting resolution.
During a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly earlier this week, Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called for "concrete and verifiable" measures to ensure that Afghan territory is not used for "terrorism".

Sweden and Finland have scrambled fighter jets to intercept Russian military aircraft over the Gulf of Finland, in their first such joint operation.
The Russian aircraft was flying in international airspace over the Gulf of Finland, an area on high alert as Russia’s war with Ukraine spills into Europe in the form of gas pipeline outages, drone sightings and airspace violations.
Ulf Kristersson, Sweden’s prime minister, said the Thursday operation showed how the so-called Quick Reaction Alert cooperation could defend the nordic countries’ airspace.
"It is a concrete expression of the readiness and trust we have built together – and an expression of the strength in the Nordic, Nordic-Baltic, and broader NATO cooperation in our part of the world," Kristersson he wrote on X.
It comes as Denmark’s intelligence has warned that there is “a low but growing risk” that Russia would launch a limited military attack against one or several Nato countries that border it.
Such attacks could include isolated strikes with long-range weapons like drones or missiles on infrastructure supporting Ukraine, or false-flag operations using Ukrainian-made drones, intelligence service chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said at a press conference.
Recap: Ukraine WILL receive Patriot licences, says Zelensky
Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday that Donald Trump had at last agreed to issue Ukraine with the licences to produce vital Patriot interceptor missiles in house, reducing reliance on foreign imports and allowing the country to defend against Russian aerial attacks.
“There are concrete agreements regarding Patriot licenses,” the Ukrainian president said.
“At our meeting, President Trump stressed that he had made his final decision: Ukraine will receive licenses to produce Patriot missiles.”
100,000 homes without internet following Russian strikes on data centres, says Ukraine
Ukraine has accused Russia of ramping up strikes on its data centres and telecommunications facilities, causing massive disruption to internet access across the capital.
Some 100,000 homes in Kyiv and the surrounding areas were hit by temporary internet outages following strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, Ukraine’s digital transformation ministry said.
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said on Wednesday the attacks on the data centres endangered people's lives.
"Russia has targeted major Ukrainian data centers, seeking to disrupt the flow of information. Rapid alerts about missile and drone threats are essential - they save lives," he wrote on X.
Russia's Defence Ministry, in a post on Telegram, said its forces had launched strikes on a number of data centres and logistics and warehouse sites it said were being used for the benefit of the Ukrainian military.
Finland asks Musk to expand Starlink coverage for Ukraine
Finnish president Alexander Stubb said he has asked Elon Musk to extend Starlink coverage into Russian territory, arguing that it could help Ukraine locate Russian ballistic missile launchers.
Starlink has been a key part of Ukraine’s battlefield communications since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 and is also used to support drone operations, but its coverage does not extend over Russia.
Ukraine faces a shortage of air defences against ballistic missiles and believes access to Starlink over Russian territory could improve its ability to identify launch sites.
Nato says it is prepared for sabotage and drone incidents
Nato secretary general Mark Rutte has reassured member states that the alliance has plans to respond to drone and sabotage incidents, following a Danish warning that Russia could intensify hybrid operations across Europe.
The concerns were heightened by a fire at a Starlink facility in Poland, which Polish officials said was deliberate, although they have not identified those responsible.
Rutte said Nato was prepared for such threats, as European governments increasingly focus on protecting critical infrastructure from cyberattacks, sabotage and other forms of disruption.
Moscow has denied involvement in sabotage incidents attributed to Russia.
Swedish, Finnish fighter jets intercept Russian military aircraft
Swedish and Finnish fighter jets were scrambled on Thursday to intercept and identify Russian military aircraft flying in international airspace over the Gulf of Finland, the Finnish Air Force said on Friday.
The operation was carried out as part of a joint Swedish-Finnish framework for monitoring and protecting the two countries’ airspace, the Finnish Air Force said in a statement.
The fighter jets tracked and identified a group of Russian aircraft, including a transport plane and several fighter jets, it added.
Zelensky broke confidentiality with North Korea POWs disclosure, South Korean president Lee Jae Myung says
South Korean president Lee Jae Myung accused Ukraine of breaking a confidentiality agreement by publicly revealing that two North Korean soldiers captured while fighting for Russia had been sent to South Korea.
Zelensky announced the transfer during his UN speech, saying Ukraine had handed over the two POWs to South Korea after consultations.
Lee wrote on X: “I do not know why the Ukrainian side broke the agreement and made the matter public, but it is very disappointing.
“The issue of bringing North Korean prisoners to South Korea is a highly sensitive one that could have a major impact on diplomacy, security and the situation on the Korean Peninsula,” he said.
His comments came as opposition parties in South Korea questioned Lee for hiding arrival of North Korean troops in South Korea after it was first revealed by Zelensky.
Lee said those who “harm someone's life, national interest, or security for their own petty gain are called murderers or traitors”.
“Criticising valid and justified confidentiality measures is wrong,” he said.
Russian strikes kill eight across Ukraine
Russian missile and drone strikes across Ukraine killed eight people on Thursday, including six people at a vegetable storage facility in the northeastern Kharkiv region, according to Ukrainian officials.
Two people were killed in Kyiv, where strikes damaged residential buildings, a maternity hospital, a post office, warehouses and dozens of cars.
Ukraine’s air force said the overnight barrage involved 282 drones as well as an unspecified number of hypersonic and ballistic missiles, authorities said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine needed more ballistic interceptors to protect civilians, while claiming Kyiv had reached an agreement for a new package of missiles for Patriot air defence systems.
Europe's crackdown sharply reduces number of shadow fleet ships, report says
Western efforts to crack down on Russia’s shadow fleet have sharply reduced the number of vessels sailing under false flags, according to a 25 September report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
The number of such vessels fell from a peak of 101 in October 2025 to 45 by the end of June 2026, as European countries stepped up enforcement and traditional open ship registries tightened oversight, The Kyiv Independent reported.
The crackdown has pushed many vessels towards Russia’s own registry: the number of ships registered under the Russian flag rose 36 per cent to 382 between January 2025 and June 2026, with 87 per cent of the newly registered vessels already under sanctions, CREA said.

New York continues to fight prediction markets with a lawsuit against Polymarket
The state now has illegal gambling charges underway against four of these businesses.
The state of New York continues to take action against prediction markets, arguing that they are running illegal gambling businesses. Today, the state's Attorney General Letitia James and Governor Kathy Hochul announced a new lawsuit against the domestic branch of Polymarket. The duo are seeking a court order "stopping Polymarket from operating as an unlicensed gambling business in New York state," according to the AG's office.
James also has a similar lawsuit underway against Kalshi that launched in July and she sued Coinbase Financial Markets and Gemini Titan in April. New York is one of several states attempting to reign in prediction markets and regulate them as gambling operations. Some of the state-level suits, including this latest action by New York against Polymarket, also argue that the prediction markets allow underage betting. Most prediction market users must be over 18, but the minimum age for sports betting in many states is 21.
However, the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission has intervened and counter-sued some states for those efforts. The federal agency has alleged that it should be the sole regulator for prediction markets and claims that the states' legal actions fall outside their jurisdiction.
The courts have been divided thus far on the question of prediction market regulation. The first ruling on the topic, which came from a panel from the 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals, sided with the CFTC over New Jersey. However, the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals favored Nevada's case against Kalshi last month, blocking the company's attempt to prevent the state from regulating its activities.

‘Strongest El Niño on record’ could keep extreme weather raging for months
The hurricane season in the Pacific Ocean already has been very active, thanks to the El Nino weather phenomenon

The Pacific Ocean is experiencing an unusually severe hurricane season, with weeks of persistent storm activity and several months still remaining in the cycle.
An uninterrupted sequence of tropical storms has developed in recent weeks, driven by El Niño conditions that emerged in June. Higher-than-average ocean temperatures have subsequently disrupted global weather patterns across much of the world.
"It’s ramping up to be perhaps the strongest El Niño on record," said University of Miami hurricane expert Brian McNoldy.
Storm counts in the eastern Pacific have already outpaced an average season. Hurricane Polo has been drenching Mexico's Pacific coast while shifting between Category 4 and 5 strength, and Hawaii faces potential catastrophic flooding from the growing Tropical Storm Nolo.
When El Niño forms, the low-level easterly surface winds across the Pacific weaken or reverse direction. This alters the jet stream and contributes to record atmospheric temperatures, intense droughts, wildfires, and reduced freshwater availability worldwide.
These climate phenomena occur unpredictably every two to seven years on average and range from mild to severe. McNoldy anticipates the current pattern will peak this coming winter and persist through 2027.
"It doesn’t turn off right away," he said.
Although Pacific storm numbers are surging, El Niño typically suppresses storm formation across the Atlantic Ocean, where tropical activity has remained virtually silent this year.
Matthew Rosencrans, lead hurricane season forecaster at NOAA’s National Weather Service, noted that both the eastern and central Pacific regions have logged four more named storms than average, despite having over two months remaining in the hurricane season.
Historical data from 1991 to 2020 shows an average of 15 named storms per season in the eastern Pacific, which spans from May 15 to Nov. 30.
Exceeding that figure by September is unusual, Rosencrans pointed out: "That's a different story," he said.
Adding to the severity, three Pacific hurricanes have reached Category 5 intensity this season, tying a record set during another El Niño year in 2002, Rosencrans explained.
The most active season on record for the eastern Pacific occurred in 1992 with 25 named storms, while the central Pacific recorded its peak of 14 storms in 2015.
During that 2015 season, the eastern Pacific produced nine major storms of Category 3 or higher without causing any reported fatalities. The El Niño pattern directed those storms further west, allowing them to remain over open ocean waters throughout their cycle.
In contrast, a powerful El Niño in 1997 brought Hurricane Pauline across Mexico’s Pacific shore, leaving hundreds dead. That same year, Tropical Storm Nora delivered rare heavy rainfall to landlocked southwestern Arizona, while a December storm in Southern California triggered severe flooding that swept cars into storm channels and prompted mobile home evacuations.
In 1998, El Niño was blamed for devastating floods along China's Yangtze River that killed 4,150 people.
Hawaii has faced repeated threats in recent weeks, having already suffered damage from two hurricanes over the past month. Hurricanes Lala in August and Lowell in early September combined to destroy or damage more than 510 homes and caused $168 million in damage to public infrastructure, alongside $21.5 million in destruction to 38 schools from Lala.
If Tropical Storm Nola follows forecasts and strengthens dramatically as it tracks south of the islands, it will mark the third system to impact the state. Weather forecasters warn the storm could drop several feet of rain across parts of the region.
The state was already recovering from severe March rainfall—the worst flooding in two decades—and a magnitude-6.0 earthquake in May, leading Gov. Josh Green to say this year has been "unlike anything I can recall."
Two hurricanes came within 200 miles (320 kilometers) of Hawaii in 1957, an occurrence that did not repeat for over half a century until similar threats occurred in 2014, 2016, 2018, and now this year.
While meteorologists frequently monitor "preparedness fatigue"—where residents gear up for storms that fail to materialize—John Bravender, a weather service warning coordination meteorologist, explained that 2026 has introduced a distinct form of exhaustion in Hawaii.
"The fact that we’ve had these damaging impacts that keep happening, and as we’re recovering from them, we have to get ready for the next event — that’s a new one that really drains the resources and leads to this overall sense that this is a very busy hurricane season for us," he said.
Island residents understand the risks and are growing more accustomed to preparing.
"I think community members realize how dangerous the weather can be, how important it is for them to be self-sufficient, have food, water and also look out for their neighbors," Bravender added.

China and the US are racing ahead on AI. Can they manage risks together?
Beijing and Washington told to tackle rising AI threats together at Singapore forum, but some argue fears about runaway technology are overblown
The United States and China must work together to establish safety guardrails for artificial intelligence, leading scholars and industry leaders said at a Singapore forum, warning that rapid advances in the technology demand stronger risk controls.
Speaking at the FutureChina Business Forum on Friday, Jude Blanchette, managing director of consultancy Macro Advisory Partners, urged the two superpowers to find common ground despite escalating geopolitical tensions.
“If ever there was a moment for [the US and China] to feel a strong impetus to come together, it would be now … given the shared concerns about the impact of emerging technologies, not only AI but also robotics,” Blanchette said.
He argued that the world was moving from an era shaped by traditional human behaviour to a “technocene” in which exponential technological leaps would dramatically reshape global power dynamics.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday lauded the rhino conservation efforts in the country and said the Project Rhino has been initiated for financial and technical support to the range states for protection, habitat management, and understanding population dynamics of the endangered species.
On the occasion of World Rhino Day, Modi said the country celebrates the magnificent greater one-horned rhinoceros and lauds all those at the forefront of its protection.
“Assam now holds nearly 80 per cent of the world’s rhino population and Kaziranga’s efforts to end rhino poaching have been extensively appreciated,” he said in a post on ‘X’.
The prime minister said on one hand, rhinos have either returned or are well protected in parts of Bihar and West Bengal, on the other hand, success of reintroduction of rhinos in Dudhwa (Uttar Pradesh) is creating history.
“This shows the sustained commitment of our people towards animal protection and active wildlife management in the range states,” he said.
Taking species conservation in the country forward, Modi said he was happy to share that Project Rhino has been initiated for financial and technical support to the range states for protection, habitat management, genetic improvement and understanding population dynamics.
World Rhino Day is a day of awareness for all five rhino species and the work being done to save them. Since 2011, World Rhino Day has been celebrated internationally on September 22 by rhino experts and advocates around the world.
The day is especially important to raise awareness of the plight of rhinos because they are regularly poached for their horns which are sold illegally and used in traditional medicine — despite no scientific proof that these remedies work.

South Sudan's president dissolves government ahead of country's first elections
- Published
South Sudan President Salva Kiir has dissolved the transitional government, three months before the country's first election since its independence in 2011.
The country has previously postponed elections twice and extended the transitional period several times.
Under the amended law, signed on Monday, Kiir removed the country's five vice-presidents and dissolved parliament, as well as national and state governments.
Kiir is the presidential candidate of his Sudan People's Liberation Movement (SPLM). No prominent figures have announced plans to challenge him in the December poll. The main opposition leader Riek Machar was sacked as vice-president last year and charged with treason.
He is under house arrest.
Machar had been named vice-president as part of a 2018 peace deal to end a five-year civil war between forces loyal to the two men.
Kiir will remain in office with full constitutional powers until an elected president is sworn in. He also reappointed some ministers and governors in caretaker positions until the 22 December elections.
Ahead of Tuesday's announcement a heavy security presence was reported in the capital, Juba. Soldiers from the army and national security services blocked access to government ministries. Soldiers were also seen patrolling parts of the city.
A senior government official told the BBC that staff arriving for work were turned away and told to return the following Monday.
UN agencies in Juba also asked staff to work remotely while the situation was monitored.
- South Sudan's leader sacks aides after dead man appointed 
  - Published3 February
Kiir last week dismissed the chairman of the national elections commission, Abednego Akok Kacuol, without giving a reason. He was replaced by the commission's secretary-general, Gabriel Bol Deng.
Akok had said in August that the commission needed $250m (£190m) to conduct the election but had received only $21m.
The main opposition group, the Sudan People's Liberation Movement in Opposition (SPLM-IO), the party of Machar, said on Thursday it would not take part in the polls.
It has written to the African Union and other agencies warning that the country had entered a "constitutional and legitimacy crisis".
"We will not participate in, validate, or lend legitimacy to an electoral process held without key constitutional, security and legal reforms," the party said in the letter.
"Parts of the country remained outside of the government's control and we are wondering how people in those areas would be able to vote," acting SPLM-IO chairman Nathaniel Oyet told the BBC.
"This means that the the elections are a way for Kiir to seek legitimacy," he said.
The body which oversees implementation of the 2018 peace agreement, the Reconstituted Joint Monitoring and Evaluation Commission (RJMEC), said South Sudan had entered a "critical phase".
It said several key talks under the agreement remained incomplete and urged the parties to agree on a path towards credible elections and a peaceful end to the transitional period, which has lasted since independence.
The latest 24-month extension was due to end on 22 February 2027.

Internet restricted after fighting breaks out in Ethiopia's Tigray region
- Published
Internet and call services have been disrupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray after fighting broke out this week between regional forces and the national army.
Services provided by state-owned telecoms operator Ethio Telecom have been completely cut, although those from the much smaller private firm Safaricom remain operational. Internet monitoring group NetBlocks earlier posted on X that network data indicated a sub-national internet shutdown in northern Tigray.
"Last night telecommunications got knocked out," Duke Burbridge, an American humanitarian worker in Tigray's capital, Mekelle, told the BBC's Newsday programme.
The BBC has contacted Ethiopia's authorities for comment.
Burbridge said there had been a scarcity of cash in Tigray for the past eight months, with people unable to access ATMs so the lack of internet services would be "devastating for everybody".
Many people rely on banking and mobile money applications for transactions, with the majority using Ethio Telecom and Safaricom's networks to access these services.
Clashes between Tigrayan forces and their allies and Ethiopia's federal troops broke out on Wednesday, prompting heightened tension and reports of panic buying.
During the two-year civil which ended in 2022, Tigray was totally cut off from the outside world.
Limited access to cash, food and medicine pushed hundreds of thousands into famine-like conditions.

Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome is a seldom-discussed group of conditions that affect the connective tissue of the human body, typically loosening or weakening it. Connective tissue supports and provides flexibility to the skin, tendons, ligaments, bones, blood vessels, and organs.
EDS is generally inherited and is commonly associated with hypermobility, meaning one’s joints can move past their normal range of motion. But hypermobile EDS, or hEDS, which often comes with a higher risk of bruising and injury, is only the most common among the 13 types of EDS, some of which are very rare.
In fact, one of the rare forms of the condition, vascular EDS, can be life-threatening. Here’s all you need to know about Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome.
Why does EDS occur?
EDS is caused by certain genetic changes and is generally passed down to children by their parents. These genetic changes affect how one’s body makes and uses collagen, a protein that gives structure and strength to joints, skin, blood vessels, and other tissues.
However, in some people, it can occur randomly due to genetic mutations with no family history of the condition.
What are the different types of EDS and their symptoms?
The most common form of EDS is hEDS. Hypermobile EDS, like some other types of EDS, presents with symptoms such as stretchy, fragile skin, loose and clicky joints that dislocate easily, joint pain, and joint hypermobility. hEDS may also manifest as extreme fatigue, skin that bruises quickly, digestive issues, and poor bladder control, among other symptoms.
Classical EDS, which is another, less common type of EDS, also exhibits similar symptoms, but it mostly affects the skin. A person with this condition might have very stretchy and fragile skin that bruises easily or splits easily, especially around the elbows, on the forehead, and on the knees. Wounds may also take longer to heal, and they may leave obvious scars.
The rarer form, vascular EDS, affects one’s internal organs. This results in fragile blood vessels that can tear easily and cause internal bleeding, which can be life-threatening. This condition poses a serious risk of bowel tearing, womb tearing during pregnancy, and lung collapse, among others. Pregnant women with EDS must, therefore, discuss this condition with their gynaecologist/obstetrician.
Another type of EDS, called kyphoscoliotic EDS (kEDS), which is also rare, affects the curvature of the spine. It might manifest during early childhood and is also characterised by joint hypermobility and loose joints.
How is EDS diagnosed?
Most people with EDS generally show symptoms of hEDS, which is diagnosed through physical and not genetic testing. It is also important to note that joint hypermobility is common, and it need not necessarily be caused by hEDS; it could also be a result of hypermobility spectrum disorder. Consult a general practitioner, who may refer you to a specialist if you exhibit symptoms of hEDS.
Some of the rarer forms of EDS may be diagnosed through genetic testing.
How can EDS be treated?
There is no cure for EDS, but symptoms, especially those of hEDS, can be managed. For some, however, the symptoms can be disabling.
A physiotherapist could help recommend muscle and joint strengthening exercises that could have both short- and long-term benefits. In addition to this, doctors may also recommend pain management and appropriate treatment for bowel-related issues.
Depending on the severity of the condition, persons may have to avoid certain activities, such as weight-lifting or contact sports, that put undue pressure on the joints. However, low-risk activities including swimming and pilates could help individuals stay fit.

How to Get and Hatch Eggs in Ride A Pet
Most eggs appear as world spawns that you must locate and carry back in Ride A Pet. Here is how you can do so:
- Use a Radar: Equip the appropriate Radar when you need help locating the target.
- Follow the marker: Travel toward the location shown by your active Radar.
- Pick up the egg: Interact with the egg after reaching its location.
- Return home: Carry the egg back to your plot before the timer runs out.
- Place the egg: Put the egg inside your ranch by clicking anywhere.
- Wait for the hatch: Allow the egg to finish growing before clicking E to hatch it.
If you are looking for rare eggs, they spawn pretty far from the main hub. We suggest you keep your fastest pet equipped and leave enough space in your Egg Basket. There is a chance of eggs being stolen, so it is better to reach the egg before others do.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

US backs Elon Musk's bid to overturn €120m EU fine against X
- Published
The US government is seeking to join Elon Musk's legal challenge to overturn a €120m (£105m) EU fine against X over its blue tick badges.
In December 2025, the European Commission said the platform "deceives users" by allowing people to pay for a blue verified check mark, because it is not "meaningfully verifying" who is behind the account.
But US Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said on Thursday that the commission had "inappropriately attempted" to expand its reach to American companies outside its control.
Musk, who spent millions helping elect Donald Trump and other Republicans, has previously claimed EU tech regulation "inhibits progress" for companies.
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has filed an application, external with the EU's General Court in support of Musk's and X's attempts to dismiss the case.
It claims that under a section of law in the Statute of the Court of Justice of the EU, a state may intervene in disputes before the court if it "can establish an interest in the result of the case to the court".
The DOJ said the US "has a clear interest" in ensuring any decision by the commission was applied consistently with "how territorial jurisdiction is generally understood in international law".
It also wants to make sure it would not "otherwise prejudice" US-headquartered digital services that "contribute significantly" to its economy.
In a press briefing on Friday, external, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said it was "ready to defend" its position in court.
He added that the commission had an "solid case" at its disposal, due to the alleged breach of its Digital Services Act.
In addition to its use of blue ticks, EU regulators had accused X of failing to provide transparency around its adverts and denying researchers access to public data.
Henna Virkkunen, the regulator's executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, said at the time of the fine's issue it was "holding X responsible for undermining users' rights and evading accountability".
"Deceiving users with blue checkmarks, obscuring information on ads and shutting out researchers have no place online in the EU," she said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had criticised the EU regulator, accusing it of attacking and censoring US firms.
"The European Commission's fine isn't just an attack on X, it's an attack on all American tech platforms and the American people by foreign governments," Rubio wrote in a post on X.
"The days of censoring Americans online are over."
His remarks were reposted by Musk, who added "absolutely".
The European Commission denied targeting any specific nationality, stating it is simply protecting its digital and democratic standards to maintain its role as a global benchmark.
The action marked the Commission's first official non-compliance decision under the Digital Services Act (DSA), one of two mandatory rulebooks governing online platforms in the EU.
However, the EU is also conducting several other investigations into the platform, including one into its integrated AI assistant Grok over concerns it was used to create sexualised images of real people.
