Srinagar, Sep 22: The ongoing Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly session has come under criticism from All Party Sikh Coordination Committee Chairman and senior political leader Jagmohan Singh Raina, who alleged that the House is spending more time on political confrontations and Jammu-versus-Kashmir rhetoric than on issues directly affecting the public.
The Assembly witnessed uproar over the cancellation of the December 5 holiday commemorating the birth anniversary of Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah, founder and leader of the National Conference. During the proceedings, questions were also raised over the continuation of the holiday marking the birth anniversary of Maharaja Hari Singh, with demands for its cancellation as well.
Reacting to the developments, Raina, as per a statement issued on Tuesday, said people elect legislators with the expectation that their problems will be raised in the Assembly, debated and followed by concrete efforts to find solutions.
He questioned why legislators were engaging in political confrontation instead of using the Assembly to bring resolutions on issues affecting ordinary citizens.
Raina also expressed concern over what he described as increasing Jammu-versus-Kashmir rhetoric inside the House. He said issues surrounding Article 370 and Article 35A should not overshadow the pressing concerns for which people expect their elected representatives to work.
According to Raina, the Assembly should give greater attention to unemployment, vacant posts in the health sector, shortage of doctors and paramedical staff, and vacancies in educational institutions.
He alleged that thousands of posts remain vacant across different departments and questioned whether the government has a clear long-term strategy to address unemployment and staffing shortages, particularly in healthcare and education.
Raina said every MLA should use the Assembly platform to highlight problems faced by people in their respective constituencies and seek practical solutions.
He also referred to earlier Assemblies, saying that, in his view, legislators had maintained greater decorum and devoted more attention to government programmes, policies and public welfare.

It took MapQuest until 2026 to add public transit directions
The 30-year-old map service is quickly getting with the times.
MapQuest is having a moment after refusing to follow along with Google Maps and Apple Maps and rename Lake Ontario. Its decision to hold firm led many folks to turn to its app, which rocketed up the App Store and Google Play charts. The service is now capitalizing on that by adding public transit directions, a feature it probably should have had in 2009 or so. It's available in the iOS and Android MapQuest app now and it's coming to the web soon.
At the outset, MapQuest supports transit directions for almost 2,000 cities across 70 countries. The feature includes door-to-door trip planning (factoring in buses, trains, trams and walking); real-time departure and delay information for more than 350 cities; details about station entrances and access points; and multiple route options. Y'know, much like MapQuest's competitors have had for well over a decade.
MapQuest says millions of people "rediscovered the brand overnight" after it declined to start referring to Lake Ontario as "Lake America," following an executive order from President Donald Trump. It said that many of the returning or new users, particularly those in major cities, wanted to make MapQuest their go-to navigation app, but they needed transit directions first. Updates are in the works, including expanded coverage and live navigation to guide users to their destinations.
The platform's developers have been racing to add other features, including Android Auto support. Having public transit directions is especially important, though. It's great that the 30-year-old MapQuest has finally added that critical feature, even if it took the stupidest possible catalyst to get there.

We’re not even a full year into the new regulations, and Formula 1 is already thinking hard about its next iteration, set to be introduced as early as the start of 2030.
This was supposed to be a big year for F1, with the introduction of a bold new technical rules package that puts far more emphasis on the electric side of the cars’ hybrid power units than before. But those rules were perhaps too ambitious for 2026, with batteries that can only power the electric motor for a tiny fraction of a lap. Such was the shock of getting it wrong that F1 may fast-track a fix for 2030 rather than 2031, when the next set of rules is currently set to start. And according to a report in Autosport, there is now some agreement on what those power units will look like.
Where are we now?
The current rules were finalized several years ago, when optimism about electrification among automakers was high. F1 wanted more of those automakers, and automakers wanted more electrification. The sport would give it to them with a near 50:50 split between a small 1.6 L V6 turbo and an electric motor, both driving the rear wheels. The idea worked. Audi, Cadillac, and Ford have all signed up since, joining Mercedes, Ferrari, and Honda, which recommitted after pulling out in 2021.
But an F1 car is of limited size, and energy density is such that the 4 MJ (1.1 kWh) battery can last maybe 11 or 12 seconds at full throttle. Meanwhile, even the shortest lap time recorded in 2026, during qualifying in Austria, took George Russell 1 minute and 6.113 seconds from start to finish. So one can see the issue. Even allowing for regenerating energy under braking, many of F1’s most classic venues lack sufficient brake zones to recharge more than a fraction of the energy demand of an entire lap.
Adding a front electric motor would have made the cars more efficient and allowed them to recapture more energy under braking. But the existing power unit manufacturers allegedly feared new entrant Audi’s expertise with all-wheel drive hybrids and blocked the idea.

Israel game should not go ahead - Republic of Ireland's Knight
- Published
Jason Knight has become the first Republic of Ireland player to publicly voice his opposition to playing Israel on Sunday.
The sides are due to meet in Debrecen, Hungary at 19:45 BST, with the return fixture in Backa Topola, Serbia on 4 October.
Since the sides were drawn together in Group B3, there has been increasing calls in Ireland to withdraw from the games due to the ongoing war in Gaza with a 'Stop The Game' campaign gathering pace.
Speaking before Thursday's 1-0 defeat by Kosovo in Pristina, Republic stand-in skipper Dara O'Shea confirmed the players would meet on Friday to discuss their approach to Sunday's 'home' game against Israel, which will have no Irish fans in attendance, before their behind-closed-doors match the following week.
"Look, it's difficult, the manager, and Dara, and Nathan [Collins] spoke well about it, I don't think the game should be going ahead but it is going ahead," Knight said following the Kosovo game.
"We'll have a deeper talk about it and what that means, we'll get our thoughts as a group and go from there.
"I think it was a difficult one. It's obviously big talk in Ireland. I have been focusing on my football in England in the Championship. But I knew this was coming so I had a think about it."
The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.
In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations (UN).
"We had chats about it with the players, and more senior players on what the step will be," added Bristol City midfielder Knight.
"Now we're here, we can have a really in depth talk of what that means and what the consequences are. We'll do that [on Friday] and go from there.
"I am quite experienced. None of us have gone through this scenario before but I'd like to think I'm experienced, thick skin and can get through most things and that is what I will try and do.
"I'll try and focus on the football as much as I can. I'll give my view and my thoughts on when I see fit, but I'll be trying to focus on the football as much as possible."

Child predators are arguably the most reviled demographic in society.
So when someone like Chris Hansen, the former NBC Dateline journalist and host of the To Catch a Predator series, decides to take up the mantle of exposing them to the public, he is naturally praised as a hero.
But, as is revealed in Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime—a dramatized snapshot of Hansen’s life at the show’s peak—it’s not as simple as that. Exposing allegedly bad people for public entertainment brings up a lot of ethical concerns and unintended consequences. And while many of the vigilantes carrying out these sting operations claim they are doing a public service, their motivations become a lot more suspect when fame and money are involved.
To Catch a Predator launched in 2004. In the show, Hansen’s team would pair up with civilian watchdog group Perverted Justice, using adult “decoys” to pose as minors online and exchange messages with men in chatrooms and private DMs. After the conversations became sexual, the crew would set up a sting, inviting these men to a home to meet the decoy, only to have Hansen confront them, uttering his catchphrase, “Have a seat.” The men were technically free to leave instead of sitting for an on-camera interview, but often police were waiting outside to arrest them.
The show developed an intense fandom that remains active to this day in subreddits like r/tcap, which has 52,000 weekly visitors, despite the fact that NBC stopped airing the original series in 2007.
In A24's Primetime, a darkly told character study in theaters September 25, Hansen (Robert Pattinson) clearly enjoys the praise and seems desperate for more accolades. He brags to his two young sons that he’s about to be on prime-time television, despite them not understanding the importance of that, and complains that the show has “never won an Emmy or any of the significance it deserves.” When a fan recognizes Hansen on a flight and becomes bloodthirsty, asking the TV host if he ever wants to “bleed” the predators he’s outing, Hansen smiles and admits that what he does by disgracing them on national television is “a little worse.”
In real life, Hansen cofounded the streaming service Trublu in November 2022, where he continues his investigations into alleged child predators. But these days, he’s far from alone. His work has inspired copycats, who thrive on social media and streaming platforms like YouTube, Kick, and Facebook. These groups and individuals are largely disorganized, and as such, hard to track, but a 2022 Washington Post investigation identified at least 160 in the US. Arguably, the people running these operations are more reckless, in part because they’re driven by virality.
One of them, who goes by Skeet Hansen, was featured in the 2025 MTV documentary Predators, about the Dateline show. In the film, directed by David Osit, Skeet Hansen responds to the criticism of the movement by saying, “There’s never been a detective that solved a murder that didn't get paid for it. So why shouldn't I be able to monetize off of catching these guys like the original show and making this content for people’s entertainment?”
One of many issues with that argument is that these hunters aren’t professional investigators—and sometimes they get things wrong.
In April, YouTuber and Kick streamer Vitaly Zdorovetskiy apologized after publicly—and wrongly— accosting a man of Indian descent. He accused the man of wanting to “rape a 16-year-old” in a mock Indian accent and called him “Mr. Mumbai.” In March 2025, The New York Times reported that Zdorovetskiy’s tactics for ambushing suspected creeps included beating some of them up, dressing like the Joker; the Times piece found that there have been more than 170 violent vigilante attacks by predator-hunting groups since 2023.
I spent over a year investigating similar groups in Canada for Vice, starting in 2015, and found that some of the people being targeted in stings had severe intellectual and physical disabilities.
Law enforcement groups, meanwhile, have repeatedly denounced vigilantes, noting that their evidence often can’t be used within the criminal justice system and that confronting alleged pedophiles can allow the targeted person to escape before police can step in. In some cases, the so-called predator hunters have ended up being charged with child-porn offenses themselves.
Warning: The following contains spoilers for Primetime.
In Primetime, the catastrophic consequences of these rogue busts culminate in a sting taking down Louis William “Bill” Conradt Jr., a chief felony assistant district attorney in Rockwall County, Texas. Conradt doesn’t agree to come to a decoy house, so both the TV crew and police show up at his home, where he shoots and kills himself. (The real-life Hansen told the Hollywood Reporter he doesn’t regret the November 2006 sting. Neither he nor NBC responded to a request for comment for this story.)
There are no heroes in Primetime, and the movie doesn’t wrap up any of these threads neatly.
At the end, struggling actor “Decoy Dan,” played excellently by Skyler Gisondo, finally gets career validation when his appearances on the show earn him a SAG-AFTRA card, but it’s clear from his expression that he’s not comfortable with what he had to do to get it.
Meanwhile, Hansen’s character, who repeats the phrase “What would have happened if I wasn’t here?” to suspected predators throughout the film, leaves the audience to grapple with that question. The answers are far from black-and-white.

In March this year, the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and the American Heart Association (AHA), both globally recognised premier organisations in cardiovascular medicine, handed down their newest dyslipidemia guideline, and gave universal Lipoprotein(a) screening in every adult a ‘Class I’ recommendation -- the strongest tier there is. The High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hsCRP) test got a lighter endorsement: checked selectively, alongside coronary calcium scoring, to sharpen risk estimates when they’re uncertain. These two long-debated biomarkers, were both freshly blessed by the field’s governing societies.
Then arrived the irony. On July 31, pharma major Novo Nordisk’s ziltivekimab — a drug built to block the inflammatory pathway behind elevated C-Reactive Protein (CRP) — fully hit its target in a Phase 3 clinical trial and still didn’t move the needle on heart attacks or strokes. Five weeks later, pelacarsenm, a drug that lowers high levels of Lp(a) failed the same way. Within six months of the guideline telling every clinician to start checking these numbers, the two flagship drugs built to act on them came up empty.
It’s a familiar shape for cardiology. Heart disease mortality fell almost every year through the back half of the last century — statins, blood pressure control, smoking cessation, better acute care — and that decline has visibly slowed this past decade, even as the drug arsenal has never been more sophisticated. LDL (’bad cholesterol’) is already driven remarkably low in anyone on a serious statin; medicine needed a new lever, and reached for the two candidates the guidelines had just endorsed. Neither has delivered yet.
What actually happened
On September 4, Novartis announced pelacarsen missed the primary endpoint of Lp(a)HORIZON, the first cardiovascular outcomes trial ever run for a drug built to lower lipoprotein(a). Pelacarsen is an antisense drug — a short, lab-made strand of genetic material injected monthly, designed to intercept the liver’s instructions for building Lp(a) before it’s ever made, rather than mopping up what’s already circulating. In 8,323 patients with established heart disease, it cut Lp(a) by roughly 80%. And yet, there was no reduction in heart attacks or stroke.
What we were taught
Lp(a) was drilled into me in medical school as one of the ‘unfair’ risk factors — a number you’re essentially born with, indifferent to diet or willpower, and loaded disproportionately onto South Asian patients, who as a population carry some of the highest mean Lp(a) levels of any group studied. It helped explain a pattern every cardiology rotation eventually shows you: South Asian patients with premature, multi-vessel disease and normal LDL numbers. That teaching isn’t wrong, and this trial doesn’t overturn it — Lp(a) is a real, heritable, biologically active risk factor. What it disputes is narrower: whether lowering it, this late and this fast, changes what happens next.
What Lp(a) actually is
Here’s the plain version of how a heart attack builds. LDL particles, commonly known as ‘bad cholesterol’ work their way into the artery wall and get stuck there. Once trapped, immune cells chemically alter them and swallow them up, ballooning into fat-filled ‘foam cells.’ Over years, those dying cells pile up into a fatty core, and the artery seals it off with a cap of scar-like tissue. When that cap eventually cracks or wears thin, a blood clot forms on top of it — that’s the heart attack.
Statins, ezetimibe, and the newer PCSK9-inhibitor injections all lower LDL through different mechanisms, but the trial data lines up the same way every time: about a 22% drop in heart attacks and strokes for every 39-point drop in LDL, no matter how you get there.
Lp(a) is an LDL particle with one extra piece stuck to it — a protein called apolipoprotein(a), built from the same molecular parts as the protein your body uses to break up blood clots. But it’s a decoy, not a copy: it fits into the same docking spots on a forming clot, without carrying the working part that actually gets activated into a clot-dissolving enzyme. So instead of helping to break clots down, it crowds out the real thing and makes clots a little harder to clear. That’s what makes Lp(a) different from LDL: it builds plaque the same way LDL does, but it also nudges the body toward clotting rather than away from it. And unlike LDL, your Lp(a) level is almost entirely set by your genes at birth — diet, exercise, and statins barely move it.
Why did the trial fail?
A floor effect: Mean background LDL in the trial was 66 mg/dL as most patients were already on aggressive therapy. Whatever risk Lp(a) adds on top of that may be smaller than older, less-treated cohorts suggested, offering little room for an 80% reduction to matter.
Too late in the game: Every patient entered with 50-plus years of Lp(a) exposure already built into their arteries. Lowering the level for three or four years in someone’s sixties, after a cardiac event, may be too late to undo a lifetime of exposure the genetic data actually measured.
This isn’t cardiology’s first time at this wall. The CANTOS trial suggested a decade ago that quieting the immune system could work, independent of cholesterol reduction. Hitting the biomarkers still doesn’t seem to be enough: Lp(a) may just be writing the newest chapter of the same story.
Back to basics
The interventions with the deepest trial evidence are still the boring ones: eat well, move, don’t smoke, stay lean. LDL, blood pressure, glucose, and tobacco remain the pillars with decades of reproducible data behind them.
Lp(a) will likely still matter — as a flag for who needs those basics enforced hardest, and maybe eventually as a target that is treated decades earlier than this trial tried. But for now, the fanciest number on the panel failed its biggest test, and the oldest advice in medicine didn’t.
No antisense drug, no anti-inflammatory antibody, has found a way around the same wall. In Greek mythology, Icarus didn’t fall because he was foolish — he flew exactly as high as anyone reasonably could, and the sun turned out to be closer than he’d been told. Despite everything medicine can now measure, alter and silence, the quest for a healthy long life perhaps rests on the same principles it has rested on for centuries: eat well, move well, sleep well.
(Dr. Dinesh Arab is director, interventional and structural cardiology, AdventHealth Daytona Beach and clinical assistant professor of medicine, Florida State University. dinarab@yahoo.com)

Manchester City has been found guilty of all but one of the 115 alleged breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules.
According to a report in the Athletic, City is expected to appeal any possible sanction imposed on the club.
The outcome of an independent hearing that began more than two years ago could send shock waves through English football.
The legacy of City’s trophy-laden era is on the line over accusations it had been built on financial impropriety.
City was charged by the Premier League in 2023 following an investigation into alleged breaches between 2009 and 2018.
The club, which has always denied the allegations, was accused of failing to provide accurate financial information and details of payments to players and coaches, as well as breaches of financial sustainability rules.
Under the ownership of Sheikh Mansour, whose Abu Dhabi United Group acquired the club in 2008, City has become the dominant force in English football.

The Central Railway’s Solapur Division will operate 102 festival special train trips, including 64 services between Kolhapur and Kalaburagi, to meet the additional passenger rush during the Dasara and Deepavali festive season.
The special services will be operated between Mumbai and Chennai, Mumbai and Latur, and Kolhapur and Kalaburagi between October 10 and November 24, according to a revised press release issued by the Solapur Division on Friday.
On the Kolhapur-Kalaburagi route, 64 special trips will be operated daily except on Fridays from October 10 to November 15. Train No. 01451 will leave Kolhapur at 6.10 a.m. and reach Kalaburagi at 4.10 p.m. the same day. The return train, No. 01452, will leave Kalaburagi at 6.10 p.m. and reach Kolhapur at 5.40 a.m. the next day.
The train will stop at Hatkanangale, Jayasingpur, Miraj Junction, Arag, Belanki, Sulgare, Kavathe Mahankal, Langarpeth, Dhalgaon, Mhasoba Dongargaon, Javale, Wasud, Sangola, Pandharpur, Modnimb, Kurduwadi Junction, Solapur and Kalaburagi Junction.
The Kolhapur-Kalaburagi special will comprise four AC III-tier, six Sleeper Class, six General Second Class and two luggage-cum-brake vans, totalling 18 ICF coaches.
On the CSMT Mumbai-Chennai Beach route, 12 weekly special trips will be operated. Train No. 01015 will leave CSMT Mumbai at 12.35 a.m. every Wednesday from October 14 to November 18 and reach Chennai Beach at 11.30 p.m. the same day. The return train, No. 01016, will leave Chennai Beach at 4 a.m. every Thursday from October 15 to November 19 and reach CSMT Mumbai at 4 a.m. the following day.
These trains will halt at Dadar, Thane, Kalyan, Lonavala, Pune, Daund, Kurduwadi, Solapur, Kalaburagi, Wadi, Krishna, Raichur, Mantralayam Road, Adoni, Guntakal, Gooty, Tadipatri, Yerraguntla, Cuddapah, Razampeta, Renigunta, Arakkonam and Perambur. They will have 22 LHB coaches, including two AC II-tier, two AC III-tier and two luggage-cum-generator-cum-brake vans.
Another 26 special trips will be operated between CSMT Mumbai and Latur every Tuesday and Thursday from October 13 to November 24. Train No. 01105 will leave CSMT Mumbai at 12.35 a.m. and reach Latur at 11.40 a.m. the same day. Train No. 01106 will leave Latur at 4.30 p.m. and reach CSMT Mumbai at 4.10 a.m. the next day.
These trains will halt at Dadar, Thane, Kalyan, Lonavala, Pune, Uruli, Daund, Bhigwan, Jeur, Kurduwadi, Barshi Town, Dharashiv and Harangul. The service will comprise four AC III-tier, 11 Sleeper Class, five General Second Class and two luggage-cum-brake vans, totalling 22 ICF coaches.
Reservations for the festival special trains, which will run on special charges, will open on September 27 at all computerised reservation centres and through the IRCTC website and RailOne app.
Passengers have been advised to travel with valid tickets and make use of the additional services during the festive season. Detailed timings at intermediate stations can be checked through the Indian Railways enquiry system, RailOne app and NTES app.

Disney+ got its fourth price hike in four years today. Hulu prices also went up.
Disney+ and Hulu’s respective standalone, ad-free plans (which also support 4K and HDR) are each increasing 13 percent from $19 per month to $21.50/month.
Disney+ and Hulu’s respective standalone plans with ads increased from $12 to $12.50.
The Walt Disney Company also increased prices for bundles of the streaming services, including those with ESPN.
The price for the Disney+ and Hulu bundle without ads increased from $20/month to $22/month. The Disney+ and Hulu bundle with ads ($13) didn’t get more expensive.
However, prices increased for the Disney+, Hulu, and ESPN Select bundles with ads (from $20 to $22) and without ads (from $29 to $33).
Monthly subscription prices for Hulu + Live, which adds cable channels delivered over the Internet to Hulu’s on-demand options, went up by $10.
For comparison, Netflix is currently $9/month with ads and starts at $20/month without ads. There’s also a $27/month ad-free plan for premium features, like 4K. That means Disney+ and Hulu are both more expensive than the most popular streaming service now, unless you want 4K or HDR.

New Delhi, Sep 23: Expansive red flags raised by two Election Commissioners within the poll panel over the Special Intensive Revision of voters list triggered a massive political storm on Wednesday, with the Opposition accusing CEC Gyanesh Kumar of indulging in "one-man autocracy" and demanding his removal.
Officials said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had flagged multiple issues, including deletion of names, in various states during the voter roll cleanup but the poll body was unanimous in its decisions related to the pan-India Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voters' list.
The reactions poured in after a report in The Indian Express revealed that questions were raised on issues related to the SIR of electoral rolls within the three-member Election Commission (EC) itself, time and again by two of the three Election Commissioners.
The national rollout of the SIR has been under the supervision of all three Commissioners. But Sandhu and Joshi have formally objected, on record, at least 14 times over the last 10 months -- four times on a single day -- to decisions taken and orders issued, they say, without their knowledge, the report in the English daily said.
Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh shared the screenshot of the media report on X.
Ramesh said that on behalf of the party, his colleague Abhishek Singhvi will be speaking in detail to the media on the sensational revelations made in the leading national newspaper on the way "the CEC has destroyed the credibility and integrity of the Election Commission of India".
Congress general secretary in-charge organisation K C Venugopal said there is no doubt remaining that Kumar has no right to remain in office.
"How the hell can one man, acting on His Master's orders, strike off names at whim? How can he sideline fellow Constitutional officers to only take blatantly illegal steps that put our democracy in danger?" he said.
"The right to vote is an essential Constitutional power given to every citizen, the fundamental bedrock of our democracy. If it is to be taken away, due process must be followed with utmost probity," he said.
"Today, when we are staring at crores of genuine voters being excluded and a similar number of bogus voters being added to the rolls, it is clear that Gyanesh Kumar was the Chief Architect of the nationwide 'Vote Chori' exercise, with the the Modi top brass pulling the strings," he alleged.
"We demand Gyanesh Kumar's immediate removal and a Supreme Court-monitored impartial investigation to expose the rot that has destroyed the ECI's credibility," Venugopal said.
If Kumar remains in office, the people of India will come forward and make sure that our democracy is not destroyed by a mere bureaucrat, he added.
Congress' media and publicity department head Pawan Khera lashed out at Kumar, saying he is "planted" and being "protected" by the BJP to hollow out the Election Commission of India from within.
"It was already known that things were not exactly well within the ECI. But just how messy, dysfunctional and, frankly, disturbing things had become is laid bare by this brilliant expose by @IndianExpress," he said on X.
Kumar has to be the single most sold-out bureaucrat of the Modi era who has disenfranchised crores of Indians, and he must face the law, he alleged.
Congress MP Manish Tewari also reacted to the media report, saying that if the ostensible facts as reported are correct then it seems to suggest that there is an "invisible hand" running the Election Commission.
"If rules were not allegedly followed and decisions were taken that were not unanimous or by majority then all the decisions of @ECISVEEP are per -se arbitrary and capricious if not completely illegal," Tewari said on X.
"This is perhaps a fit case for serious considering an impeachment proceeding but more importantly the fundamental question is as to how will the credibility of @ECISVEEP be ever resurrected," he said.
Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal demanded Kumar's suspension and filing of an FIR to probe who is behind his actions.
Former chief election commissioner O P Rawat said changes to the statutory voter registration Form 6 are "absolutely wrong and illegal", while describing revelations of differences within the Election Commission as "very serious" and "unfortunate".
CPI(M) MP John Brittas said this is no longer an Election Commission, it is a "one-man autocracy" under CEC Kumar.
"Two Election Commissioners have formally objected 14 times in 10 months. They branded the addition of new voters and mass deletion 'unauthorised and illegal'. They recorded objections to secret deletions, restorations, and form 6 changes that harass young first-time voters - all while being kept in the dark," he said.
This is the open subversion of the EC and our democracy too, Brittas said.
"Parliament must immediately start the process for the removal of the CEC. We had in fact submitted a notice for removal on 24th April, 2026 as per the constitutional stipulations - solid grounds and around 70 members signing( 50 in the stipulated number)," he said.
The Constitution provides this power for precisely such moments of institutional capture and subversion, he said.
"The Supreme Court must annul the entire SIR process without delay. When two of the three Commissioners put on record that the exercise is illegal and destructive of the electoral roll's integrity, judicial silence becomes complicity," Brittas said.
What Kumar is doing is the death knell of a democratic nation, he said.
"Remove the CEC. Strike down the SIR. Or accept that free and fair elections in India are already being buried," the CPI(M) MP said.
Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut also cited the media report, and said "A-Gyanesh Kumar will go to jail! He will have to go! His masters will flee the country and run away!"
TMC Rajya Sabha leader Derek O'Brien said on X, "Five months ago, 60+ Rajya Sabha MPs (50 needed) wrote to Chairman RS moving Motion to remove CEC Gyanesh Kumar. After big news break today that two Election Commissioners objected to many of CEC's actions, it's time to bring out the RS Motion today. Impeach CEC to save democracy".

Nintendo wins $4.5 million from lawsuit over pirated Switch games
It's easy to win when the defendant is a no-show.
Nintendo of America has been awarded $4.5 million in damages from a lawsuit brought by the company against an individual who allegedly sold pirated versions of Switch games. The target of the lawsuit was James Williams, known online by the handle Archbox and reportedly a moderator for the r/SwitchPirates Reddit community. The subreddit in question is still active, although Aftermath noted that Williams does not currently appear listed as a mod.
Nintendo claimed in its suit, originally filed in 2024, that Williams was the "operator, overseer and driving force behind several Pirate Shops." Although Nintendo has a big legal team that it has been known to deploy aggressively, the lawyers had comparatively less to do this time around because Williams did not respond to the suit in court, which granted the game company a win by default. Williams has still been ordered to "immediately disable access to all online 'shops' that he operates or otherwise controls which have offered to the public extensive libraries of pirated Nintendo Switch games for download."

Hundreds of thousands expected in Paris for Pope's visit
- Published
Pope Leo XIV embarks on a four-day visit to France on Friday, with the highpoint being a giant Mass attended by more than half a million people in central Paris.
For Saturday's afternoon celebration, an altar has been built on the Place de la Concorde and a large area around the Champs-Élysées sealed off by police.
Some 600,000 Catholic faithful are expected to cram the avenue up to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond.
Large crowds are also due at other stages in the Pope's itinerary, reflecting an enthusiasm that the Church attributes to growing spiritual thirst among the French and other Europeans.
President Emmanuel Macron will greet the Pope at Orly airport on Friday morning, and then hold talks with him at the Élysée Palace on geopolitical issues and artificial intelligence (AI). He will also deliver a speech with the Pope in Metz.
However, the president will not be at any of the Pope's Masses, largely to avoid breaching France's strict separation of state and religion.
Instead, the Champs-Élysées Mass will be attended by his wife Brigitte and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. Several candidates for next year's presidential election are also due, including Marine Le Pen of the nationalist right, centrists Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, and conservative Bruno Retailleau.
There were reports of tensions between Macron and the Vatican team sent to make arrangements, with the president allegedly frustrated in his wish for a more ceremonial aspect to the visit.
This was dismissed this week by Élysée officials, who said it was customary to offer a visiting head of state – which the Pope is – a range of high-profile events, such as a cavalry escort down the Champs-Élysées. But they said it was never expected that the Pope would actually take the offer up.
They did confirm that Pope Leo turned down Macron's idea of a meeting with artisans who helped rebuild the fire-devastated Notre-Dame cathedral. This was because his agenda was too tight, they said.
After a Popemobile ride through crowds to Notre-Dame cathedral on Friday afternoon, Pope Leo XIV will be joined in the evening by 80,000 young people at the Stade de France in northern Paris.
On Sunday 150,000 have signed up to attend mass in the Pyrenean sanctuary of Lourdes.
On Monday the Pope will be in Metz, in northeast France, where he will pay tribute to Robert Schuman (1886-1963), a founding father of the European Union and a fervent Catholic who is today a candidate for beatification.
The Pope will also meet a group of migrants in Paris, and in Lourdes some victims of sexual abuse by members of the Catholic clergy.
Born in Chicago in 1955, Pope Leo XIV was originally called Robert Prevost – a French name.
In fact his paternal grandmother was born in Le Havre in Normandy in 1894. When she married in the US many years later she and her Italian husband took the name Prevost, which had been her mother's maiden-name.
France has a historically complex relationship with the Catholic Church of Rome. The country was long known as the "Eldest Daughter of the Church" because supposedly, but inaccurately, it was the first kingdom to convert to Christianity. Actually Armenia, Georgia and Ethiopia preceded it.
In the 14th Century the papacy came in exile to Avignon in southern France, and over following centuries French armies periodically intervened in Italian politics, where popes were secular rulers as well as heads of the Church.
Napoleon held two popes in captivity.
Recent popes have all come to France, most notably John-Paul II, who came several times between 1980 and 2004, and Pope Francis who came three times, but avoided Paris, going instead to Strasbourg, Marseilles and Corsica.
Today France has secularised with the rest of Europe, and less than half of the population identifies as Catholic.
The number of regular worshippers has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000.
But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025.
"France has indeed secularised, but there is a void where God and values used to be," said Cardinal François Bustillo, Bishop of Ajaccio.
"People are searching for something. Maybe they go to India or Tibet or the Amazon. And now the Pope comes here from Rome, bringing a reminder to people of their own roots.
"It was John-Paul II who awoke the East. Now Leo XIV will awake the West," he said.

The Taliban has claimed that Pakistan is striking Afghanistan to avoid its commitments under a recently signed defence agreement, the Makkah defence pact, as Saudi Arabia faces heightened security risks following attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi movement. Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid alleged that Pakistan was deliberately portraying the situation as a conflict with Afghanistan to sidestep its obligations under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement signed with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, CNN-News18 reported. “Pakistan’s recent attacks on Afghanistan were carried out with the aim of escaping the Makkah agreement with Saudi Arabia, while portraying the situation as though Pakistan is engaged in a war in Afghanistan,” Mujahid said, according to CNN-News18. Pakistan has said it carried out strikes against identified military targets in Afghanistan, while Kabul has accused Islamabad of targeting Afghan territory and civilians. Pakistan claimed it had foiled an “attempted Afghan aggression” along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border, according to Reuters. Pakistani security sources said several Taliban members were killed in an exchange of fire in the Gulistan area of the border on Friday, with fighting continuing. The escalation follows a period of relative calm between the two sides. Tensions have resurfaced after a recent militant attack on a police facility in northwestern Pakistan that killed at least 24 people. Afghanistan’s Taliban government, meanwhile, said Pakistani air strikes killed four civilians. Mujahid’s allegation comes against the backdrop of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey in Mecca on August 7. Under the agreement, an armed attack against any one of the three countries is to be regarded as an attack against all three. The language of the pact has drawn comparisons with NATO’s Article 5, under which an armed attack against one member is treated as an attack against the alliance. The conflict along the Durand line comes as Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi movement have escalated attacks upon each other, ending a period of relative calm following the 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire. Earlier, Pakistan Defence Minister Khawaja Asif had suggested that the defence pact could become operational if Saudi Arabia faced “unprovoked aggression” or if the Yemen conflict spilt over into Saudi territory, according to Geo News. In a flip-flop, Islamabad later sought to narrow expectations. On September 10, Pakistan Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said there was no military response under discussion in connection with the Houthi attacks. Pakistan’s confrontation with the Taliban government is rooted in its long-running allegations that militants operating from Afghanistan are responsible for attacks inside Pakistan. Islamabad has repeatedly accused Kabul of providing space to the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and other militant groups. The Taliban government denies the allegations and maintains that militancy inside Pakistan is an internal issue. 'I don't even know if my parents are alive' - the war heroes jailed 25 years ago
- Published
Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrested in Eritrea and jailed without trial. Their mother was subsequently detained - and no-one has heard from either of them - or of them - since.
"He had a towel on his shoulders like a sportsman," she tells the BBC about the last time she saw her father when she was 10 years old, and he had gone out for a jog.
"He used to work out every morning."
Her parents met when they both fought in the long liberation war that saw Eritrea gain independence from Ethiopia in 1993.
Her father Petros Solomon had been one of the senior leaders during the war and is regarded by many as a national hero for his critical role.
After independence, he had served as defence minister, then foreign minister and had been heading the fisheries ministry when his troubles began.
That was in May 2001 when he and 14 other high-profile politicians signed an open letter to President Isaias Afewerki calling for the implementation of a constitution that was ratified after independence and demanding national elections. They became known as the G-15.
Isaias, the leader of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) which had fought against Ethiopia, did not take the criticism well.
Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day.
It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isais's displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history.
In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders.
Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit.
The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US.
It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories.
"My classmates told me that my father sold out his country.
"That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt."
In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home.
After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return.
Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried.
"I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers.
"She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'"
Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers.
Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home.
"First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport."
Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home.
All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring.
The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara.
Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives.
At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero.
The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive.
Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport.
Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents.
As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days."
She also hankers after her mother's "unmatched" egg and potato sandwiches.
On trips down to the coast when her father was the minister of fisheries, Hanna remembers him organising singing competitions in the car: "He would ask us to sing one by one and whoever won would get a present."
One of his favourite songs included the lyrics: "I had a sweater, a blue sweater, that my sister took" - which reminded him of his sister who was also a freedom fighter and had been killed during the war.
She also has memories of her mother loving music - playing and singing hits by Abba, Dolly Parton and Whitney Houston.
Until her father's arrest, Hanna remembers September as being full of hope with its three big Orthodox Christian festivals, including the Geez New Year. Now the month brings her no joy.
Ibrahim Sherifo knows exactly how she feels. Both his parents, who were senior members of the ruling People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), were among the G-15 people arrested 25 years ago.
He was 13 years old at the time
"For me 18 September 2001 is a dark day, but not only for me, it is a dark day for Eritrea and its people, because it is the day when law and democracy was detained," he tells the BBC.
He is now 38 and living in exile in the Netherlands, where he was granted asylum, and is pursuing an MA in political science - following in his father's footsteps.
His dad Mahmoud Ahmed Sherifo was the local government minister and de facto deputy president before his detention.
Ibrahim was with his mother, Aster Fissehatsion, staying with her sister when he remembers security agents knocking on the door early in the morning and taking her away in her pyjamas.
Worried about his father, Ibrahim immediately ran to his nearby house but was told he had already been picked up when he had gone out for exercise.
Both Hanna and Ibrahim say they are forever grateful to the friends and family who offered them care and supported them as they grew up without their parents, despite the risks.
They are also proud of what their parents stood for and daring to call for reforms.
"They had conscience and couldn't observe idly while what they fought for what had been hijacked by Isaias and his coterie," says Ibrahim.
"As a family, we should be informed whether they are alive or not," he adds, accusing the government of wanting to erase all memory of the political prisoners.
Hanna also wants the plight of the many others whose relatives have disappeared over the years to be heard too.
Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down"
Human rights groups, including the UN, consider the G-15 prisoners of conscience and have been calling for their release.
President Isaias, now 80, has still not implemented the country's first constitution - approved in 1997 - and remains in power without ever holding an election.
Hanna recalls that on the eve of her father's disappearance, she had a "bad feeling" - and had crept into his bed and tied his legs to her own with string while he slept.
"In the morning he woke up to find he was tied up and to release himself he pulled my legs and I woke up. I begged him not to leave but he assured me that he would return [after his run]."
Describing the years of sorrow since, she says it is like living in the deep sea.
"Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down.
"Sometimes you lose hope and you are out of breath."
Asked what she would say if she could get a message to her parents, she replies: "Don't worry about us.
"Like you survived the struggle through sheer steadfastness, we hope you can pull through this too and return to us."

Africa's richest man, Ethiopia and Djibouti to build $660m fuel pipeline
- Published
Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote, Ethiopia and Djibouti have agreed to develop a $660m (£500m) petroleum pipeline and storage project linking the two countries.
The project will include a 120km- (75 mile-) pipeline connecting Djibouti's Damerjog port to a distribution facility in Dewele, Ethiopia, as well as storage capacity of about 400 million litres.
It is expected to begin operations within 18 months.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said the pipeline would reduce the time needed to transport fuel from Djibouti's port to the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, from five days to one.
The first phase will transport key petroleum products, including jet fuel, diesel and petrol.
Speaking at the groundbreaking ceremony, Dangote said the project would strengthen Ethiopia's energy security and make its fuel supply chain more resilient.
Landlocked Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti's port for imports, including petroleum products. The new infrastructure is expected to reduce pressure on existing transport systems supporting industries, including transport, aviation, agriculture and construction.
Djibouti is also expected to benefit from increased port activity, job creation and higher government revenues.
The project is part of Dangote's wider expansion of infrastructure and manufacturing businesses across Africa.
Dangote Cement has production capacity of about 55 million tonnes a year, while his oil refinery in Nigeria currently has capacity to process 700,000 barrels of crude a day and is seeking to double that to 1.4 million barrels a day.
The refinery recently listed 4.1 billion ordinary shares on the Nigerian stock exchange, aiming to raise about $1.63bn (£1.2bn).
In Kenya, the company is due to break ground next week on a proposed 700,000-barrel-a-day crude oil refinery in Lamu.

The Senate has only one more week before it breaks so that incumbents can hit the campaign trail. Polling shows that Americans are worried about AI running amok and rising gas prices amid President Donald Trump’s unilaterally waged war in Iran.
Republicans seem to know the Iran war is politically toxic and could lose them control of not just the House, but also the Senate. But are they doing anything to stop it? Heavens, no. Is the Senate doing anything on AI? Nope. Not after Trump decreed he should be the only guardrail.
So what is the Senate focused on? The Protecting College Sports Act, legislation co-sponsored by Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), which would create regulations on athletes’ share of revenue from sports; create an antitrust exemption to allow colleges and conferences to share media rights; limits players to one transfer without penalty and prevents college football personnel from leaving mid-season to become a head coach at another institution.
And that has some Republicans skeptical fuming with one week left before the Senate breaks for midterm campaigning back home.
“We’ve been spending all week trying to make the football coaches happy,” Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told a gaggle of reporters Thursday. “I can assure you that moms and dads out there across America, when they lie down to sleep at night — they’re not worried about football.”
Anyone who watches ESPN is familiar with how much coaches and sports television wants this bill to pass. ESPN even allowed Cruz to appear on College Gameday earlier this month without offering the opposing viewpoint, which featured University of Texas Longhorns fans booing Cruz.
Kennedy might be biased considering Lane Kiffin left the University of Mississippi to become head coach of Louisiana State University only for Ole Miss to beat LSU, but he’s not wrong. A CNN/SRSS poll shows that only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s foreign policy. Combine that with the way Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz has caused gas prices to skyrocket and Republicans have every reason to panic.
And it’s not just Republicans going along with it; it’s split the Democratic caucus in half, as 25 Democrats voted for bill. The NAACP has come out against the bill, saying it puts athletes, many of whom are Black, at a disadvantage. The normally jovial Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), a former tight end at Stanford University, railed against his colleagues.
“The fact that Democrats would participate in this being the last thing of consideration is shameful to me,” he told The Independent.
Meanwhile, the Senate spent much of last week focused on the CLARITY Act, which would have provided a regulatory framework for digital assets like cryptocurrency. Democrats ultimately blocked the legislation, with some arguing it would allow Trump to continue to profit off of cryptocurrency.
“I mean, the Senate only works on things that are a personal priority to President Trump,” Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) told The Independent. “So he told the Senate to to give the crypto industry what it wants because he makes money off the crypto industry and he told the Senate to fix college sports because he's got a lot of buddies that are boosters.”
Even Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), who voted to allow the bill to proceed, cast doubt on the focus on college sports.
“Republicans set the calendar, and there's a reason why they're going to lose this election,” he told The Independent.
All of this comes as many Americans continue to fear AI running out of control. This week, OpenAI admitted that one of the company’s systems broke into the Australian government’s website.
But Trump has insisted that “The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades.” He’s also attempted to rebrand AI as “super intelligence” amid anxieties around artificial intelligence.
Meanwhile, amid the debate around college sports, the Senate held a vote on the War Powers Act to rein in Trump’s war in Iran, that summarily went down. While Sen. Collins (R-Maine), the most endangered incumbent voted for it, the other endangered Republicans like Sens. Roger Marshall of Kansas and Dan Sullivan in Alaska voted against the resolution, even as the price of gas and diesel has turned these blood-red states competitive.
Regardless, there will likely be little action to address the concerns Americans have. As has been the case throughout this Congress, the Senate has deferred to Trump wholesale. The only new Republican to vote with the War Powers Act resolution was Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who is retiring.
And as votes wrapped on Thursday, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a former college basketball player at Biola University, seemed almost resigned to his fate that Democrats will win when he spoke in a gaggle about staving off a midterm loss.
“I think midterms when both parties have had the presidency–there have been a number of them–the time I've been in office that have been tough environments for the incumbent party,” he said. “Yeah, there were some parallels, but I don't don't want to get into specifics.”
Republicans are essentially in the fourth quarter. But Trump, who is supposed to be quarterback, is not even benched; he is on the field not even interested in throwing passes that could connect. And Republicans could pay a price ultimately.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi attended a ‘Bhajan Clubbing’ programme at Deen Dayal Upadhyay Park in Delhi on Friday, 25 September, to mark the 110th birth anniversary of Bharatiya Jana Sangh leader Pandit Deendayal Upadhyaya. Modi was seen listening to devotional songs at the event, clapping along and playing a tambourine as performers led the gathering. The programme brought a newer format of devotional music into the spotlight, with large groups coming together to sing and engage with bhajans in a setting more closely associated with a concert than a traditional prayer gathering. ‘Bhajan Clubbing’ refers to devotional music events that retain traditional bhajans while presenting them through a modern, high-energy concert format. Performances can include amplified music, guitars, drums, electronic beats, stage lighting and large-scale production, while the lyrics remain rooted in devotional songs. The format has increasingly attracted younger audiences, including Gen Z. Events are generally positioned as alcohol- and drug-free gatherings where people can sing, dance, clap and participate in devotional music in a social setting. Reports on the trend have described it as a meeting point between traditional religious music and contemporary concert culture. The idea is not entirely new. Devotional singing has long been part of temples, community gatherings and religious celebrations, but organisers and performers have increasingly adapted its presentation for younger audiences and larger venues. Some events now resemble music concerts, complete with stage lighting and rock or electronic arrangements. Bhajan clubbing has emerged as a visible cultural trend in several Indian cities, with events attracting both younger participants and families. Organisers have presented it as a way of connecting traditional devotional music with contemporary audiences without changing the religious songs themselves. Modi had already spoken about the trend during an episode of his monthly Mann Ki Baat radio programme in January 2026. He described bhajan clubbing as a combination of devotion, culture, spirituality and modernity, and said such gatherings had found resonance among young people. He also said the events could resemble global concerts while retaining the sanctity of bhajans. The format has also prompted debate about how religious traditions are being adapted for modern entertainment spaces. Supporters see it as a new way of engaging younger audiences with devotional music, while some critics have questioned the commercialisation and changing presentation of religious practices. Friday’s programme was organised on the birth anniversary of Deendayal Upadhyaya, a prominent leader of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, the political organisation that preceded the Bharatiya Janata Party. Upadhyaya is associated with the philosophy of Antyodaya, which emphasises the upliftment and welfare of the poorest and most marginalised sections of society. The event therefore brought together a commemorative occasion and a contemporary devotional music format that has gained visibility in recent months. Inside the confines of Manchester City's sophisticated data operation is a fundamental phrase its experts work towards: "What does it take to win?"
In practice, the motto is broken down into three sections: identifying players, evaluating them and assessing how the club could improve them, all with a view to enhancing the statistical probability of City winning the Premier League.
Last season, the club's data department projected they would be there or thereabouts when it came to the title race, but their metrics indicated Arsenal were favourites to be champions. They were accurate.
This time around, City prefer to keep their projections under wraps - but five wins from five Premier League games have prompted predictions from supporters and pundits they will again be the Gunners' closest challengers.
City's devotion to data is at the heart of their efforts to close the gap on Arsenal and BBC Sport has been given unprecedent access to the inner workings of the club's metrics machine as we uncover some of the secrets guiding their work - particularly regarding player recruitment and sales.
Their work is a sign of the times in the Premier League, with clubs across the top flight and beyond increasingly using data for transfers and monitoring their teams' performance.
At City, one of the fundamental aims is to reduce risk of any market transaction, be it a purchase or a sale.
City grade players based on:
- Ability;
- Overall characteristics;
- The system they play in at their current club and how the manager is asking him and the team to play.
Once those four aspects are observed, City's aim is to understand not just how good the player is but how good he could become at the Etihad.
Since winning the Treble in 2023, City's squad has undergone a vast overhaul using this approach. Only four players from that historic campaign remain.
It is crucial to stress, however, that while data has made an indefinite impact on how City operate in the transfer market, the work of traditional scouts continues to be the primary gauge of whether they decide to move for a player.
"Data plays a role in our decision-making, but it is just one part of the overall picture," City sporting director Hugo Viana told BBC Sport.
"We know data cannot tell us everything about a player. It cannot fully show a person's character, mentality or behaviour.
"That is why we study data insights but focus on the expertise of our scouts and other specialists."
The prominence of data, however, has grown significantly behind the scenes at the Etihad.
Here BBC Sport can take you to the core of some of City's key transfer calls from their extensive three-year squad revamp - including the £116m signing of Elliot Anderson.
From 650,000 players to the No 1 target
The starting point for any new signing is City's database of 650,000 footballers from around the world.
The next step is the brief: what sort of player is the club wanting to recruit.
This usually starts with a position, though that process isn't as simple as it sounds.
City, for example, categorise their full-backs into three types: those who are defensive, those who come inside, and those who play high and wide.
Once the club's data departments have the brief, filters that grade a player's overall ability are applied to whittle down the 650,000-man database to 20-50 names.
Juventus full-back Andrea Cambiaso is one player who has been on City's radar after the data highlighted him, particularly his ability to coming inside to build play in midfield.
That he is comfortable with both feet rated highly on the data, too.
In accordance with the data and the scouting reports it was decided the club would not proceed with their interest in Cambiaso in the previous window, but City's approach is likely to mean he will continue to be monitored.
The longlist of 20-50 names is cross-referenced with the scouting longlist. Generally there is a significant overlap between the players identified by data and the ones already on scouts' radar.
From there, further, more refined metrics are applied to rank and prioritise the longlist.
Scouts will then complete further diligence on the players to reduce the list to a maximum of about six players.
At this point, the club will complete deeper dives into the remaining players, including diligence on their injury record, athletic performance and behavioural habits.
The information is then collated into individual reports called acquisition packs which contain all the key metrics used to inform the decision on a player.
This includes a 'radar chart', which rates a range of specific on-field metrics.
For example, when Jeremy Doku was signed in 2023, then manager Pep Guardiola decided he wanted a winger who was direct, akin to Leroy Sane, because at the time they had Jack Grealish and Riyad Mahrez, who preferred to keep the ball and cut inside.
Among the criteria applied in City's brief were the following: making (running into) the box, pressure regains, take-on percentage and opposition-half pressure.
Doku's overall numbers ticked the boxes Guardiola was looking for, although the Belgian's 'making the box' score was among his lowest readings.
Since his arrival, Doku has improved this rating - an example City say shows how their data systems are helping to improve existing players.
There is also a 'utilisation chart' that records how often the player has been used over a three-year period, as well as a scouting grade that indicates how highly the traditional scouts rate the individual.
Each player is also awarded an overall "current impact score" - which predicts what impression he would be expected to make immediately on signing - and a "potential impact score" that projects the contribution the player could make in the future.
Perhaps the most intriguing reading on the acquisition packs is a player's "action value score". This positions them in a league table that includes City players and ones from rival clubs who play in a similar role.
Once the acquisition reports are evaluated, the list is further reduced to 2-3 players once City's valuation of the player has been factored in.
Data contributes heavily to the price range City believe a player falls in, and the valuation is never a single number.
A decision is then made on which player is the priority, though all players on the shortlist are worked on simultaneously in the event of changing circumstances, for example if a player becomes unavailable.
Indeed, being able to move according to the market is something the data team feel they have become adept at.
The sudden emergence of Yan Diomande last season led to City completing checks on him before he joined Real Madrid from RB Leipzig.
The club also paid close attention to Eduardo Camavinga's metrics in case Real decided to sell a midfielder.
Anderson - the signing that shows City's forensic approach
Anderson was an obvious signing for a top Premier League club.
The 23-year-old had developed into a key player for Nottingham Forest. An added appeal was the fact he is English, and had cemented his position in the national team.
City fought off other top clubs, including Manchester United, to sign him.
It would seem, on the face of it, a straightforward decision.
But the way City analysed it underlines their incredibly forensic approach even when, outwardly, it might be considered they did not need to be so comprehensive given Anderson's obvious talents.
The fact they still used their algorithm and went through all their normal steps says a lot about elite football in the modern day - and also the limitations of data alone.
That is because - perhaps surprisingly - Anderson's metrics didn't necessarily catch the eye.
At the start of last season, despite emerging uncertainty over Guardiola's future, the club knew they would be in the market for at least one central midfielder come the summer.
They knew Bernardo Silva was leaving while there were doubts over the futures of Rodri and Nico Gonzalez.
There was an acknowledgement that replacing Silva and Rodri like-for-like would be virtually impossible, so they looked for a player who was equally adept at building play from either deep or high central midfield.
As last season developed, doubt also emerged over the future of Tijjani Reijnders - but Enzo Fernandez was viewed as the favoured replacement for the Dutchman.
Anderson made the initial cut from the 650,000-man database to the longlist - but was not high in that group. However, his metric readings didn't immediately scream out the "no-brainer" he ultimately became.
As City took a closer look, there was an acknowledgement Anderson's case does highlight some of the limitations of data.
Anderson did not score lots of goals for Forest, or consistently provide assists. Because, generally speaking, Forest aren't a possession team like City, his general metrics in their algorithm did not grab the attention.
With that in mind, City's data analysts had to consider that, because Anderson was generally playing closer to his own goal than he would at City, he wasn't getting the opportunities to impress in the final third of the pitch.
So they paid close attention to what he was doing at Forest and modelled his potential role in a City team that generally plays closer to the opposition's goal, dominates possession and has more elite players.
Among the criteria graded on Anderson's 'radar chart' were defensive regains, duel success, line-breaking passes, aerial-duel success and defensive errors.
With his reading for defensive errors, it was acknowledged that, because Forest were a transitional side, some were a result of the area of the pitch in which he was asked to operate.
He may, for example, have regained possession deep inside his own half but lost the ball because he had to play a longer and a riskier pass after being asked to play forward quickly.
In the same scenario at City, it is anticipated Anderson would have options to play a shorter pass with a greater success rate.
"Just because a player doesn't have the opportunity to perform a particular action on a regular basis because of the team he is playing doesn't mean he can't do it," said a source.
Anderson's data readings improved significantly as the season developed, which compelled the club's scouts to watch him on a regular basis.
He stood up very favourably against City's existing midfielders - and a list of rival players the club had identified as possible signings in that area.
The results of the diligence completed by City's data team, scouts and other experts meant that even though Anderson's price increased beyond what City believed was his true valuation, they felt the risk was low.
"Elliot Anderson is a great example of how the process works," Viana said.
"The data was positive for Elliot and gave us real confidence in his profile, but it was the insight from our scouts and wider performance team that helped us understand the player and his attributes and this proved our belief that he was the right fit for the club."
The success of Alvarez and Khusanov
BBC Sport was also provided with fascinating insight into how data was used to sign Julian Alvarez from River Plate for £14m in 2022.
The initial recommendation came from scouts, and given Alvarez was not a player originally identified by his metrics, the data team had to take a closer look.
Because the Argentine league isn't recognised as one of the strongest globally, City's general data settings mean players will reach a natural ceiling with their readings in comparison to those playing in one of Europe's top five divisions.
So, City dug deeper into Alvarez's stats, and his impact on both the ball and River's scorelines.
The stats showed he was by far the best player in the Argentine top flight, and City believed they had enough evidence to say he would develop into a starter for a top-half club in one of Europe's top five leagues within two-and-half years.
The data model valued Alvarez between £26m and £40m. City signed him for £14m so believed they were signing an undervalued player.
Alvarez's projected value was £70m after three years. They eventually sold him to Atletico Madrid in 2024 for £81m.
The signing of Abdukodir Khusanov from Lens also provides intriguing insight into City's reliance on data.
The 22-year-old didn't initially make City's 50-man longlist, but on closer inspection they found while his output on the ball needed to improve, his physical data - for example his covering runs behind - was through the roof.
Khusanov's on-the-ball metrics, City say, have improved significantly since he signed in January 2025.
The impact of Guardiola leaving and squad building
The departure of Guardiola and the arrival of Enzo Maresca is not expected to alter the club's approach significantly.
The key metrics Maresca looks for in a player are understood to be very similar to Guardiola's, with the notable difference that the Italian prefers his full-backs to be more direct.
Rooted in City's coach recruitment process is a certain team philosophy and way of playing, with any new manager expected to produce a side that is possession dominant, can press high, regain possession high up the pitch, produce quality chances and entertain.
That philosophy was designed before Guardiola's appointment, and the Spaniard produced the purest form of City's footballing ideology.
With that in mind, the change in manager has not drastically altered the way City's data department approach their work.
Maresca will continue to work closely with them as he looks to build his own dynasty - but much of the hard work in building a squad to last is complete.
Before City's Treble-winning season, the internal data indicators were such that the club knew they would soon need to overhaul a squad that had reached its peak.
Selling players such as Kevin de Bruyne, Kyle Walker, Riyad Mahrez and Ilkay Gundogan wasn't easy given their illustrious service and the fact they were still performing at a very high level.
Data, though, allows the club to spot declining trends well in advance - often two or three years - before a player is offloaded.
Those particular metrics help City identify when the right time is to sell a player is - perhaps even before the buying club have spotted a drop in performance.
And when those trends are identified, the club can plan well in advance.
From there the club decide whether to start embedding a player from the academy or enter the market to replace.
Ayyoub Bouaddi's arrival from Lille this summer is a prime example. At 18, City realise he isn't necessarily going to have a profound impact this season - but the club believe the Moroccan will be able to make a bigger contribution within two years.
After the Treble season, the recruitment remit at City was to lower the average age of the squad and build a set of players that could deliver sustained success.
But doing that at City comes with a catch. Because at City, the team are always expected to compete for trophies.
Lowering the age of a squad is one thing; doing so while continuing to win is far more complicated.
In previous years, for example, City's data systems identified former Brighton trio Moises Caicedo, Marc Cucurella and Carlos Baleba, who have been lauded as data successes.
But there was a sense at City that the development of such signings would take too long for them to make an impact on a team that has the remit of winning titles or assets that could be developed and sold for a profit.
City have successfully lowered the average age of the squad to the extent they now have the third youngest set of players in the Premier League behind Newcastle and Chelsea.
But with the signings of goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, defender Marc Guehi, and Fernandez and Anderson they have added players who can not only grow with that new generation but also already have vast experience of top-level football.
City's data indicates their current squad will not peak for another two to three years - but also projects they are likely be among the title challengers this season.
Time will tell if they are right.
