Step 4: Add your UI reference images

Now enter this prompt to ask Google Antigravity to create an app.
Please build an Expo React Native app in TypeScript based on the attached UI designs.

Replicate the layout, typography, colors, and components from the attached screenshots as closely as possible.

Implement full client-side state with local persistence using AsyncStorage so added tasks and items persist across app reloads.
Keep the code modular with clean components in a src/ folder.
Ensure there are zero TypeScript compile errors.

- Go to expo.dev/settings/access-tokens.
- Create a token, name it “Antigravity”, and generate the new token.
- Open the terminal and run this command:

Step 8: Build the Android app
You can simply enter the prompt and wait for some time until Google Antigravity starts an Expo build in the Expo build app. Once it finishes, it will give you a direct download link for the app.

If this is your first time installing a third-party app, Google Chrome will block the app download from unknown sources. When prompted, you can enable unknown sources; once enabled, you can use the package installer to install the app on your Android phone.
Connect your Android app to Supabase (Optional)

Once a project is created, go to your project settings and then API, and copy the following details:
- Project URL – You can go to Project Settings > General

Step 13: Connect the app to Supabase
And now, once you have connected your Supabase account to Google Antigravity, open Google Antigravity and enter the following prompt: Next, ask Google Antigravity to create a new Supabase database to use for storing the data.

“I want to sync this app’s data with Supabase.

Please do the following:

Create a Supabase client configuration file in src/services/supabase.ts.
Provide the SQL table definition script I need to run in the Supabase SQL Editor for our tasks and projects.

Sharon Levy is exiting Banijay’s Endemol Shine North America after nearly a decade at the company — including most recently as CEO.
The restructure comes following this summer’s completion of the $8 billion merger between Banijay and All3Media, with Banijay Americas CEO Ben Samek overseeing the combined company’s U.S. entity.
“Sharon has played an integral role in building ESNA into the creative powerhouse it is today, and her influence has been felt across Banijay America and the wider Banijay group,” a Banijay Americas spokesperson said in a statement. “She has built a varied and healthy slate of titles that continue to thrive year-over year, spanning global franchises, creative IP extensions and scripted hits.”
Popular on Variety
As CEO, Levy led the indie Endemol Shine North America shingle’s output, which has included unscripted fare like “Lego Masters,” “MasterChef” and “Deal or No Deal,” as well as Netflix’s scripted series “Ripley.” She first joined Endemol Shine North America in 2017 as president, unscripted and scripted TV.
In 2021, Levy was named chief content officer, and then upped to CEO in 2023 at Endemol Shine North America as it shifted from its dual role as a studio and Banijay Americas’ holding company to solely an independent production company.
Besides the Emmy Award-nominated “Lego Masters” and the “MasterChef” and “MasterChef Junior” franchises on Fox, Levy’s oversight at Endemol Shine included Fox’s TBS’ revamped “Wipeout,” USA/Peacock’s “The Courtship,” the revived “Extreme Makeover: Home Edition” for ABC, “Fear Factor: House of Fear” at Fox, “Deal or No Deal Island” at NBC and “The Summit” on CBS.
Prior to her time at Endemol Shine, Levy was executive vice president of original series for Spike TV for seven years, where she led acquisition, creation and production of the network’s entertainment with shows like “Ink Master,” “Bar Rescue,” “Auction Hunters” and “Deadliest Warrior.”
Deadline was first with the news of Levy’s departure.

Russell takes pole in Baku as Antonelli hits wall
- Published
George Russell took an imperious pole position for Mercedes at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix as his team-mate and championship leader Kimi Antonelli crashed out.
Russell beat Ferrari's Charles Leclerc by a massive 0.837 seconds while Antonelli, who leads the Britain by 81 points in the championship, will start in 16th.
The Italian hit the inside wall at Turn One in the first session and was knocked out.
McLaren's Oscar Piastri was third ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar and McLaren's Lando Norris.
Lewis Hamilton, compromised by running without a tow from another car, was sixth, ahead of the Alpine of Pierre Gasly and Red Bull's Max Verstappen.
With a tow or slipstream worth as much as 0.5 seconds, Verstappen was following Norris on their final laps when the Briton made a mistake and went off track.
That scuppered Verstappen's chances of competing closer to the front.
But although the four-time champion said he believed he could have been on the front row, he acknolweged that he could not have beaten Russell.
On a weekend in which Antonelli's running has been compromised by reliability problems that meant he missed out on half the possible running on Thursday, Russell absolutely delivered on Mercedes' dominant position on this unique track.
Russell has looked comfortable all weekend and never looked in danger of being beaten for pole, his first since the Austrian Grand Prix at the end of June.
"That's probably the biggest margin I've had in my whole career," Russell said. "The lap felt really sweet and the car has been feeling great all weekend."
Leclerc was somewhat taken aback by Mercedes' superiority, saying that the position was what he expected but the gap most definitely was not.
At the bottom of the top 10, there was finally some good news for Williams, for whom Carlos Sainz achieved the team's first top 10 qualifying performance of the year.
Williams have introduced a new chassis this weekend which has brought them down to the weight limit for the first time this season, after being as much as 25kg over at the start of the year.
Along with some additional developments, it appears to have produced a big step forwards, although the caveat is that Baku is a track that suits the characteristics of the Williams car and does not expose its weaknesses.
Team-mate Alex Albon did not manage to secure a tow in the second part of qualifying, and was "anyway struggling with straight-line speed all session", and was 13th, just under 0.4secs behind the Spaniard.
Antonelli's error came on his second lap of the first session.
He turned into the first corner too early, and the left front wheel clouted the inside wall, breaking the suspension.
He initially tried to get the car back to the pits but was told by engineer Peter Bonnington to park up.
"Let me try," Antonelli pleaded, before Bonnington told him that either the track rod or upright was broken and there was no way Mercedes could fix that in the time they had to turn the car around before the next session.
Antonelli had been on the back foot all Friday trying to catch up time lost to a hydraulic problem that had stopped his car on track halfway through first practice, and was not repaired until halfway into the second.
It was Antonelli's first major mistake of the season since he crashed heavily in final practice at the first race of the season in Australia.

At least five candidates are in the running to become the next director-general of the World Health Organization, a job that will come with extraordinary challenges.
The withdrawal of the WHO’s largest funder — the United States — and an overall contraction of international spending on global health has raised crucial questions about how the Geneva-based agency will respond once a successor to Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus takes office. Among many significant issues awaiting this individual will be deciding whether or how to entice the U.S. to either return to the fold, or at least interact more frequently and collaboratively with the WHO.
Tedros’ successor will take office on Aug. 16, 2027.
“I think this DG election is the most consequential DG election in modern WHO history,” said Lawrence Gostin, director of Georgetown University’s World Health Organization Collaborating Center on Public Health Law and Human Rights “Because the organization is more vulnerable, in a more perilous position, than it’s been at any time in the last 25 years that I can recall.”
The nomination period closed Thursday. Five candidates are listed on the WHO’s website, including late entrant Maria Neira, director of the WHO’s environment, climate change, and migration division, who was nominated by Spain. In theory, additional candidates could be named over the coming weeks. The WHO will not release the official list of candidates until all the regional WHO divisions have had their fall meetings; they conclude in early November.
These are the five known candidates:
Hanan Mohammed Al-Kuwari
Qatar’s former public health minister (2016-2024)
Al-Kuwari also served as managing director of Qatar’s largest public health provider, Hamad Medical Corporation from 2007 to 2024. She has previously served on the WHO’s Executive Board.
She received a Ph.D. in health care management from Brunel University in the United Kingdom.
Hanan Balkhy
Director of the WHO’s Eastern Mediterranean region since early 2024
Balkhy previously worked at WHO headquarters as assistant director-general for antimicrobial resistance. She is a pediatrician who trained in Saudi Arabia and the U.S.
Balkhy was born in the United States and has dual citizenship, a fact she doesn’t emphasize. “I’m Saudi,” she told STAT in an interview in April.
Hans Henri P. Kluge
Director of the WHO’s European regional directorship since early 2020
A family physician, he received medical degrees from Belgium’s Catholic University of Leuven and the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp. Prior to joining WHO, he worked internationally for Doctors Without Borders in Africa, Asia, and Russia, where his work focused on tuberculosis and HIV. He led the WHO’s Europe region through the Covid-19 pandemic and the emergence in Europe of mpox.
Maria P. Neira
Director of the WHO’s environment, climate change, and migration division
A last-minute entry into the race, Neira was nominated by Spain, where she worked previously as vice minister of health and consumer affairs and as president of the Spanish Food Safety and Nutrition Agency.
Neira has worked for the past 21 years at the WHO. She is a physician who trained in endocrinology and metabolic diseases.
Budi Gunadi Sadikin
Indonesia’s health minister since late 2020
If he is successful, Budi (Indonesians generally use their first name on second reference) would be the first director-general with neither a medical degree nor an advanced degree.
Budi has a bachelor of science degree in engineering physics from the Bandung Institute of Technology. He has had a long and successful business career, primarily in banking. He steered his country through the Covid pandemic.
Thomas Bollyky, director of the Council on Foreign Relations’ global health program, said he wasn’t surprised by the number of candidates, but he had expected a field that was more geographically diverse.
There has never been a director-general from the Eastern Mediterranean region. (Before Tedros, there had never been a director-general from Africa either.) But experts told STAT they thought it was unlikely that would be a factor in the race.
Suerie Moon, director of the global health center at the Geneva Graduate Institute, said with two candidates from the Eastern European region and two from the Europe region, it seems likely votes within at least one of those regions will be split.
“I doubt most regions will vote as unified blocks, in any case, and the idea of ‘taking turns’ across the regions is no longer carrying much weight,” she said.
Bollyky doesn’t believe there is a current frontrunner. Gostin believes there is a groundswell of support for Budi.
“WHO really needs a technically excellent person, and it seems to me that, rather than the usual person that’s got mostly the health/public health/science chops, having a former banker and corporate executive is quite attractive,” Gostin said. “I think having a technocrat, particularly an economic and corporate technocrat, might be very appealing to countries, particularly since he’s from the global south and a very powerful mover on the equity front.”
The U.S. withdrawal from the WHO — attributed largely on Trump’s belief that the agency had mishandled the response to the Covid pandemic — left a gaping hole in the agency’s coffers. It was the single largest funder of the agency, with assessed contributions for 2025 of $130 million — which the country did not pay before departing. (Though the congressional resolution that allowed the U.S. to withdraw from the WHO stipulated that it should pay all outstanding monies owed first, the Trump administration left nearly $278 million in unpaid fees when it quit.)
In addition to assessed contributions, which are effectively dues, the U.S. was a major provider of voluntary contributions, used to fund work deemed of importance to the donor country. In the 2022-2023 budget period, the U.S. contributed nearly $1.3 billion in dues and voluntary contributions. The next largest contributor was Germany, which added $856 million.
This year has seen major cost-cutting at the WHO and the financing issue will continue to be daunting, said Moon.
Bollyky agreed. “I absolutely think that finding a WHO leader who can stabilize institution financing, rebuild its credibility, and make hard choices about its future role is going to be key,” he said.
Another major challenge the next director-general will face is what to do with the United States. While there is still some communication between the country and the WHO — Tedros recently told a group of reporters that he speaks at times with health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the agency interacted regularly with the U.S. during this spring’s hantavirus outbreak — there are no official ties.
“Everybody I talk to thinks that this is one of the factors going on: Will there be somebody that can work with the United States?” said Gostin.
There appears to be little hope of a rapprochement while President Trump is in office. And Moon said she isn’t sure there’s even universal willingness among the WHO member states to try to change that.
“I think views are divided on how big a priority it is for the next DG to be able to rebuild bridges with the United States. But I think that decision is much less in the hands of the DG and much more in the hands of the U.S.,” she said.
Another looming question is whether the U.S. — or Trump himself — might try to influence the outcome of the election through political horse-trading in response to requests for help from a nominating country. That could backfire, several experts suggested.
The next phase in the election process occurs in mid-November, when a candidates’ forum will be held. When the WHO’s executive board, a committee of 34 members from around the globe, meets in January, it will shortlist five candidates to interview, then whittle the list down to three. The election will take place by secret ballot in May during the WHO’s annual general meeting, the World Health Assembly.

In China, the Xi-Trump summit is seen as projecting image of the country’s rise
U.S. President Donald Trump’s elaborate reception of Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., has impressed the Chinese public
BEIJING -- It’s unclear if U.S. President Donald Trump’s elaborate reception of his Chinese counterpart in Washington dazzled President Xi Jinping, but for the Chinese public, it made quite an impression.
Trump’s rare welcome of Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at the airport, as well as the bilateral and cultural events the leaders attended were closely covered — and praised — by Chinese state media. Those who watched at home saw a China elevated in status.
“I read the news that the U.S. reception standards for President Xi are very high,” Xiang Ziyu, a postgraduate student in Beijing, told The Associated Press. “I’m quite impressed because it shows that our country has become really powerful.”
That takeaway was shared by several people interviewed by the AP as well as in comments on Chinese social media, which praised China's cooperation with the United States.
The official People’s Daily newspaper allocated the entire front page to the trip, featuring six photos of the Xi-Trump meetings.
Meanwhile, on the Chinese search engine Baidu, the three most popular search topics on Friday were the talks between Trump and Xi; the state dinner attended by Xi and Peng; and greetings extended by Xi to Chinese people on the occasion of the Mid-Autumn Festival being celebrated on Friday.
Shen Zuohang, a Beijing resident, felt reassured by the coverage and by Trump and Xi’s seeming agreeability on topics like trade, artificial intelligence and security.
“We have no trade war and no military conflict. Even on the issue of Taiwan we are moving in a good direction instead of having heated confrontation,” Shen said.
“The two sides are handling issues in a more acquiescent way.”
According to China’s Foreign Ministry, Xi called on Trump to oppose the independence of Taiwan, an island democracy China claims as its own territory, and to handle the issue with caution. Trump did not immediately make comments on Taiwan, but had previously described U.S. arms sales to the island as open to negotiations with China.
Xiang, the student, said the summit overall sent a positive signal and will help improve the Chinese public’s opinion of the relations between the two countries.
“It is better than not communicating,” he said.

The organisers of France’s most prestigious literary prize said they had removed a critically acclaimed novel by a Canadian-Haitian writer from the longlist after an anonymous online account claimed the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.
The Académie Goncourt, a Paris-based literary organisation, said on Friday its decision to withdraw Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était ça ou mourir (It Was That or Die) was “driven by the desire to preserve the integrity of the Goncourt prize and the academy itself, whose central role is to promote and honour literature written by women and men”.
The Haiti-born author’s book is a lyrical first-person account of how a history and geography teacher flees a home country mired in gang violence and embarks on a perilous journey across 12 countries before finding a haven in Canada.
Published in France by Grasset in August, it has sold about 35,000 copies and won the Prix du roman Fnac, with translation rights sold to more than 20 countries.
Allegations that the book was written using AI emerged on X on 21 September, the same day It Was That or Die won the Fnac prize for best novel.
An anonymous account called Balance ton Claude – a reference to Anthropic’s AI agent – said it had fed the novel into the AI detection software Pangram and found it to be “almost entirely” written by artificial intelligence.
Questions have been raised over Pangram’s accuracy, and French media outlets have found other AI detection programmes that identified It Was That or Die as very probably written by a human.
Orélien, 38, has denied the allegation, saying it was racially motivated. “I’ve always loved creating and writing,” he said. “I don’t see why I would use a machine.”
He told the newspaper Libération that he used traditional language and rhythms that were Haitian and Caribbean. “The imagery, repetition and rhythm are a living language, they are mine.”
The author of the anonymous X account was later identified on the pages of the centre-right newspaper Le Figaro as one of its own columnists, Samuel Fitoussi, the author of an essay against “wokeism” on film and TV.
On his own X account, Fitoussi said he had initiated his campaign because even though he was “techno-optimistic”, he feared that “AI will cause the disappearance of reading and writing”.
On Wednesday Philippe Claudel, the Académie Goncourt’s president, had urged caution over the allegations. But separate accusations of plagiarism against Orélien published in French media appeared to have caused a change of heart.
Libération alleged in an article that the author plagiarised an award-winning short story from the preface of the French journalist Louis Pauwels’ book The Morning of the Magicians, originally published in 1960.
In its statement the academy referred to the “plagiarisms of which its author has been guilty over time and which have just been revealed, as well as the convergent result of several analyses by trustworthy researchers and journalists highlighting the fact that [the book] is in all likelihood very largely the product of artificial intelligence”.
“The aim is to send a clear message,” it added, “to affirm that we neither endorse nor condone in any way the creation of texts generated with the help of AI.”
In a statement shared with the Guardian, the novel’s original publisher, Le Éditions du Boréal, said: “Unfortunately, at this stage, we are unable to confirm or deny the allegations the author is facing.”
The Canada-based publisher said it was important not tojump to conclusions, adding: “Without credible, concrete evidence, it is not our place to decide whether this book has a right to exist.”
Boréal said it was “concerned” about the newer plagiarism allegations, but added it was important to remember there was a real person behind the book. “We unequivocally condemn the hateful messages and personal attacks of recent days, and we urge everyone to show restraint,” it said.
Orélien has said he will not comment further on the latest allegations. Speaking on Thursday at Les Correspondances literary festival in Manosque, southern France, he said: “There’s this desire not only to attack the book, but especially my voice … to silence me,” adding that he would therefore “take a step back and wait until things have calmed down”.
The Académie Goncourt will publish its shortlist on 6 October and announce the winner of the prize on 4 November.

The FBI is now investigating claims from a hacker group that thousands of current and former employees’ personal data was stolen after the group exploited a previously unknown bug found on an agency jobs website.
On Tuesday, 404 Media reported that ShinyHunters took down the agency site, FBIJobs.gov, then posted a banner on the homepage that said “THIS SITE HAS BEEN SEIZED BY SHINYHUNTERS.”
About two to three terabytes of data were taken, ShinyHunters told The New York Times. None of the data has been leaked yet, but it included “names of current and former agents as well as applicants and corresponding home addresses, phone numbers, names of spouses, certain medical information, and other data.” According to Bloomberg, the data could be used to potentially retaliate against agents, with one sample appearing to include “potentially sensitive professional information on the FBI employees’ work focus such as counter-intelligence work on China, Russia and Iran, as well as work against street gangs.”
The group’s motive was not to extort the FBI or seek a ransom, it claimed. Instead, the strike was meant to force the FBI to either remove or edit a May advisory warning about ShinyHunters that the group said circulated “disinformation in an attempt to ‘disrupt’ our operations.”
In a message posted on the dark web that was reviewed by Ars, ShinyHunters said it was “severely offended” that the FBI alleged that they sometimes use “exaggerated claims” to extract payments from victims. “We wish to state unequivocally our threats and claims are very real,” the group said. “Not exaggerated and never a bluff.”
ShinyHunters was also upset that the FBI claimed the group conducts swatting attacks against corporate workers and makes sextortion threats. That “never” happens, ShinyHunters said.

Japan says Trump voiced concern over weak yen in summit with PM Takaichi
The weak yen is driving up energy import costs that are already high due to the Iran war, fuelling concerns about an inflation overshoot
US President Donald Trump raised concerns about yen weakness at a summit with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Japan’s Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Friday, offering an unusually detailed account of the leaders’ talks on currencies.
“At the recent Japan-US summit meeting, President Trump expressed concern about the yen’s weakness,” Katayama said at a regular news conference, adding that she was disclosing the exchange for the first time after consulting with the Prime Minister’s Office.

Bellamy wants more from Wales after loss to Portugal
- Published
Wales earned plaudits but Craig Bellamy wants more from his side, after admitting they were forced to suffer in their narrow 1-0 defeat in Portugal.
Joao Felix's deflected strike proved enough to earn victory in Lisbon for the hosts, who also saw Cristiano Ronaldo's effort ruled out by VAR.
It was a winning start to the Nations League title defence for Portugal and for new manager Jorge Jesus.
Despite being under pressure for long spells in Lisbon, Bellamy's injury-hit side ended strongly as Brennan Johnson and Lewis Koumas both went close to snatching a draw.
"It was a difficult game for us. We had to suffer a lot," said Bellamy.
"I think that's the longest we've been in a game without the ball.
"We could have done more with the ball but I'm beyond proud as well.
"We have a lot of players who weren't here. That's OK, we can handle it.
"A lot of players who don't play, week-in, week-out. So for them to use the energy they were able to, we've got to have a big heart to be able to do that. They've always shown that and they showed that again."
Wales have a short turnaround to their second League A fixture against Denmark in Copenhagen on Sunday (17:00 BST).
But Bellamy feels his squad - missing Harry Wilson, Karl Darlow, Dylan Lawlor, Joe Rodon and Nathan Broadhead through injury - are capable of improving.
"There's more for us, so that's something we always look at as a positive," he said.
"How can we improve? How can we get better?"

Ronaldo unsurprisingly took the spotlight in the build-up to the contest at Jose Alvalade Stadium - where the 41-year-old began his professional career with Sporting in 2002.

The organizers of the annual Global Citizen Festival in New York City’s Central Park have canceled this year’s event due to the Nor’easter-caused extreme weather forecast for this weekend.
“Due to the extreme weather forecast for New York City this weekend, we have made the difficult decision, in consultation with the City of New York and NYC Parks, to cancel this year’s Global Citizen Festival,” organizers said. “Forecasts predict dangerous conditions and circumstances in which we cannot safely bring tens of thousands of Global Citizens, artists, crew, vendors, partners, and staff onto the Great Lawn, let alone all of the equipment required.”
The statement continued, “Safety has to come first. This is the first time in 14 years we’ve had to cancel. We have spent this week working through countless contingencies, which were ultimately not possible, and cancelling is a decision we have not taken lightly.”
Watch on Deadline
The annual festival, which raises money and awareness to end extreme poverty around the world, was to have taken place this year on Saturday, September 26, on the Great Lawn in Central Park. Hosted by Hugh Jackman, the festival was to have featured appearances by Alicia Keys, Yeonjun, Ms. Lauryn Hill & Wyclef Jean, Lenny Kravitz, John Legend, Lainey Wilson, Shaboozey and Tomorrow X Together, among many others.
Following the success of the first-ever FIFA World Cup Final Halftime Show, which was produced by Global Citizen and helped raise $60 million for the FIFA Global Citizen Education Fund, this year’s festival was designed to raise awareness and raise funds for childrens’ global educational opportunities, smallholder farmers and electricity for 2.5 million homes.
According to Global Citizen, the organization over the last six weeks has secured $208.8 million in financial commitments to help more than 2 million children access education and stay in school, and support 7.5 million people, including smallholder farmers, women, youth, and indigenous communities. Ireland and Canada committed $151.6 million to help children get in and stay in school; and Burundi, Chad, Ethiopia, Kenya, Guinea, Rwanda, Somalia, Sudan, and Zimbabwe, the Minderoo Foundation, and the Green Climate Fund will support small farming businesses.
“The Festival is one day,” the organization said, “but the actions you took and the impact you created will reach far beyond Central Park. Conflict, extreme weather, and rising costs are forcing millions of families from their homes, disrupting education, threatening food supplies and pushing communities back into extreme poverty, but we have seen what is possible when we take action together.”
Tickets to the Global Citizen Festival were free and could be secured by visiting the Global Citizen app and earning points by completing “action journeys” related to the core issues.
“You took action to earn your tickets,” today’s statement said. “You made plans, booked travel, and in many cases came to New York from across the country and around the world to be with us in Central Park, and we are sincerely grateful for your commitment to our mission.”
Festival tickets that were purchased outright will be refunded automatically. People who made a donation to secure tickets can also receive refunds, with email instructions being sent to outline options.
Food that was due to be available at the Festival will be donated to local organizations serving the people of New York City.
“We are enormously proud of what we have achieved together this year – one of the most impactful years for our movement around the world – and we are deeply grateful to every artist, world leader, partner, crew member, vendor, global citizen, and our team,” Global Citizen said, adding that the festival “will be back in Central Park next year.”

IPO-bound fintech startup Navi saw its net loss for the fiscal year FY26 widen by 268.7% to ₹465.99 from ₹126.4 Cr in the prior fiscal year. The bottom line swelled despite a 16.2% uptick in Navi’s top line, with its operating revenue for the fiscal increasing to ₹2,981.7 Cr from ₹2,565 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Including other income of ₹108.9 Cr, Navi’s total income for the year stood at ₹3,090.6 Cr. While the company’s total expense for the fiscal crossed the ₹3,500 Cr mark, its tax expenses halved YoY to ₹42.2 Cr. In terms of operational metrics, Navi claims its FY26 lending book grew 57.2% YoY to ₹13,138 Cr. Meanwhile, its monthly transacting users more than doubled to 2.9 Cr. Loan disbursements in the fiscal also grew 73% YoY to ₹23,332 Cr while its assets under management amounted to ₹19,740 Cr. Furthermore, its gross and net NPA ratios also declined to 1.25% and 0.16% respectively. Important to note that Navi is India’s fourth largest UPI player, commanding 3.5% market share and processing about 80 Cr transactions monthly. As per a report by CareEdge Ratings, Navi turned profitable on PBT basis in Q1 FY27, registering a profit of ₹104 Cr . As per a report by CareEdge Ratings, Navi's total income for the quarter stood ₹1,165 Cr. Based on the company’s improving QoQ profitability status, CareEdge Ratings upgraded Navi’s credit rating to CARE A+. Important to note that the ratings agency cited unaudited financials from Navi for the quarter. “Ratings continue to derive strength from Navi’s experienced promoter, Sachin Bansal, its scalable technology-led business model and integrated financial services ecosystem, supported by adequate capitalisation and a diversified resource profile,” the ratings agency said. However, it flagged asset quality risks due to high concentration of personal loans, comprising 92% of Navi’s AUM. Founded by Sachin Bansal and Ankit Agarwal in 2018, Navi offers financial products across lending, insurance, mutual funds and UPI payments. Its lending business provides home loans, personal loans and loans against property through its NBFC and partner institutions. Bansal stepped down as the startup’s CEO in February 2025 and transitioned into the role of executive chairman while Rajiv Naresh took over as CEO. Abhishek Dwivedi was named CEO of its NBFC arm Navi Finserv. Notably, the fintech startup raised its maiden institutional funding round for the first time last month when it announced that it was raising $100 Mn from global tech investor Prosus, subject to regulatory approval. According to reports, it is also gearing up to file its IPO papers by December as it seeks to raise ₹3,000 Cr through a fresh issue of shares. Notably, the startup earlier filed for an IPO in 2022, but eventually deferred its plans to list on the bourses. Where Did Navi Spend In FY26? In FY26, Navi’s total expenses grew faster than its top line, surging 28.8% YoY to ₹3,514.4 Cr from ₹2,729.1 Cr in FY25. Finance Costs: Finance costs increased 32.7% to ₹1,123.2 Cr from ₹846.6 Cr. Other Expenses: Navi’s other expenses grew 79.5% to ₹1,111.6 Cr from ₹619.3 Cr. Employee Benefits Expense: Navi’s staff-related expenditure grew 13.4% to ₹619.2 Cr from ₹546 Cr. Impairment On Financial Instruments: Impairment costs decreased 29.4% to ₹407.9 Cr from ₹577.6 Cr. Policyholders’ Expense In Insurance Operations: Spending under this line item more than doubled to ₹199.7 Cr from ₹79.3 Cr. Depreciation And Amortisation: Depreciation expenses slipped 12.7% to ₹52.8 Cr from ₹60.3 Cr.

Why teenagers have become a huge part of football's transfer market
- Published
A 15-year-old growing up in the UK faces many tough personal decisions about their future - which school subjects to study, which social circle suits them, and where their priorities lie in life.
But in the past few weeks the choices teenage Manchester United striker JJ Gabriel has been making about his future in football have drawn huge public attention in sports media and online.
Gabriel has informed United he wants to leave the club and join another. BBC Sport has reported that he has stayed away from training and begun talking to other clubs because he and his representatives are unhappy with United's handling of the 15-year-old's progress.
That a transfer saga involving a footballer so young could generate so much interest highlights a truth that to many is uncomfortable - money is changing how the football transfer market works, and children are increasingly deemed to be among its most valuable commodities.
So what is behind the rise in transfers involving boys who in some cases are not even old enough to have taken their GCSEs, what kind of influence can the money on offer have on agents and parents, and what exactly are the country's top football clubs getting out of it?
'Race for talent is huge'
"It's crazy when you think about it," says Ryan Cardwell, former youth scout at Liverpool and Southampton.
"In what other kind of world would 15 and 16-year-olds be spoken about in the media like this?"
This summer alone, all six of the Premier League's wealthiest clubs either signed a highly-rated academy player from another, or lost a youngster to a direct rival.
"It is such a competitive market," Cardwell explains. "There are now tens of transfers between the elite academies every summer, when it used to be the case that if you were already at one of those, you would likely stay the course.
"The race for talent is huge – you look at what teams are spending on transfers for senior players and it's enormous, so if you can spot a player earlier and offset some of that financial risk, you're going to do so."
Some inside football claim that the transfer of Rio Ngumoha - the now 18-year-old winger who was called up to this month's senior England squad - from Chelsea to Liverpool at the age of 15 in 2024 ushered in a new era of competition for academy players among the nation's elite.
One of the major factors is Brexit. Before 2021 English clubs were allowed to sign academy players over the age of 16 who held European Union passports.
Since the UK left the EU, foreign players cannot join English clubs until they reach 18.
"Heathrow and Gatwick [airports] on a Friday night were inundated with scouts going to other countries to look for young players", says Caldwell.
"Belgium and the Netherlands were full of scouts for Premier League clubs.
"Now it's the competition between English clubs that has increased, looking at each other's players, including the old-school 'top six' but also the likes of Southampton, Aston Villa, and Fulham."
Young players have further added financial value - youth signings don't count towards the Premier League's squad cost ratio rules, and any future sale counts as 'pure profit' in club accounts.
Advances in video technology and data analysis mean more young players are being identified, tracked and approached by rival clubs than ever before.
'Money can mean agents or parents push a player to move'
Players can de-register from their academy at the end of their under-12, under-14 and under-16 seasons if they wish to explore options elsewhere.
They can be offered paid scholarship contracts from the season in which they turn 14, and can sign professional deals from the season in which they turn 16.
Some pundits and fans have criticised Gabriel's family over the controversy in recent weeks.
Gabriel can potentially join clubs in Europe because he has an Irish passport.
"It's a really tough world - players and families want the best for their kids and you can't give them stick without knowing what their motivations are," says Phil Jagielka, whose son Zac left Liverpool in 2024 and signed a scholarship deal at Hull City at 16.
"The harsh reality is that if a young player fails to progress, or gets a bad injury, teams will stop being interested in them. So there is an element of strike while the iron's hot."
When a club signs a player from a rival academy, they pay a set compensation fee based on how long they had been trained there.
Depending on the player's age, the fee can reach millions of pounds.
The increasing allure of signing young academy players from rivals means some parents are now compiling data packs on their sons to give to potential clubs, and more and more children are represented by football agents.
"There are good agents and bad agents," Cardwell says.
"You certainly speak to some and think 'that's completely the wrong idea', or, ' this player is going to be misguided'. Sometimes they push for a move when a player isn't ready.
"The contracts can be enormous and [money] can be a huge motivation to move. It could set a young player's family up for life.
"I would quite like to see some form of financial cap. My fear for some of the young players is they're on the biggest salaries they'll ever have, because if they don't make it at the top level, they can go from being on tens of thousands (of pounds) a week to one or two thousand lower down the pyramid."
'Far more people are prepared to rock the boat'
In decades gone by, development of academy players would be combined with menial tasks around the training ground.
The idea was to keep young footballers grounded and make them feel a part of the wider club.
But the Gabriel case demonstrates the significant changes football has undergone.
"We would clean boots, sweep floors, tidy the changing rooms," says Jagielka, who came through Sheffield United's academy in the late 1990s.
"I fully back that system. It taught us responsibility and discipline. It was a way of getting to know the first-team players, and you would get a proper telling off if you didn't do your jobs properly.
"There was nowhere near as much outside influence on young players back then. Now there is an entourage, people wanting to play the long game with, 9, 10, 11-year-olds because of the millions of pounds of commission if they turn out to be a superstar.
"There are far more people out there now who are prepared to rock the boat between the different clubs."
The public scrutiny on young players has increased significantly, and the elite clubs' desire to succeed in the market means that high-profile youth transfers involving big money seem to be here to stay.
"Young players now have such a big platform on social media that intrigue is part of day-to-day life for them," says Cardwell.
"When you're in elite sport you have to grow up really, really fast. Teenagers are expected to cope with the pressure and naturally some people fall into the trap of thinking 'well, he's a young man already' and forget about everything else.
"The race for talent is never, ever going to change."

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”
What else we’re reading about
Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.
The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.
Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
4,756,000
One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about 4.76 million voters, have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express reported.
Vibe check
Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).
It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.
It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships
- Published
Kenya's President William Ruto says the World Athletics Championship will be "coming home", with Nairobi set to make history after being selected as the first African city to host the event in 2029.
Ruto hailed the winning bid as a "victory for generations of athletes" who have made the nation "synonymous with excellence" on the track and road.
Nairobi beat London and Rome to the hosting rights, with Munich selected to stage the 2031 edition.
After missing out on the 2025 World Championships to Tokyo, a series of factors helped Kenya see off its European rivals this time around.
A sport 'woven into the fabric' of the nation
When World Athletics president Lord Coe announced the decision in Budapest on Tuesday, he described Kenya's bid as "compelling and emotional".
The East African nation is the second-most successful nation in the history of the World Championships with 72 gold medals, placing it behind the United States.
The vast majority of those glories, alongside 38 Olympic gold medals, have come in middle- and long-distance running.
Lord Coe said that athletics is "woven into the fabric" of the nation and that Kenyans have helped "shape the history" of the sport.
He name-checked several runners including two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge - who was involved in the lobbying for Kenya's bid - men's 800m world record holder David Rudisha and multiple world and Olympic medallist Faith Kipyegon.
A passionate fanbase is also one of the country's great strengths.
Some 68% of Kenyans surveyed by World Athletics rated their interest in athletics as high, compared with a global average of 39%.
Athletics is the country's second-most followed sport, behind only football, and when World Athletics assessed its social media channels, Kenya was the fourth-highest nation in terms of followers.
Upgraded facilities
Kenya's previous bid for the 2025 edition fell down largely on the facilities which the country possessed.
This time around, the Kasarani Stadium will have gone through a complete structural upgrade well before the world's top athletes descend on Nairobi.
The 48,000-capacity venue will be used when Kenya co-hosts football's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) next June and July alongside Tanzania and Uganda.
"We learned from the 2025 bid because there were areas that we did not score well," Barnaba Korir, who worked on the successful bid, told the BBC World Service.
"Because of that, we managed to improve on those areas.
"I'm happy that the infrastructure that we have already developed will also meet the standards that we have seen all over the world."
Hotel space is one area not expected to be a problem, with Nairobi a regular host for large conventions.
"Kenya is also known for its very dynamic hospitality, the tourism sector," Elijah Mwangi, principal secretary at the State Department for Sports, told the BBC.
"It has a game park within the city, so we are waiting to welcome everybody."
President Ruto made financial and security guarantees in order to secure the Championships.
"We thank World Athletics for the confidence it has placed in Kenya," Ruto said.
"We will honour that confidence by delivering an unforgettable championship worthy of our athletes, our country and our continent."
Expanding athletics
Lord Coe became president of World Athletics (then known as the IAAF) in 2015 and has pledged to grow the sport around the globe.
During his time in office the World Championships have been hosted in Qatar (2019), the United States (2022) and Tokyo, while China's capital Beijing will stage them in 2027.
Kenya has successfully hosted age-grade events in Nairobi and the World Cross Country Championships in Mombasa, while the World Athletics Relays were held in Botswana's capital Gaborone in May.
With Coe's third term in office coming to an end next year, one official involved in Kenya's bid, speaking before the host announcement, said it was "unthinkable" that Nairobi would not succeed.
"With this decision we continue to fulfil our mission of growing athletics worldwide," Coe said.
"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances.
Coe hailed the "quality, ambition and commitment" of all four bidding cities.
London, Munich and Rome have all previously held the Olympics, with the World Championships in London as recently as 2017, but the chance to break new ground in Africa was clearly compelling.
UK Athletics chief executive Jack Buckner said his team was "deeply disappointed" to see London miss out.
What is needed next?
Kenya now faces logistical and organisational challenges over the next three years as it prepares to deliver Africa's first World Championships.
With the 2027 Afcon looming large on the horizon, Nairobi will have a chance to test-run getting fans in and out of the Kasarani Stadium, which lies about a half-hour drive from the city's central business district.
The venue does not have any rail connections but Korir says World Athletics officials were "very satisfied" by Kenya's transport plan.
There were instances of overcrowding when the stadium hosted Kenya games at football's African Nations Championships last year, which led to the capacity being reduced for some matches.
Delays in preparations for Afcon have raised concerns, and the funding for the World Championships will come entirely from the Kenyan government.
Mwangi revealed that $78m (£58.5m) is the current estimate for the government's contribution, with sponsorship deals also playing a role.
"We are prepared to ensure that whatever is expected to be paid, it is paid in the due time," he added.
Presidential elections are scheduled for next year, but Korir is confident organisers will secure the "huge" and "legally binding" figure earmarked even if there is a change in government.
"Whatever the government assigns now will be observed by the next government. It is an international agreement," he said.
Then comes ticketing, first to make sure the local population are not priced out and then to ensure the stands are filled.
The cheapest tickets for the Under-18 World Championships in 2017 were priced at 200 Kenyan shillings ($1.15, £1.14) but attendances were low until entry was made free.
World Athletics generated $522m in revenue from Tokyo 2025, with a total of 619,000 tickets sold over the nine days of competition, while London sold a record 705,000 tickets in 2017.
In passing up the opportunity of returning to the British capital, World Athletics has chosen expansion over guaranteed ticket sales, but attendances will be scrutinised - especially after the sparse numbers seen in the stands in Doha in 2019.
Korir, however, is confident the Kasarani Stadium "will be full" on "every day" of competition, including morning sessions, if sales begin early enough.
Meanwhile, Kenya has endured a spate of doping scandals in recent years, with 11 individuals banned by the Athletics Integrity Unit so far this year alone.
The pressure is now on the East African nation to deliver on its promises in the build-up to Nairobi 2029 and ensure the Championships pass off without any major issues.
Additional reporting by Ian Williams and Celestine Karoney.

Phones don’t have lights

Spacetech startup GalaxEye has secured ₹63.84 Cr in financial support under the Centre’s Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund to develop its next-generation multisensor satellite technology. The Technology Development Board (TDB), under the Department of Science and Technology (DST), has signed an agreement with the Bengaluru-based startup to provide the support through optionally convertible debentures. The project has a total approved cost of ₹247.69 Cr, the Centre said in a statement. It aims to develop an indigenous satellite capable of OptoSAR imaging at a resolution finer than 0.5 metres. The project will take the technology from Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 6 to TRL 9, progressing from a demonstrated prototype towards a system proven in operation. GalaxEye's technology combines synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and electro-optical (EO) imaging. While optical imaging can be affected by cloud cover and lighting conditions, SAR can capture images through clouds and without daylight. By combining the two, the startup aims to provide high-resolution Earth observation across different weather and lighting conditions. The proposed satellite’s applications include wide-area and long-range surveillance, detection of people and vehicles, and target classification, the government said. “The agreement with GalaxEye reflects TDB’s focus on enabling indigenous capabilities in emerging space technologies and supporting their journey towards commercialisation,” TDB secretary Rajesh Kumar Pathak said. GalaxEye Builds Its Satellite Capabilities Founded in 2021 by Suyash Singh, Denil Chawda, Kishan Thakkar, Pranit Mehta, and Rakshit Bhatt, GalaxEye builds multi-sensor earth observation satellites designed to provide high-resolution imaging and geospatial intelligence catering to sectors such as defence, agriculture, infrastructure and disaster management. The startup raised ₹44.2 Cr as part of an ongoing Series A round earlier this year, with investors including Speciale Invest, Rainmatter, MV Core and Mounttech Growth Fund. The IIT Madras-incubated startup has raised nearly $27 Mn in funding to date from investors like Speciale Invest, Mela Ventures, and Anicut Capital. The startup claims to be building the world’s first multi-sensor earth observation satellite and aims to deploy a constellation of indigenous micro-satellites with data fusion capabilities. Earlier this month, GalaxEye received a US patent for satellite imaging technology, the first of its kind for an Indian spacetech startup. The patent covers the core architecture behind the startup’s proprietary OptoSAR technology. This came after the startup launched its maiden OptoSAR satellite under ‘Mission Drishti’ in May, which was touted as India’s largest privately built earth observation satellite and the world’s first imaging satellite using OptoSAR. However, it lost communication with the satellite in July due to an anomaly linked to a geomagnetic solar storm. The startup is now targeting the launch of two new OptoSAR satellites in the next two years while expanding its in-house capabilities to further strengthen quality, reliability, and execution. Spacetech Funding Enters New Phase The agreement adds to support for spacetech startups under the Centre’s ₹1 Lakh Cr RDI Fund, approved in July 2025 to increase private-sector participation in research, development, and innovation. The fund is designed to finance technology development and commercialisation through long-term capital. It operates through a two-tier structure, with the Anusandhan National Research Foundation acting as the first-level custodian and institutions such as TDB and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council serving as second-level fund managers. According to the government statement, TDB has approved 22 projects with a combined project cost of ₹4,744 Cr, involving ₹2,192 Cr in RDI support. GalaxEye joins other spacetech startups backed under the programme. In May, Dhruva Space secured ₹105 Cr for Project Garud, which aims to develop a standardised satellite platform for large-scale deployments across telecom, earth observation, and national security applications. The public funding comes alongside larger private investments in the sector. Indian spacetech startups have raised nearly $250 Mn in 2026 so far. These include Skyroot Aerospace’s $60 Mn round, which made it India’s first spacetech unicorn, and Pixxel’s $100 Mn Series C to expand satellite manufacturing and imaging capabilities.

Rows of hardware and car-part shops line Garstin Bastion Road, with faded signs crammed together above their shutters. By day, the street is one of Old Delhi’s busiest commercial thoroughfares. But as dusk falls, GB Road, as it is known locally, transforms into one of the city’s most notorious red-light districts.
An estimated 2,800 sex workers live and work in brothels that occupy the upper floors of the dilapidated buildings, their entrances tucked behind narrow stairways and unmarked doors. Women sit on plastic stools beneath the stairways, calling out to men passing on the street, while others watch from windows above, their eyes following the movement below before customers are directed upstairs.
The challenges the women of GB Road face are numerous and well documented – from health risks to abuse, debt to poor sanitation. Now they face a new struggle: India’s controversial electoral reform process. The Election Commission’s special intensive revision, or SIR, is a nationwide exercise in which electoral rolls have shrunk by more than 58 million voters across the 13 states covered in the first two of three main phases. In Delhi, covered in the third phase, the scale of exclusion is the highest recorded as a percentage: 4.76 million names – 33% of the city’s previous electorate – do not appear on the city’s draft roll published on 31 August.
The government says SIR is meant to “purify” the electoral rolls by removing ineligible voters, including alleged undocumented migrants, but critics have accused Narendra Modi’s government of using it to target minority voters and reshape electoral rolls in ways that could benefit his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
On GB Road, the proportion of those excluded is even higher. Data shared by officials overseeing about 1,300 voters in the area show that about 650 were sex workers on the previous electoral roll. Of these, at least 500 have either been marked as “shifted”, meaning they have moved home or location, or have been unable to establish their eligibility because of missing documentation – more than three-quarters of the sex workers on the local roll.
One of them is 36-year-old Beauty*, who has lived on GB Road for more than two decades. She got her first voter ID in 2008. At the time, the address where she lived and worked as a sex worker and verification by a government official called a booth-level officer (BLO) were enough to put her on the electoral roll. She voted in previous elections.
But under the new rules, voters had to establish eligibility by proving their link to the relevant previous electoral roll or by producing prescribed documents such as a passport, birth or education certificate – a paper trail Beauty struggled to reconstruct. Trafficked at 16 and brought to the brothels of GB Road, she has no contact with her family. She does have an Aadhaar card, India’s biometric identity document used widely to establish identity and access government services, with her GB Road address. But Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship and does not, by itself, establish eligibility to vote under the SIR process.
She tried to get a copy of her matriculation certificate, which is evidence of schooling, from the village in Rajasthan where she grew up. One of her regular customers of the past 10 years – a man she refers to as her husband, agreed to help track down the old record but failed.
“If I had the papers to show my father’s birth certificate, or even my own matriculation certificate, then I could prove who I am,” she says. “But how can I go back to my village to ask for these things when my trafficking has brought so much shame to my family that they no longer accept me?”
Now Beauty has lost hope – and, for now, her vote. Her name was left out of Delhi’s recent draft electoral roll. For her, the voter ID had meant more than a piece of identification. Sex workers, she says, are accustomed to being treated as immoral, degraded and less worthy than others.
“We all shit. That is what makes us equal as human beings. Voting is the same in the realm of rights. When I stand in that queue, nobody is more or less than me. It reminds me that whatever people think about my work, I am still equal to everyone else.”
Beauty is not alone in struggling to prove her eligibility. The SIR requirements have exposed the precarious paper trails of women across GB Road, a roughly 1.5km stretch running between two of Delhi’s historic landmarks, Ajmeri Gate and Lahori Gate.
Of the nine sex workers interviewed for this story, none had successfully completed the SIR process: six said they had never received the enumeration form distributed by BLOs to verify voters’ details and collect information for the electoral-roll revision, while the remaining three were unable to meet the documentation requirements.
According to Kiran Deshmukh, a sex worker and coordinator at the National Network of Sex Workers (NNSW), many have spent years, even decades, in Delhi but possess few documents establishing their family histories or links to earlier electoral rolls. “Some were trafficked as children and lost contact with their families; others never attended school or have moved between rooms and brothels without leaving a stable documentary trail,” says Deshmukh. “It is impossible in such circumstances to prove such rigid eligibility requirements under SIR.”
The process is so cumbersome that even people who are literate and have institutional and organisational support can struggle to establish their eligibility. “The process of receiving the enumeration form, knowing when you have not received it, reaching out, then trying to create a paper trail is so daunting that the entire burden of proving your eligibility is placed on the citizen to protect their own constitutional right,” says Deshmukh.
Sagrika Rajora, a researcher and member of Voter Adhikar Manch, a citizens’ collective, argues that the burden falls particularly heavily on people whose lives do not fit neatly into the categories used by the verification process. “To identify people of such marginality is a tedious task. These categories of ‘shifted’ become an easy way forward for booth-level officers, when finding people on the ground is already time-consuming.”
BLOs are often drawn from occupations such as auxiliary nurses or health workers, adding electoral duties to already demanding jobs. Some have raised concerns about the workload and unrealistic timelines of the exercise. Yet, Rajora says, there has been little effort to streamline the process to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out”, the aim outlined by the Delhi chief electoral officer, Ashok Kumar.
“There is so much discretion vested in one BLO. Even if you leave citizenship aside and talk only about voter rights, the entire process of delivering and collecting these forms depends on that one person. There are no grounds for entrusting one person with such a huge responsibility without any accountability at all,” Rajora says.
“It is not surprising that sex workers are among those being excluded. When people have lives that are so complex and mobile, you are going to be untraceable, absent from the system. These are the people for whom such a verification system is simply not designed to work.”
The gaps also cause problems for workers’ children when they reach adulthood. “Children may not possess documents establishing parentage in the manner expected for verification. Some are raised by relatives, guardians or members of the community, while others grow up in institutional care, making conventional family records difficult to establish,” says Deshmukh.
For 23-year-old Dinesh*, whose mother was a sex worker, the problem is not abstract. His mother died three years ago, but she never had a birth certificate. Without one, obtaining her death certificate became nearly impossible, leaving Dinesh with little documentation through which to establish his maternal lineage.
When Dinesh submitted his enumeration form, he relied on his matriculation certificate as proof of his identity. But the booth-level officer pointed out that it did not have his father’s name. “If my mother gave birth to me, why do I need a man’s name on any official certificate?” he asks.
Dinesh says his name is missing from the draft electoral roll. He is still unsure why, but suspects the absence of his father’s name may have been a factor.
The NNSW has written to the chief electoral officer seeking special measures to ensure that sex workers and their children are not excluded from the SIR. But the joint chief electoral officer, Balram Meena, told The Hindu there was no separate process for sex workers. “If their mapping can’t be done and there are no documents either, their names will be removed as per the process.”
The fear of losing the vote is not only about voting rights. In West Bengal, where the SIR has already been completed, the BJP government has used lists of voters deleted during the exercise to scrutinise eligibility for welfare schemes. The BJP chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, says welfare programmes will continue under a “transparent process”, but adds: “No deceased person, illegal infiltrator, or non-Indian individual will be allowed to avail benefits meant for citizens of the state.” The government has excluded about 3 million beneficiaries from its new Annapurna Bhandar welfare for women scheme, using SIR deletion data in its verification process.
In Delhi, the next stage of the SIR process – issuing notices to those whose eligibility or previous electoral-roll details could not be established or matched, and dealing with claims and objections – has now begun and will continue until 29 October. Those excluded from the draft roll can challenge their omission. But Dinesh says he does not intend to.
After years of being asked to produce documents that his family never had, he is unsure what more he can submit to prove that he exists.
“Even if my mother were alive today, I don’t think that would be enough to prove anything. She never had the documents they are asking for. So how am I supposed to get those documents now, especially after her death?”
* Names have been changed. Workers and residents did not permit any photography during the Guardian’s visit

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has proposed a draft amendment to the Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations, 2011, to restrict the manufacture and sale of analogue products as “Paneer” and prevent consumers from being misled about the nature and composition of such products, noted a release issued by the Union Health Ministry on Thursday.
The proposed Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Amendment Regulations, 2026 seek to insert a new clause under Regulation 2.1.1 of the existing regulations, specifically covering “paneer made of constituents not derived from milk”.
Under the proposed amendment, products already licensed or registered under the ‘Analogue in Dairy Context’ category would be required to discontinue the use of the term “Paneer” in their nomenclature, labelling or marketing.
The proposed amendment is aimed at ensuring that the nomenclature and presentation of food products accurately reflect their nature and composition, thereby enabling consumers to make informed choices.
As the notification is a draft regulation, FSSAI has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public. US president Donald Trump called told Xi Jinping that China 'helping Iran' was unacceptable, during the China president' Washington visit, said US Ambassador to China David Perdue on Friday.
"We made it very clear to them weeks ago that, you know, any help that they would give Iran, whether it be direct or indirect, whether it be intelligence or parts or military equipment, was totally unacceptable. President Trump made that very clear again yesterday. This is an ongoing drumbeat," said Perdue said in a CNBC interview.
"These two leaders are beginning to develop a relationship of somewhat trust and also working on the issues. I mean, this was a very candid and open conversation, and every time they talk, I think we see a different level of intimacy about these difficult issues that we're dealing with," he added.
Xi Jinping made a three-day state visit to Washington at the invitation of Trump, with the trip focused on maintaining stability in ties between the world's two largest economies. Xi and Trump held a 90-minute closed-door meeting on Thursday, discussing the Middle East, Ukraine and the Korean Peninsula, according to China's official readout. 
No major breakthroughs were reported on trade or artificial intelligence.
Although, Trump made a post on social media hailing the "productive meeting", saying, "Tremendous things will be happening. Like almost everyone else, he seemed to like calling the poorly and inaccurately named Artificial Intelligence to a far more accurate and important name, SUPER INTELLIGENCE. That would be “SUPER!” Everyone last night agreed, also."
Trump also hosted Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at a black-tie state dinner attended by prominent US technology executives and other business leaders. Earlier, Trump gave Xi a tour of parts of the White House, including the Oval Office, a gallery of presidential portraits, the new helicopter landing pad and the ballroom under construction. Melania Trump and Peng separately visited the Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art.
On Friday, Trump was taking Xi to the National Archives, where the US Constitution, Declaration of Independence and Bill of Rights are preserved. The visit comes as the US marks its 250th anniversary, with Trump saying he wanted to show Xi some of the country's historic treasures. Xi's visit also coincides with China's Mid-Autumn Festival, a major family holiday.

Japanese municipalities are turning their low name recognition into tourism promotion opportunities, using self-deprecating jokes to attract attention.
The Akita prefectural government’s tourism strategy division launched a campaign from May to July this year to distribute accommodation coupons under a catchy slogan, “Akita Prefecture: Still Unnoticed.”
The northeastern prefecture has struggled with its low name recognition despite its rich tourist attractions, including the Shirakami-Sanchi mountain range, a UNESCO World Heritage site, which also straddles Aomori Prefecture, and the Akita Kanto Festival, a traditional summer event in August.
In June, the number of overnight stays in Akita totaled 339,100, up 34.4% from a year earlier, marking the highest growth rate nationwide, according to the Japan Tourism Agency’s statistics.
“The campaign appears to have had an effect,” a prefectural government official said.
The city of Kusatsu in Shiga Prefecture, aims to raise its name recognition by promoting itself as “Kusatsu without onsen hot springs,” setting itself apart from the town of Kusatsu in Gunma Prefecture, one of the country’s leading hot spring resorts.
Last year, the city’s tourism and products association released a mascot character named “Onsen Dorobou,” a thief who steals hot spring water from all over Japan to turn Lake Biwa in Shiga into a hot spring. The character attracted widespread attention, leading to its appearance at the Kusatsu onsen festival in Gunma in August.
“It may seem like self-deprecation, but we hope it will provide an opportunity for people to learn about the charm of Kusatsu,” Kana Sakamoto, 29, an official of the tourism and products association said.
Among Japan’s 47 prefectures, Tottori became the only one without a Matsuya gyūdon beef-on-rice restaurant after Matsuya Foods Holdings opened an outlet in Izumo, Shimane Prefecture, this spring.
The prefectural character, “Toripy,” posted on X, “I don’t care about it at all!” Even so, the attached photo shows him sitting at a desk with a fan bearing the slogan “Come here!” The post drew attention and recorded more than 800,000 page views.
In April, the Tottori prefectural government launched a campaign using the hashtag “#If Matsuya comes to Tottori” to solicit collaborative menus using ingredients produced in the prefecture on its X account.
“We don’t take it negatively that we became the last prefecture, but we want to make it positive and convey our charm,” said Saki Nakagaki, 35, an official of the prefecture’s public relations division, who organized the campaign.
