Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s presidential campaign has accused Donald Trump of wanting to “colonise” Brazil in order to capture its natural resources by meddling in next month’s presidential election.
The accusation came in a televised campaign advert that was broadcast on Thursday by Lula’s team amid growing fears over the impact alleged US interference could have on the vote.
The TV spot claimed the US president was trying to sway the election in favour of Lula’s far-right adversary in the election, Flávio Bolsonaro, in order to advance Trump’s interests in the South American nation.
“Flávio Bolsonaro is Trump’s candidate and what Trump wants is to colonise Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust,” the female narrator tells viewers in the minute-long video.
The state department has denied claims the US is meddling in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” it said last month in a statement.
Writing on X, Lula accused Bolsonaro of wanting to “hand our natural resources over to the United States”.
“If it’s up to him, Brazil will become a colony again,” the incumbent leftwing president added.
With just over a week to go until the 4 October first round vote, Lula and Bolsonaro are neck and neck in the polls. A second round run-off will be held on 25 October if no candidate secures more than half of the votes.
In recent weeks, there has been growing alarm – both in Brazil and overseas – about Washington’s apparent attempts to influence the result, with a campaign of diplomatic and economic pressure, including 25% tariffs on Brazilian imports.
Speaking at the UN general assembly in New York this week, Lula indirectly criticised the US’ perceived meddling, telling delegates: “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians.”
Earlier this week, dozens of Democratic party congresspeople wrote to secretary of state, Marco Rubio, to denounce the Trump administration’s “apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s elections through what they called a “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilisation in Brazil”.
The narrator of Lula’s campaign ad cited a series of recent media stories relating to alleged acts of US meddling.
They include reports about the alleged interference of Big Tech companies as well as a confidential document sent to electoral authorities by Brazil’s intelligence agency warning of a “critical level” of risk of US interference. The campaign video also highlighted recent claims about links between Bolsonaro’s campaign and the conservative donor network Rockbridge, which was co-founded by Trump’s vice-president JD Vance.
Éden Valadares, the communications secretary for Lula’s Worker’s party (PT), said the campaign ad was part of efforts to “alert the Brazilian people” to the ideologically-driven US campaign. “We don’t believe it will work but nor will we sit back and do nothing,” Valadares said.
“President Lula has instructed us … to mobilise Brazilian society … [and] to react in the streets,” added Valadares, who said a nationwide series of events were being planned for this Sunday.
Fears over US meddling are not confined to the Brazilian left. This week, another of the right-wing candidates in Brazil’s election, Renan Santos, also denounced Trump’s behaviour and said he did not want Brazil to become a US vassal state. “They want to interfere in Brazil’s elections to secure satisfactory contracts involving rare earths,” Santos claimed in a social media video.
Recalling the US invasion of Venezuela in January, Santos added: “I don’t want to see Latin America become an American protectorate.”
In the letter sent to Rubio on Friday, the Democratic lawmakers wrote that “rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy”, the US was “acting as an agent of interference and destabilisation – using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic US ally and trading partner”.
They asked Rubio if Trump’s administration would commit to respecting Brazil’s electoral process and requested a response by 1 October. The state department has not yet responded to a request for comment.

Divers recover a total of 52 bodies from capsized ferry in Indonesia after a dayslong search
Divers in Indonesia have recovered 52 bodies following the capsizing of a ferry in rough seas earlier this month
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Divers in Indonesia have recovered a total of 52 bodies in a dayslong operation that followed the capsizing of a ferry in rough seas earlier this month, officials said Friday. Authorities had rescued 108 people, but 83 people remain missing.
The Virgo Transport 8 ferry was en route from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan on Borneo island with 243 people on board when it issued a distress call on Sept. 13, reporting the vessel was listing in rough seas, with waves reaching 3 meters (10 feet).
Authorities later learned the ferry had capsized in the waters of the Masalembo archipelago in the Java Sea.
During the search operation, divers recovered bodies of passengers after smashing ferry windows underwater to enter the ship. Indonesia’s Search and Rescue Agency said all available resources were being deployed in the search operation.
“Our primary focus is to locate the missing victims and provide closure to their families,” said Mohammad Syafii, head of Indonesia’s National Search and Rescue Agency.
The agency is still planning to salvage the ferry and pull the wreckage from a depth of about 30 meters (98 feet).
The recovered bodies have been taken to the police hospital in the Borneo city of Banjarmasin for identification before being handed over to their families.
Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands where ferries are a common method of travel. Disasters occur regularly, with weak safety enforcement often blamed.

With an eye toward pandemic preparedness, a U.N.-backed agency has signed sub-licensing deals with 11 manufacturers to develop and manufacture generic versions of a Roche influenza treatment.
Under the agreements, brokered by the Medicines Patent Pool, the companies can develop, manufacture, and supply Xofluza in 129 countries, covering nearly all low- and middle-income countries. The manufacturers will also have access to technical data, reference products for bioequivalence studies, and other support intended to help with regulatory approval in those countries.
This marks the latest effort to widen access for a needed medication to poor countries, a goal that has often required the pharmaceutical industry to balance its financial priorities with ensuring its medicines can be affordably obtained by the largest number of patients possible.

Google is taking its first step toward making Project Suncatcher a reality. Announced last year, Suncatcher is Google’s “moonshot” effort to design orbital AI data centers, which AI boosters like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos have pitched as an alternative to divisive terrestrial data centers. Google’s first experimental satellite will launch on October 1 with the aim of validating Google’s vision for a constellation of AI satellites.
The satellite, dubbed MVP, is about the size of a refrigerator. Inside, it has four of Google’s custom TPU AI accelerators, which are used to train AI models and run inference to generate tokens for AI workloads. On Earth, a data center will run thousands of these chips, which consume massive amounts of power—one of the reasons putting solar-powered AI hardware in space is so attractive.
MVP is starting small, with solar panels that supply only about one kilowatt of power, The New York Times reports. That’s enough to power a microwave or a hair dryer. Google did not build the satellite from scratch. While the AI hardware inside is Google’s, the spacecraft comes from a satellite imagery firm called Planet Labs. The initial plan was to launch two custom satellites in 2027, but Google wanted to accelerate its efforts. So the company opted to integrate its chips into a satellite that Planet Labs had already built for an early test.
Google’s AI test will launch as part of the upcoming Transporter-18 rideshare aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Eventually, Google wants to have networks of orbiting satellites that communicate over high-speed laser connections, probably requiring expensive dedicated launches. This lone satellite will serve as a test of several technologies and will operate for just a few months.

President Droupadi Murmu on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) urged popular film artists not to endorse products harmful to people's health, saying a “true star” spreads light, not darkness, highlighting the impact of words and actions of celebrities on young minds.
Ms. Murmu distributed the 72nd National Film Awards for 2024 in various categories of cinema at Ekta Nagar (Kevadia), near the Statue of Unity, in a glittering ceremony attended by top talents of the film industry.

"I hope you are paying heed to these requests," she said.
Describing film artists as key representatives of the creative economy, the President said highly popular artists possessed immense potential to influence citizens, especially the youth.
She also praised the quality of films being produced in the country, saying it strengthened her conviction that Indian films would set world-class benchmarks for quality.
"Learning about the quality films being produced in the country strengthens my conviction that our films will set world-class benchmarks for quality. I wish you all and the film industry a golden future," Ms. Murmu said.

Government hospitals across Tamil Nadu are facing a shortage of surfactant medicines, a critical and life-saving medicine for pre-term babies.
The shortage has been persisting for the past few months, and several Special Newborn Care Units (SNCUs) at government hospitals have been flagging it up for the Health Department.
Doctors said surfactant medicines are essential to inflate the lungs of pre-term babies in need of the therapy. They utilised external bovine or porcine surfactants (intratracheal) in pre-term babies. These surfactants were part of the speciality drug rate contract purchases of the Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation (TNMSC).
Inquiries with a number of hospitals and doctors revealed that a number of centres were facing short supply of surfactants in the past few months. Official sources confirmed that government hospitals, among them medical college hospitals in Theni, Dharmapuri, Tiruppur, Cuddalore, Tiruvannamalai, Vellore and Karur districts and in Chennai, reported surfactant vial shortage, while some hospitals said they had uninterrupted supply.
A doctor, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the shortage prevailed in the past three to four months owing to a number of factors. “First, we got no allotment. Secondly, some centres miscalculated their requirement, which is based on the average number of pre-term babies delivered, and thirdly, there was higher utilisation. This is a life-saving medicine essential to inflate the lungs of pre-term babies who are otherwise solid,” he said.
A doctor at another hospital said continuous supply was not assured, and shortage occurred frequently. “Currently, we are borrowing from other sub-centres which are referring babies to us. It is very difficult for us to manage newborn units without surfactants. Sometimes, we purchase them privately using SNCU funds to save the babies,” another doctor said.
A senior paediatrician said that after 34 weeks of gestation, the foetal lungs are generally mature enough to support exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide after birth. “However, in very pre-term babies, the alveoli, which are the tiny air sacs in the lungs, may not be sufficiently mature to function effectively on their own. Surfactant, a substance produced in the lungs, helps keep the alveoli open. But in babies born very prematurely, not enough surfactant may be produced, making it difficult for them to maintain adequate oxygen levels. Depending on the baby’s condition, doctors may use respiratory support such as CPAP or a mechanical ventilator. Surfactant is delivered directly into the lungs through the endotracheal tube to prevent hyaline membrane disease.”
Lung maturity in a newborn is critical as decreased oxygen could cause hypoxia and conditions such as retinopathy of prematurity and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, he said.
A Health Department source denied that there was any shortage. “There was no procurement delay. Some centres may have miscalculated their requirement, resulting in shortage, or may have utilised more vials. In such circumstances, they have obtained the required supply from neighbouring facilities. A six-month purchase order, worth nearly ₹9 crore, has been issued. Additionally, operational costs are provided for paediatricians to make local purchases whenever required,” he said.

Pope Leo warns a 'paradise of machines' could undermine humanity on his France visit
PARIS — Pope Leo XIV warned Friday that a "paradise of machines" risked undermining humanity as he opened a trip to France by posing fundamental questions about what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence, a nuclear arms race and other threats to life itself.
Leo raised existential concerns about scientific progress, life and human rights during his opening speech to President Emmanuel Macron and authorities at the Élysée Palace and then to diplomats and United Nations employees at the headquarters of UNESCO, the U.N. culture and education organization.
With wars plaguing Europe and the Middle East, he reaffirmed the Vatican's opposition to nuclear weapons and said the nuclear deterrence doctrine was "mistaken" since it was just fueling a new arms race.
"Peace is not a balance of power; rather, it is built day by day through dialogue and justice," he said.
Leo has an intense four days in France, where the Catholic Church has lost ground on influencing ethical issues given the strict approach to secularism that is enshrined in the French Constitution.
Church bells tolled across the country when Leo's charter flight landed at Paris' Orly airport, and more than a million people are expected to turn out to see him. They lined the streets of the capital as Leo's motorcade passed by, underscoring the surprising level of interest in Leo's visit, the first official state visit by a pope in 18 years.
Macron said Leo's visit brings "a source of hope" to many French people.
"France stands on the side of peace, effective multilateralism, respect for international law and the United Nations Charter ... because every life has equal value, and all peoples must be defended," he said.
A capstone visit as Macron's term ends
For Macron, who is barred from seeking a third term in May elections, hosting the American pope is something of a capstone. Pope Francis had refused repeatedly to make a proper state visit to France during his 12-year pontificate and pointedly refused to join the inauguration of the rebuilt Notre Dame cathedral in 2024.
"For a president of the republic as Macron, who is at the end of his mandate, it can be important to be aside the pope and to capture a part of his popularity," said Charles Mercier, director of history and sociology of Catholicism studies at Paris EPHE university.
With seven months left in his term, Macron's approval ratings are near record lows, driven by anger over the rising cost of living and criticism of France's growing debt and deficit and deteriorating public services.
Smiling broadly as Leo spoke French, Macron thanked the pope for visiting, saying: "You are here with us for an extended visit, giving us your time, and that is moving."
The Rev. Aristide Ahidote, from Ivory Coast, was among those who planned to attend the pope's vespers service in Notre Dame later Friday. "God has given us a pope with vigor and strength," he said.
While acknowledging the French church has declined in popularity, Ahidote said "it still has small remnants and these small remnants have been edifying for me."
Leo appeals to loftier questions about life
Unlike Francis, who liked to travel to small Catholic communities far from Rome, Leo has been keen to emphasize and reawaken Europe's Christian roots. He is seeking to push the church's message about the value and dignity of human life in a country where the right to abortion was enshrined in the constitution in 2024, and where lawmakers recently gave final approval to a bill allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication.
The French Catholic hierarchy strongly opposed the measures, in keeping with Catholic teaching that human life must be protected and defended from conception until natural death.
In his speech to Macron and other government and diplomatic authorities, Leo reminded France of its "deep Christian roots" and called especially for the French to remember that the right to life is the "indispensable foundation of every other human right."
His concern about the dignity of human life and humanity as a whole extended to the threats posed by artificial intelligence.
"The paradox has become increasingly evident: while 'intelligence' is attributed to computational systems, we struggle to recognize the inalienable dignity of human persons, whose lives are judged according to the criterion of efficiency and, when deemed no longer productive, are rejected and discarded," he said.
From the very start of his pontificate, Leo has identified AI as one of the greatest challenges facing humanity. He dedicated his first encyclical to the topic, "Magnificent Humanity," calling for robust regulation and for AI developers to work for the common good rather than profit.
Leo also appealed to AI developers and political leaders responsible for regulating them to slow down, an appeal that several top AI companies seem to have taken to heart in recently.
"If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a 'paradise of machines' invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for education in ethical discernment and the capacity to acknowledge the moral good," he said.
Speaking to reporters en route to Paris, Leo said he was pleased that his message was being heard and said he hoped the dialogue that the Vatican had initiated with tech companies would continue.
"And I think from their perspective, many of them, they're very much open to looking for ways of making sure that AI does not displace or ultimately destroy humanity, but rather than be a tool for human beings," he said. "Good things are beginning at least."

Education, Barcelona & Basque culture - why Spain are dominating football
- Published
World champions. European champions. Olympic champions. Undefeated in two and a half years. Spain are the dominant force in men's world football.
Of the past 10 major international tournaments, they have won five.
Going into Saturday's Nations League meeting with England at Wembley (19:45 BST), they are on an international record 38-match unbeaten run. They have not lost since a 1-0 defeat by Colombia in a 2024 friendly.
And the success does not stop with the senior men's team. During that time, Spain have also won:
- Six Under-19 European Championships
- Three Under-21 European Championships
- The Women's World Cup in 2023
At club level, Spanish teams have won half of all available Champions League and Europa League titles since 2009.
Spain football expert Guillem Balague told BBC Radio 5 Live there are "three pillars" that explain Spain's coaching culture and its unprecedented success.
"The first one was university, and in particular something called the National Institute of Physical Education," he said. "University entered physical education in Spain a long time ago, in the 1990s, and they created physical coaches and football coaches with a deep understanding of learning and training processes.
"Some of those fitness coaches became really big managers, like Rafa Benitez or Marcelino Garcia Toral. They came from learning and studying what football was about ahead of anybody else.
"The second pillar is the Basque culture. The Basque Country represents historically a special reference within Spanish football because they relate to work ethic, massive work ethic, daily effort.
"And the third pillar is what everybody knows: the Barcelona influence, Johan Cruyff and the tactical revolution that followed through him."
The Barcelona influence
Eight players from Barcelona's La Masia academy were in the Spain squad who won the 2010 World Cup under Vicente del Bosque, and another eight were in Luis de la Fuente's group as they lifted the trophy again this summer.
Barcelona won their first European Cup in 1992 under Cruyff playing total football - a style pioneered by the Netherlands team of the 1970s in which he played, and later mirrored at the Nou Camp under Pep Guardiola's management between 2008 and 2012.
That was a period where Barcelona won three consecutive La Liga titles, while Spain won back-to-back European Championships in 2008 and 2012 either side of their 2010 World Cup triumph.
Xavi, Andres Iniesta and Sergio Busquets were brought through in a system where players learn the art of ball possession and positional play in its purest form.
Jordi Gratacos, Barcelona's international director of academies from 2009 to 2011, and then from 2016 to 2020, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "The number one thing is to understand the tactical meaning of the technical action. What I mean is to create intelligent players [who are] very good in technical aspects.
"In this level, all players are very good in the technical aspects. The most important are these players who always decide the best option inside the field and make others better.
"The main objective is to prepare the players to take the position. It's an open education when you create some scenarios, context and ecosystem where the player needs to decide, and the coach needs also to say: 'This was the best option - next time, take the other option.'
"The most important thing is that they need to decide inside the game."
In his first two seasons as Barcelona manager, Hansi Flick is repeating what Guardiola did - not only in the sense that he has won two La Liga titles in a row and chasing a third.
Academy products form the engine of his project, with Lamine Yamal, Dani Olmo and Pau Cubarsi forming key components of success at both club and international level - just as the generation of 2008-12 did.
Spain have found the formula to repeat success, and Barcelona are at the heart of it.
The Basque Country
If Barcelona and Catalonia represents the artistry of Spanish football, the Basque Country represents its character.
Five players in the 2026 World Cup squad were from the region and came through at either Athletic Bilbao or Real Sociedad - clubs where eight players were playing at the time Spain won Euro 2024.
Then there is Mikel Merino, who scored a quarter-final winner against Germany at Euro 2024, before going on to score six goals in six games in World Cup qualifying, and late winners against Portugal and Belgium over the summer.
Although not Basque, Merino is from Pamplona in the autonomous community of Navarre - a region that has a significant influence of both Spanish and Basque culture.
Just five kilometres away from Pamplona is Zizur Mayor - the town where former Chelsea captain and Spain international Cesar Azpilicueta grew up.
When asked to describe Basque culture, Azpilicueta told BBC Radio 5 Live: "The discipline, the culture of working hard, of not giving up or being resilient, not very flashy.
"Normally, people want to display this culture of fight, being tough - like English football - more duels, more physical, less technical.
"But also in terms of tactical approach, more compact, great knowledge of knowing where to go, and with the ball keep it simple and try to go forward as quick as possible."
The five Basque players from the 2026 squad have formed an important part of Spain's recent success and are an embodiment of what Cruyff thought of players from that region.
Cruyff once said: "The first thing I did as a coach, was to sign four players from the Basque region. They are not afraid of anything."
For current Spain boss De la Fuente in 2026, Unai Simon played in goal, with former Manchester City defender Aymeric Laporte a key cornerstone of a defence that conceded just one goal in eight matches all tournament.
Nico Williams assisted the winning goal for Ferran Torres in the final against Argentina, Martin Zubimendi made a positive impact from the bench in both the Euro 2024 and World Cup finals, while Mikel Oyarzabal has scored 18 goals in his past 20 Spain appearances.
This influence stretches beyond the pitch as Basque coaches are in charge at four of England's biggest clubs - Mikel Arteta at Arsenal, Unai Emery at Aston Villa, Xabi Alonso at Chelsea and Andoni Iraola at Liverpool.
Education of the coaches
On to the final pillar - education.
Former Liverpool boss Rafael Benitez explained: "We were creating in Spain a group of fitness coaches who knew about football.
"I went to Liverpool John Moores University to see the programme of the sports scientists and they didn't have the knowledge in football that we had.
"They were really good in fitness, but with the ball and on the pitch, they didn't know how to manage. So you didn't have in England, this professional, this specialist in football, sports medicine and everything that we were studying in university.
"That was a crucial part of the formation of why Spain was improving and has been improving since then."

When I was in college in New York City, I loved the theater department so much that it became a punchline: my friends and I joked that after graduation, I would take a job there and stay forever. Little did we know that would actually become my reality.
After earning my degree in May 2022, I faced an uncertain job market in an industry still struggling to recover from the COVID-19 pandemic, which had forced my hands-on theater program to transition to remote learning.
Even though I was beginning to build a freelance career in theater, I wanted a day job to offer some stability in an unpredictable field. So, when a job as the administrator of my college theater department opened up, I applied, and a yearslong joke came true.
On paper, it was the perfect position: stable, better-paying than a comparable administrative role at a commercial theater, with ample time off and the flexibility to freelance as a director and writer. Above all, it was something I loved doing — managing the operations of a place I knew inside and out, surrounded by colleagues who had been my teachers, mentors, and friends for years.
In reality, the job was so much more than that: It allowed me to retrace the footsteps of my college self in a way I never would've imagined.
The theater department became my lifeline, but after a while, it made me feel stuck in the past
At the start of the pandemic, I was a sophomore in college. Like universities everywhere, we had to adjust to online learning, with campus operations not "returning to normal" until the spring of 2021.
So, two years later, by the end of my senior year, as I started preparing to say goodbye to a place that had become a lifeline, I balked.
I thought it was unfair that half my undergraduate career had been in a virtual or hybrid format, and this sense of betrayal froze me in my tracks. So, because I felt I hadn't had a full college experience and that I was unprepared to make the high-stakes choices required of graduates, I decided to stay.
There's a touching scene in Greta Gerwig and Noah Baumbach's film "Frances Ha," in which the titular character returns to her alma mater as a resident assistant for a summer program. Frances, expecting to fall back into the comfort of her old routine, shows up for a dance class only to be told it's just for students. It's a bittersweet moment in which she is forced to realize that, even if she doesn't feel like it, she has grown up.
I felt some version of this embarrassing alienation almost every day at work. Not only did I miss being a student in the department more than I was willing to admit, but I yearned for the experiences I never got to have. I couldn't help but feel jealous as new generations of students enjoyed field trips to theater productions around New York City, studied abroad, and took classes I would never get to take.
I watched each class of graduates displace me further from my own school days with a mixture of pride, melancholy, and envy that they were ready to inhabit the world beyond these halls.
Why couldn't I bring myself to do the same?
It took 4 more years, but I finally felt ready to leave
Despite these complicated feelings, I thrived in my job. The more I did, the more confident I became, until one day I looked around and realized that both my skill set and my confidence had grown beyond my circumstances.
I produced dozens of plays, elevated the visibility of our productions within the university and beyond, built lasting professional relationships with individuals I admire, and most importantly, helped students find their artistic voices.
In the end, forces outside my control dictated my exit, and after four years in the role, my job was eliminated as part of restructuring. I was heartbroken — and almost immediately relieved.
Having this choice made for me was easier than making it for myself: I could leave the party while I was still having fun.
I had stayed for an additional four years, an entire college life-cycle, and in that time, the school and I had both changed.
I realized I had finally maximized what I could learn at the place that taught me most of what I know. This, I thought, is how people are supposed to feel at the end of college. It was time to use what I had learned without losing the fondness for the place I had loved as a student.
Leaving felt like a second graduation, except this time, I actually feel prepared to leave the world of higher education behind and pursue a career as a freelance writer and director.
Without the sometimes messy, painful, wonderful experience I had in that job, I might never have felt prepared to make that leap.

A video showing a group of people removing and breaking metal barricades near a water body is being widely shared with a claim that it shows people in Karnataka vandalising barricades after authorities restricted Ganesh idol immersion (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: A video shows devotees in Karnataka vandalising barricades after authorities restricted Ganesh idol immersion.
Fact: The video is from Hyderabad. It shows members of the Bhagyanagar Ganesh Utsav Samithi removing barricades at Tank Bund while protesting restrictions on Ganesh idol immersion. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to an Instagram post by South Matters featuring the same visuals. According to the post, the visuals show tension at Tank Bund in Hyderabad, where representatives of the Bhagyanagar Ganesh Utsav Samithi staged a protest against restrictions on Ganesh idol immersion. We also found a post by the BNN channel on X stating the same.
Based on this, we conducted a relevant keyword search and found multiple media reports about the incident (here, here, here). According to these reports, the barricades were installed to prevent devotees from immersing Ganesh idols along the Tank Bund stretch. Members of the Bhagyanagar Ganesh Utsav Samithi (BGUS) protested against the restrictions and demanded that devotees be allowed to continue idol immersion at Tank Bund.
The comparison between the viral visuals and the visuals reported by the media can be seen below.
To sum up, this viral video of devotees removing barricades is from Hyderabad, not Karnataka.

The Supreme Court revives a controversial data system for citizenship checks
The U.S. Supreme Court has revived for now a federal data system the Department of Homeland Security revamped into a tool to check the citizenship of millions of Americans on voter rolls. The tool has mistakenly flagged some eligible voters as potential noncitizens.
The news comes as the Trump administration has been pouring resources into searching for noncitizens on voter rolls ahead of the upcoming election. The Supreme Court's decision opens the way for the administration to use its expanded version of the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements data system — known as SAVE — in that hunt, as well as in its unprecedented project of compiling lists of adult citizens in each state.
SAVE is a 40-year-old federal data system that was created to check the immigration status of noncitizens to determine their eligibility for public benefits. Then, DHS overhauled SAVE last year by linking it for the first time with Social Security Administration records, which include most Americans. The overhaul also allowed bulk queries to SAVE, and DHS encouraged states to upload their entire voter rolls to SAVE to verify those registered are U.S. citizens and not listed as deceased in federal records.
In June, U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan, a Biden appointee, blocked use of the modified version of SAVE, finding that its aggregation and disclosure of sensitive data violated the Social Security Act, the Privacy Act and the Administrative Procedures Act. "The federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote," she wrote.
After an appeals court panel refused to stay the lower court's decision in a 2-1 vote, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer appealed to the Supreme Court earlier this month.
In his appeal, Sauer wrote that since May 2025, the updated version of SAVE has verified more than 65 million voters across 26 states, and has flagged 28,635 as potential noncitizens.
"The district court's order, however, makes it harder to detect ineligible voters, undermining the integrity of federal elections and public confidence in the results of those elections," he wrote.
The League of Women Voters and the Electronic Privacy Information Center, which first challenged the legality of the SAVE overhaul a year ago, argued in a brief to the Supreme Court that Congress has not authorized the federal government to create a "master database of U.S. Citizens," nor does it have data that could do that accurately. The brief added that multiple statutes restrict repurposing and sharing Americans' sensitive data.
"Disregarding these laws, the government has recklessly created an error-laden master citizenship database that endangers millions of Americans' privacy and voting rights," the groups wrote.
They wrote that even though 65 million voters had been verified by the revamped SAVE, the government had not yet released the system's error rate, or how many Americans' citizenship was misrepresented "and who consequently have been forced to reverify their citizenship to retain their voter registration or obtain government benefits."
Even though Election Day is just over a month away and voting is underway, the Trump administration could try to make use of the expanded version of SAVE right away in its quest to check registered voters' citizenship.
An executive order President Trump signed in March calls for federal agencies to consult SAVE data, along with other federal records, to create state-by-state lists of adult U.S. citizens. The same order directs the U.S. attorney general to prioritize investigating and prosecuting election officials who provide ballots to ineligible voters. Even though the executive order says such state lists are to be completed 60 days before an election and that deadline has already passed, federal officials have indicated the project is still underway — although it is facing a legal challenge.
One factor with the election so near is that federal law bars states from "systematically" removing voters from rolls within 90 days of a federal election. Though the Trump administration and Republican state officials have argued that rule should not apply to removing noncitizens who were improperly registered. And the federal government argued to the Supreme Court that at a minimum, the updated SAVE should be able to be used for individual removal decisions ahead of an election.
Yet eligible voters have been erroneously flagged by SAVE, which has been unable to confirm the citizenship of certain categories of foreign-born people who become U.S. citizens.
After Texas ran its entire voter list of 18 million voters through SAVE, the system flagged 2,724 voters as potential noncitizens. County election officials then gave those individuals 30 days to prove their citizenship and, following state law, removed anyone who did not respond in time.
As NPR first reported in December, that effort resulted in citizens being removed from the rolls. Anthony Nel, whose story NPR highlighted in that reporting, gave a declaration in this lawsuit.
A recent press release from the Texas secretary of state revealed that of the 2,724 voters that were initially flagged by SAVE as potential noncitizens, some 20% were later found to be citizens who were reinstated. The same release said the office referred 117 cases identified by SAVE, or 4.2% of those flagged, for investigation for possible noncitizen voting.

- A video shared on social media in September 2026 by the conservative pundit Rob Smith featured an interview with a woman who claimed to live on the South side of Chicago andsaid that immigrants who entered the United States without authorization ("illegals") were receiving $20,000 in benefits from the Democratic-led governments of Chicago and Illinois.
- Snopes found that the interview was originally conducted by Brooke Shirley (the mother of the conservative social media personality Nick Shirley, who is herself a conservative social media personality) in August 2024, while the Democratic National Convention was happening in Chicago.
- The woman interviewed in the video made several claims that closely resembled major Republican talking points at the time. Some of those claims referenced policies that have become outdated, while others were misleading or exaggerated. As a result, we have not rated the claim.
- We contacted Smith for comment on the fact that his posts sharing the video never mentioned that the interview took place in 2024, and will update this story if we learn more. We also reached out to the Illinois Housing Development Authority to confirm that a program that provided up to 6 months or $15,000 in renter's assistance for asylum seekers was no longer active; it said that program stopped processing applications in June 2024.
In September 2026, a video posted by the conservative pundit Rob Smith appeared online claiming that Democrats were giving $20,000 in benefits to "illegals" in Chicago.
Snopes readers asked us to verify or disprove the claims made in the video, the latest in a long stretch of Republican-promoted rumors suggesting Democrats give large amounts of money or other benefits to immigrants living in the country without authorization. (Snopes fact-checked a version of that claim from the White House here).
Oftentimes, as is the case here, such claims are accompanied by the idea that these payments are the first step in a Democratic-led plot to permanently control the federal government.
The video presents its narrative without providing any additional evidence to support any of its claims, which are as follows:
Immigrants living in the country illegally receive $15,000 in food stamps from the government; - These immigrants receive $5,000 in cash from the government;
- These immigrants receive free, government subsidized Wi-Fi;
- The government covers these immigrants' rent for two years;
- Democrats give immigrants living in the country illegally these benefits as a sort of "bribe," with the later goal of granting them the right to vote. The immigrants would then repay the favor by voting for Democrats in large numbers, effectively diluting the voting power of non-immigrant Americans and giving the party long-term control.
We have refrained from rating this article because of the complexity of the claims in the video. Our research indicated that the first two claims were unfounded at best, while the third and fourth are exaggerated, though the fourth might have been the source behind the $15,000 figure. (The fifth claim is also unfounded, since it depends on the other four being true.)
We also noted that much of the rhetoric resembled common claims made during the last two years of President Joe Biden's administration, when Texas Gov. Greg Abbott made a show of busing migrants entering the U.S. to cities like Chicago. Much of the reporting around these issues also came from that time, leading us to suspect that the interview took place in the lead-up to the 2024 election, rather than in 2026.
We were able to confirm the theory using a reverse image search. The original video first appeared on the Instagram (archived) and TikTok accounts of conservative social media personality Brooke Shirley in late August 2024. Shirley, the mother of conservative social media personality Nick Shirley, originally posted the video in the days following the 2024 Democratic National Convention, which was held in Chicago. She has reposted the video at least twice since then.
As part of reporting this story, we contacted the Illinois Housing Development Authority, which ran a program that paid some rent costs for immigrants legally seeking asylum, though not to the extent suggested in the video
We also contacted Smith seeking clarification on the time discrepancy, since his September 2026 video never mentioned that the interview originally took place two years prior. We also asked whether Smith believed the policies described in the interview were active in 2026, but had not heard back.
Wealso attempted to confirm that the interview featured in the video, conducted with a woman who said she lived on Chicago's south side, was real — if it was instead generated using AI tools, for instance, the person who generated it 
Immigrants did not get $15,000 in food stamps
Immigrants who are in the country without authorization have never been eligible for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, and the video's assertion otherwise is not based on concrete evidence.
SNAP eligibility is extended to some non-citizens, but there are strict requirements, which were made even more strict after the passage of the Trump administration's much-touted "One Big Beautiful Bill" budget act in July 2025.
The principal requirement is that an immigrant must have a permanent residency card and have lived in the U.S. for at least five years, or be under the age of 18. Prior to July 2025, however, there were exceptions for refugees and individuals granted asylum. Even before these exceptions were eliminated, however, the claim would still have been untrue. SNAP benefits are calculated using the number of individuals in a household (in 2024, for instance, a family of four could receive a maximum of $973 each month, or just over $11,500 per year, with money subtracted based on an individual's household income. Immigration status does not factor into the calculation at all.
Immigrants are not getting $5,000 in cash
This claim also spread significantly around the time the video was originally shared.. It, too, is not based on any evidence. Snopes disproved a claim that immigrants got roughly $3,800 in 2017, and many prominent fact-checking organizations have disproved the claim that immigrants are getting $5,000 in cash or gift cards.
Furthermore, although exposing and cutting alleged wasteful government spending has been a major policy platform of the second Trump administration, there was no evidence the administration has identified or targeted programs matching the claims in the video.
Chicago has a free WiFi program ... for families of students
It's worth noting that many libraries in 
However, we found that the city does offer a free home internet program that immigrants can access. The program is eligible for families of students enrolled in Chicago Public Schools who receive free or reduced meals, and there are no eligibility requirements based on immigration status.
According to a city fact-sheet about the program, the internet access is valued at $10 per month — a drop in the bucket compared to the alleged $20,000 in benefits each immigrant allegedly receives.
Chicago did pay some immigrants' rent ... for up to 6 months, or $15,000
Snopes found that in the fall of 2022, months after Greg Abbott's busing program began, the state of Illinois did implement a program through the Illinois Housing Development Authority to cover the housing costs for the influx of migrants seeking asylum entering Chicago. (It should be noted that migrants are legally entitled to claim asylum, and therefore the description of these individuals as "illegal immigrants" is suspect at best).  
However, contrary to the claim, this program did not cover rent for two years. Several outlets have separately investigated a similar claim about the government of Michigan, too.
Instead, it covered a security deposit and rent for three months, with an optional extension for another three months, making six months in total. Applicants could receive a maximum of $15,000, which we suspect may have been the source of the food stamps figure.
According to an IHDA document detailing the program's accomplishments, it gave $3.7 million in grants to 681 families by the beginning of 2023, and another $1.4 million went toward additional three-month extensions. The authority claimed households received an average of $6,369, which is significant, but still below the fictitious $15,000 in food stamps described previously.
The program provided $53 million in rental assistance to 6,623 asylum seekers and families over the course of its lifespan, meaning that each successfully applicant received an average of just over $8,000.
One last note on this program: the IDHA's program paid landlords directly wherever possible — the money for rental assistance offered through the program was not given to immigrants.

In sum, the claims were a combination of 
It is true that immigrants were eligible for some welfare programs in Chicago during the later years of Joe Biden's presidency. However, the emergency housing program ended in 2024, while the additional restrictions on SNAP implemented by the Trump administration specifically bars refugees and asylum seekers — the individuals generally being incorrectly described as "illegal immigrants."

Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, speaks to Navin Gnanasekaran, longevity physician and head of Radiology, Apollo Hospitals, Chennai, about healthy ageing and the distinction between lifespan and healthspan.
India’s population is ageing. According to the United Nations Population Fund’s India Ageing Report 2023, the share of people aged 60 and above is projected to increase from 10.5% in 2022 to 20.8% by 2050. The episode discusses what this demographic change means for maintaining health and functional ability in later life.
The conversation covers racquet sports as a key form of physical activity, along with nutrition, sleep, muscle strength, stress, metabolism, inflammation and cognition. It also examines the importance of establishing sustainable health habits.
Physical activity is a key part of the discussion. The World Health Organisation recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week for adults, along with muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days. For older adults, the guidelines also recommend activities that improve balance and help prevent falls.
Racquet sports are discussed as one form of physical activity. Dr. Gnanasekaran looks at how they can combine exercise with social interaction and cognitive engagement.
The episode also discusses whether longevity advice needs to account for Indian lifestyles and health needs, including food habits, physical activity and other aspects of daily life.
The discussion focuses on the practical aspects of maintaining health and physical function as people live longer, and on the difference between simply extending lifespan and maintaining health during those additional years.

Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda
- Published
Teenage brothers Olly and Seb Fisher are closing in on their dream of international recognition - but it won't come from their homeland of Scotland.
Instead, the Partick Thistle duo are in line to play for Uganda.
They believe they would become the first white players ever to represent the African nation, thanks to their mother Kate being born there.
"My gran and grandad lived out here for, I think, four or five years," Olly, 18, tells BBC Sport Scotland. "My grandfather came out here to teach in a school then my mum was born here. So, it's a bit of a strange one."
The siblings became aware of interest from Uganda about six months ago, following a chance conversation some time before between their father and a football consultant at a game in Nigeria.
And, at the start of August, they were invited to attend under-20 and under-17s training camps.
They spent last week in Jinja in the country's eastern region and will stay on for one more week, with the pair saying they're "shocked" and "honoured" at the call-ups.
"I couldn't believe it," 16-year-old striker Seb said. "It's one of those things you look at and you're shocked. You can't believe it. Most other people couldn't as well."
Goalkeeper Olly had a similar reaction. "A real mixture of emotions," he said. "I was quite shocked. I didn't really think that this was a possibility but I was honoured to be asked to represent Uganda. I thought it was a real big opportunity."
Mum Kate is "ecstatic" and "thinks it'd be a great experience for us", adds Seb.
'The other boys have been brand new'
There is another Scottish link with Uganda, with former Hearts and Ghana midfielder Laryea Kingston currently coach of Uganda's under-20s.
And he is the one who believes the Fisher brothers are on the verge of making history.
"Coach Kingston was saying we'd be the first white boys to play for Uganda, which would be history in the making," Seb explained. "It is very special."
And Olly added: "It's never been done before, so definitely it is very special."
The pair feel like they're making connections with the African nation, having been reared on stories about Uganda from their grandparents.
And even though they have been training in oppressively warm conditions, they are embracing the opportunity.
"Everyone has been brilliant, welcoming, really great," Seb said. "The other boys have been brand new with us. Some of the boys actually come from the same area where my mum was born. So, they were all talking about that."
The boys will return to Scotland soon, combining training and playing with Thistle with university and school, but are planning to rejoin their new international team-mates in the near future.
Olly hopes to be part of his squad if they qualify for the Under-20's Africa Cup of Nations early next year, and Seb could be in the Under-17 squad for November's World Cup in Qatar.
"That's what you want as a footballer, being in an international environment," Seb said. "It makes you a better player and hopefully it does for the two of us, and I think it will, and benefit us very much going back to Scotland playing at Thistle."

The 51st episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu explores what constitutes a healthy diet amid the growing focus on protein, along with recent developments in osteoarthritis research, corneal donation and rabies prevention.
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss nutrition, weight management, osteoarthritis, corneal donation and transplantation, and rabies prevention.
Protein has become a major focus of nutrition advice, particularly on social media. The episode discusses the role of protein in the diet and why a healthy diet needs to be considered as a whole rather than through the lens of a single nutrient or product.
The conversation also looks at what happens to protein consumed in excess of the body’s requirements. Unlike carbohydrates and fat, protein is not stored in the body as a dedicated reserve. Amino acids from protein are used for functions including tissue repair, muscle maintenance and the production of enzymes and hormones, while excess intake can be used for energy or other metabolic processes.
The episode examines the role of diet and exercise in weight management, including research suggesting that combining dietary changes with physical activity can help support sustained weight loss. It also discusses why overall dietary patterns matter when assessing healthy eating.
Another segment looks at new research into osteoarthritis and cartilage regeneration. The research involves stromal-cell extracellular vesicles derived from menstrual blood and their potential role in cartilage repair. The findings are preliminary and are discussed in the context of ongoing research into new approaches to osteoarthritis care.
The episode also examines challenges in corneal donation and transplantation. Despite the potential of donated corneas to restore vision, some donated tissue does not reach patients who need it. The discussion looks at gaps in the process and the need to improve the use of donated corneal tissue.
Rabies prevention is another focus of the episode. The discussion looks at dog vaccination as an important part of preventing human rabies, given the role of dogs in transmission of the disease.
The episode can also be viewed here at The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap .

Danielle Smith’s popularity dips as her party now tied with NDP in support: poll
UCP sees support drop in Calgary by 10 points since the spring
New polling suggests both impressions of Premier Danielle Smith personally and support for her party are slipping in Alberta, with the UCP now essentially neck-and-neck with the opposition NDP.
The Janet Brown Opinion Research Poll for CBC News suggests 41 per cent of respondents would vote for the UCP if an election were held today, while 41 per cent would vote for the NDP.
In a similar poll conducted this spring, pollster Janet Brown said Smith’s government was enjoying the longest honeymoon period since the Ralph Klein-era.
But now?
“I think the UCP is having a struggle navigating this difficult situation that we're in right now,” said Brown. “Having a controversial referendum, the premier taking one position on the referendum [and] also trying to advocate for the nine other questions.”
Brown says it appears the party is shedding support on both sides of the independence debate: from separatists who wish Smith had taken a stance of support, and federalists frustrated by the question in the first place.
“She’s trying to walk the middle of the road, between the moderate, business conservatives and the far-right populist base that’s still angry over COVID restrictions,” said John Santos, data scientist with Janet Brown Opinion Research.
“And she’s getting hit by traffic on both sides of the road.”
The random survey of 1,200 Albertans was conducted between Sept. 8 and Sept. 21, with a margin of error of +/-2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.
Breaking down the numbers
The poll suggests the UCP has dropped eight points since April, while the NDP has seen its share of voter intention rise five points over that same time, putting the two parties at a tie.
“Obviously the NDP would take a lot of pleasure in seeing these numbers,” said Lisa Young, political science professor at the University of Calgary. “It suggests that they're on a trajectory that might make them competitive in the election.”
There’s also an increase in the number of respondents who say they would vote for another party, up six points since April, and the number of political “orphans” in the province: those who wouldn’t vote UCP or NDP, but also could not name which party they’d support instead.
Regionally since the April poll, the UCP saw a drop of 14 points in areas outside Calgary and Edmonton, and a drop of 10 points in Calgary.
“That would have surprised me, were it not for the Calgary-Shaw byelection,” said Brown. The NDP pulled out a victory in that byelection, claiming what had been a UCP riding.
Brown says the drop in UCP voter intention in Calgary is likely among those supporting the remain side, while rurally it reflects a drop in voter support from those who would vote to separate.
Young says the numbers mean Calgary should be a key battleground in coming months.
“But we're a year away from the election. If the referendum is in fact what's driving support away from the UCP, the government will have an opportunity to try to win that support back,” Young said.
And with the price of oil still high and the province’s finances looking to be in better shape, Young says that could give the government more money in the coffers to spend big and woo voters.
Albertans’ impressions of Danielle Smith have also soured slightly in recent months, with the poll suggesting a drop of six percentage points in those very or somewhat impressed with her, and a seven point increase in those not at all impressed with her.
Twenty-five per cent of respondents are very impressed with NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi, the poll suggests.
“What Albertans are saying is they're not feeling highly impressed with either of these leaders right now,” Brown said.
Carney’s popularity keeps rising
But the honeymoon period seems to be still going strong for Prime Minister Mark Carney in Alberta. Fifty-two per cent of respondents said they are very impressed with him, up six points since the last poll.
“We're in this strange universe where a Liberal Prime Minister is doing better than either the premier, or the leader of the Opposition here, and doing much better than the leader of the federal Conservative Party in terms of popularity,” Young said.
Young credits approval largely to Carney’s handling of trade tensions with the United States. He’s also likely benefitting from Albertans happy with his commitment to get a pipeline to the B.C. Coast, she says.
It’s a project Smith is, of course, also pushing for.
“I think there's a bit of an irony here that the MOU is working well for Mark Carney and his popularity, but Danielle Smith doesn't seem to be benefitting from her part in creating the MOU,” said Brown.
Brown notes favourability does not equal voter intention, and some Albertans might appreciate Carney’s style but still be unlikely to cast a ballot for the Liberals.
But Carney does boast a higher score than Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, with just 26 per cent of those polled saying they are very impressed with him.
"Which has got to be a concern for the Conservative Party, because this is the Conservative heartland,” Brown said.
The CBC News random survey of 1,200 Albertans was conducted using a hybrid method between Sept. 8 and Sept. 21, 2026, by Edmonton-based Trend Research under the direction of Janet Brown Opinion Research. The sample is representative of regional, age and gender factors. The margin of error is +/- 2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. For subsets, the margin of error is larger.
The survey used a hybrid methodology that involved contacting survey respondents by telephone and giving them the option of completing the survey at that time, at another more convenient time, or receiving an email link and completing the survey online. Trend Research contacted people using a random list of numbers, consisting of 30 per cent landlines and 70 per cent cellphone numbers.
Telephone numbers were dialed up to five times at five different times of day before another telephone number was added to the sample. The response rate among valid numbers (i.e., residential and personal) was 11.3 per cent.

Engaged in a flirtatious conversation at a bar in Manhattan, 23-year-old Gary stood with a Guinness in hand as he explained to a woman why he took an engineering job at Palantir, the data analytics company cofounded by Alex Karp and Peter Thiel. Raking in a $250,000 salary would allow him to help pay off his parents’ mounting medical bills, he explained.
Gary wasn’t met with sympathy. Medical debt, the woman told him, was “not an excuse to work somewhere like that.” She was referring, of course, to Palantir’s controversial work with governments, including the US and Israel, which use the company’s surveillance tools for law enforcement and military operations.
Since joining the tech company in 2025, Gary has noticed that naming his employer prompts brutal reactions from prospective paramours. One woman, he says, called him the devil; another asked how he lives with himself. “Sometimes people would just straight up stop talking to me,” he says.
Recently, Gary’s buddies requested he not mention Palantir on their nights out together so as to not tank the whole group’s chances of getting laid. “I get nervous now. I don’t bring it up,” he says. (Gary, along with the other daters in this piece, have been given pseudonyms to protect against professional, if not romantic, repercussions.)
Gary has resorted to saying he works in AI. “Even that gets some pretty bad responses sometimes,” he says. His Hinge profile doesn’t mention his employer. And sometimes he makes up stories out of thin air to justify working for Palantir—like that line about the medical debt. His parents don’t have any, nor are they ill.
The bachelors of Palantir aren’t the only tech bros dealing with the industry’s fall from grace. Take 29-year-old James, who lives in San Francisco and works at Tesla. Earlier this year, on his third date with a woman he met on Raya, she asked whether he’d voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 election. A self-described “moderate liberal or moderate progressive” who “always votes blue and always will, probably,” James was offended. “I was like, ‘Are you kidding me? Did I really give that off?’” She replied, “You work for Tesla, so I just need to check.”
James says skepticism of his politics has “come up repeatedly” in his dating life. “If I don’t immediately say that I don’t like Elon Musk, people think that I’m conservative, which is generally not something that people like in San Francisco,” he says.
Once seen as a groundbreaking leader in sustainability and a quirky futurist, Musk—recently crowned the world’s first trillionaire—is better known these days for his record-breaking donation to Trump’s 2024 campaign, being the brain behind DOGE, the dismantling of Twitter, an apparent Nazi salute, frequent ketamine use, racist tweets, and something of a breeding kink.
Long gone is the cliché of the optimistic tech guy in flip-flops and a ratty old hoodie. The tech industry is now seen as the locus of unchecked power. Meta created an environment where Russian bots could influence elections and designed features that foster social media addiction among teens. Amazon, which has been widely accused of unfair labor practices and of generating a staggering amount of waste, has aided in the collapse of small, independent businesses, while a glowed-up Jeff Bezos has become a poster child for extreme wealth inequality. More recently, the AI industry is being widely maligned over claims that it’s exacerbating job loss, pollution, and a critical-thinking crisis.
Amy Laurent, the founder of a high-end matchmaking company, has a front-row seat to the way Big Tech’s moral failings are causing problems for single, rank-and-file tech bros. Turns out their cushy paychecks often aren’t enough of an upside anymore.
“I think 10 years ago, saying you worked in tech was more about innovation, ambition, intelligence,” says Laurent. Now, many people charge Big Tech with “causing the breakdown of society,” whether they’re worried about “AI, job displacement, wealth inequality, privacy and surveillance, content moderation, or political influence.”
Laurent says that when she pitches her tech-employed male clients to women, she acknowledges their hesitation right off the bat: “Listen, I have a great guy to tell you about. He’s such a good match for you. Now hear me out: He’s in tech.” The justifications are a new feature of her work.
Jessica Engle, a family and marriage therapist, has noticed that men in tech worry about being perceived as red pilled. Recently, one of her clients expressed concern about having his Apple Watch visible in his dating profile photos. He wondered whether the gadget “would make him look like a tech bro” and whether it might signal a “very particular kind of toxic masculinity that we’re seeing more and more in the news.”
Engle’s client wasn’t wrong to worry. Mira, a 29-year-old Bay Area resident, says she perceives a career in tech as a possible “right-wing flag” or a sign that someone might be “manosphere-coded” or libertarian.
When 28-year-old Helen was an undergraduate at Stanford from 2016 to 2020, she viewed men in tech as guys who “stay up late and maybe have bad hygiene.” But her feelings toward them have gotten even worse over time as she’s questioned the industry’s overall impact.
Helen’s family is from the Tigray region of Ethiopia, whose population, beginning in 2020, was subjected to a prolonged period of human rights abuses. “When I started thinking about questions around genocide and the technology that kills or tracks or excludes,” Helen says, “I realized that the things these people are building are secretly, or under the surface, really nefarious, and I could not personally be with someone who is a puzzle piece in that tapestry.”
Helen herself has worked in tech. Soon after graduating from college, she accepted a job at Grammarly. But after about a year, she went to work for a mutual-aid platform and now is employed at an impact investing firm funding technology for underserved communities. Similarly, Sasha, a 31-year-old Oakland resident, had a brief stint working in AI before heading to a sustainability-focused tech company, where she is now chief of staff. In dating, when she meets someone who works or wants to work in AI, she wonders, “Does that mean that we have the same values in terms of climate and sustainability and thinking about human rights?”
Even if they do, she adds, “then the issue I have is there’s clearly this cognitive dissonance happening between what you’re working on and what you care about, which I have a really hard time accepting.”
James, the Tesla employee, confesses that he embodies plenty of tech bro stereotypes that might work against him, including “paying too much in rent” (or “just generally gentrifying”), ordering most of his meals on DoorDash (“I suck at cooking”), and not “really contributing to the culture of the city that much.”
“I really fit the mold so much that it’s sort of like, I have to at least be self-aware of it,” James says.
The pushback James gets IRL makes him wonder how much more happens behind screens. “There’s less visible rejection because you kind of get prefiltered out,” he says. “If I were to write on the dating app that I work at Tesla, I think it would just cut a lot of people right away.” His experience seems to bear this out. On his Hinge profile, he disclosed his place of work; on Raya he decided against it. He says he’s had more success on Raya.
In fact, about four months after joining Raya, he met someone. His new girlfriend had recently moved to the Bay Area for medical school and, before dating James, had managed to stay insulated from tech culture. “I was talking to my now girlfriend, and she was like, ‘Yeah, I feel like I’ve gotten lucky. I didn’t really know what the tech bro stereotype is.’”
“I was like, ‘Thank God. I don’t think I would have made it if you did.’”

In Summary
- Google recently unveiled the first batch of Googlebooks, its new kind of notebook, with devices from Lenovo, Dell, Asus, Acer and HP.
- The first batch of Googlebooks comes packed with top-of-the-line hardware and premium design, and has premium prices beginning at USD 899.
- While we wait for them to hit the market (they go on sale on October 4 and 5), we take a look at eleven features of Google’s new notebook concept.
Is it a rejigged Chromebook? Or is it a new attempt by Google to get Android into the notebook space? Google took the wraps off its much-talked-about Googlebook notebook recently, with Googlebooks from five leading brands: HP, Asus. Acer, Lenovo and Dell. What exactly is so special about them, and should you be interested in one? Here are eleven things that we think you need to know about the new Googlebook that might help you make up your mind about them, even as the first batch of Googlebooks gets set to arrive in early October:
Table of Contents
Built on Android, designed to work in sync with your (Android) phone
“If you use an Android phone, your laptop shouldn’t treat it like a stranger,” says Google, so it is hardly surprising that one of the USPs of the Googlebook is the fact that it works seamlessly with your phone, provided it is an Android phone. Googlebooks are built on what Google calls a “share Android foundation,” so you can log in to them with your Android username and password, and access apps and files on your phone on the Googlebook, and do much more, effortlessly. We have no news on compatibility with iPhones at the time of writing.
Comes with a touchscreen
While touchscreens were broadly optional with Chromebooks, as of now, all Googlebooks come with a touchscreen display of up to 2.8K resolution. The touch interface is an integral part of the Googlebook experience. As of now, there is no talk of Googlebook tablets, but given the touch UI, we expect to see them at some stage.
Premium innards (Top-of-the-line chips, lots of RAM)
Unlike Android and ChromeOS, which were both optimized to run even on relatively modest specs, the Googlebook is clearly a high-end beast. All Googlebooks have to come with Intel Core Ultra Series 3 or Snapdragon X Elite with dedicated NPUs capable of over 45 TOPS. They also come with a minimum of 16 GB RAM. The Googlebook at this point seems clearly to be designed for high-end work.
…and outards too
It is not just their hardware; the Googlebook itself also has to be made of premium materials, such as carbon fiber, magnesium and aluminum. Trackpads also have to be made of glass, and the keyboards have to be backlit.
A bar that glows!
They might be sleekly designed and made of premium materials, but perhaps the most striking feature of the Googlebooks is the thin glowing bar on their lids. This Glow Bar lights up in different shades when one starts up the Googlebook, shows battery level, and also “supports other playful patterns” on different occasions, such as when one is using Gemini.
Keyboards that are slightly different
While the keyboards on Googlebooks are broadly similar to those seen on Windows notebooks, there are some subtle differences. Keyboards on the Googlebook come with two special keys – a special key labeled G to invoke Gemini. The capslock key on a Googlebook also acts as a Quick Insert key. Pressing it gives you access to a number of features such as clipboard history, instant translation, emojis, and local search tools. There is also a dedicated shortcut key for Rambler, Google’s voice dictation app that’s making waves these days. Don’t get fooled by those classic keys – there’s a lot under the surface of a Googlebook keyboard!
Runs on Googlebook OS
The operating system of the Googlebooks is – well – Googlebook OS. It is a blend of Android and ChromeOS, and was codenamed Aluminum. It is built on Android and has the same security architecture as ChromeOS. Yes, not many prizes for innovative nomenclature, but then this is the tech world which has operating systems called One and Nothing, so who are we to judge?
Gemini is literally a cursor wriggle away
Every Googlebook comes packed with AI and AI tools, and a super special way of summoning Gemini, Google’s AI assistant. You do not need to hit a button; just wriggle the cursor, and Gemini will pop up! Google calls it the Magic Pointer, and it certainly adds a new dimension to accessing AI on notebooks.
All of Android’s apps and a “desktop Chrome” experience
At the time of writing and based on what has been made public, the Googlebook’s main source of apps is the Google Play Store for Android. What’s more. Android apps and games run natively rather than in a special environment (as on Chromebooks), delivering smooth performance. You also get a proper “desktop” Chrome experience, so all extensions will work, and there is also support for Office 365. What’s more, Android apps and games on a connected Android phone will also work smoothly on a Googlebook. Many of the apps are optimized to run on the large screen and come with support for keyboard and mouse. We do not know if APK files can be installed or if apps can be “sideloaded” onto Googlebooks at this time, though.
PC games can be played…but on the cloud!
But what about PC games? After all, the Googlebooks do boast some seriously powerful hardware, including high-resolution displays, flagship chips, and stacks of RAM. Well, at the time of writing, PC games cannot be directly installed on the, but one can stream PC games via GeForce NOW. We hope that changes in the coming days, given Google’s specs and price tags.
10 years software support
Impressed by the seven years of software support on the Pixel phones? Well, the Googlebooks come with a massive ten years of software support. And given that the hardware inside is top-notch and the frame is made of premium materials, there is every chance that these notebooks will stand the test of time.
And one more thing: They are going to be premium devices as of now!
The current set of Googlebooks unveiled by Google starts at USD 899, with some even starting at prices in excess of USD 1000. Given the current hardware and material requirements laid down for them and the trend of rising component prices, it is likely that Googlebooks will remain premium devices for a while. Of course, we would love it if they became more affordable. Premium tech is wonderful, but affordable tech is love.

The death of an Anna University student at Government Kilpauk Medical College Hospital (KMCH) on Friday (September 18, 2026), due to scrub typhus, has once again brought this bacterial infection to the fore. University authorities have said they have started screening students for scrub typhus as well, along with dengue and leptospirosis
What is scrub typhus?
Scrub typhus is a bacterial infection caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi. It is spread by the bite of infected larval mites or chiggers -- it is not a mosquito-borne disease.
Scrub typhus is a major public health burden in South and Southeast Asia. A 2021 systematic review noted that scrub typhus, a common acute febrile illness, is “a grossly under-recognised public health problem in India.” It stated that the proportion of scrub typhus among acute undifferentiated febrile illness (AUFI) studies was 25.3%, and community seroprevalence was 34.2%. The review also noted that the disease causes severe morbidity and accounts for a large number of deaths, with its bueden “underappreciated.”
A 2025 multi-centre study of 587 children with acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) from Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu revealed that scrub typhus is now the most common infectious cause of AES in southern India.
What are the symptoms?
Symptoms usually begin within 10 days of infection. The United States Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) lists symptoms of scrub typhus as: fever and chills, headache, body aches and muscle pain, a dark, scab-like region at the site of the chigger bite (also known as eschar), mental changes ranging from confusion to coma, enlarged lymph nodes and a rash.
Timely treatment is critical. If left untreated, severe illness from scrub typhus infection can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), shock, meningitis and kidney failure, which can be fatal, notes a research paper, Incidence of Scrub Typhus in Rural South India published in The New England Journal of Medicine last year.
In India, there is a high mortality of scrub typhus, primarily due to late diagnosis and treatment.
How is it diagnosed and treated?
Since the symptoms of scrub typhus are common to those of several other diseases, diagnosis is often delayed. A blood test (IgM ELISA or PCR) can help confirm the diagnosis.
Scrub typhus should be treated with the antibiotics doxycycline or azithromycin. If the treatment is begun in time, it is effective. Results of a trial carried out in seven centres in India, published in 2023, in which patients were randomly assigned to receive a combination therapy of doxycycline and azithromycin, showed faster resolution of complications compared with two other arms where patients were given monotherapy with either doxycycline or azithromycin. The frequencies of respiratory, renal, hepatic, and central nervous system complications were lower in the combination-therapy group than in either of the monotherapy groups.
How can it be prevented?
There is no vaccine as yet for scrub typhus. The infection is not contagious.
Chiggers live in areas with lots of grass, thick vegetation, agricultural fields, plant litter and bare soil across rural areas of Asia, and usually feed on small mammals such as rats and shrews.
Keeping oneself safe from bites through protective clothing, covered footwear and the use of insect repellent may help. Ensuring surroundings are clean and well maintained can also go some way towards reducing mite habitats.
“Early diagnosis and prompt treatment can significantly reduce complications and mortality. Establishing good surveillance and instituting appropriate control measures are urgently needed,” the 2021 review notes.
